This paper aims to address the following challenges, including (C1) how to incorporate explicit relationship networks of the time series; (C2) how to model the implicit relationship of the temporal dynamics. We propose a novel model called Network of Tensor Time Series, which is comprised of two modules, including Tensor Graph Convolutional Network (TGCN) and Tensor Recurrent Neural Network (TRNN). TGCN tackles the first challenge by generalizing Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) for flat graphs to tensor graphs, which captures the synergy between multiple graphs associated with the tensors. TRNN leverages tensor decomposition to model the implicit relationships among co-evolving time series. The experimental results on five real-world datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method.

Crowd-sourcing has become a popular means of acquiring labeled data for a wide variety of tasks where humans are more accurate than computers, e.g., labeling images, matching objects, or analyzing sentiment. However, relying solely on the crowd is often impractical even for data sets with thousands of items, due to time and cost constraints of acquiring human input (which cost pennies and minutes per label). In this paper, we propose algorithms for integrating machine learning into crowd-sourced databases, with the goal of allowing crowd-sourcing applications to scale, i.e., to handle larger datasets at lower costs. The key observation is that, in many of the above tasks, humans and machine learning algorithms can be complementary, as humans are often more accurate but slow and expensive, while algorithms are usually less accurate, but faster and cheaper. Based on this observation, we present two new active learning algorithms to combine humans and algorithms together in a crowd-sourced database. Our algorithms are based on the theory of non-parametric bootstrap, which makes our results applicable to a broad class of machine learning models. Our results, on three real-life datasets collected with Amazon's Mechanical Turk, and on 15 well-known UCI data sets, show that our methods
AI: In this paper, we introduce $\epsilon$-Consistent Mixup ($\epsilon$mu), a data-driven structural regularization method that integrates Mixup's linear interpolation with consistency regularization along the Mixup direction. This approach enforces a simple, adaptive balance between the two techniques. By combining consistency and interpolation in a learnable manner, $\epsilon$mu introduces greater flexibility in how model responses evolve across the feature space. Experimental results on the SVHN and CIFAR10 benchmark datasets demonstrate that $\epsilon$mu enhances semi-supervised classification performance, achieving the most significant improvements in scenarios with limited labeled data. Empirical comparisons between $\epsilon$mu and standard Mixup provide insights into the underlying mechanisms that contribute to its effectiveness. Notably, $\epsilon$mu generates more accurate synthetic labels and produces more confident predictions than traditional Mixup.

Autoencoders find valuable applications in high-energy physics, particularly in anomaly detection, where they are used to analyze jets—collimated sprays of particles produced in collisions, such as those at the CERN Large Hadron Collider. In this work, we investigate the potential of graph-based autoencoders that process jets in their "particle cloud" representation, enabling them to capture complex relationships between particles within a jet. Furthermore, we introduce a differentiable approximation of the energy mover's distance using a graph neural network, which can serve as an effective reconstruction loss function for autoencoders.

Recent exciting challenges in contemporary machine learning have been formulated within the classical framework of tree search, with the game of Go being the most prominent example. Interestingly, the state spaces underlying these sequential decision-making problems often exhibit a more complex latent structure than what can be represented by a simple tree. In this work, we introduce a probabilistic framework designed to leverage the latent structure of the search space, enabling information sharing across different branches of the search tree. Our approach combines approximate inference in jointly Gaussian models for the explored regions of the problem with an ad hoc abstraction for the unexplored parts, which helps reduce computational complexity. Empirical evaluations show that our algorithm performs competitively against non-probabilistic methods in applications such as Tic-Tac-Toe and feature selection.

Ticks are a major global cause of transmitting various bacterial, viral, and parasitic diseases. Over the past decade, the prevalence of tick-borne illnesses has risen sharply, with Lyme disease alone affecting an estimated 300,000 people in the United States each year. This increase underscores the urgent need for improved methods of identifying and diagnosing tick-related skin conditions. The goal of this study is to build on the approach developed by Burlina et al., utilizing multiple convolutional neural network models to detect tick-borne skin lesions. To enhance the diversity of the training data, we expanded our image dataset by collecting images from Google in seven different languages. The final dataset comprised nearly 6,080 images and was trained using a combination of deep learning architectures, including ResNet 34, ResNet 50, VGG 19, and DenseNet 121. Our model achieved an accuracy of 80.72% when trained on the DenseNet 121 architecture.

Deep neural networks have become highly influential in various computer vision tasks. However, their effectiveness often requires large amounts of annotated data for supervised training. In this work, we review and compare different techniques presented in the literature that aim to enhance training performance without the need for additional real-world annotated data. These approaches typically involve applying transformations that preserve annotations to existing data or generating synthetic data to supplement the training set.

The diagnosis and evaluation of therapeutic effects in Parkinson's disease using voice data hold significant importance, yet they present a challenging few-shot learning problem. Although deep learning excels in automatic feature extraction, it often struggles with limited data scenarios. Consequently, a commonly effective approach involves first leveraging prior knowledge for feature extraction, followed by dimensionality reduction to support subsequent classification tasks. However, two major limitations remain: (1) the structural information within speech features has not been adequately explored, and higher-quality features have not been effectively reconstructed; and (2) the structural relationships between data samples have not been sufficiently mined, leading to a lack of high-quality sample reconstruction.

To address these challenges, this paper proposes a deep double-side learning ensemble model that simultaneously and deeply reconstructs both speech features and samples based on an existing Parkinson's disease speech dataset. For feature reconstruction, an embedded deep stacked group sparse autoencoder is designed to perform nonlinear feature transformation, thereby generating high-level deep features. These deep features are then combined with the original speech features through an L1 regularization-based feature selection method. For speech sample reconstruction, a deep sample learning algorithm is introduced to enhance the quality and representativeness of the data samples.

We examine the challenges of identity and closeness testing in a discrete population based on random samples. Our objective is to design efficient testing algorithms while ensuring Differential Privacy for the individuals involved. We present an approach that leads to sample-efficient differentially private testers for these tasks. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that private identity and closeness testers can achieve performance nearly as good as their non-private counterparts in terms of sample efficiency. We evaluate our algorithms experimentally on synthetic data, showing that our private testers achieve low type I and type II errors with sample sizes that grow sublinearly with the domain size of the underlying distributions.

Smart cities around the world have started monitoring parking areas to estimate available spots and assist drivers in finding parking. The initial results are encouraging. However, existing methods are constrained by the high cost of deploying sensors across the entire city to achieve accurate estimates. This study explores the possibility of extending parking information estimation from sensor-equipped areas to those without sensors. To do this, we assess the similarity between city neighborhoods using background data, such as geographic information system (GIS) data. Based on these similarity measures, we examine how occupancy rates can be adapted from monitored to unmonitored parking areas.

The capacity to measure similarity between documents plays a crucial role in enabling intelligent summarization and analysis of large text collections. Traditional distance metrics between documents often fail to account for semantic relationships between words or face challenges in scalability. To address these limitations, we propose hierarchical optimal transport as a meta-distance for comparing documents. In this approach, documents are represented as distributions over topics, which are themselves modeled as distributions over words. By solving an optimal transport problem on the topic level, we compute a similarity score that captures both semantic and structural information. We establish conditions under which this construction forms a valid distance metric and demonstrate its connection to the word mover's distance. Our experiments show that this method achieves competitive performance in k-NN classification while offering improved interpretability and significantly better scalability at a lower computational cost.

Speaker diarization, the process of identifying speech segments corresponding to specific speakers, is widely applied in human-centered systems such as video conferences and human-computer interaction platforms. In this paper, we present a self-supervised audio-video synchronization learning method to tackle speaker diarization without requiring extensive manual labeling. To enhance existing approaches, we introduce two novel loss functions: the dynamic triplet loss and the multinomial loss. We evaluate our method on a real-world human-computer interaction system, where the results demonstrate that our best model achieves a significant improvement of +8% in F1-score, along with a notable reduction in diarization error rate. Finally, we introduce a large-scale audio-video corpus specifically designed to address the lack of comprehensive audio-video datasets in Chinese.

The development of network-centric artificial intelligence (AI) and Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled cyber-physical systems (CPS) and services presents significant challenges in design and validation. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach rooted in model-driven software engineering, with a focus on domain-specific modeling. We concentrate on a key area of AI—machine learning (ML)—and propose the delegation of data analytics and ML tasks to the IoT edge. This strategy enhances the quality of ML services, such as availability and performance, under varying network conditions, while also preserving privacy, security, and sustainability. 

We enable practitioners to assign ML tasks to a variety of edge devices, including resource-constrained embedded microcontrollers with memory sizes in the kilobyte range and power consumption in the milliwatt scale—commonly referred to as TinyML. Additionally, we demonstrate how software models at different abstraction levels—platform-independent and platform-specific—can be effectively integrated into the software development lifecycle. Finally, we validate our approach through a case study on predictive maintenance of a hydraulic system, incorporating multiple networked sensors and actuators.

Despite significant advances in maternal healthcare, high rates of maternal and perinatal mortality persist in low- and middle-income countries. Fetal ultrasound plays a critical role in antenatal care, yet its widespread use is hindered by a shortage of skilled healthcare providers. To address this challenge, we developed and validated an artificial intelligence (AI) system capable of estimating gestational age (GA) and detecting fetal malpresentation from "blind sweep" ultrasound videos acquired by novice operators. We also designed the system to overcome common barriers in resource-limited settings. By implementing a streamlined scanning protocol with real-time AI feedback on image quality, we demonstrated that the AI models can achieve reliable performance even when used by minimally trained operators with low-cost ultrasound devices equipped with on-device AI capabilities. The GA estimation model performed comparably to traditional biometric methods with as few as two sweeps, while the fetal malpresentation model showed strong diagnostic accuracy across different operators and devices. These AI models hold promise for enhancing the diagnostic capabilities of under-trained ultrasound operators in low-resource environments.

In this paper, we advocate for a declarative foundation as the basis for data-intensive machine learning systems. Rather than developing new systems for each type of machine learning task or hardcoding specific optimizations, we propose using recursive queries to implement a wide range of machine learning models. This approach allows us to leverage database query optimization techniques to generate efficient execution plans, which can then be executed on a unified, data-parallel query processing engine.

As a proof of concept, we examine two common programming models in the machine learning domain—Pregel and Iterative Map-Reduce-Update—and demonstrate how they can be expressed in Datalog. These models can then be tailored for specific tasks and compiled into optimized physical execution plans. Experiments conducted on a large-scale computing cluster using real-world data show that this declarative approach delivers strong performance while also enhancing both the generality and ease of programming.

Data poisoning attacks seek to influence the model generated by a learning algorithm by strategically altering the training data. In this work, we explore differential privacy as a defense mechanism against such attacks. We demonstrate that learners incorporating differential privacy are resilient to data poisoning when the adversary can only corrupt a limited number of training examples. However, this resilience diminishes as the number of poisoned samples increases. To support this claim, we develop attack algorithms targeting two common differentially private learning methods: objective perturbation and output perturbation. Our experimental results confirm the effectiveness of these attacks when the adversary is allowed to poison a substantial portion of the training data.

Given a sample drawn from a probability distribution supported on a submanifold embedded in Euclidean space, one can construct a neighborhood graph that serves as an approximation of the underlying submanifold. The graph Laplacian associated with this graph is widely used in various machine learning techniques, including semi-supervised learning, dimensionality reduction, and clustering. In this paper, we analyze the pointwise limit of three commonly used graph Laplacians as the number of samples increases and the neighborhood size shrinks to zero. We demonstrate that, for a uniform distribution on the submanifold, all three graph Laplacians converge to the same operator up to constant factors. However, when the measure on the submanifold is non-uniform, only the random walk graph Laplacian converges to the weighted Laplace-Beltrami operator.

We present two-scale loss functions designed for use in various gradient descent algorithms applied to classification tasks using deep neural networks. This novel approach is general-purpose, as it can be effectively integrated into a broad range of machine learning models, including deep neural networks and support vector machines. The two-scale loss functions enable the training process to concentrate on instances within the training set that are poorly classified, thereby improving model performance. Experimental results on standard datasets such as MNIST, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100 demonstrate that appropriately defined two-scale loss functions lead to enhanced performance metrics compared to traditional cross-entropy loss when used with deep neural networks.

We revisit the lower bounds on regret in the context of multi-armed bandit problems. We derive non-asymptotic, distribution-dependent bounds and present concise proofs that rely solely on well-established properties of Kullback-Leibler divergences. These bounds reveal that, during an initial phase, the regret grows nearly linearly, while the well-known logarithmic growth of regret only emerges in a later stage. The proof techniques capture the core of the information-theoretic arguments, eliminating any superfluous complexity.

Reparameterizing variational auto-encoders with continuous random variables is a powerful technique for reducing the variance of gradient estimates. In the discrete setting, the Gumbel-Max trick enables reparameterization, but the resulting objective involves an $\arg \max$ operation, which is not differentiable. Unlike prior approaches that rely on softmax-based approximations, we propose directly optimizing the model using a direct loss minimization strategy. This approach naturally extends to structured discrete latent variable models when the $\arg \max$ operation can be efficiently evaluated. We empirically validate the effectiveness of this direct loss minimization method in variational auto-encoders with both unstructured and structured discrete latent variables.

This paper presents an evaluation of various machine learning models designed to predict both diagnosed diabetes and undiagnosed diabetes, utilizing eight years of data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES). The models were optimized and evaluated based on their Brier Scores. The most significant features from the top-performing models were analyzed for both prediction tasks. A Support Vector Machine with a linear kernel achieved the best performance in predicting diabetes, achieving a Brier score of 0.0654 and an AUROC of 0.9235 on the test set. For undiagnosed diabetes, elastic net regression outperformed other models, with a Brier score of 0.0294 and an AUROC of 0.9439 on the test set. Notably, similar key variables emerged across both sets of models, including blood osmolality, family history, the prevalence of certain compounds, and hypertension, which are strong indicators of diabetes risk. In addition, for undiagnosed diabetes, ethnicity and genetic factors showed significant correlations.

Federated learning (FL) is a powerful distributed machine learning framework, renowned for its ability to preserve data privacy and enhance communication efficiency. However, full client participation is often impractical due to resource limitations, prompting the development of partial participation FL algorithms that actively select or sample a subset of clients to achieve performance close to that of full participation. This paper explores a less-studied scenario—passive partial client participation—where client dropout occurs as a result of external factors rather than being an intentional design choice of the FL algorithm. We frame FL with client dropout as a special case within a broader class of FL problems where clients may submit substitute (and potentially inaccurate) local model updates. Based on our convergence analysis, we propose a novel algorithm called FL-FDMS, which dynamically identifies "friends" of clients—those with similar data distributions—and uses their local updates as substitutes for those who have dropped out. This approach reduces substitution errors and enhances overall convergence performance. Additionally, FL-FDMS incorporates a complexity reduction mechanism, ensuring both theoretical rigor and practical applicability. Experimental results on MNIST and CIFAR-10 demonstrate the effectiveness of FL-FDMS in mitigating the impact of client dropout in federated learning settings.

With the rapid increase in energy demand from data centers and computing systems overall, it is essential to integrate energy efficiency into the design of scheduling algorithms. Machine learning offers a promising approach by enabling predictions of future system load, often based on historical data. However, the success of such methods heavily relies on the accuracy of these predictions, and their performance may fall significantly short of optimal when predictions are poor. In contrast, classical online algorithms provide strong worst-case guarantees but can be overly conservative for many practical scenarios. This paper explores the emerging field of machine learning-augmented algorithms, aiming to combine the strengths of both approaches in the context of the classic deadline-based online speed-scaling problem. By introducing a new prediction framework, we propose algorithms that (i) achieve provably low energy consumption when accurate predictions are available, (ii) remain robust even when predictions are unreliable, and (iii) exhibit smooth degradation in performance as prediction accuracy decreases.

Recent studies have investigated the potential of large-scale Transformer-based pre-trained models, particularly Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs), in the field of natural language processing. However, this advancement has raised significant concerns from multiple perspectives, including financial costs and environmental impact. To address these challenges, compressing PLMs such as BERT with minimal performance degradation has become a promising direction, offering faster inference and more cost-effective deployment.

In this work, we focus on achieving even higher compression ratios for PLMs, with tensor decomposition emerging as a promising but underexplored technique. We introduce two novel decomposition and reconstruction protocols to enhance both the effectiveness and efficiency of the compression process. Our compressed BERT model, which reduces the number of parameters in the Transformer layers by a factor of 7, performs comparably to, and in some cases slightly better than, the original BERT on the GLUE benchmark.

Furthermore, a highly compact version of our model achieves 96.7% of BERT-base's performance while using only 1/48th of the encoder parameters (i.e., fewer than 2 million parameters excluding the embedding layer) and demonstrates a 2.7-fold speedup during inference. To demonstrate that our approach is orthogonal to existing compression techniques such as knowledge distillation, we also evaluate its effectiveness on a distilled BERT model, showing additional benefits.

The problem of minimizing the rank of a matrix subject to affine constraints appears in a wide range of applications, including signal processing and machine learning. The nuclear norm is a widely used convex relaxation for this problem, and it can accurately recover the true rank under certain theoretical conditions. However, in many real-world scenarios, the nuclear norm approximation often yields results that are far from the optimal solution. To achieve higher accuracy, this paper introduces a novel rank approximation based on the logarithm-determinant function. We apply this approach to subspace clustering, where it effectively models various types of errors and noise. An efficient optimization algorithm is proposed, with strong theoretical guarantees ensuring convergence to a stationary point. Experimental results on face clustering and motion segmentation demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art subspace clustering techniques.

We propose two general and testable hypotheses regarding expectations about generalization error in the context of concept drift. The first hypothesis suggests that as the drift rate increases, the optimal forgetting rate that minimizes generalization error also increases, and conversely, as the drift rate decreases, the optimal forgetting rate decreases. The second hypothesis posits that as a learner’s forgetting rate increases, the bias-variance profile that minimizes generalization error will exhibit lower variance, with the inverse holding true for lower forgetting rates.

These hypotheses give rise to the concept of the "sweet path"—a trajectory through the three-dimensional space defined by alternative drift rates, forgetting rates, and bias-variance profiles, along which generalization error is minimized. On this sweet path, slow drift is paired with low forgetting and low bias, while rapid drift is associated with high forgetting and reduced variance. We present experimental results that support the existence of such a sweet path.

Furthermore, we demonstrate that simple learners capable of adapting their forgetting rates and bias-variance profiles can achieve performance comparable to state-of-the-art incremental learners on real-world concept drift problems.

We present Coarse-Grained Nonlinear Dynamics, an efficient and general parameterization of nonlinear system behavior derived from the Volterra series expansion. These models scale their parameter count nearly linearly with the system's memory length, irrespective of the truncation order of the Volterra expansion—resulting in a superpolynomial reduction in parameters as the order increases. This efficiency is achieved by coarse-graining components of the dynamics that involve products of input samples separated by long time intervals, a concept analogous to the coarse-graining used in the fast multipole method for simulating n-body problems in $\mathcal{O}(n)$ time. Our approach enables regularization, giving rise to Coarse-Grained Nonlinear System Identification, a technique that can accurately model complex nonlinear dynamics using minimal experimental data. We validate this method on a synthetic example and demonstrate its effectiveness experimentally by identifying a precise model of the nonlinear relationship between voltage and luminosity in a tungsten filament using less than one second of data.

Adversarial training—defined as training neural networks on data that has been perturbed in a way designed to fool the model—has long been explored as a strategy to enhance model robustness against adversarial attacks during inference. However, this improved resilience often comes at the cost of reduced overall accuracy and performance. In the context of real-world robot learning, recent studies have revealed that the trade-off between robustness and accuracy is not favorable; instead, adversarial training can result in a net decline in holistic robot performance. This paper re-examines the robustness-accuracy trade-off in robot learning by systematically investigating whether recent advances in robust training techniques and theoretical understanding, combined with adversarial learning approaches, can make adversarial training viable for practical robotic applications. We evaluate a broad range of robot learning tasks, including autonomous driving in high-fidelity simulation environments suitable for sim-to-real deployment, as well as mobile robot gesture recognition. Our findings show that while these methods yield modest improvements in the trade-off on a relative scale, the negative side effects introduced by adversarial training remain significantly more impactful, often by an order of magnitude. Based on these results, we conclude that substantial progress in robust learning methods is still required before adversarial training can effectively benefit real-world robot learning tasks.

Adversarial learning has become a powerful approach for mitigating the vulnerability of existing methods to adversarial perturbations. However, most current defense strategies are designed to counter a single type of attack, such as $\ell_\infty$-based perturbations. In safety-critical applications, this limitation makes them ineffective, as attackers can employ a variety of adversarial techniques to bypass the system. Furthermore, training with multiple perturbations at once leads to a substantial increase in computational costs. To tackle these issues, we introduce a novel meta-learning framework that explicitly learns to generate noise in order to enhance the model's robustness against multiple types of attacks. The core of our approach is the Meta Noise Generator (MNG), which produces optimal noise to stochastically perturb a given sample, thereby reducing errors across diverse adversarial perturbations. By leveraging samples generated by MNG, we train the model by enforcing label consistency across different perturbations. We evaluate the robustness of models trained using our method on various datasets and under a wide range of attack scenarios, demonstrating that it significantly outperforms existing baselines while incurring only a minimal computational overhead.

Enhancing the explainability of deep neural networks (DNNs) necessitates assessing whether they perform symbolic computation. A key aspect of symbolic processing is variable binding—linking an input value to an abstract variable stored in the system's internal memory. Previous research on the computational capabilities of DNNs has not conclusively determined whether their internal processes involve variable binding. We contend that this lack of clarity stems from a fundamental limitation in the design of prior experiments. In this work, we present the first systematic investigation into the variable binding abilities of state-of-the-art Transformer models, BERT and RoBERTa. Our experimental setup requires the model to generalize a rule across distinct subsets of the input vocabulary, preventing reliance solely on associative pattern matching. The results reveal a significant difference between classification and sequence-to-sequence tasks: BERT and RoBERTa can readily learn to copy or reverse strings, even when trained on task-specific vocabularies that change during testing; however, both models fail entirely to generalize across vocabularies in similar sequence classification tasks. These findings suggest that the success of Transformers in sequence modeling may stem from their extensive use of the input as an external "memory," rather than from internal symbolic operations involving variable binding.

Visual Question Answering (VQA) has garnered significant attention from the research community due to its wide-ranging applications, including assisting visually impaired users and enhancing image-based search systems. In this work, we investigate the potential of scene graphs in addressing the VQA task. We conduct experiments on the GQA dataset, which features a complex set of questions requiring counting, compositional reasoning, and advanced logical inference, along with scene graphs for a large number of images. Our approach involves using image-plus-question architectures tailored for scene graphs, evaluating different scene graph generation methods for unseen images, introducing a training curriculum that integrates both human-annotated and automatically generated scene graphs, and developing late fusion architectures to combine multiple image representations. This comprehensive study marks the first of its kind to explore the role of scene graphs in VQA, offering new insights into their effectiveness and potential.

The widespread use of monitoring devices in urban flow monitoring systems incurs substantial maintenance and operational costs. To address this, there is a need for a technique that reduces the number of deployed devices while maintaining data accuracy and granularity. In this paper, we propose an approach for estimating real-time, fine-grained crowd flows across a city based on coarse-grained observations. This task presents two main challenges: capturing the spatial correlations between coarse- and fine-grained urban flows, and accounting for the complexities introduced by external factors. To overcome these challenges, we introduce UrbanFM, a model composed of two key components: 1) an inference network that generates fine-grained flow distributions from coarse-grained inputs, utilizing a feature extraction module and a novel distributional upsampling module; and 2) a general fusion subnet designed to enhance performance by incorporating the effects of various external influences. UrbanFM demonstrates strong effectiveness and efficiency for small-scale upsampling tasks. However, its single-pass upsampling mechanism proves inadequate at higher upscaling rates. To address this limitation, we further propose UrbanPy, a cascading model that enables progressive inference of fine-grained urban flows by breaking down the original task into multiple subtasks. Compared to UrbanFM, UrbanPy achieves superior performance for large-scale inference scenarios.

Eligibility traces in reinforcement learning serve as a tool for balancing bias and variance, often accelerating training by propagating information backward across time steps within a single update. In this work, we explore the integration of eligibility traces with recurrent neural networks within the Atari gaming environment. We demonstrate the advantages of combining recurrent networks with eligibility traces in several Atari games, while also emphasizing the critical role of the optimization method employed during training.

Language identification (LI) serves as a crucial initial step in various speech processing systems. As the use of voice-based assistants continues to grow, speech-based language identification has become a widely studied area. To address the challenge of language detection, two main approaches can be considered: an implicit method, which relies solely on speech signals, and an explicit method, which uses text along with its corresponding transcription. This paper focuses on the implicit approach, as transcriptive data is often unavailable. 

We evaluate existing models and introduce a novel attention-based model for language identification that takes log-Mel spectrogram images as input. Additionally, we explore the effectiveness of raw waveforms as features for neural network models in LI tasks. For training and evaluation, we classified six languages—English, French, German, Spanish, Russian, and Italian—with an accuracy of 95.4%, and four languages—English, French, German, and Spanish—with an accuracy of 96.3%, using the VoxForge dataset. This framework can be extended to include additional languages in future work.

In this paper, we introduce methods for addressing two key challenges in time series (TS) analysis through the lens of quantum computing: reconstruction and classification. We frame the problem of reconstructing a given time series from a training dataset as an unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem, which can be efficiently solved using both quantum annealers and gate-model quantum computers. This is achieved by discretizing the time series and transforming the reconstruction task into a set cover problem, enabling a one-versus-all approach for reconstruction. Building on the results of the reconstruction process, we demonstrate how to adapt the method for semi-supervised classification of time series data. Our experimental results show that the proposed approach performs competitively with existing semi- and unsupervised classification techniques, while requiring significantly less data compared to classical methods.

We address the challenge of jointly encoding structured data, such as natural language, over a noisy communication channel. Traditionally, this problem is tackled by first applying source coding to compress the text and then using channel coding to enhance transmission reliability. This two-step approach is theoretically optimal for minimizing end-to-end distortion when using arbitrarily long block lengths for both source and channel codes, particularly over discrete memoryless channels. However, this optimality breaks down in practical scenarios involving finite-length documents and constrained encoding lengths.

In such cases, we demonstrate that a deep learning-based encoder-decoder architecture can achieve lower word error rates. Unlike conventional methods that focus on minimizing bit error rates, our approach preserves the semantic structure of sentences by first embedding them into a semantic space, where semantically similar sentences are represented closely. Subsequently, we perform joint source and channel coding directly on these embeddings, thereby maintaining meaningful information throughout the transmission process.

I specialize in training neural machine translation (NMT) models for the English-Hungarian and Hungarian-English language pairs, utilizing the Hunglish2 corpus. The primary contribution of this work lies in the evaluation of various data augmentation strategies during the training of NMT models. I introduce five structure-aware augmentation methods, which differ from conventional approaches by leveraging the dependency tree of sentences rather than randomly selecting words for masking or replacement. My thesis begins with an extensive literature review covering neural networks, sequential modeling, neural machine translation, dependency parsing, and data augmentation. Following a thorough exploratory data analysis and preprocessing of the Hunglish2 corpus, I conduct experiments using the proposed augmentation techniques. The best-performing model for Hungarian-English achieves a BLEU score of 33.9, while the best model for English-Hungarian attains a BLEU score of 28.6.

Integer quantization of neural networks refers to the process of approximating the high-precision computations of standard neural network models using lower-precision integer arithmetic. This technique plays a crucial role in the efficient deployment and execution of machine learning systems, as it significantly reduces memory usage and enables faster computations. In this work, we introduce an integer-only quantization approach tailored for Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network architectures, which form the backbone of many real-world machine learning systems. Our quantization strategy is accurate—demonstrating strong performance even when applied post-training—efficient, and fast, utilizing 8-bit integer weights and predominantly 8-bit activations. Furthermore, it is designed to be compatible with a wide range of hardware platforms, leveraging instruction sets available in common CPU architectures as well as dedicated neural accelerators.

Automated design synthesis holds the promise of transforming the modern engineering design process, enabling broader access to highly optimized and customized products across a wide range of industries. The successful integration of generative machine learning into design engineering could unlock this potential, making it a critical area of research. In this paper, we present a comprehensive review and analysis of deep generative machine learning models in the context of engineering design. 

Deep Generative Models (DGMs) typically employ deep neural networks to learn patterns from input datasets and generate new, original designs. Recent advancements have demonstrated the effectiveness of DGMs such as feedforward neural networks (NNs), generative adversarial networks (GANs), variational autoencoders (VAEs), and specific deep reinforcement learning (DRL) frameworks in various design applications, including structural optimization, materials discovery, and shape generation. 

Since 2016, the use of DGMs in engineering design has seen a significant rise. Anticipating continued growth in this field, we conduct a review of recent developments to provide valuable insights for researchers interested in applying DGMs to design tasks. Our review is structured around key aspects of current literature, including algorithms, datasets, representation methods, and practical applications. In particular, we highlight influential works that have introduced novel techniques in DGMs, successfully applied these models to design domains, or contributed to their advancement through the creation of specialized datasets or supporting tools.

Although NLP systems perform well on many tasks, they are vulnerable to small adversarial perturbations in the input. Current defense mechanisms either rely on heuristic approaches that can be bypassed by stronger attacks or provide theoretical robustness against worst-case scenarios but are incompatible with advanced models like BERT. In this work, we propose Robust Encodings (RobEn), a straightforward framework that ensures robustness without requiring changes to the model architecture. At its core, RobEn employs an encoding function that maps sentences into a smaller, discrete space of representations. By using these encodings as a bottleneck, systems can achieve guaranteed robustness through standard training, and the same encodings can be applied across multiple tasks. To build effective encoding functions, we define two key requirements: (1) perturbations of a sentence should map to a limited set of encodings (stability), and (2) models using these encodings should maintain strong performance (fidelity). We apply RobEn to defend against a wide range of adversarial typos. On six GLUE tasks, our implementation of RobEn combined with BERT achieves an average robust accuracy of 71.3% against all considered adversarial typos, compared to just 35.3% accuracy achieved by prior methods using a typo-corrector against a simple greedy attack.

This paper presents a study focused on reservoir history matching through the integration of 4D seismic data into the inversion process, employing machine learning techniques. A novel integrated framework is introduced for reconstructing petrophysical properties using a modified Ensemble Smoother with Multiple Data Assimilation (ES-MDA) in a synthetic reservoir setting. The permeability field is represented using an unsupervised learning method—K-means combined with Singular Value Decomposition (K-SVD)—which is further enhanced by the Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (OMP) algorithm, known for its effectiveness in promoting sparsity. Additionally, seismic attributes, particularly acoustic impedance, are parametrized using the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT). This innovative combination of machine learning, sparsity-promoting regularization, seismic imaging, and history matching aims to efficiently address the ill-posed nature of historical production data inversion via ES-MDA. The numerical experiments demonstrate that the sparse representations of petrophysical properties and seismic attributes lead to improved matches with actual production data and more accurate quantification of the advancing water front, outperforming conventional methods that lack such advanced parametrization strategies.

Neural Architecture Search (NAS) is an emerging field that holds the potential to be as transformative as Convolutional Neural Networks were in 2012. Although numerous significant advancements have been made across a range of tasks, comparing different NAS methods remains a challenging and unresolved issue. While most algorithms are evaluated on the same datasets, there is no unified experimental protocol followed by all researchers. Consequently, and due to the limited use of ablation studies, it remains unclear why certain approaches outperform others. Our first contribution is the creation of a benchmark that evaluates 8 NAS methods across 5 datasets. To address the challenge of comparing methods with varying search spaces, we introduce a metric based on a method's relative improvement over a randomly sampled average architecture. This approach effectively neutralizes advantages stemming from manually designed search spaces or training procedures. Surprisingly, we find that many NAS techniques struggle to significantly surpass the baseline performance of the average architecture. To further investigate, we conduct experiments using the widely adopted DARTS search space, aiming to assess the impact of each component in the NAS pipeline. These experiments reveal that: (i) the use of specific tricks in the evaluation protocol has a substantial influence on performance.

While randomized clinical trials typically have sufficiently large sample sizes to estimate the average treatment effect accurately, they often lack the power to reliably estimate treatment-covariate interactions, which are essential for data-driven precision medicine. Observational data from real-world practice may help address this limitation. A common approach in trials is to use separate regression models for each treatment arm to predict the outcome of interest and then estimate the treatment effect by comparing these predictions. However, this straightforward method can lead to spurious treatment-covariate interactions in observational studies when the underlying regression model is misspecified.

Motivated by the need to model the number of relapses in multiple sclerosis patients, where the ratio of relapse rates naturally represents the treatment effect, we propose estimating the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) as the ratio of expected potential outcomes. We derive a doubly robust estimator for this CATE within a semiparametric model that incorporates treatment-covariate interactions. Additionally, we introduce a validation procedure to assess the performance of the estimator on an independent dataset. Through simulations, we demonstrate the finite-sample properties of the proposed methods and illustrate their practical advantages using real-world data to explore treatment effects.

Code smell, much like an unpleasant odor, serves as a surface-level indicator of underlying issues in software development practices. This metric reflects deeper problems within the codebase and is often recognized by experienced developers as a sign of poor coding conventions. Recent research has shown that code containing code smells is more likely to undergo frequent changes during the software development lifecycle. In this paper, we developed code smell prediction models using features extracted from source code to identify eight different types of code smells. Our work also explores the use of data sampling techniques to address class imbalance and feature selection methods to identify the most relevant features. While previous studies have employed techniques such as Naive Bayes and Random Forest, they have not extensively investigated deep learning approaches for code smell prediction. A total of 576 distinct deep learning models were trained using the features and datasets described. The study found that deep learning models utilizing data generated by the Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique achieved superior performance in terms of accuracy and AUC, with some models showing an improvement in accuracy from 88.47%.

We investigate $Q$-learning with knowledge transfer, leveraging samples from a target reinforcement learning (RL) task as well as data from related but distinct source tasks. We introduce transfer learning algorithms tailored for both batch and online $Q$-learning scenarios, where the source data is obtained in an offline manner. The proposed transferred $Q$-learning method incorporates a novel re-targeting mechanism that facilitates vertical information propagation across multiple steps within an RL task, complementing the traditional horizontal information aggregation seen in transfer learning for supervised settings. We provide the first theoretical analysis of transfer learning in RL, demonstrating a faster convergence rate for $Q$-function estimation in offline RL transfer, as well as a reduced regret bound in the transition from offline to online RL under specific similarity conditions. Empirical results on both synthetic and real-world datasets are presented to validate the effectiveness of our algorithm and support our theoretical findings.

Through the quantification of physical activity energy expenditure (PAEE), healthcare monitoring holds promise for promoting healthy and active aging. By encouraging behavioral changes in older adults and linking these to tangible health benefits, PAEE measurement can play a key role in supporting longevity and well-being. To assess PAEE in a monitoring context, wearable accelerometers have been widely used; however, most existing methods are designed for younger populations. Given that older adults have distinct energy needs and activity patterns, current models may not accurately estimate PAEE in this demographic. Since past activity levels influence current energy expenditure, we propose the use of a modeling technique well-suited for sequential data: the Recurrent Neural Network (RNN). To train the RNN for an elderly population, we utilized the GOTOV dataset, which includes 34 healthy participants aged 60 and above (mean age 65) performing 16 different activities. Accelerometer data were collected from both the wrist and ankle, while energy expenditure was measured using indirect calorimetry. Following model optimization, we developed an architecture combining an RNN with three GRU layers and a feedforward network that integrates both accelerometer signals and participant-specific information. In this paper, we present our efforts to go beyond the standard capabilities of a GRU-based RNN, with the goal of achieving more accurate and personalized PAEE estimation for older adults.

Symmetry transformations give rise to invariances that are often captured using deep latent variable models. In complex domains like chemical space, such invariances can be observed, but the corresponding symmetry transformations are typically not expressible in closed form. To address this challenge, we propose a model that learns the symmetry transformation through two distinct latent subspaces: one that encodes the target variable and another that captures the remaining invariant information. Our method leverages the deep information bottleneck framework combined with a continuous mutual information regularizer. Unlike prior approaches, we focus specifically on the difficult task of minimizing mutual information in continuous settings. To achieve this, we compute mutual information using correlation matrices alongside a bijective variable transformation. Extensive experiments show that our model outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on both synthetic and molecular datasets.

Gaussian processes have emerged as a powerful tool in safety-critical applications, thanks to their ability to provide posterior variance estimates that directly reflect model uncertainty and enable risk quantification. However, existing methods for such settings typically rely on the assumption that kernel hyperparameters are known, an assumption that does not hold in general scenarios. To address this limitation, we propose robust Gaussian process uniform error bounds that account for unknown hyperparameters. Our approach constructs a confidence region over the hyperparameter space, allowing us to derive a probabilistic upper bound on the model error for any set of hyperparameters. Unlike many existing approaches, we do not require prior knowledge of hyperparameter bounds; instead, we derive these bounds directly from the data in a straightforward manner. Furthermore, we apply the proposed technique to establish performance guarantees for a class of learning-based control problems. Experimental results demonstrate that our bound significantly outperforms both standard and fully Bayesian Gaussian processes.

We introduce the first learning-based visual odometry (VO) model that demonstrates strong generalization across multiple datasets and real-world scenarios, outperforming traditional geometry-based methods in complex environments. This is achieved through the use of the SLAM dataset TartanAir, which offers a rich and diverse collection of synthetic data in challenging settings. To enhance the model's adaptability across different datasets, we propose an up-to-scale loss function and integrate camera intrinsic parameters directly into the model architecture. Experimental results show that a single model, TartanVO, trained exclusively on synthetic data without any fine-tuning, can effectively generalize to real-world datasets such as KITTI and EuRoC, showcasing significant performance advantages over geometry-based approaches on difficult trajectories. Our code is available at https://github.com/castacks/tartanvo.

We study online sequential decision-making problems in which an agent must carefully balance exploration and exploitation. We introduce a family of Bayesian "optimistic" policies, which, in the context of stochastic multi-armed bandits, encompasses the Thompson sampling strategy. We present a novel analysis demonstrating that any algorithm generating policies from this optimistic set achieves $\tilde O(\sqrt{AT})$ Bayesian regret in a setting with $A$ actions over $T$ rounds. 

We extend this analysis to bilinear saddle-point problems, which include zero-sum matrix games and constrained bandits as special cases. In such settings, we show that Thompson sampling may produce policies outside the optimistic set and can incur linear regret in certain scenarios. 

To address this, we propose a method called "Variational Bayesian Optimistic Sampling" (VBOS), where finding a policy within the optimistic set reduces to solving a convex optimization problem. This approach is applicable to any posterior distribution, without requiring assumptions like log-concavity, unimodality, or smoothness. The variational formulation offers several advantages, including flexibility in tuning the exploration-exploitation tradeoff, incorporating regularization, enforcing constraints, and parameterizing the policy in a linear fashion.

Current deep learning architectures demonstrate impressive performance when trained on large-scale, controlled datasets. However, their predictive accuracy tends to decline significantly when learning new classes incrementally. This decline is attributed to catastrophic forgetting—the tendency of these models to lose previously acquired knowledge. In contrast, Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) can effectively model the input space using a constrained k-means approach, allowing them to retain prior knowledge. 

Inspired by the structure and function of biological neurons, we introduce a novel algorithm called the Dendritic-Self-Organizing Map (DendSOM). DendSOM consists of a single layer of SOMs that extract patterns from specific regions of the input space, along with a set of hit matrices—each corresponding to a SOM—that estimate the relationship between units and labels. The best-matching unit for an input pattern is determined using the maximum cosine similarity rule, while point-wise mutual information is used for class inference.

Unlike traditional approaches, DendSOM performs unsupervised feature extraction, as it does not rely on labels for weight updates. It outperforms classical SOMs and several state-of-the-art continual learning methods on benchmark datasets such as Split-MNIST and Split-CIFAR-10. Our results suggest that integrating neuronal properties into SOMs may offer a promising solution to the challenge of catastrophic forgetting.

This study investigates the denoising of piecewise smooth graph signals that display varying levels of smoothness across different regions of the graph, where each node's value may be vector-valued. We extend the graph trend filtering framework to handle vector-valued signals by introducing a family of non-convex regularizers, which demonstrate improved recovery performance compared to traditional convex approaches. By leveraging an oracle inequality, we derive statistical error bounds for the first-order stationary points of the proposed non-convex method on general graphs. Additionally, we develop an ADMM-based algorithm for solving the resulting optimization problem and establish its convergence properties. The effectiveness of the method is demonstrated through extensive numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, focusing on tasks such as denoising, support recovery, event detection, and semi-supervised classification.

In this paper, we introduce DiffWave, a flexible diffusion probabilistic model designed for both conditional and unconditional waveform generation. Unlike autoregressive models, DiffWave operates without sequential dependency, transforming white noise into structured audio signals through a Markov chain with a fixed number of steps during synthesis. The model is efficiently trained by optimizing a modified version of the variational lower bound on data likelihood. DiffWave achieves high-fidelity audio output across multiple waveform generation tasks, such as neural vocoding conditioned on mel spectrograms, class-conditional synthesis, and fully unconditional generation. We show that DiffWave matches the speech quality of a strong WaveNet vocoder (MOS: 4.44 vs. 4.43) while generating audio significantly faster. Moreover, it substantially outperforms autoregressive and GAN-based models in the challenging task of unconditional generation, demonstrating superior audio quality and sample diversity according to both automated and human evaluations.

Due to the ease of modern data collection, applied statisticians frequently have access to a large number of covariates that they aim to relate to an observed outcome. Generalized linear models (GLMs) provide a highly interpretable framework for such analyses. However, in high-dimensional settings—where the number of covariates is large relative to the number of observations—inferential uncertainty becomes non-trivial. A Bayesian approach offers a coherent way to quantify this uncertainty. Unfortunately, current methods for Bayesian inference in GLMs typically require computation times that scale roughly cubically with the number of parameters, limiting their use to problems with at most tens of thousands of parameters. To address this, we introduce LR-GLM, an approach that leverages a low-rank approximation of the data to reduce both time and memory costs. When combined with the Laplace approximation or Markov chain Monte Carlo, LR-GLM delivers a full Bayesian posterior approximation while significantly reducing computational complexity by a factor proportional to the parameter dimension. We rigorously analyze the accuracy of our approximation and demonstrate how the choice of rank enables a flexible trade-off between computational efficiency and statistical precision. Empirical results on real-world large-scale datasets support our theoretical findings and highlight the effectiveness of LR-GLM.

Fairness in machine learning (ML)—the process of understanding and mitigating algorithmic bias—has attracted growing attention, with a wealth of literature emerging. Most existing work assumes that the underlying data is independent and identically distributed (IID). However, graphs are a common data structure used to represent relationships among individual entities, and they are inherently non-IID. Bridging the gap between traditional fairness research, which is typically designed for IID data, and the widespread use of non-IID graph representations is therefore crucial for addressing bias in ML systems. In this survey, we review recent advances in fairness under non-IID graph data, highlight available datasets and evaluation metrics for future research, and discuss the limitations of current approaches as well as promising directions for future work.

When designing variational autoencoders (VAEs) or other latent space models, the dimensionality of the latent space is typically set in advance. However, this predefinition may lead to either an insufficient or excessive number of dimensions for the specific task at hand. When the latent dimension is not fixed, it is commonly determined through computationally intensive and resource-heavy cross-validation procedures. To address this challenge, we have developed a technique that automatically and dynamically reduces the latent space dimensionality during training. This approach leverages Generalized ELBO with Constrained Optimization (GECO) and the $L_0$-Augment-REINFORCE-Merge ($L_0$-ARM) gradient estimator. The GECO framework ensures that the reconstruction error remains within a specified upper bound. In this paper, we present the algorithmic details of our method and evaluate its performance on five different datasets. Our experiments demonstrate that the training process is stable and that the latent space can be effectively pruned without violating the constraints imposed by GECO.

This article presents Jigsaw, a convolutional neural network (CNN) designed for geoscience applications and inspired by the Inception architecture, but specifically adapted for geoscientific analysis. It introduces JigsawHSI, a variant of Jigsaw, and applies it to the land-use and land-cover (LULC) classification task using three hyperspectral image datasets: Indian Pines, Pavia University, and Salinas. The performance of JigsawHSI is evaluated against HybridSN, a state-of-the-art spectral-spatial 3D-CNN followed by a 2D-CNN that has achieved top results on these datasets. The study demonstrates that JigsawHSI matches or outperforms HybridSN across all three datasets. Furthermore, the paper emphasizes the potential of Jigsaw in geoscience applications and provides access to the code and toolkit for reproducibility.

We examine the optimal posteriors for recently introduced \cite{begin2016pac} PAC-Bayesian bounds based on the chi-squared divergence, focusing on the nature of their distribution, computational scalability, and test set performance. For a finite set of classifiers, we derive bounds using three different distance functions: KL-divergence, linear distance, and squared distance. The optimal posterior weights are found to be proportional to deviations in empirical risks, typically with support restricted to subsets of classifiers. When a uniform prior is used, it suffices to consider posteriors defined over classifier subsets ordered by their empirical risk.

We demonstrate that minimizing the bound for the linear distance formulation corresponds to a convex optimization problem, allowing for a closed-form solution for the optimal posterior. In contrast, the minimization for the squared distance results in a quasi-convex program under specific conditions, while the KL-divergence case involves non-convex optimization (a difference of convex functions). To efficiently compute these optimal posteriors, we derive fast-converging fixed-point (FP) equations.

These methods are applied to a finite set of SVM regularization parameter values, resulting in stochastic SVMs with tight PAC-Bayesian bounds. A comprehensive evaluation is conducted comparing our optimal posteriors with existing KL-divergence-based posteriors across various UCI datasets, considering differences in risk value ranges and variances. The results show that chi-squared divergence-based posteriors yield weaker bounds and higher test errors, suggesting potential limitations in their effectiveness.

Due to limited measurements in the distribution system state estimation (DSSE), achieving full observability and obtaining redundant measurements is challenging without the use of pseudo-measurements. Matrix completion state estimation (MCSE) addresses this by integrating matrix completion techniques with power system models, leveraging the low-rank structure of the measurement matrix to estimate voltage. This paper introduces a robust matrix completion state estimation (RMCSE) method designed to estimate voltages in distribution systems under conditions of low observability. 

Traditional state estimation methods, such as the weighted least squares (WLS) approach, require full observability to compute system states and rely on redundant measurements for bad data detection. In contrast, the proposed RMCSE enhances the robustness against bad data by simultaneously minimizing the matrix rank and the weighted measurement residuals. This enables accurate state estimation even in low-observability scenarios, without the need for an explicit bad data detection process in the presence of multiple erroneous measurements.

The performance of the RMCSE is evaluated numerically on the IEEE 33-bus radial distribution system. The results are compared with those of the WLS method combined with the largest normalized residual-based bad data identification (WLS-LNR) and the standard MCSE, demonstrating the improved accuracy and robustness of the proposed approach.

This paper introduces a representational model for image pairs, such as consecutive video frames, which are connected by local pixel displacements. The goal is to gain insights into motion perception in the primary visual cortex (V1). The model integrates two key components: (1) vector representations of local image content, and (2) matrix representations of local pixel displacements resulting from the relative motion between the observer and objects in a 3D scene. When an image frame changes due to local displacements, the corresponding vectors are multiplied by the displacement matrices, leading to an equivariant representation that adapts in response to motion. Our experiments demonstrate that the model can learn Gabor-like filter pairs with quadrature phases, whose characteristics closely resemble those of simple cells in the macaque V1. Furthermore, we show that the model can infer local motion either through supervised or unsupervised learning. Despite its simplicity, the model achieves competitive performance in optical flow estimation.

Energy-based modeling represents a promising direction in unsupervised learning, as it enables the development of numerous downstream applications from a single, unified model. A key challenge in training energy-based models using contrastive methods lies in generating samples from the current energy function at each iteration. While significant progress has been made in making this sampling process more efficient, existing approaches typically rely on Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods that target the current model. These methods require infinitely long chains to accurately sample from the true energy distribution, which poses practical limitations. 

This paper introduces an alternative strategy for generating samples without resorting to computationally expensive MCMC procedures. Our approach involves viewing the evolution of the modeling distribution as two interrelated processes: (i) the evolution of the energy function itself, and (ii) the evolution of the samples drawn from this distribution along a specific vector field. By deriving a time-dependent vector field that guides particles to follow a trajectory closely aligned with the current density model, we effectively synchronize the dynamics of the samples with the energy function as it is updated during learning. 

Unlike traditional Monte Carlo methods, our technique aims to approximate the target distribution within a finite time frame. We validate the effectiveness of our approach through empirical experiments, demonstrating its advantages over existing methods.

Optimal decision-making in social contexts often relies on forecasts derived from time series (TS) data. In recent years, deep neural networks (DNNs), particularly recurrent neural networks (RNNs), have been widely adopted for TS forecasting and have demonstrated encouraging results. However, their effectiveness is increasingly being challenged in scenarios where high-quality training data is scarce and the time series to be forecasted exhibit complex, non-linear dynamics. Such challenges are prevalent in domains like financial forecasting, where achieving accurate and consistent long-term predictions remains a significant hurdle.

In this work, we explore whether DNN-based models can enhance forecasting performance by learning a joint representation of multiple time series, rather than relying on raw TS inputs. To achieve this, we employ a dynamic factor graph (DFG) to construct a multivariate autoregressive model. We identify a key limitation of RNNs within the DFG framework and introduce a novel variable-length attention-based mechanism (ACTM) to overcome it. The ACTM enables the model to dynamically adjust the autoregressive order over time, thereby capturing a broader range of probability distributions compared to existing methods. Leveraging this mechanism, we propose a self-supervised DNN architecture that improves forecasting accuracy in complex and data-scarce environments.

Most online reviews are composed of plain-text feedback along with a single numeric rating. However, products and user opinions are multidimensional, and understanding the specific "aspects" that influence a user's rating can provide deeper insights into their preferences. For instance, a user's experience with an audiobook likely depends on factors such as the story and the narrator, and knowing their views on these aspects could enable more accurate product recommendations. In this paper, we develop models for rating systems where these dimensions are explicitly represented through separate ratings for each aspect of a product. By introducing new corpora containing five million reviews, each rated across three to six aspects, we evaluate our models on three key prediction tasks: first, identifying which parts of a review correspond to each rated aspect; second, summarizing reviews by selecting the sentences that best reflect a user's overall rating; and third, inferring missing aspect ratings in datasets where such ratings are optional. Our model performs competitively with state-of-the-art approaches.

The Gauss-Manin connection for a family of hypersurfaces dictates how the period matrix varies across the family. Despite the simplicity of the equations defining the family, this connection can become highly complex. In such cases, computing the period matrices of individual varieties in the family using homotopy continuation becomes computationally intensive. To address this challenge, we train neural networks capable of rapidly and accurately estimating the complexity of the Gauss-Manin connection for a pencil of hypersurfaces. As an application, we compute the periods of 96% of smooth quartic surfaces in projective 3-space whose defining equations are sums of five monomials. From these periods, we determine their Picard numbers and the endomorphism fields of their transcendental lattices.

Idioms present significant challenges for nearly all Machine Translation systems. This type of language is commonly used in everyday communication and cannot be easily overlooked. Recently, the growing interest in memory-augmented models within Language Modeling has helped improve system performance by effectively handling long-range dependencies. In this paper, we investigate the application of such techniques in a Neural Machine Translation system to enhance the translation of idiomatic expressions.

The recognition network in deep latent variable models, such as variational autoencoders (VAEs), employs amortized inference to efficiently approximate the posterior distribution, enabling scalability to large datasets. However, this approach has been shown to produce suboptimal variational parameters, leading to an additional source of error known as the amortization gap. To address this issue and enhance the training of the generative model, recent studies have introduced an additional refinement step that applies stochastic variational inference (SVI) to further optimize the variational parameters obtained from the amortized inference model. In this paper, we propose Buffered Stochastic Variational Inference (BSVI), a novel refinement method that leverages the sequence of intermediate variational proposal distributions and their corresponding importance weights generated by SVI to construct a more generalized importance-weighted lower bound. Our experimental results show that training VAEs with BSVI consistently outperforms standard SVI, offering a more effective training framework for variational autoencoders.

This paper introduces an improvement to convolutional neural networks for object detection in resource-limited robotic systems by incorporating a geometric input transformation known as Visual Mesh. By leveraging object geometry, Visual Mesh constructs a graph within the visual space, thereby reducing computational complexity through the normalization of pixel and feature density. Experimental comparisons with several fast convolutional neural networks show that Visual Mesh achieves execution times up to sixteen times faster than the fastest competitor, while maintaining high accuracy.

In this paper, we introduce a novel two-stage metric learning algorithm. First, we transform each data instance into a probability distribution by computing its similarities to a set of fixed anchor points. Next, we define the distance in the input space using the Fisher information distance on the corresponding statistical manifold. This approach gives rise to a new class of distance metrics with distinctive properties. Unlike kernel-based metric learning methods, our approach does not require the similarity measure to be positive semi-definite. Additionally, it can be viewed as a local metric learning method that provides a well-defined approximation of distances. We evaluate the performance of our algorithm on several datasets and demonstrate that it significantly outperforms existing metric learning methods as well as SVM.

In recent years, money laundering schemes have become increasingly complex and rapid in execution, impacting financial institutions and millions of customers worldwide. Enhanced privacy policies, combined with local regulatory requirements, have made it challenging for banks to internally and cross-share data or report suspicious activities in the context of Anti-Money Laundering (AML) efforts. Current AML analysis frameworks and information-sharing models face significant limitations, including compliance with regulatory constraints, the need for extensive infrastructure to support high-computation algorithms, issues related to data quality and scope, and the overall complexity and cost of execution, integration, and interpretation. This paper introduces a novel topology for analyzing multi-banking customer social relationships within an AML framework—focusing on customer-to-customer, customer-to-transaction, and transaction-to-transaction relationships—using a 3D modeling topological algebra based on Poincaré embeddings.

Generative adversarial networks (GANs) represent a powerful class of deep learning models that have achieved significant success across a wide range of applications. As part of the broader generative modeling family, GANs generate new data by learning the underlying distribution of real-world examples through a probabilistic approach. In the clinical domain, GANs have demonstrated superior ability to model complex, nonlinear, and subtle disease-related patterns—particularly in capturing spatially intricate features—when compared to traditional generative techniques. This review provides an overview of the current literature on the use of GANs in neuroimaging studies related to various neurological conditions, such as Alzheimer’s disease, brain tumors, brain aging, and multiple sclerosis. For each application, we offer an intuitive explanation of the relevant GAN methodologies, while also addressing key challenges, unresolved questions, and potential future directions for the integration of GANs in neuroimaging research. Our goal is to bridge the gap between advanced deep learning techniques and neurology by illustrating how GANs can enhance clinical decision-making and deepen our understanding of the structural and functional characteristics of brain diseases.

Existing literature highlights the value of limit order book data in predicting short-term volatility in stock markets. Given that stocks are not independent, movements in one asset can influence related assets. In this paper, we focus on forecasting short-term realized volatility using a multivariate approach that integrates limit order book data with relational information. To this end, we propose the Graph Transformer Network for Volatility Forecasting, a model capable of incorporating limit order book features along with an unlimited number of temporal and cross-sectional relationships from diverse sources. Experimental results on a dataset comprising approximately 500 stocks from the S&P 500 index demonstrate that our model outperforms existing benchmarks.

Muscle-actuated organisms can learn an extraordinary range of dexterous movements, despite having a large number of muscles. However, reinforcement learning (RL) on complex musculoskeletal models has yet to achieve comparable performance. We propose that the primary challenge lies in ineffective exploration within large, overactuated action spaces. This is supported by evidence showing that standard exploration strategies based on noise are insufficient in synthetic overactuated systems. We identify differential extrinsic plasticity (DEP), a concept from the field of self-organization, as a promising approach capable of inducing comprehensive state-space exploration within seconds of interaction. By incorporating DEP into RL, we enable rapid learning of reaching and locomotion tasks in musculoskeletal systems, achieving superior sample efficiency and robustness compared to existing methods across all evaluated tasks.

Pruning less critical parameters can significantly reduce the computational and memory demands of deep neural networks (DNNs). A saliency metric helps identify which parameters can be removed without substantially affecting the model's classification performance. Numerous saliency metrics have been proposed, often as part of broader pruning strategies. As a result, it becomes challenging to isolate the true effectiveness of a saliency metric from the overall pruning framework in which it is embedded. Even similar-looking metrics can produce vastly different outcomes due to subtle design differences. To address this, we introduce a taxonomy of saliency metrics based on four largely independent principal components. This classification enables us to categorize a wide variety of metrics from the pruning literature. Beyond serving as a reference for existing work, our taxonomy facilitates the development of new saliency metrics by exploring innovative combinations of its components. We conduct an extensive experimental analysis involving over 300 distinct saliency metrics. Our findings provide clear insights into unresolved research questions and highlight the significance of reduction and scaling when pruning weight groups. Notably, some of the metrics we constructed outperform the most advanced existing methods for convolutional neural networks.
