Protein secondary structure plays a vital role in establishing an information bridge between the primary and tertiary (3D) structures. Accurate prediction of the eight-state protein secondary structure (PSS) has become a key tool in the structural and functional analysis of proteins within the field of bioinformatics. Recently, deep learning techniques have been increasingly applied to this area, leading to significant improvements in the accuracy of eight-state (Q8) PSS prediction. However, from a theoretical perspective, there remains considerable room for further advancement, particularly in the precision of eight-state PSS prediction.

In this study, we introduce a novel deep convolutional neural network (DCNN), named PS8-Net, designed to enhance the accuracy of eight-class PSS prediction. The architecture is built upon a carefully constructed feature matrix derived from both sequence and profile features of proteins. A key innovation in our model is the introduction of a new PS8 module, which incorporates skip connections to effectively capture long-range interdependencies from higher layers, extract local contexts from earlier layers, and integrate global information during the secondary structure prediction process.

Our proposed PS8-Net achieves Q8 prediction accuracies of 76.89%, 71.94%, 76.86%, and 75.26% on the benchmark datasets CullPdb6133, CB513, CASP10, and CASP11, respectively. This architecture enables efficient processing of both local and global interactions among amino acids, thereby improving the accuracy of predictions across all secondary structure classes.

The deployment of machine learning models in high-stakes environments, such as healthcare, requires more than just high accuracy—it also demands fairness, robustness, and interpretability. Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) have long been favored in these critical domains due to their interpretability, but they often fall short in terms of scalability and flexibility compared to deep learning methods. In this work, we introduce two novel models: the Neural GAM (NODE-GAM) and the Neural GA$^2$M (NODE-GA$^2$M). These models retain the interpretability of traditional GAMs while offering improved performance on large datasets and better scalability than conventional GAMs. Compared to other ensemble and deep learning approaches, our models maintain transparency without sacrificing accuracy. We demonstrate that they uncover meaningful patterns in complex data. Furthermore, we show that self-supervised pre-training enhances model performance, an advantage that is not available to non-differentiable GAMs.

In the field of convex optimization, the problem of identifying near-stationary points remains underexplored compared to other optimality criteria such as function value. Even in the deterministic setting, the optimal method—OGM-G, introduced by Kim and Fessler (2021)—was only recently discovered. In this paper, we perform a comprehensive investigation into algorithmic approaches for finding near-stationary points in convex finite-sum problems. Our key contributions include: (1) the development of a memory-efficient variant of OGM-G, derived using the performance estimation problem framework (Drori and Teboulle, 2014); (2) the design of a novel accelerated SVRG variant that attains fast convergence rates for both minimizing the gradient norm and the function value; and (3) the proposal of an adaptively regularized accelerated SVRG method that eliminates the need for prior knowledge of certain unknown initial constants and achieves nearly optimal complexity bounds. We emphasize the simplicity and practicality of our proposed methods, which are intended to support and advance future research in this area.

In knowledge distillation, since a single, all-powerful teacher network is unable to address all challenges, recent research has focused on multiple teacher-based approaches. However, these methods sometimes fail to deliver the expected improvements, as some underdeveloped teachers may pass on incorrect knowledge to the student. To address this limitation and fully leverage the potential of multiple networks, we propose dividing the networks into two groups: a teacher group and a student group. Specifically, the student group consists of immature networks that benefit from learning from the teacher group, which comprises well-performing networks. Moreover, our online role-switching strategy allows the top-performing networks in the student group to be promoted to the teacher group, and vice versa, at each iteration. After refining the teacher group using the error samples from the student group, we successfully transfer the collective knowledge from the teacher group to the student group. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets, achieving strong performance. Additionally, we validate the generality of our approach across various backbone architectures, including ResNet, WRN, VGG, MobileNet, and ShuffleNet.

Recent studies have demonstrated that modern machine learning techniques offer a promising alternative to the long-standing joint source-channel coding (JSCC) problem. Initial results have shown that deep neural networks (DNNs) can outperform traditional digital schemes that rely on separate source and channel codes, particularly in wireless image and video transmission. However, end-to-end training of such systems typically requires a differentiable channel input representation, leading prior work to assume that any complex value can be transmitted over the channel. This assumption may limit the applicability of these methods in scenarios where hardware or protocol constraints restrict the set of allowable channel inputs to specific digital constellations. In this paper, we introduce DeepJSCC-Q, an end-to-end optimized JSCC framework for wireless image transmission that uses a finite channel input alphabet. We demonstrate that DeepJSCC-Q achieves performance comparable to previous approaches that allow arbitrary complex-valued channel inputs, especially when high modulation orders are used. Furthermore, its performance asymptotically converges to that of unconstrained channel inputs as the modulation order increases. Notably, DeepJSCC-Q maintains graceful degradation of image quality under unpredictable channel conditions, making it well-suited for deployment in mobile systems operating in dynamic environments.

Several learning applications involve solving high-dimensional regression problems in which the relevant features belong to a small number of (overlapping) groups. For large-scale datasets under standard sparsity assumptions, hard thresholding methods have shown remarkable efficiency. However, these methods often require NP-hard projections when handling overlapping group structures. In this paper, we demonstrate that such NP-hard projections can be circumvented through submodular optimization, leading to algorithms with strong theoretical guarantees—even in the presence of poorly conditioned data, such as when two features are highly correlated (e.g., with a correlation of ≥ 0.99), a scenario that existing analyses fail to address. The proposed methods offer an intriguing trade-off between computational efficiency and accuracy and can be extended to more challenging problems, including those involving sparse overlapping groups. Experimental results on both real and synthetic datasets confirm the effectiveness of our approach, showing that it is orders of magnitude faster than existing greedy and convex relaxation techniques for learning with group-structured sparsity.

We introduce a fast, scalable, and data-driven approach for solving linear relaxations of 0-1 integer linear programs by leveraging a graph neural network. Our solver is built upon the Lagrange decomposition-based algorithm FastDOG (Abbas et al., 2022). We make the algorithm differentiable and enable backpropagation through its dual update scheme, allowing for end-to-end training of its algorithmic parameters. This ensures that the algorithm retains its theoretical guarantees, including feasibility and a non-decreasing lower bound.

To address the issue of FastDOG potentially getting trapped in suboptimal fixed points, we enhance the graph neural network with the ability to predict non-parametric update steps that help escape these points while preserving dual feasibility. For training, we employ an unsupervised loss function and evaluate the model on large-scale real-world datasets. We train on smaller problems and test on larger ones, demonstrating strong generalization performance with a graph neural network containing only around 10,000 parameters.

Our solver significantly outperforms its non-learned counterpart in terms of speed and dual objective quality. Compared to commercial solvers, our learned approach achieves near-optimal results for LP relaxations and demonstrates up to an order-of-magnitude speed improvement on very large instances from structured prediction and selected combinatorial problems.

Variance reduction is a simple yet powerful technique that enhances the efficiency of convex (or non-convex) stochastic optimization. Among existing variance reduction methods, SVRG and SAGA stand out due to their use of unbiased gradient estimators and have become widely adopted in recent years. While several accelerated variants of SVRG, such as Katyusha and Acc-Prox-SVRG, have been proposed, a direct acceleration of SAGA has remained an open problem. In this paper, we introduce a directly accelerated version of SAGA based on a novel technique called Sampled Negative Momentum (SSNM). This approach achieves the best-known oracle complexity for strongly convex problems with a known strong convexity parameter. Our work thus addresses the long-standing gap in the direct acceleration of SAGA.

In this paper, we introduce a service-oriented architecture (SOA)-based platform designed to facilitate the retrieval and analysis of large-scale datasets originating from social networking (SN) platforms and Internet of Things (IoT) devices. These datasets are collected through smart city applications and socially-aware data aggregation services. A diverse range of urban applications—spanning areas such as Participatory Urbanism, Augmented Reality, and Sound-Mapping—are deployed across multiple cities, generating millions of user-generated events and online SN reports that are integrated into the RADICAL platform. Additionally, we explore the use of data analytics techniques, including sentiment analysis, on the combined IoT and SN data stored in an SQL database. We also investigate various algorithms and configurations aimed at reducing processing delays and improving the efficiency of result retrieval.

We investigate the interval estimation of the effect of a treatment $ T $ on an outcome $ Y $, in the presence of an unobserved confounder $ U $. By applying Hölder's inequality, we derive a set of bounds on the confounding bias $ |E[Y|T=t] - E[Y|\text{do}(T=t)]| $, which depend on the extent of unmeasured confounding—specifically, the strength of the relationship between $ U $ and $ T $, as well as between $ U $ and $ Y $. These bounds are tight when $ U $ is independent of $ T $ or when $ U $ is independent of $ Y $ given $ T $, corresponding to scenarios without unobserved confounding. We focus on a specific instance of these bounds that depends on two key components: the total variation distance between the distributions $ p(U) $ and $ p(U|T=t) $, and the maximum deviation (over all possible values of $ U $) of the conditional expected outcome $ E[Y|U=u, T=t] $ from the average expected outcome $ E[Y|T=t] $. We explore various calibration strategies for constructing interval estimates of treatment effects based on this bound and validate its performance through experiments on synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets.

Bayesian optimization is often challenging to apply in high-dimensional settings, as the acquisition step involves solving a non-convex optimization problem within the full search space. To address this limitation while preserving the advantages of Bayesian optimization, we introduce LineBO—a method that reduces the problem to a sequence of one-dimensional sub-problems, which can be efficiently solved. We establish that LineBO converges globally and achieves a fast local convergence rate when the objective function is strongly convex. Moreover, if the objective function has an invariant subspace, the algorithm automatically adapts to the effective dimension without requiring any modifications. When integrated with the SafeOpt algorithm to solve the sub-problems, LineBO becomes the first safe Bayesian optimization method with theoretical guarantees applicable in high-dimensional scenarios. We evaluate our approach on multiple synthetic benchmarks, demonstrating competitive performance. Additionally, we apply LineBO to optimize the beam intensity of the Swiss Free Electron Laser, involving up to 40 parameters, while ensuring compliance with safety constraints.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing various aspects of human life, science, and technology. One such area is polymer informatics, where AI and machine learning (ML) tools are playing a crucial role in the efficient development, design, and discovery of polymers. Surrogate models, trained on existing polymer data, enable rapid prediction of material properties, facilitating the identification of promising polymer candidates that meet specific performance criteria. Researchers are also employing statistical methods to address questions related to synthesizability and potential (retro)synthesis pathways for creating target polymers. Data-driven approaches are being developed to overcome the unique challenges posed by the vast chemical and physical diversity of polymers at both small and large scales. A major challenge in polymer informatics remains the limited availability of well-curated, structured data, as well as the need for machine-readable representations that accurately capture not only the structural complexity of polymeric systems but also their synthesis and processing conditions. Methods for solving inverse problems—where advanced AI algorithms recommend polymers that fulfill specific application requirements—are currently under investigation. As different components of the growing polymer informatics ecosystem continue to evolve and integrate, they hold the potential to enhance efficiency, accelerate discoveries, and boost productivity. In this review, we explore the emerging elements of this polymer informatics ecosystem and their implications.

Prompt-Tuning represents a novel approach to fine-tuning pre-trained language models in a parameter-efficient manner. In this work, we investigate the use of HyperNetworks to generate hyper-prompts, introducing HyperPrompt—a new architecture for task-conditioning self-attention mechanisms in Transformers through prompts. These hyper-prompts are end-to-end learnable, generated by a HyperNetwork, and serve as task-specific global memories that queries can attend to. This design enables both task-specific feature learning and efficient information sharing across tasks. We demonstrate that HyperPrompt achieves strong performance compared to established multi-task learning baselines, using as few as 0.14% of additional task-conditioning parameters, thereby offering significant improvements in both parameter and computational efficiency. Extensive experiments on Natural Language Understanding benchmarks such as GLUE and SuperGLUE show that HyperPrompt outperforms strong T5-based multi-task learning approaches as well as parameter-efficient methods like Prompt-Tuning and HyperFormer++ across a range of model sizes.

We aim to interpret a black-box classifier of the form: "data X is classified as class Y because X *has* A and B, and *does not have* C," where A, B, and C represent high-level concepts. The main challenge lies in discovering these concepts in an unsupervised manner, as they must be meaningful for explaining the classifier's decision-making process. To address this, we first introduce a structural generative model capable of expressing and uncovering such concepts. We then present a learning framework that simultaneously models the data distribution and promotes certain concepts to exert significant causal influence on the classifier's output. Additionally, our approach facilitates the integration of user-provided prior knowledge, enhancing the interpretability of the discovered concepts. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate that our method effectively identifies useful binary concepts for explanation.

Ridge, or more formally $\ell_2$ regularization, is a fundamental concept that appears across various fields of statistics and machine learning. It is an essential tool that every skilled data scientist should master. In this concise exploration of ridge regression, I have gathered some of the elegance and insights we've encountered over the past four decades in applied statistical practice.

One challenge in automated audio captioning (AAC) is the ambiguity in selecting appropriate words to describe an audio event or scene. Since a single acoustic event or scene can be expressed using multiple words, this leads to a vast number of possible captions and complicates the training process. To address this issue, we introduce TRACKE, a Transformer-based audio-captioning model that incorporates keyword estimation. TRACKE tackles the word-selection ambiguity as part of its main task while also performing a sub-task of acoustic event detection and acoustic scene classification—essentially estimating relevant keywords. By identifying keywords that correspond to the audio events or scenes present in the input, TRACKE generates captions that reference these keywords, thereby reducing the uncertainty in word selection. Experimental results on a public AAC dataset demonstrate that TRACKE achieves state-of-the-art performance and effectively captures both the caption and its associated keywords.

We present DeepPSL, a variant of Probabilistic Soft Logic (PSL), designed to create an end-to-end trainable system that seamlessly integrates reasoning and perception. PSL expresses first-order logic through a convex graphical model known as Hinge Loss Markov Random Fields (HL-MRFs). Its tractability has enabled its application to systems involving over 1 billion ground rules, setting it apart from other probabilistic logic frameworks. The core of our approach lies in representing predicates from first-order logic using deep neural networks, followed by approximate backpropagation through the HL-MRF, allowing for the training of every component within the logical system. We believe this method offers a promising direction for combining deep learning with reasoning techniques, with potential applications in knowledge base learning, multi-task learning, and explainability. We evaluate DeepPSL on a zero-shot learning task in image classification, where state-of-the-art results highlight the effectiveness and adaptability of our approach.

Most existing federated learning algorithms operate in a manner where, in each round, each client minimizes a loss function to learn an optimal local model, which is then aggregated at the server. However, these methods typically rely on point estimates of model parameters at the clients, neglecting the uncertainty inherent in the models learned locally. In many scenarios—particularly when data is limited—it can be advantageous to account for this uncertainty to improve the accuracy and robustness of predictions. Moreover, uncertainty information can be valuable for other critical tasks, such as active learning and out-of-distribution (OOD) detection.

In this work, we propose a framework for Bayesian federated learning, where each client infers the posterior predictive distribution based on its local training data. We explore multiple strategies for aggregating these client-specific predictive distributions at the server. To address the challenges and computational costs associated with communicating and aggregating full predictive distributions, our approach involves distilling each client’s predictive distribution into a single deep neural network. This enables us to seamlessly integrate advancements from standard federated learning into the Bayesian setting.

Unlike some recent approaches that focus solely on estimating model uncertainty at the client level, our method does not impose restrictive assumptions and provides a more flexible and practical framework for incorporating uncertainty into federated learning systems.

Classifiers trained using traditional empirical risk minimization or maximum likelihood approaches are known to experience significant performance drops when evaluated on adversarially crafted examples that exploit knowledge of the classifier's decision rule. As Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) have become dominant in classification tasks, their vulnerability to adversarial examples, along with methods for robust training, has become a major focus of recent research. In this paper, we present the first study on the susceptibility of spiking neural networks (SNNs), also referred to as third-generation neural networks, to adversarial attacks. The investigation examines both rate and time encoding schemes, as well as rate and first-to-spike decoding strategies. Additionally, we propose a robust training framework that is shown to improve the resilience of SNNs against white-box adversarial attacks.

This paper introduces a novel U-Net variant, termed SDU-Net, which employs stacked dilated convolutions for medical image segmentation. SDU-Net is based on the standard U-Net architecture but modifies the encoder and decoder operations—defined as all processing steps applied to feature maps at the same resolution. While the original U-Net uses two standard convolutions in each encoder/decoder operation, SDU-Net replaces this with one standard convolution followed by multiple dilated convolutions. The outputs from these dilated convolutions are concatenated and used as input for the next operation. Experimental results demonstrate that SDU-Net achieves superior performance compared to vanilla U-Net, attention U-Net (AttU-Net), and recurrent residual U-Net (R2U-Net) across four segmentation tasks. Furthermore, SDU-Net significantly reduces the number of parameters, using approximately 40% of those in vanilla U-Net, 17% of those in AttU-Net, and 15% of those in R2U-Net.

Distributed Gradient Descent (DGD) is an effective approach to implement Gradient Descent (GD), particularly for large-scale datasets, by partitioning the computational tasks into smaller subtasks and distributing them across multiple computing servers (CSs) for parallel execution. In conventional parallel setups, the per-iteration waiting time is often constrained by the slowest, or "straggling," servers. To address this issue, coded DGD techniques have been recently proposed, which introduce redundancy in computation tasks to mitigate the impact of stragglers. 

In most existing DGD frameworks—whether based on coded computation or coded communication—non-straggling CSs typically send a single message per iteration once they finish their assigned tasks. However, even though straggling servers may not complete all their tasks, they are often able to finish a portion of them. In this paper, we propose allowing multiple transmissions from each CS during each iteration, ensuring that as many completed computations as possible are reported to the aggregating server (AS), including those from straggling servers. Numerical results demonstrate that this approach can significantly reduce the average completion time per iteration, with only a slight increase in the communication load per server.

Recognition tasks, such as object detection, keypoint estimation, and instance segmentation, have become widely adopted in recent years. However, most state-of-the-art methods rely on deep neural networks that are computationally intensive and require significant memory, making them challenging to deploy on low-power embedded systems. As a result, reducing both the storage requirements and computational cost of these models has become a critical research focus.

The recently introduced Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) suggests that large neural networks trained on extensive datasets contain smaller, sparse subnetworks that can achieve comparable performance to their dense counterparts. In this work, we conduct the first empirical investigation into applying LTH for model pruning within the context of object detection, instance segmentation, and keypoint estimation. Our findings show that lottery tickets derived from ImageNet pretraining do not generalize well to downstream tasks. We present practical guidelines for identifying lottery tickets that achieve up to 80% overall sparsity without compromising performance across different sub-tasks. Additionally, we analyze the behavior of these trained subnetworks in relation to various task-specific factors, including object size, frequency, and detection difficulty.

We establish quantitative bounds that measure the $ L^2 $-norm difference between the trajectory of a finite-width neural network trained on a finite number of samples and the idealized kernel dynamics of an infinite-width, infinite-data network. A key implication of these bounds is that the network exhibits a bias toward learning the top eigenfunctions of the Neural Tangent Kernel—not only on the training set but across the entire input space. This bias is determined solely by the model architecture and the input distribution, and it persists regardless of the target function, which need not lie in the Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) of the kernel. Our results apply to deep architectures incorporating fully connected, convolutional, and residual layers. Moreover, we show that high-probability bounds can be achieved without requiring the network width to grow polynomially with the number of samples, up to a given stopping time. The proof leverages the low effective rank of the Fisher Information Matrix at initialization, which implies a much lower effective dimension of the model compared to its parameter count. We conclude that the theoretical understanding of local capacity control arising from the low effective rank of the Fisher Information Matrix remains underdeveloped.

The global spread of pneumonia caused by a novel coronavirus presents an unprecedented challenge to the world’s healthcare systems and public health measures. COVID-19 not only affects the lungs, leading to severe breathing difficulties and life-threatening conditions, but can also damage other vital organs such as the heart, kidneys, and brain, potentially resulting in long-term complications. Currently, the detection of COVID-19 relies primarily on reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) testing. However, many countries are currently experiencing outbreaks, and their medical resources are severely constrained, limiting the availability of gene sequencing tests. As a result, many patients may not be isolated or treated in a timely manner.

In response to this critical situation, we explored the potential of deep learning models in analyzing chest radiographs for diagnostic purposes and proposed a cascaded architecture called Cascade-SEMEnet, which integrates SEME-ResNet50 and SEME-DenseNet169. Both networks in the Cascade-SEMEnet framework utilize large input sizes and incorporate SE-Structure to enhance feature extraction. Additionally, they employ MoEx and histogram equalization techniques to improve image quality and data representation.

Initially, SEME-ResNet50 is used to screen chest X-rays and classify them into three categories: normal, bacterial pneumonia, and viral pneumonia. Subsequently, SEME-DenseNet169 performs a more detailed classification of the viral pneumonia cases to determine whether the infection is caused by SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19. To ensure accurate diagnosis, we also take steps to eliminate the impact of non-pathological factors.

Model discovery seeks to automatically uncover the underlying differential equations governing a given dataset. While approaches based on Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have shown significant potential, a fully differentiable model that explicitly learns the governing equation has remained challenging. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach by combining neural network-based surrogates with Sparse Bayesian Learning (SBL), resulting in a robust algorithm for model discovery. We demonstrate its effectiveness across multiple datasets. Furthermore, we reveal a connection between our method and multitask learning, which inspires the development of a Physics-Informed Normalizing Flow (PINF). As a proof of concept, we apply the PINF to directly learn a density model from single-particle data. Our work extends the applicability of PINNs to diverse neural network architectures and bridges neural network surrogates with the well-established field of Bayesian parameter inference.

**Objective:** This study explores the application of deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for the automated measurement of fetal body parts, including head circumference, biparietal diameter, abdominal circumference, and femur length, as well as the estimation of gestational age and fetal weight from fetal ultrasound videos.

**Approach:** A novel multi-task CNN-based spatio-temporal fetal ultrasound feature extraction and standard plane detection algorithm, named FUVAI, was developed and evaluated on 50 freehand fetal ultrasound video scans. The performance of FUVAI in measuring fetal biometrics was compared to that of five experienced sonographers at two time points separated by at least two weeks. Intra- and inter-observer variability were also assessed.

**Main Results:** The automated fetal biometric measurements generated by FUVAI were found to be comparable to those obtained by experienced sonographers. The differences in measurement values fell within the range of both intra- and inter-observer variability. Furthermore, statistical analysis revealed that these differences were not significant when comparing individual medical experts to the model.

**Significance:** We propose that FUVAI has the potential to support sonographers in clinical settings by offering guidance on the most appropriate frames for measurement, alongside automated results. Additionally, FUVAI is capable of performing these tasks efficiently, significantly reducing the time required for manual assessments.

Federated Learning enables the training of machine learning models across decentralized devices without requiring data to be centralized, thus preserving data privacy. A critical challenge in achieving broader adoption of Federated Learning is its ability to effectively handle data heterogeneity—specifically, non-IID (non-independent and identically distributed) data. In this paper, we introduce a novel Divide-and-Conquer training approach that allows the effective use of the widely adopted FedAvg aggregation algorithm, overcoming its known limitations in non-IID settings. Our method introduces a novel application of a Cosine-distance based Weight Divergence metric to identify the optimal point at which a deep neural network can be split into class-agnostic initial layers and class-specific deeper layers for efficient Divide-and-Conquer training. We demonstrate that our approach achieves model accuracy comparable to, and in some cases surpasses, that of state-of-the-art aggregation methods such as FedProx and FedMA. Furthermore, we show that the proposed methodology leads to significant improvements in computational efficiency and bandwidth usage under specific conditions.

Gradient Boosting Decision Trees (GBDTs) are widely used machine learning algorithms, with popular implementations such as LightGBM and support in toolkits like Scikit-Learn. Most existing implementations generate trees in an offline and greedy fashion. In this work, we investigate methods to transform established GBDT frameworks into neural network architectures with minimal loss of performance. This transformation enables online updates of decision splits and allows for the adaptation of split points through the lens of neural architecture search. We also establish theoretical learning bounds for our proposed neural network framework.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have emerged as one of the most prominent techniques in machine learning. However, due to their black-box nature, DNNs often lack transparency and interpretability in their predictions. To address this limitation, neural additive models (NAMs) have been introduced as a promising approach that balances predictive accuracy with model explainability. In this paper, we present a novel NAM-based method tailored for multivariate nowcasting (NC) problems, which represent a critical area within machine learning. For multivariate time-series data commonly encountered in NC tasks, it is essential to provide explanations for each input value across distinct time steps. By leveraging generalized additive models, our proposed NAM-NC effectively captures the importance of each input variable at different time points. Experimental evaluations on a toy example and two real-world datasets demonstrate that NAM-NC achieves prediction performance comparable to state-of-the-art neural networks while offering clear interpretability. Additionally, we explore parameter-sharing architectures using NAM-NC to reduce model complexity, and we show that NAM-MC's hard-tied feature network can extract meaningful explanations with strong performance.

We introduce a novel method for detecting anomalies in time series, a critical task across various domains such as autonomous vehicles, finance, marketing, medical diagnosis, and epidemiology. Our approach leverages self-supervised deep learning, a technique that has significantly advanced anomaly detection in image data through the use of powerful image transformations. However, such transformations are typically not available for time series data. To address this challenge, we propose Local Neural Transformations (LNT), a method that learns local transformations directly from the data. This approach generates an anomaly score for each time step, enabling precise detection of anomalies within time series. Theoretical analysis shows that our proposed training objective is more effective for transformation learning compared to existing deep anomaly detection methods. Experimental results demonstrate that LNT outperforms previous approaches in identifying anomalies in speech segments from the LibriSpeech dataset and in detecting disruptions in cyber-physical systems. Furthermore, visualizing the learned transformations provides valuable insights into the types of patterns the model identifies as anomalous.

The operation and management of intelligent transportation systems (ITS), such as traffic monitoring, depend on real-time aggregation of vehicular traffic data, including the types of vehicles—such as cars, trucks, and buses—on critical roads and highways. Traditional methods that rely on embedded GPS sensors or camera networks often raise privacy concerns or incur high deployment costs. To address these challenges, this paper presents a low-cost alternative called **SenseMag**, which identifies vehicle types using a pair of non-invasive magnetic sensors installed on straight road sections.

SenseMag processes incoming magnetic signals by filtering out noise and segmenting the data based on the exact times when vehicles arrive at or depart from each sensor node. It then employs a hierarchical recognition model: first estimating the vehicle's speed, then determining its length using the predicted speed, sampling frequency, and the distance between sensor nodes. With the vehicle's length identified and temporal and spectral features extracted from the magnetic signals, SenseMag classifies the vehicle type accordingly.

To enhance performance, semi-automated learning techniques are used in designing filters, selecting features, and tuning hyperparameters. Extensive experiments conducted through real-world field deployments on highways in Shenzhen, China, demonstrate that SenseMag significantly outperforms existing methods in both accuracy and efficiency.

As training deep learning models on large datasets is time-consuming and resource-intensive, there is a growing need to construct a small, synthetic dataset that can effectively train these models. Recent research has explored methods for condensing image datasets using complex bi-level optimization techniques. For example, Dataset Condensation (DC) aligns the network's gradients with respect to both large real data and small synthetic data, optimizing network weights over multiple steps in each outer iteration. However, existing approaches have several limitations: (1) they are not directly applicable to graph-structured data, which is inherently discrete; and (2) the condensation process is computationally expensive due to the nested optimization involved. To address these challenges, we propose an efficient approach tailored for graph datasets, where we model the discrete graph structure as a probabilistic model. We further introduce a one-step gradient matching scheme that performs gradient alignment in just a single step without explicitly training the network weights. Theoretical analysis shows that this strategy can generate synthetic graphs that achieve lower classification loss on real graphs. Extensive experiments across various graph datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our method. In particular, we are able to significantly reduce the dataset size while maintaining high model performance.

Although fine-grained recognition has become increasingly prominent in our field, the term "fine-grained" has yet to be precisely defined. In this work, we develop a framework for quantifying dataset granularity based on clustering theory. We argue that dataset granularity should not only depend on the data samples and their labels, but also on the distance function used. To capture the essential properties of a granularity measure, we introduce an axiomatic framework and present several examples of measures that satisfy these properties. We evaluate each measure through experiments on datasets with hierarchical labels of varying granularity. When applying our measure to commonly used datasets, we find that some datasets widely regarded as fine-grained actually contain large subsets that are significantly coarser than datasets typically considered coarse-grained. Additionally, we explore the relationship between dataset granularity and various factors, revealing that fine-grained datasets are more challenging to learn from, harder to transfer to, less effective for few-shot learning, and more susceptible to adversarial attacks.

This paper investigates the approximation capabilities of ReLU neural networks under weight norm constraints. We establish both upper and lower bounds on the approximation error for smooth function classes. The lower bound is derived using the Rademacher complexity of neural networks, a result that may be of broader interest. These approximation bounds are then applied to analyze the convergence of regression tasks with norm-constrained neural networks and to study distribution estimation via GANs. In particular, we derive convergence rates for over-parameterized neural networks. Additionally, we show that GANs can achieve optimal learning rates for probability distributions when the discriminator is a well-chosen norm-constrained neural network.

Feature learning seeks to automatically extract meaningful information from data sets. It is the driving force behind the current surge in deep learning, a collection of techniques that have achieved broad empirical success. However, a comprehensive theoretical understanding of various feature learning approaches remains lacking. This work introduces a theoretical framework for feature learning and investigates under what conditions features can be learned in an unsupervised manner. Additionally, we present methods for evaluating the quality of features using rate-distortion theory and its extensions.

Deep learning models (DLMs) represent the state-of-the-art in speech recognition. However, training high-performing DLMs can be computationally intensive, particularly for large-scale models and datasets. While various parallel training algorithms have been proposed to enhance training efficiency, there remains a lack of clear guidance on which method to choose for a given task, due to the absence of systematic and fair comparisons among them. In this paper, we address this gap by conducting a comprehensive comparison of four widely used parallel training algorithms—namely, asynchronous stochastic gradient descent (ASGD), blockwise model-update filtering (BMUF), bulk synchronous parallel (BSP), and elastic averaging stochastic gradient descent (EASGD)—on the 1000-hour LibriSpeech corpus. We evaluate these methods using feed-forward deep neural networks (DNNs) and convolutional, long short-term memory, DNNs (CLDNNs). Our experimental results indicate that BMUF is the preferred choice for training acoustic models, as it offers the best stability, scales effectively with the number of GPUs, produces reproducible results, and often outperforms single-GPU SGD. ASGD may serve as a viable alternative in certain scenarios.

Design optimization techniques are commonly employed early in the design process to explore the range of potential solutions. In such domains, illumination algorithms like MAP-Elites offer a compelling alternative to traditional optimization methods, as they generate a diverse set of high-quality solutions in a single run, rather than just one near-optimal result. However, these algorithms often require a large number of function evaluations, which restricts their practical use. In this paper, we present a novel illumination algorithm called Surrogate-Assisted Illumination (SAIL), which utilizes surrogate modeling to build a map of the design space based on user-defined criteria while significantly reducing the number of fitness evaluations needed. When applied to a 2D airfoil optimization problem, SAIL generates hundreds of diverse and high-performing designs using several orders of magnitude fewer evaluations compared to MAP-Elites or CMA-ES. We also show that SAIL can effectively create maps of high-performing designs in real-world 3D aerodynamic tasks, even when using accurate flow simulations. By enabling data-efficient design exploration, SAIL allows designers to discover what is possible—beyond mere optimality—by considering factors beyond simple objective-based optimization.

Network data is increasingly being leveraged in quantitative, data-driven public policy research. These datasets are often highly complex, containing intricate relationships and interdependencies. While this richness offers significant potential for advancing policy analysis, it also presents substantial challenges in effectively extracting meaningful insights—challenges that require innovative data analysis techniques. In this report, we outline a research agenda focused on key methodological issues that, if addressed, could drive significant progress across various domains of policy research. We then examine recent developments in applying deep learning to network data and demonstrate how these approaches can help tackle the methodological challenges we identify. Particular emphasis is placed on deep generative methods, which can produce realistic synthetic networks useful for microsimulation and agent-based modeling—tools that can inform critical public policy decisions. Building on these advances, we introduce a new generative framework tailored for large social contact networks frequently used in epidemiological modeling. To provide context, we compare and contrast these neural network-based approaches with traditional Exponential Random Graph Models. Finally, we highlight several open problems where further research is needed.

As deep learning increasingly captures the attention of the research community for the prediction and control of real-world physical systems, the ability to learn meaningful and physically coherent representations has become more critical than ever. Ensuring that deep learning models align with physical principles is essential, especially when working with discrete data. While incorporating prior knowledge can help enforce physical consistency, not all discretization strategies preserve the fundamental structures inherent in physical systems.

In this paper, we propose Symplectic Momentum Neural Networks (SyMo), a class of models derived from a discrete formulation of mechanics tailored for non-separable systems. This formulation naturally enforces constraints that preserve key geometric properties such as momentum and the symplectic structure, enabling effective learning even from limited data. Moreover, SyMo can learn dynamical behavior directly from pose information without requiring explicit velocity or force data.

We further extend SyMo by integrating variational integrators into the learning framework through the development of an implicit root-finding layer, resulting in End-to-End Symplectic Momentum Neural Networks (E2E-SyMo). Experimental results on benchmark systems such as the pendulum and cartpole demonstrate that this approach enables the models to learn effectively from sparse data while maintaining the symplectic structure. Additionally, these models exhibit superior long-term stability and accuracy compared to traditional methods.

We present new depth-based separation results for feed-forward neural networks, demonstrating that certain simple and natural functions can be more efficiently approximated by deeper networks compared to shallower ones—even when the shallower networks are significantly larger. These functions include indicators of balls and ellipses, non-linear radial functions with respect to the $ L_1 $ norm, and smooth non-linear functions. Furthermore, we provide experimental evidence supporting these theoretical findings: increasing network depth leads to better learning performance than increasing width when training neural networks to approximate the indicator of a unit ball.

Neural networks have emerged as a powerful tool in medical image segmentation, capable of delivering highly accurate results when trained on a GPU. However, for scenarios where GPUs are not available, alternative methods such as random forests can also be considered. In this study, two random forest-based approaches were compared with a state-of-the-art deep convolutional neural network (CNN). The comparison was conducted using the PhC-C2DH-U373 and retinal imaging datasets. The results demonstrated that the deep convolutional neural network achieved the highest performance. Nevertheless, one of the random forest methods also delivered comparable levels of accuracy. These findings suggest that random forest techniques can serve as a viable alternative to deep learning models in medical image segmentation, enabling effective segmentation without the need for GPU resources.

Microarray technology is a powerful method that enables the simultaneous monitoring of thousands of genes under various experimental conditions. It is widely used to identify co-expressed genes in specific cells or tissues that are actively involved in protein synthesis. This technique plays a crucial role in analyzing gene expression, which is a key aspect of bioinformatics research. Cluster analysis of gene expression data has proven to be an effective approach for identifying groups of co-expressed genes, as well as biologically meaningful groupings of both genes and samples.

In this paper, we analyzed K-Means with Automatic Generation of Merge Factor for ISODATA-AGMFI, a method designed to cluster microarray datasets based on the ISODATA algorithm. AGMFI automatically generates initial values for the merge and split factors, as well as the maximum number of merge iterations, eliminating the need for manual selection of optimal parameters as required in traditional ISODATA. Typically, the initial seeds for each cluster are selected either sequentially or randomly, and the quality of the resulting clusters is significantly influenced by these initial choices.

In real-world applications, it is often difficult to determine the appropriate number of clusters in advance. To address this limitation, the current research focuses on developing clustering algorithms that do not require the initial specification of the number of clusters.

This paper represents an initial effort to bridge the gap between advanced Deep Reinforcement Learning techniques and the challenge of exploring and covering unknown terrains. As part of this work, we introduce MarsExplorer—a custom environment compatible with OpenAI Gym—designed specifically for the exploration and coverage of uncharted areas. MarsExplorer transforms the original robotics problem into a Reinforcement Learning framework, enabling a range of off-the-shelf algorithms to effectively address it. Notably, any policy learned in this environment can be directly deployed on a physical robotic platform without the need for a detailed simulation of the robot’s dynamics, thereby simplifying the transition from learning to real-world application.

A key feature of MarsExplorer is its controllable, multi-dimensional procedural terrain generation, which plays a crucial role in developing policies with strong generalization capabilities. To evaluate the effectiveness of the environment, four state-of-the-art RL algorithms—A3C, PPO, Rainbow, and SAC—are trained on MarsExplorer, and their performance is compared against human-level benchmarks. 

In a follow-up analysis, the impact of varying multi-dimensional difficulty settings on the learning performance of the top-performing algorithm (PPO) is investigated. A significant outcome of this research is the emergence of an exploration policy that follows a Hilbert curve pattern, even though no prior information about the curve was provided to the environment, nor were Hilbert-like trajectories explicitly rewarded. The study concludes with an evaluation of the PPO-learned policy, demonstrating its robustness and adaptability in complex, dynamically generated environments.

Designing optimal controllers for dynamic systems typically requires solving optimization problems under strict real-time constraints. These constraints limit the choice of numerical methods, often leading to the use of fast but less accurate techniques in place of more computationally intensive ones, thereby compromising solution quality for speed. This paper introduces methods to enhance the performance of optimized control policies within a fixed computational budget. We achieve this through a hypersolvers framework, which combines a differential equation solver with a neural network. The approach is evaluated on both direct and receding-horizon optimal control tasks across low- and high-dimensional settings, demonstrating consistent improvements in solution accuracy and control performance.

Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) is a powerful method for identifying whether hidden sources are jointly present across two or more datasets. It is widely valued for its ability to perform dimensionality reduction, clustering, classification, feature selection, and data fusion. However, the standard CCA does not take into account the geometric structure of these common sources, which may be inherent in the data or inferred from cross-correlations. In this paper, we encode the additional information provided by the common sources—derived from the data or from correlations—into a graph structure and incorporate it as a graph regularizer. This leads to a new variant of CCA called graph (g) CCA, which integrates the geometric knowledge of common sources while minimizing the distance between the canonical variables. To address scenarios where the number of samples is smaller than the dimensionality of the data vectors, we also develop a dual formulation of gCCA. Furthermore, we extend the approach by incorporating kernels to model nonlinear relationships, resulting in a graph-kernel (gk) CCA that is derived in closed form. Finally, we present experimental results on real-world image classification tasks to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed linear, dual, and kernel-based approaches compared to existing methods.

Sparse subspace clustering methods that enforce sparsity through the $\ell^0$-norm, such as $\ell^0$-Sparse Subspace Clustering ($\ell^0$-SSC)~\citep{YangFJYH16-L0SSC-ijcv}, have been shown to be more effective than their $\ell^1$-based counterpart, Sparse Subspace Clustering (SSC)~\citep{ElhamifarV13}. However, the theoretical analysis of $\ell^0$-SSC has so far been limited to scenarios where data lie exactly in subspaces. In practice, real-world data are often corrupted by noise and may only approximately lie near subspaces.

In this paper, we demonstrate that an optimal solution to the noisy $\ell^0$-SSC optimization problem achieves the subspace detection property (SDP), which ensures that data points from different subspaces are correctly separated. This result holds under both deterministic and semi-random models. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first theoretical guarantee for the correctness of noisy $\ell^0$-SSC in terms of SDP on noisy data, highlighting its advantage in requiring much weaker conditions on subspace affinity compared to other methods.

To enhance the computational efficiency of noisy $\ell^0$-SSC, we propose Noisy-DR-$\ell^0$-SSC, a method that provably recovers the underlying subspaces from dimensionality-reduced data. The approach involves first projecting the data into a lower-dimensional space using random projections, followed by applying noisy $\ell^0$-SSC on the reduced data. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of Noisy-DR-$\ell^0$-SSC in achieving accurate subspace clustering while significantly improving computational efficiency.

This paper presents a joint analysis approach for multiple functionally related structures in classification tasks. Specifically, our method is motivated by how functionally connected brain structures differ between individuals with autism and control groups. To achieve this, we developed a technique that integrates two key components: (1) non-Euclidean statistics, which enable the accurate representation of non-Euclidean data within Euclidean spaces, and (2) a non-parametric integrative analysis method capable of decomposing multi-block Euclidean data into joint, individual, and residual components. The resulting joint structure demonstrates effectiveness, robustness, and interpretability in capturing the underlying patterns of variation across multiple non-Euclidean data blocks. We validated the method on structural shape data from individuals who either developed or did not develop into Autistic Spectrum Disorder (ASD).

In recent years, cybersecurity has emerged as a critical concern in the development and adoption of smart applications. Particularly in smart homes, where a large number of IoT devices are interconnected, having secure and trustworthy mechanisms is essential to ensure user confidence and peace of mind. Accurate detection of cyber threats is vital, but the precise identification of attack types is equally important for developing effective countermeasures to protect the system.

Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) have shown promising results in detecting security threats in smart applications. However, the complexity of ANN models often makes it difficult for average users to trust these solutions. Additionally, selecting the appropriate hyperparameters for an ANN architecture plays a crucial role in achieving accurate threat detection, especially when distinguishing between different subcategories of attacks.

In this paper, we propose a model that addresses both the challenges of ANN explainability and hyperparameter selection, making the approach more transparent and trustworthy for users of smart home applications. Our method also incorporates a subset of the dataset to optimize hyperparameter selection, thereby reducing the computational overhead associated with designing the ANN architecture. Distinctively, this approach enhances both the usability and reliability of AI-based security solutions in smart environments.

Semi-supervised learning (SSL) offers an efficient way to enhance model performance by utilizing unlabeled data. In this paper, we highlight the effectiveness of a straightforward combination of two widely used SSL techniques: consistency regularization and pseudo-labeling. Our proposed method, FixMatch, first generates pseudo-labels by applying the model to weakly augmented versions of unlabeled images. A pseudo-label is only kept if the model's prediction is highly confident. The model is then trained to predict these pseudo-labels when given strongly augmented versions of the same images. Despite its simplicity, FixMatch achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple standard semi-supervised learning benchmarks, such as 94.93% accuracy on CIFAR-10 with just 250 labeled examples, and 88.61% accuracy with only 40 labels—4 per class. Given that FixMatch shares similarities with other SSL methods that perform less well, we conduct a comprehensive ablation study to identify the key factors contributing to its success. We have made our code publicly available at https://github.com/google-research/fixmatch.

Understanding how biological and artificial networks operate remains a complex and critical challenge. To uncover general principles governing these systems, researchers are increasingly turning to the analysis of large collections of networks that are trained or adapted for similar tasks. A standardized set of analytical tools is now essential to determine how network-level factors—such as architecture, anatomical brain regions, and model organisms—affect neural representations (i.e., hidden layer activations).  

In this work, we establish a rigorous foundation for such analyses by introducing a broad family of metric spaces that quantify representational dissimilarity. Using this framework, we refine existing representational similarity measures based on canonical correlation analysis to satisfy the triangle inequality. We also propose a novel metric that accounts for the inductive biases inherent in convolutional layers. Furthermore, we identify approximate Euclidean embeddings that allow network representations to be seamlessly integrated into a wide range of off-the-shelf machine learning models.  

We validate these methods on large-scale datasets from both biology (the Allen Institute Brain Observatory) and deep learning (NAS-Bench-101). Through this, we reveal interpretable relationships between neural representations, linking them to anatomical features and model performance.

We introduce a novel and effective adversarial defense approach that is resistant to pre-processor blind white- and black-box attacks. Our method is computationally efficient and relies solely on self-supervised learning using general images, eliminating the need for adversarial training or retraining of the classification model. 

Through an empirical analysis, we demonstrate that adversarial noise—defined as the residual between an original image and its adversarial counterpart—exhibits nearly zero mean and a symmetric distribution. Leveraging this insight, we propose a simple yet effective iterative Gaussian Smoothing (GS) technique that successfully suppresses adversarial noise and significantly enhances robust accuracy.

To further enhance performance, we introduce Neural Contextual Iterative Smoothing (NCIS), which trains a blind-spot network (BSN) in a self-supervised manner to reconstruct the discriminative features of the original image that may be lost during GS. 

Extensive experiments on the large-scale ImageNet dataset, using four different classification models, demonstrate that our method achieves both competitive standard accuracy and state-of-the-art robust accuracy against a wide range of strong purifier-blind white- and black-box attacks. Additionally, we introduce a new benchmark for evaluating purification methods using commercial image classification APIs such as AWS, Azure, Clarifai, and Google. Adversarial examples are generated using ensemble transfer-based approaches.

Correspondence-based shape models play a crucial role in various medical imaging applications that depend on statistical analysis of anatomical structures. These models are designed to capture consistent anatomical features across populations, enabling the derivation of population-specific shape statistics. Early methods for establishing correspondence typically relied on nearest neighbor search, which worked well for simpler anatomical structures. However, as anatomical complexity increases, coordinate transformation-based approaches have emerged as a promising alternative. Despite their potential, coordinate-wise correspondence often fails to align with true anatomical correspondence due to the inherent geometric complexity and population-level variability in shapes.

An alternative approach, known as group-wise correspondence placement, explicitly balances geometric accuracy with statistical compactness across populations. Nevertheless, these models have shown limited effectiveness in handling nonlinear shape correspondences. Recent research has attempted to overcome this challenge by introducing application-specific notions of correspondence through the lifting of positional data into higher-dimensional feature spaces. While effective, these methods still rely heavily on manual expertise for designing domain-specific features and consistent landmarks.

This paper presents an automated feature learning approach that leverages deep convolutional neural networks to extract correspondence-friendly features from shape ensembles. Furthermore, an unsupervised domain adaptation scheme is introduced to enhance the pretrained geometric features with new anatomical data. Experimental results on anatomical datasets of human scapula, femur, and pelvis bones demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in achieving accurate and robust shape correspondence.

Learning a regression function from censored or interval-valued output data is a critical challenge in fields such as genomics and medicine. The objective is to construct a real-valued prediction function, where the training labels represent intervals of possible values rather than exact points. While most existing methods for this problem rely on linear models, this paper explores the use of nonlinear tree-based models. We introduce an approach that learns a tree by minimizing a margin-based discriminative objective function, and we present a dynamic programming algorithm that computes the optimal solution in log-linear time. Empirical results demonstrate that our algorithm achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of both speed and prediction accuracy across multiple benchmark datasets.

Automatic Speech Scoring (ASS) refers to the computer-assisted assessment of a candidate's speaking ability in a given language. ASS systems encounter numerous challenges, including open grammatical structures, variability in pronunciation, and unstructured or semi-structured content. While recent deep learning approaches have shown some success in this area, most focus on analyzing a single audio input, which limits their ability to capture speaker-specific context essential for accurately modeling complex speech tasks.

To address this limitation, we introduce a novel deep learning approach for non-native speech scoring called *speaker-conditioned hierarchical modeling*. Our method leverages the fact that oral proficiency tests typically involve multiple responses from the same candidate. By extracting contextual vectors from these responses, we provide additional speaker-specific information to our model, enabling it to better evaluate a particular response.

Compared to strong baseline models, our approach improves average performance by 6.92% (with a maximum improvement of 12.86% and a minimum of 4.51%). We also present both quantitative and qualitative evidence demonstrating the critical role of this additional context in enhancing the accuracy and robustness of automatic speech scoring.

We present a layer-by-layer algorithm for training deep convolutional networks, in which each step consists of performing gradient updates on a two-layer network followed by a simple clustering procedure. This approach is inspired by a deep generative model that constructs images level by level, with lower-resolution representations corresponding to latent semantic classes. We analyze the convergence rate of our algorithm under the assumption that the data is generated according to this model (along with additional technical conditions). Although we do not assert that these assumptions are fully realistic for natural images, we believe they reflect certain underlying properties of real-world data. Moreover, we demonstrate that the algorithm performs effectively in practice, achieving performance comparable to standard convolutional neural networks trained via stochastic gradient descent on the CIFAR dataset. Finally, the proof techniques we employ may be of broader interest.

Accurately determining the solubility of hydrocarbon components in natural gases is a critical aspect of operational processes in petroleum and chemical engineering. In this study, a new solubility estimation tool has been developed for hydrocarbon gases—specifically methane, ethane, propane, and butane—in aqueous electrolyte solutions, utilizing the Extreme Learning Machine (ELM) algorithm. When compared against a comprehensive real-world database containing 1175 solubility data points, the model achieved R-squared values of 0.985 and 0.987 for the training and testing phases, respectively. Visual comparisons between predicted and actual solubility values further validated the effectiveness of the proposed model. Additionally, a sensitivity analysis was conducted to assess the influence of input variables on hydrocarbon solubility. This thorough and reliable investigation provides valuable insights that can assist engineers and scientists in accurately determining key thermodynamic properties, which are essential for the optimization and design of various industrial systems, including refineries and petrochemical plants.

Actively sampled data often exhibits significantly different characteristics compared to passively sampled data. As a result, it is promising to explore the use of distinct inference procedures during active learning (AL) as opposed to those used in passive learning (PL). This concept is thoroughly examined in the context of AL with cost-weighted SVMs for imbalanced data—a scenario that is common in many human language technology (HLT) tasks. The core idea of the proposed InitPA method for handling class imbalance is to construct cost models during AL based on an estimate of the overall corpus imbalance derived from a small, unbiased sample, rather than relying on the imbalance present in the labeled training data, which is the conventional approach in PL.

Weight sharing and predictor-based methods are two prominent approaches in fast neural architecture search. In this paper, we introduce a unified framework that integrates both weight sharing and predictor techniques. First, we build a SuperNet using weight sharing and probabilistically sample architectures from it. To enhance the accuracy of architecture evaluation, we not only assess architectures using the inherited weights but also employ a few-shot predictor to provide an additional evaluation. The final evaluation of each architecture is obtained by combining the direct evaluation, the predictor's prediction, and the computational cost. We treat this combined score as a reward and use a self-critical policy gradient method to update the probabilities of the sampled architectures. To mitigate the limitations of weight sharing, we propose a weakly weight-sharing strategy by introducing an additional HyperNet. Extensive experiments on datasets such as CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, under the NATS-Bench, DARTS, and MobileNet search spaces, demonstrate that our proposed WPNAS method achieves state-of-the-art performance.

We introduce a feed-forward inference approach that is applicable to both belief networks and neural networks. In belief networks, the method approximates the factorized posterior distribution of all hidden units given the input. For neural networks, it propagates input uncertainty through all layers. In networks with injected noise, the method analytically accounts for uncertainties arising from this noise. This feed-forward, analytic propagation is differentiable with respect to model parameters and can be trained end-to-end. Unlike standard neural networks, which only propagate means, our method propagates both mean and variance. This technique is particularly useful in scenarios requiring knowledge of neuron statistics, such as handling uncertain inputs, interpreting sigmoid activations as probabilities of Bernoulli units, regularizing models with injected noise (e.g., dropout), or estimating activation statistics across a dataset (as required for normalization techniques). In our experiments, we demonstrate the method's utility across these tasks, as well as its current limitations.

The concept of approachability in repeated games with vector-valued payoffs was introduced by Blackwell in the 1950s. He provided geometric conditions for approachability and developed strategies that involve computing *steering directions*—essentially, projections from the current average payoff vector to a (convex) target set. More recently, Abernethy, Bartlett, and Hazan (2011) proposed a family of approachability algorithms that leverage the no-regret properties of Online Linear Programming to generate appropriate sequences of steering directions. Their work initially focused on convex cones as target sets, and later extended to arbitrary convex sets by embedding them within a higher-dimensional convex cone. In this paper, we present a more direct formulation of approachability that utilizes the support function of the target set, combined with suitable Online Convex Optimization methods. This leads to a general class of approachability algorithms. We also demonstrate that Blackwell's original algorithm and its convergence properties emerge as a special case of this broader framework.

Research on connected vehicles represents a rapidly evolving technological field, driven by the emerging Internet of Things (IoT) paradigm and recent advancements in intelligent transportation systems. Today, vehicles serve as platforms capable of generating, receiving, and autonomously acting upon large volumes of data. In the context of assisted driving, connected vehicle technology provides real-time insights into surrounding traffic conditions. This information has the potential to enhance drivers' quality of life, for instance, by enabling more informed decision-making based on current parking availability.

In this context, we introduce an online and adaptive scheme for mapping parking availability. Specifically, we employ an information-seeking active sensing approach to selectively process incoming data, thereby conserving onboard storage and computational resources. Subsequently, we estimate parking availability using Gaussian Process Regression. When compared to several baseline methods, our proposed algorithm demonstrates superior performance in terms of both mapping convergence speed and adaptability. Furthermore, the approach imposes only a minimal computational burden.

Leveraging data to uncover the fundamental governing laws or equations that describe complex physical systems can greatly enhance our ability to model, simulate, and understand these systems across various scientific and engineering domains. This work presents a novel physics-informed deep learning framework designed to identify governing partial differential equations (PDEs) from limited and noisy data in nonlinear spatiotemporal systems. The approach effectively combines the power of deep neural networks for rich representation learning, embedded physical principles, automatic differentiation, and sparse regression to (1) approximate the system's solution variables, (2) compute critical derivatives, and (3) detect the essential derivative terms and parameters that define the structure and explicit form of the PDEs. The effectiveness and resilience of this method are validated through both numerical and experimental studies on a range of PDE systems, under varying degrees of data scarcity and noise, as well as different initial and boundary conditions. The proposed computational framework demonstrates significant potential for deriving closed-form models in practical applications where large and precise datasets are difficult or impossible to obtain.

We introduce data-driven, one-pass streaming algorithms for estimating the number of triangles and four-cycles—two core problems in graph analytics that have been extensively studied in the context of graph data streams. Recently, Hsu (2018) and Jiang (2020) demonstrated the potential of machine learning techniques in other data stream scenarios by incorporating a trained oracle capable of predicting specific properties of stream elements, thereby enhancing the performance of traditional algorithms that did not utilize such oracles. In this paper, we investigate the effectiveness of a "heavy edge" oracle across various graph edge streaming models. 

In the adjacency list model, we present a one-pass triangle counting algorithm that achieves improved space efficiency compared to prior methods that lacked such an oracle. In the arbitrary order model, we develop algorithms for both triangle and four-cycle estimation that require fewer passes while maintaining the same space complexity as previous approaches. Several of these bounds are shown to be optimal. We evaluate our algorithms under different noise models, demonstrating their robustness even when the oracle makes errors.

Our approach builds upon classical streaming algorithms, as multi-pass and random-order streaming techniques can be viewed as special cases of our framework, particularly when the first pass or random ordering is used as a baseline.

Manifold learning techniques have gained increasing importance as the volume of data continues to expand. These methods uncover a lower-dimensional representation (or embedding) of a dataset’s underlying structure, enabling significant dimensionality reduction while retaining essential information. However, many advanced manifold learning algorithms operate as "black boxes," making it difficult to understand how the embedded representation relates to the original high-dimensional space. This lack of transparency poses challenges in exploratory data analysis, where interpretability is often as important as performance.

Previously, we introduced a Genetic Programming-based approach that performed manifold learning by evolving transparent and interpretable mappings. While this method offered interpretability, it required the target dimensionality of the embedding to be specified in advance, limiting its applicability when little is known about the dataset's structure.

In this paper, we significantly extend our prior work by proposing a multi-objective framework that automatically balances the competing goals of maintaining high-quality embeddings and controlling their dimensionality. Our approach achieves performance comparable to existing baseline and state-of-the-art manifold learning methods, while providing a range of solutions that reflect different trade-offs between embedding quality and dimensionality. Moreover, the models generated by our method are often simple and efficient, relying on a minimal number of features in an interpretable way.

Practical brain-machine interfaces have been extensively researched to accurately decode human intentions from brain signals in real-world settings. However, electroencephalography (EEG) signals are often corrupted by artifacts such as movement and head motion, leading to large-amplitude signals that do not reflect the desired EEG patterns. These artifacts make it particularly challenging to accurately detect human intent in mobile environments. In this study, we propose a reconstruction framework based on generative adversarial networks (GANs), utilizing event-related potentials (ERP) recorded during walking. A pre-trained convolutional encoder was employed to extract latent representations, while a generative model reconstructed the ERP signals in a manner that mirrored the inverse of the encoder's transformation. The reconstructed ERPs were then classified using a discriminative model to validate the effectiveness of our approach. The results showed that the reconstructed signals retained key ERP components, such as N200 and P300, similar to those observed during standing. The classification accuracy of the reconstructed EEG was comparable to that of raw noisy EEG signals collected during walking. Additionally, the signal-to-noise ratio of the reconstructed EEG improved significantly, reaching 1.3 times that of the original signals. The generative model achieved a relatively low loss of 0.6301, indicating strong training performance. Overall, the reconstructed ERP demonstrated enhanced classification accuracy, highlighting the potential of our proposed framework for improving signal quality in mobile BCI applications.

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are powerful models for handling data with complex temporal dependencies. However, training them has historically been difficult due to issues like vanishing or exploding gradients. Architectures such as LSTMs and GRUs, along with their variants, address these challenges by incorporating gating mechanisms that regulate information flow. Although these gates have been shown to enhance performance empirically, the precise impact of these gates on the dynamical behavior and trainability of GRUs and LSTMs remains poorly understood.

In this work, we analyze randomly initialized LSTMs and GRUs from the perspective of dynamical systems. We investigate how the presence of gates shapes key dynamical properties, focusing on the structure of state transitions. Using tools from random matrix theory and mean-field analysis, we examine the Jacobians of the state transitions in GRUs and LSTMs. Our findings reveal that the update gate in GRUs and the forget gate in LSTMs can lead to an accumulation of slow dynamical modes. Additionally, the GRU's update gate can stabilize the system near a critical (marginally stable) state. Meanwhile, the reset gate in GRUs and the input and output gates in LSTMs influence the spectral radius of the Jacobian matrix. Notably, the GRU reset gate also affects the complexity of the optimization landscape.
