Transformer model architectures have attracted significant attention in recent years due to their remarkable performance across diverse fields such as natural language processing, computer vision, and reinforcement learning. In the realm of natural language processing, Transformers have become a fundamental component of modern deep learning systems. Recently, an impressive array of "X-former" models—such as Reformer, Linformer, Performer, and Longformer—have been introduced, each aiming to enhance the original Transformer architecture, with many focusing on improving computational and memory efficiency. To assist researchers in navigating this rapidly expanding landscape, this paper provides a detailed and structured overview of a broad and carefully selected set of efficiency-oriented "X-former" models, offering a comprehensive survey of current work across multiple domains.

We investigate the problem of adaptive sensing for Cox point processes, a widely employed model in spatial statistics. We define three key tasks: maximizing the number of detected events, locating the maximum of the intensity function, and learning its level sets. The intensity function is modeled as a sample from a truncated Gaussian process, expressed in a specially designed positive basis. This basis ensures that the positivity constraint on the intensity is straightforward to enforce. We present a method for constructing a minimal description positive basis that adapts to the covariance kernel and accounts for non-stationarity, while also establishing connections to commonly used positive bases from prior literature. Our adaptive sensing algorithms are based on Langevin dynamics and employ two sampling strategies: posterior sampling (referred to as \textsc{Cox-Thompson}) and top-two posterior sampling (\textsc{Top2}). In the latter, the difference between samples is used as a proxy for uncertainty. We illustrate the effectiveness of our approach through applications in environmental monitoring and crime rate modeling, and compare it with the classical Bayesian experimental design framework.

Inspired by StyleGAN's remarkable ability to generate highly realistic images across various domains, recent research has focused on leveraging the model's latent space for manipulating both generated and real images. However, identifying semantically meaningful latent directions often requires labor-intensive manual exploration of the many degrees of freedom or relies on annotated image datasets for each desired manipulation. In this work, we propose a text-based interface for manipulating StyleGAN-generated images by harnessing the power of Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) models, eliminating the need for extensive manual effort. We introduce an optimization framework that uses a CLIP-based loss function to adjust an input latent vector based on a user-provided text prompt. Additionally, we present a latent mapper that learns text-guided latent transformations for a given image, enabling faster and more stable text-driven manipulations. Finally, we develop a method to map text prompts to general, input-agnostic directions in StyleGAN's style space, allowing for interactive, text-driven image generation. Experimental results and comparisons validate the effectiveness of our approach.

Spectral Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are a class of GNNs that operate based on graph signal filtering in the spectral domain. Recently, several models have been proposed that can learn arbitrary spectral filters. However, the expressive power of such spectral GNNs remains underexplored. This paper provides a theoretical analysis of the expressive capabilities of spectral GNNs. We first demonstrate that even without nonlinearity, spectral GNNs can generate arbitrary graph signals, and identify two necessary conditions for achieving universality: 1) the absence of multiple eigenvalues in the graph Laplacian, and 2) the presence of all frequency components in the node features. We further establish a connection between the expressive power of spectral GNNs and Graph Isomorphism (GI) testing—a commonly used metric for evaluating the expressiveness of spatial GNNs. Additionally, we investigate the empirical performance differences among various spectral GNNs with equivalent expressive power from an optimization standpoint, and propose the use of an orthogonal basis whose weight function aligns with the spectral density of the graph signal. Based on this analysis, we introduce JacobiConv, a novel convolution operator that leverages the Jacobi basis due to its orthogonality and adaptability to a wide range of weight functions. Remarkably, JacobiConv achieves strong performance without relying on nonlinearity, outperforming all baseline models on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

The linear quadratic regulator (LQR) problem has regained prominence as a key theoretical benchmark for reinforcement learning-based control in complex dynamical systems with continuous state and action spaces. Unlike most recent work in this domain, our approach considers multiplicative noise models, which have become increasingly relevant due to their ability to explicitly account for inherent uncertainty and variability in system dynamics, thereby enhancing the robustness of the resulting controllers. Robustness remains a critical and poorly understood challenge in reinforcement learning; methods that neglect uncertainty may lead to fragile policies or fail to converge altogether. Moreover, the deliberate introduction of multiplicative noise into learning algorithms has been shown to improve policy robustness, as demonstrated in ad hoc studies on domain randomization. Although policy gradient methods typically involve optimizing a non-convex cost function, we demonstrate that the multiplicative noise LQR cost possesses a special property known as gradient domination. This property is leveraged to establish global convergence of policy gradient algorithms to the globally optimal control policy, with polynomial dependence on problem parameters. Our results are presented in both model-known and model-unknown settings, where policy gradients are estimated using samples from system trajectories.

Systems involving competing agents are frequently modeled as games. Under the assumption of rational behavior, the most probable outcomes correspond to equilibrium states, such as Nash equilibria. In many real-world scenarios, game dynamics are shaped by contextual factors—additional data not controlled by individual agents, like weather conditions in traffic systems or fiscal policies in market economies. Typically, only the observed equilibria are available, while the actual cost functions of the players remain unknown.

This work introduces **Nash Fixed Point Networks (N-FPNs)**, a class of implicit neural networks designed to predict equilibria based solely on contextual information. The architecture of N-FPNs integrates data-driven learning with explicit constraints on the feasible actions of agents. These networks are compatible with the recently developed **Jacobian-Free Backpropagation** technique, enabling significantly faster training compared to previous models. Furthermore, N-FPNs leverage a novel approach to constraint decoupling, which helps avoid computationally expensive projections. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of N-FPNs in both atomic and non-atomic games, including applications such as traffic routing.

In this paper, we introduce an unsupervised, data-driven approach for predicting real-time locational marginal prices (RTLMPs). The method is built on a versatile data structure that transforms system-wide heterogeneous market data streams into the form of market data images and videos. By leveraging this structure, the problem of system-wide RTLMP prediction is redefined as a video prediction task. A generative adversarial network (GAN)-based video prediction model is proposed to capture the spatio-temporal relationships in historical RTLMPs and forecast system-wide prices for the next hour. To enhance prediction accuracy, an autoregressive moving average (ARMA) calibration technique is integrated. The proposed RTLMP prediction framework relies solely on publicly available market data, eliminating the need for sensitive information such as system topology, model parameters, or detailed market operations. Case studies using public data from ISO New England (ISO-NE) and the Southwest Power Pool (SPP) show that the method effectively captures spatio-temporal patterns in RTLMPs and delivers accurate predictions.

Multi-label learning has garnered significant attention within the machine learning community. One popular approach, known as Binary Relevance, transforms a single-label problem into a multi-label one by treating each label independently. Due to its straightforward structure and computational efficiency, Binary Relevance is widely adopted. However, this method neglects the potential correlations among labels, which can limit its effectiveness for certain tasks. In this paper, we propose a novel multi-label learning algorithm that is also applicable to single-label classification. The method is built upon standard support vector machines (SVMs) and modifies the original single decision hyperplane into two parallel decision hyperplanes, resulting in the Multi-Label Parallel Support Vector Machine (MLPSVM). Experimental results demonstrate that MLPSVM outperforms other multi-label learning algorithms on various datasets.

Nearest neighbor methods have gained significant popularity in official statistics, particularly in applications such as imputation and statistical matching. They also play a crucial role in machine learning, where numerous variants have been developed. The choice of the distance function typically depends on the type of variables involved. However, relatively few distance measures are suitable for handling mixed-type variables, a common challenge in official statistics.

The Gower distance, derived from the Gower similarity coefficient, is one of the most widely used distance measures for mixed data. It is appealing due to its range between 0 and 1 and its ability to accommodate missing values. Nevertheless, the standard unweighted version of the Gower distance can be problematic, as it does not account for the different natures of the variables, leading to an imbalanced contribution of each variable to the overall distance.

This article aims to address the limitations of the unweighted Gower distance by proposing modifications in the calculation of distances for interval and ratio-scaled variables. These modifications include simple adjustments designed to reduce the influence of outliers on the scaled Manhattan distance. Additionally, more advanced approaches based on kernel density estimation are introduced to mitigate the uneven contribution of different variable types. The performance of these proposed methods is evaluated in the following sections.

The object proposal technique with a dense anchoring scheme has been widely used for scene text detection to achieve high recall. However, this approach leads to significant improvements in accuracy at the cost of excessive computational resources for searching, regression, and classification. In this paper, we propose an Anchor Selection-based Region Proposal Network (AS-RPN), which employs effectively selected anchors instead of densely sampled ones to generate text proposals. Unlike traditional methods that fix anchor properties, the center, scales, aspect ratios, and orientations of anchors in our approach are learnable, resulting in high recall while drastically reducing the number of anchors. By replacing the anchor-based RPN in Faster RCNN with AS-RPN, the resulting framework achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art text detection methods on standard benchmarks, including COCO-Text, ICDAR2013, ICDAR2015, and MSRA-TD500, using only single-scale and single-model (ResNet50) testing.

Given multiple source domains, domain generalization seeks to develop a model that performs effectively on any unseen but related target domain. In this work, we focus on a domain generalization setting where domain shifts occur across class-conditional distributions of different domains. Existing methods often struggle to maintain robustness when the variation in conditional distributions for the same class is significant. To address this challenge, we extend the idea of distributional robust optimization to tackle class-conditional domain generalization. Our approach optimizes the worst-case performance of a classifier over class-conditional distributions within a Wasserstein ball centered at the barycenter of the source distributions. Additionally, we introduce an iterative algorithm to automatically determine the optimal radius of these Wasserstein balls. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves superior performance on unseen target domains compared to methods that do not incorporate domain generalization.

Due to information asymmetry, identifying optimal policies for Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (Dec-POMDPs) is inherently challenging, as the computational complexity grows doubly exponentially with the horizon length. This difficulty is further exacerbated in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) settings, where the transition probabilities, observation models, and reward functions are typically unknown. To address this, we propose a general compression framework that incorporates approximate common and private state representations, enabling the construction of decentralized policies. We analyze the optimality gap when applying dynamic programming (DP) using these approximated states, deriving bounds in terms of approximation error parameters and the number of remaining time steps. When the compression is perfect (i.e., no approximation error), our DP formulation reduces to that of existing approaches. Our framework unifies and extends several methods from the literature. These results provide valuable insights for designing effective deep-MARL architectures within the "centralized learning, distributed execution" paradigm.

With the vast number of research papers in deep learning, achieving reproducibility or adopting existing work has become increasingly challenging. This is largely due to the absence of open-source implementations provided by the authors. Moreover, re-implementing these works in different libraries can be a complex and time-consuming task. To tackle these challenges, we introduce DLPaper2Code, a novel and extensible approach that extracts and interprets deep learning design flow diagrams and tables from research papers, converting them into an abstract computational graph. This graph is then automatically translated into executable source code in both Keras and Caffe in real-time. We have also developed an arXiv-like platform where the automatically generated designs are made publicly accessible for 5,000 research papers. Users can rate and modify these designs through an intuitive drag-and-drop UI, enabling collaborative improvements. To evaluate our method, we constructed a simulated dataset containing over 216,000 valid design visualizations using a manually defined grammar. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework achieves an accuracy of over 93% in extracting content from flow diagrams.

The signature is an infinite graded sequence of statistics that uniquely characterizes geometric rough paths, including those of bounded variation. It has been widely studied in the context of machine learning, with most applications focused on low-dimensional settings. However, in high-dimensional scenarios, the truncated signature transform suffers from an exponential increase in the number of features, leading to computational challenges. To address this issue, we propose a novel neural network architecture inspired by Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Our approach efficiently reduces the feature dimension in a data-dependent manner. We present empirical experiments to validate the effectiveness of our model.

In machine learning, virtually all predictive models we use are imperfect approximations of reality. As a result, most learning takes place under conditions of model misspecification. In this work, we introduce a new analysis of the generalization performance of Bayesian model averaging in the context of model misspecification and independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) data, leveraging a novel family of second-order PAC-Bayes bounds. Our analysis demonstrates, in a clear and intuitive manner, that Bayesian model averaging can lead to suboptimal generalization when the underlying model is not correctly specified.

Consequently, we present strong theoretical evidence suggesting that Bayesian methods are not optimal for building predictive models unless the model class is perfectly specified. To address this limitation, we derive a new set of Bayesian-inspired algorithms using our second-order PAC-Bayes bounds. These algorithms can be implemented as variational or ensemble methods. The resulting approach produces a posterior distribution distinct from the traditional Bayesian posterior, leading to a more effective posterior predictive distribution with improved generalization performance. Experimental results on Bayesian neural networks support these theoretical findings.

Large pre-trained language models have been increasingly utilized to generate code, offering a flexible way to synthesize programs from natural language specifications. However, these models often produce outputs that violate the syntactic and semantic rules of the target programming language, which limits their practical applicability. In this paper, we introduce Synchromesh: a framework designed to significantly enhance the reliability of pre-trained models in code generation. Synchromesh consists of two key components. First, it retrieves few-shot examples from a training bank using Target Similarity Tuning (TST), a novel approach for selecting semantically relevant examples. TST is capable of identifying utterances that correspond to similar target programs, even when the surface-level natural language expressions differ. Subsequently, Synchromesh feeds these examples into a pre-trained language model and generates programs through Constrained Semantic Decoding (CSD), a general method for restricting output to valid programs in the target language. CSD uses constraints on partial outputs to guide the generation of complete, correct programs, without requiring any re-training or fine-tuning of the underlying model. We evaluate our approach by generating code from natural language descriptions using GPT-3 and Codex across three real-world domains: SQL queries, Vega-Lite visualizations, and SMCalFlow programs. These domains feature complex constraints that CSD is well-suited to enforce, including syntax, scoping, typing rules, and contextual logic. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the Synchromesh framework in improving the accuracy and reliability of code generation.

We introduce a dataset comprising high-resolution images of 13 micro-PCBs captured from various rotations and perspectives relative to the camera, with each image labeled according to PCB type, rotation category, and perspective category. We then describe the design and outcomes of experiments examining how different combinations of rotations and perspectives during training affect test accuracy. Furthermore, we analyze the effectiveness of data augmentation techniques in simulating unseen rotations and perspectives. All experiments are conducted using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) both with and without homogeneous vector capsules (HVCs), and we investigate and demonstrate the ability of HVCs to more effectively encode the equivariance of sub-components within micro-PCBs. Our experimental results indicate that training a neural network equipped with HVCs—capable of modeling equivariance among sub-components—alongside exposure to a wide range of perspectives yields the highest classification accuracy on micro-PCB data.

This paper introduces a differentiable linear quadratic model predictive control (MPC) framework designed for safe imitation learning. By incorporating an infinite-horizon cost structure through a terminal cost derived from the discrete-time algebraic Riccati equation (DARE), the resulting controller is guaranteed to be stabilizing in closed-loop. A key contribution of this work is the analytical derivation of the derivative of the DARE solution, enabling the application of gradient-based learning methods. Another significant contribution lies in the formulation of the MPC optimization problem: an augmented Lagrangian approach ensures feasibility during training while enforcing strict constraints on both states and inputs. Additionally, a pre-stabilizing controller is employed to maintain the accuracy of the MPC solution and its derivatives at each iteration. The effectiveness of the proposed framework is validated through a series of numerical experiments.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) are increasingly being deployed in critical safety applications, where the reliability of predictions is of utmost importance. Although DNNs demonstrate remarkable predictive performance, they typically lack an inherent mechanism for quantifying and propagating significant input data uncertainty—something that is frequently encountered in safety-critical domains. This uncertainty is often epistemic, arising from various sources such as incomplete knowledge of the data generation process, imprecision, ignorance, or limited understanding of underlying physical phenomena. While recent research has primarily focused on modeling parameter uncertainty, methods for end-to-end training of DNNs that account for epistemic input data uncertainty remain scarce and largely tailored to specific problems. In this paper, we introduce the Deep Interval Neural Network (DINN), a DNN optimized using gradient-based methods that leverages interval analysis to quantify both input and parameter uncertainty. We evaluate DINN on an air pollution dataset featuring sensor uncertainties and demonstrate its ability to generate accurate, bounded predictions even when faced with uncertain input data.

Quick Shift is a widely used algorithm for mode seeking and clustering. We establish finite-sample statistical consistency guarantees for the recovery of modes and clusters under mild distributional assumptions. Building on these results, we develop a consistent modal regression method.

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are widely recognized for their success in generating realistic images. However, their application extends beyond image generation, as they can also be effectively used for generating tabular data. In this work, we review and analyze recent research on GANs applied to tabular data. We generate synthetic data to bring the training distribution closer to the test distribution. Subsequently, we compare the performance of models trained on the original training dataset with those trained on datasets augmented with GAN-generated data. Additionally, we evaluate models trained using adversarial sampling techniques. Our results demonstrate that GANs can serve as a viable solution when there is an imbalance between the training and test data distributions.

Iconography in art is the study of visual elements within artworks to identify their motifs, themes, and the ways in which these are depicted. It remains a dynamic field of research, with applications ranging from interpreting symbolic meanings to tracing the historical development and spatial distribution of visual representations, as well as examining artistic influences across different works and periods. The increasing availability of digital image archives has opened new opportunities for applying Computer Vision techniques to analyze art at an unprecedented scale, potentially enhancing both iconographic research and education.

In this paper, we present a new dataset of paintings designed for iconography classification and evaluate the performance of a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) classifier in identifying religious iconography. The proposed model achieves promising results—71.17% precision, 70.89% recall, 70.25% F1-score, and 72.73% average precision—in recognizing saints within Christian religious paintings, a challenging task due to the high similarity among visual features of different classes. A qualitative analysis of the results reveals that the CNN effectively focuses on the traditional iconic elements that define each saint's representation, leveraging these distinctive motifs for accurate classification.

Distant supervision (DS) is a powerful approach for expanding datasets to improve relation extraction (RE) models, but it often suffers from significant label noise. Existing methods based on attention mechanisms, reinforcement learning, or GANs are typically black-box models, offering neither meaningful interpretation of sample selection in DS nor consistent performance across different domains. In contrast, this work introduces a novel model-agnostic instance sampling method for DS, called REIF, which leverages influence functions (IF). Our approach identifies favorable and unfavorable instances within a bag using IF, and then performs dynamic instance sampling. We propose a fast influence sampling algorithm that reduces computational complexity from $\mathcal{O}(mn)$ to $\mathcal{O}(1)$, while analyzing the robustness of the selected sampling function. Experimental results show that simply sampling favorable instances during training allows REIF to outperform several complex baseline models. Furthermore, we demonstrate that REIF enables interpretable instance selection.

A powerful and flexible method for structured prediction involves embedding the target structures into a high- or infinite-dimensional feature space using output kernels, and then solving a regression problem in this output space. A prediction in the original domain is obtained by addressing the corresponding pre-image problem. In traditional approaches, the embedding is predefined based on the target loss function before the learning process begins. In this work, we introduce a novel approach that jointly learns a finite approximation of the output embedding and the regression function within the new feature space. By incorporating prior knowledge about the outputs and leveraging unsupervised output data—both of which are commonly available in structured prediction tasks—we enhance the learning process. We establish that the resulting structured predictor is a consistent estimator and derive an excess risk bound. Furthermore, our method exhibits significantly lower computational complexity compared to previous output kernel-based techniques. Empirical evaluations across various structured prediction tasks demonstrate the versatility and scalability of the proposed approach, making it well-suited for large-scale datasets.

Traditional neural language models often produce generic responses that lack logical coherence and emotional depth. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a syntactically constrained bidirectional-asynchronous approach for emotional conversation generation, termed E-SCBA. In our model, pre-generated emotion and topic keywords are asynchronously integrated into the decoding process, differing significantly from conventional methods that generate responses sequentially from start to finish. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach not only enhances the diversity of generated replies but also achieves improved performance in both logical consistency and emotional expression compared to baseline models.

Over-parameterized models have garnered significant attention in the era of data science and deep learning. Empirical observations show that, despite their tendency to overfit training data—such as in deep neural networks—they often achieve low test error, sometimes even outperforming traditional algorithms that are specifically designed to prevent overfitting. The primary objective of this work is to rigorously quantify the benefits of data interpolation within the context of the nearest neighbors (NN) algorithm. Specifically, we examine a class of interpolated weighting schemes and analyze their asymptotic performance characteristics. Our analysis reveals a U-shaped performance curve as a function of the degree of data interpolation. We prove that a moderate level of interpolation **strictly** enhances both prediction accuracy and statistical stability compared to the optimal, un-interpolated $ k $-NN algorithm. This result theoretically supports (and predicts) the existence of a second U-shaped curve in the recently observed double descent phenomenon. It is important to note that our aim in this study is not to advocate for the use of interpolated NN methods, but rather to gain theoretical insights into the role of data interpolation, inspired by the aforementioned empirical phenomenon.

Personalized medicine, a medical approach that tailors treatment strategies to individual patient characteristics, is gaining increasing attention in the healthcare field. A key objective of personalized medicine is to identify specific patient subgroups that derive greater benefit from a targeted treatment compared to alternative therapies. However, many existing subgroup identification methods focus primarily on maximizing the treatment effect without considering the size of the subgroup. In clinical practice, it is often crucial to identify the largest possible group of patients who can benefit from the optimal treatment.

In this paper, we introduce an optimal subgroup selection rule (SSR) that aims to maximize the number of patients selected while achieving a pre-specified clinically meaningful outcome, such as a minimum average treatment effect. We derive two equivalent theoretical formulations of the optimal SSR based on a contrast function that captures the interaction between treatment and covariates in influencing outcomes. To implement this approach, we propose the ConstrAined PolIcy Tree seArch aLgorithm (CAPITAL), which searches for the optimal SSR within the class of interpretable decision trees. The proposed method is flexible enough to incorporate multiple constraints that discourage the inclusion of patients with negative treatment effects and can also be adapted to handle time-to-event data through the use of restricted models.

Graph representation learning has attracted increasing attention due to its broad applicability in tasks such as link prediction, node classification, and recommendation. Most embedding methods aim to preserve key structural properties of the original graph within a low-dimensional space. However, real-world graphs often exhibit a complex combination of properties that are challenging to capture using a single approach. In this work, we introduce the concept of graph representation ensemble learning and present a novel framework for efficiently combining multiple graph embedding techniques. We analyze our framework theoretically and empirically, examining the dependencies among state-of-the-art embedding methods. We evaluate our approach on node classification tasks across four real-world graphs and demonstrate that the proposed ensemble methods can outperform existing state-of-the-art approaches by up to 8% in macro-F1 score. Furthermore, we show that the method is particularly effective for underrepresented classes, achieving improvements of up to 12%.

We present a general framework for establishing rigorous performance guarantees for the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm and its variant, gradient EM. Our analysis is structured in two key components: first, we examine these algorithms at the population level—under the assumption of infinite data—and then we derive results that apply when updates are based on a finite sample.

Initially, we characterize the domain of attraction of any global maximizer of the population likelihood. This characterization is grounded in a novel perspective that views EM updates as a perturbed version of likelihood ascent, or equivalently, gradient EM updates as a perturbed form of standard gradient ascent. Building upon this insight, we establish non-asymptotic guarantees for both EM and gradient EM when applied to a finite dataset.

We demonstrate the applicability of our general theory through three canonical incomplete-data problems: mixture of Gaussians, mixture of regressions, and linear regression with covariates missing completely at random. In each case, our theoretical results ensure that with appropriate initialization, a relatively small number of EM (or gradient EM) iterations will produce an estimate that is within statistical error of the maximum likelihood estimate, with high probability. We also include simulation results to support our findings.

Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) have attracted significant attention for their energy-efficient properties, but the absence of a scalable training algorithm has limited their use in practical machine learning applications. To address this, the approach of converting deep neural networks into SNNs has been extensively explored to enhance the applicability of SNNs. However, most prior work has not fully leveraged the spatio-temporal characteristics inherent in SNNs, resulting in inefficiencies in terms of spike count and inference latency. In this paper, we introduce T2FSNN, a framework that incorporates the time-to-first-spike coding mechanism into deep SNNs by utilizing kernel-based dynamic thresholds and dendritic structures to overcome these limitations. Furthermore, we propose gradient-based optimization and early firing strategies to further improve the efficiency of T2FSNN. Experimental results show that the proposed methods reduce inference latency and spike count to 22% and less than 1%, respectively, compared to burst coding—a state-of-the-art method on CIFAR-100.

Recently, the over-smoothing phenomenon in Transformer-based models has been observed in both vision and language domains. However, prior research has not thoroughly investigated the underlying causes of this issue. In this work, we aim to address this gap by analyzing the over-smoothing problem from a graph perspective, where this phenomenon was first identified and studied. Intuitively, the self-attention matrix can be interpreted as a normalized adjacency matrix of an implicit graph. Building upon this analogy, we conduct theoretical analysis and reveal that layer normalization plays a crucial role in the emergence of over-smoothing in Transformers. Specifically, when the standard deviation of layer normalization is sufficiently large, the outputs of Transformer layers tend to converge to a low-rank subspace, leading to over-smoothing. To mitigate this issue, we propose hierarchical fusion strategies that adaptively combine representations from different layers, thereby enhancing the diversity of the final output. Extensive experimental results across multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach.

In this working notes paper, we present the participation of the IBM Research AI (Almaden) team in the ImageCLEF 2019 VQA-Med competition. The challenge involved four question-answering tasks based on radiology images. The complexity of the task was heightened by the diversity of imaging modalities, organs, and disease types, combined with a small and imbalanced training dataset. To address these challenges, we developed a modular pipeline architecture that incorporated transfer learning and multi-task learning techniques. Our research led to the creation of a novel model known as the Supporting Facts Network (SFN). The core concept of SFN is to leverage information from upstream tasks to enhance performance on more challenging downstream tasks. This approach resulted in a significant improvement in validation set performance, with an 18-point increase in the F-1 score. We submitted four runs to the competition and achieved a seventh-place ranking.

Text classifiers often rely on spurious correlations—such as the term "Spielberg" being associated with positively reviewed movies, even though the word itself does not inherently express a positive sentiment. In this paper, we introduce a method for identifying and distinguishing between spurious and genuine correlations in text classification. We frame this as a supervised classification task, leveraging features derived from treatment effect estimators to differentiate spurious from true correlations. Due to the generality and low dimensionality of these features, our approach performs effectively even with limited training data, and it enables the transfer of word-level classifiers to new domains. Experiments across four datasets—covering sentiment analysis and toxicity detection—demonstrate that incorporating this method into feature selection leads to more robust classification, as evidenced by improved worst-case accuracy on samples affected by spurious correlations.

We introduce a novel approach to the Register Allocation problem, utilizing multi-agent hierarchical Reinforcement Learning. We rigorously formalize the constraints that define the problem for a specific instruction set architecture, ensuring that the generated code maintains semantic correctness. Additionally, we design a gRPC-based framework that offers a modular and efficient compiler interface for both training and inference. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our method achieves results comparable to or better than LLVM's register allocators on Intel x86 and ARM AArch64 architectures.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a widely explored approach for enhancing sequence-generation models. However, traditional reward functions used in RL training often fail to capture sufficient semantic information, leading to biased model behavior. Moreover, the sparsity and delayed nature of rewards make the exploration process in RL inefficient. To address these challenges, we introduce the concept of nested-Wasserstein distance as a means of achieving more accurate distributional semantic matching. Building on this, we propose a novel nested-Wasserstein self-imitation learning framework that encourages the model to leverage historically high-reward sequences, thereby improving both exploration efficiency and semantic alignment. Our method can be viewed as an approximation of proximal policy optimization with Wasserstein-based trust regions. Experimental results across a range of unconditional and conditional sequence-generation tasks show that our approach consistently achieves superior performance.

A deep-learning-based hybrid approach for short-term load forecasting is introduced. The proposed method features a novel tree-based ensemble technique called Warm-start Gradient Tree Boosting (WGTB). Existing approaches either combine submodels of a single type, which limits their ability to leverage the statistical strengths of diverse models, or simply aggregate outputs from entirely different models, failing to fully exploit the potential of ensemble learning. Drawing inspiration from the bias-variance trade-off, WGTB is designed to address the significant differences among various inference models in terms of accuracy, volatility, and linearity. The overall strategy integrates four distinct inference models with varying capabilities. WGTB then combines their outputs using a warm-start mechanism along with a hybrid of bagging and boosting techniques, effectively reducing both bias and variance. The method is evaluated on two real-world datasets from the State Grid Corporation of China, with hourly resolution. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed strategy in harnessing the complementary strengths of low-bias and low-variance inference models.

DeepTingle is a text prediction and classification system trained on the collected works of the acclaimed author Chuck Tingle, known for his contributions to the genre of fantastic gay erotica. Unlike the writing assistance tools we commonly use—such as predictive text, translation, and grammar checkers—which are typically trained on broad, supposedly "neutral" datasets, DeepTingle is built on a highly specific, internally coherent, yet externally unconventional dataset. This unique training set enables us to highlight and challenge the underlying norms embedded in data-driven tools that support creativity and productivity. Since such tools increasingly act as extensions of our cognitive processes, it becomes essential to examine the values and assumptions they encode—not just within themselves, but also within us. DeepTingle is implemented as a web application using LSTM networks and GloVe word embeddings, developed in JavaScript with Keras-JS.

Neural networks employed for multi-interaction trajectory reconstruction often fail to quantify the uncertainty in their predictions, a limitation that hinders a deeper analysis and understanding of the systems they model. In this paper, we enhance the Factorised Neural Relational Inference model to produce both a mean and a standard deviation for each component of the phase space vector. When combined with an appropriate loss function, this approach enables the model to effectively account for uncertainty. We explore various loss functions, including those inspired by convexification techniques and a Bayesian formulation of the problem. Our results highlight the importance of preserving the physical meaning of variables when modeling uncertainty, and we demonstrate the presence of challenging local minima that can significantly impact the training process.

Every natural text is written in a particular style. Style emerges from a complex interplay of various stylistic elements, such as formality markers, emotional expressions, and metaphors. A full comprehension of a text requires consideration of these factors. These elements interact and co-vary in intricate ways to shape distinct styles. Investigating the nature of these co-varying combinations offers valuable insights into the broader phenomenon of stylistic language, often referred to as cross-style language understanding.

This paper introduces xSLUE, a benchmark corpus designed for sentence-level cross-style language understanding and evaluation. It integrates existing datasets and includes a newly collected one. The benchmark encompasses texts spanning 15 distinct styles, organized under four theoretical categories: figurative, personal, affective, and interpersonal. To ensure robust evaluation, we also created an additional diagnostic set by annotating all 15 styles on the same text.

Using xSLUE, we explore three compelling cross-style applications in classification, correlation, and generation. First, our cross-style classifier, trained on multiple styles simultaneously, demonstrates improved performance compared to classifiers trained on individual styles. Second, our analysis reveals that certain styles are strongly interdependent in human-written texts. Third, we observe that combining contradictory styles can lead to stylistically inconsistent or inappropriate outputs.

We believe that our benchmark and case studies contribute significantly to the advancement of cross-style language understanding and provide a foundation for future research in this area.

Deep learning has emerged as the dominant approach for analyzing and interpreting whole-slide digital pathology images (WSIs). Traditionally, it is assumed that tumor regions contain the majority of predictive information. In this study, we introduce an unsupervised clustering-based multiple-instance learning framework and apply it to develop deep-learning models for predicting gene mutations using WSIs from three cancer types in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) studies: colorectal cancer (CRC), lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), and head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). Our results demonstrate that unsupervised clustering of image patches can effectively identify informative regions, filter out non-predictive patches, and enhance mutation prediction across all three cancer types, when compared to WSI-based methods that do not select specific patches or models focused solely on tumor regions. Furthermore, our proposed method outperforms two recently published baseline approaches that also use unsupervised clustering to support model predictions. The clustering-based approach enables the identification of spatial regions associated with specific gene mutations through probability scores, revealing the heterogeneity of genotypes within the tumor microenvironment. Finally, our study highlights that selecting only tumor regions in WSIs is not always the optimal strategy for identifying predictive patches in mutation prediction, as other tissue types may also contain valuable information.

Given a gallery of uncaptioned video sequences, this paper addresses the challenge of retrieving relevant videos based on an unseen text query. To overcome the absence of annotations, we leverage a related video gallery containing video-caption pairs, referred to as the source gallery, which, however, exhibits a domain gap relative to the target gallery. We introduce the problem of Unsupervised Domain Adaptation for Cross-modal Video Retrieval, along with a new benchmark focused on fine-grained actions. Our approach proposes a novel iterative domain alignment method that utilizes pseudo-labeling of target videos and cross-domain (source-target) ranking. This method effectively adapts the embedding space to the target domain, consistently outperforming approaches that rely solely on the source data, as well as those based on marginal or conditional alignment.

An increasing number of machine learning models are being deployed in high-stakes domains such as finance and healthcare. While these models often achieve impressive performance, many are inherently "black boxes," making it difficult to interpret their decisions. As a result, there has been growing interest among researchers in developing techniques to enhance model interpretability. One widely used approach is post hoc explanation methods based on perturbations, such as LIME, which provide insights into a model's behavior after it has been trained. However, this class of methods has been shown to suffer from significant instability, raising concerns about their reliability and undermining user trust. In this paper, we introduce S-LIME, a method that leverages a hypothesis testing framework grounded in the central limit theorem to determine the optimal number of perturbation points required to ensure stable explanations. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on both simulated and real-world datasets.

We introduce a decentralized "local2global" approach for graph representation learning, designed to scale any embedding method from the outset. The local2global framework operates in two main stages: first, it partitions the input graph into overlapping subgraphs, or "patches," and learns local representations for each independently. In the second stage, these local representations are combined into a globally coherent embedding by estimating the optimal set of rigid transformations that align them, leveraging information from overlapping regions through group synchronization.

A key advantage of the local2global method over existing approaches is that it enables independent training of patches without requiring costly parameter synchronization during distributed training. This makes it particularly well-suited for large-scale industrial applications, where the input graph may exceed memory limits and is often stored in a distributed manner.

Preliminary results on medium-scale datasets (up to approximately 7,000 nodes and 200,000 edges) show promising performance, with the graph reconstruction capability of local2global matching that of globally trained embeddings. Ongoing work includes a comprehensive evaluation of the method on large-scale data and its application to downstream tasks such as node classification and link prediction.

The performance of deep neural networks degrades when the feature distribution in the test environment (target domain) differs from that in the training environment (source domain). To address this issue, test-time adaptation (TTA) offers a solution by allowing a model to adapt to the target domain without access to the source dataset. However, existing TTA methods often fail to align the feature distributions between the source and target domains, a challenge that unsupervised domain adaptation typically addresses. In the TTA setting, though, access to the source data is not allowed.

In this paper, we introduce a novel TTA method called Covariance-Aware Feature Alignment (CAFe), which explicitly aligns the source and target feature distributions during testing. To achieve this alignment without direct access to the source data, CAFe leverages pre-computed auxiliary statistics—such as mean and covariance—from the source domain. These statistics are lightweight and can be efficiently computed during training.

To enhance both efficiency and stability, we propose a technique called feature grouping, which organizes feature dimensions into correlated groups using spectral clustering. This approach helps prevent the covariance matrix from becoming singular or ill-conditioned. Empirical results demonstrate that CAFe consistently outperforms previous TTA methods across various distribution shifts.

In this expository note, we explore a surprising phenomenon in overparameterized linear regression—where the number of features exceeds the number of samples. We observe that in certain regimes, the test risk of the estimator obtained via gradient descent actually increases as more data is added. In other words, additional samples can be detrimental to the performance of the estimator. This behavior is implicitly discussed in recent theoretical work on the "double descent" phenomenon in linear models. Here, we aim to isolate and clarify this effect in a simple setting: linear regression with isotropic Gaussian covariates. Specifically, the phenomenon arises due to an unusual form of the bias-variance tradeoff in the overparameterized regime: while the bias decreases with more samples, the variance increases.

Solving symbolic mathematics has long been a domain that requires compositional reasoning and recursive thinking—hallmarks of human ingenuity. However, recent research has revealed that large-scale language models, such as transformers, are remarkably capable of tackling complex mathematical problems when trained as sequence-to-sequence models. These models typically require vast amounts of training data to effectively generalize to new symbolic mathematics tasks.

In this paper, we introduce a sample-efficient approach to solving symbolic tasks by first pretraining the transformer model on language translation tasks and then fine-tuning it for the specific goal of solving symbolic mathematics. Our pretrained model achieves comparable accuracy on integration tasks while using approximately 1.5 orders of magnitude fewer training samples than state-of-the-art deep learning methods for symbolic mathematics.

However, the test performance on differential equation tasks is significantly lower compared to integration, as these problems demand higher-order recursion, which is not commonly present in language translation tasks. To explore the impact of language on symbolic reasoning, we pretrain our model using various pairs of language translations. Our results reveal a clear language bias in the performance of symbolic mathematics tasks.

Finally, we evaluate the robustness of the fine-tuned model on symbolic math tasks under distribution shifts, and our findings highlight the challenges and limitations of current approaches in this area.

The diagnostic process for colorectal cancer primarily involves identifying and characterizing abnormal growths in the colon, known as polyps. Although recent advances in deep learning have improved object localization, localizing polyps remains a challenge due to the similarity between different tissue types and the high prevalence of artifacts. Recent research has highlighted the detrimental effect of artifacts on polyp detection and has begun to integrate artifact awareness into the training process. However, the use of prior knowledge regarding the spatial relationships between polyps and artifacts has not been widely explored. In this work, we introduce a method that incorporates artifact-related knowledge during a post-processing stage. Our approach frames the task as an inductive graph representation learning problem, consisting of both a training and an inference phase. Detected bounding boxes around polyps and artifacts are treated as nodes in a graph, connected based on a predefined criterion. During training, a node classifier is learned using ground truth bounding boxes. In the inference phase, this classifier is applied to a second graph constructed from artifact and polyp predictions generated by region proposal networks. We evaluate the impact of different connectivity criteria and artifact handling strategies on the performance of our method and demonstrate its effectiveness.

Self-reinforcing feedback loops in interactive recommender systems act as both a cause and an effect of the over- or under-presentation of certain content. This dynamic leads to inaccurate estimates of user preferences—specifically, it results in an overestimation of the content that is repeatedly shown, while undermining the visibility of other alternatives. Such a scenario violates the principle of equitable exposure, which we define as a fair system. We examine two models: one that explicitly accounts for systematic and limited exposure to alternatives, and another that disregards these factors. Through simulations, we show that failing to consider systematic exposure leads to an exaggerated assessment of promoted items and an undervaluation of censored options. However, simply accounting for limited exposure serves as an effective remedy for these biases.

We explore the challenge of truth discovery in scenarios where multiple agents provide potentially unreliable or biased opinions. We consider a setting in which the reliability or bias of agents is correlated when they belong to the same community, defined as a group of agents sharing similar views on a specific event. An agent may belong to different communities for different events, and these communities are not known in advance. To address this, we integrate the agents' social network information into our truth discovery framework and propose Laplace variational inference methods to estimate agent reliability, community memberships, and event states. Additionally, we develop a stochastic variational inference approach to enable our model to scale effectively to large social networks. Experimental results on both simulated and real-world data demonstrate that, in cases of sparse observations, our proposed methods outperform existing approaches such as majority voting, TruthFinder, AccuSim, the Confidence-Aware Truth Discovery method, the Bayesian Classifier Combination (BCC) method, and the Community BCC method.

Split-Merge MCMC (Monte Carlo Markov Chain) is a key and widely used variant of MCMC for problems where the state involves an unknown number of components. It is well established that existing split-merge MCMC methods suffer from poor scalability. Efficient mixing typically requires intelligent and informative proposal distributions to minimize rejection rates. However, all known informative proposals involve computationally intensive operations, leading to high per-iteration costs. This makes them impractical for large-scale datasets. On the other hand, uninformative but efficient proposals, such as random split-merge, result in very slow convergence. This trade-off between mixing efficiency and computational cost has long been considered a major challenge. In this paper, we identify a favorable balance. By leveraging unique properties of weighted MinHash—a popular locality-sensitive hashing technique—we introduce a novel class of split-merge proposals that are significantly more informative than random sampling while remaining computationally efficient. As a result, our approach achieves a superior trade-off between convergence speed and per-iteration cost. Empirically, our method is approximately 6 times faster than state-of-the-art techniques on two large real-world datasets, KDDCUP and PubMed, which contain several million records.

We introduce **CLSRIL-23**, a self-supervised learning-based audio pre-trained model designed to learn cross-lingual speech representations from raw audio across 23 Indic languages. Built upon the **wav2vec 2.0** framework, it leverages a contrastive training task over masked latent speech representations and jointly learns quantized latents that are shared across all languages. During pretraining, we analyze language-specific losses to evaluate the impact of monolingual versus multilingual pretraining approaches. 

Our experiments demonstrate that multilingual pretraining outperforms monolingual training in two key aspects: (1) capturing phonetic similarities among languages, and (2) achieving better performance on downstream speech recognition tasks. Specifically, when fine-tuned on Hindi, a multilingual pretrained model shows a 5% reduction in Word Error Rate (WER) and a 9.5% decrease in Character Error Rate (CER). 

All code and models are open-sourced to support further research. CLSRIL-23 is trained on 23 Indic languages and nearly 10,000 hours of audio data, aiming to advance speech recognition research for these languages. We hope this work will inspire new state-of-the-art systems, particularly for low-resource Indic languages, by leveraging self-supervised learning techniques.

Label space expansion for multi-label classification (MLC) is a technique that transforms original label vectors into higher-dimensional representations before training, and then maps the predicted codes back to the original label space during testing. This approach has been shown to enhance the performance of MLC algorithms when combined with standard error-correcting codes for encoding and decoding. However, such coding schemes can be complex to implement and often struggle to meet the practical requirement of cost-sensitive MLC—adapting to different evaluation metrics of interest.

In this work, we introduce a simpler coding strategy based on the concept of a reference pair of label vectors, which enables cost-sensitivity in a more natural and effective manner. Our proposed method, called Cost-Sensitive Reference Pair Encoding (CSRPE), incorporates three key steps: cluster-based encoding, weight-based training, and voting-based decoding, all of which take cost information into account. Moreover, we exploit the cost structure embedded within the code space of CSRPE to develop a new active learning algorithm tailored for cost-sensitive MLC.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that CSRPE outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods across various MLC evaluation criteria. Additionally, the active learning approach built upon CSRPE significantly surpasses current methods in active MLC scenarios, further validating the effectiveness and versatility of our proposed framework.

Sparse R-CNN is a recent powerful object detection baseline that performs set prediction using sparse, learnable proposal boxes and their corresponding features. In this work, we introduce two dynamic improvements to enhance the performance of Sparse R-CNN. First, the original approach employs a one-to-one label assignment strategy, in which the Hungarian algorithm matches only a single positive sample to each ground truth. However, this rigid matching may not be optimal for aligning the learned proposal boxes with the actual objects. To address this, we propose Dynamic Label Assignment (DLA), which leverages the optimal transport algorithm to gradually increase the number of positive samples assigned during the iterative training stages. As training progresses, the matching becomes progressively more flexible, reflecting the improved precision of refined proposals in later stages. Second, in the inference phase of Sparse R-CNN, the learned proposal boxes and features remain static across different images. Inspired by dynamic convolution, we introduce Dynamic Proposal Generation (DPG), which dynamically combines multiple proposal experts to generate more accurate initial proposal boxes and features for subsequent training stages. This enables the model to produce sample-dependent proposal boxes and features during inference. Experimental results show that our proposed method, Dynamic Sparse R-CNN, significantly improves upon the strong baseline.

End-to-end Speech Translation (ST) models offer several advantages over traditional cascaded systems that combine Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and text Machine Translation (MT). These benefits include reduced inference latency and the elimination of error propagation between modules. However, the performance of end-to-end ST is often constrained by the limited availability of large-scale parallel datasets consisting of aligned speech and translated transcripts. To address this challenge, prior research has explored the use of pre-trained components and multi-task learning to leverage weakly supervised data, such as speech-to-transcript or text-to-foreign-text pairs. In this paper, we show that leveraging pre-trained Machine Translation (MT) or text-to-speech (TTS) models to convert weakly supervised data into speech-to-translation pairs for ST training can yield better results than multi-task learning approaches. Moreover, we demonstrate that a high-quality end-to-end ST model can be trained using only weakly supervised data, and that synthetic data generated from unlabeled monolingual text or speech can further enhance performance. Finally, we present methods for preventing overfitting to synthetic speech data, supported by a detailed quantitative ablation study.

We train multi-task autoencoders on various linguistic tasks and examine the resulting hidden sentence representations. The inclusion of translation and part-of-speech decoders leads to significant changes in these representations. The more decoders a model incorporates, the better it groups sentences based on their syntactic similarity, as the representation space becomes less entangled. To investigate the structure of this space, we interpolate between sentences, producing intriguing pseudo-English sentences that often exhibit recognizable syntactic patterns. Finally, we highlight an interesting property of our models: the difference vector between two sentences can be applied to a third sentence with similar characteristics, resulting in meaningful modifications.

Hyperbolic spaces are more effective in representing data that exhibits hierarchical structures, such as tree-like data. However, it is often necessary to align different but related representations in a meaningful way. This alignment process constitutes an important class of machine learning problems, with applications in areas like ontology matching and cross-lingual alignment. Optimal transport (OT)-based methods offer a natural framework for addressing alignment tasks, as they aim to find a transformation that maps the source dataset to match the target dataset, under certain distributional constraints. In this work, we introduce a novel approach to alignment based on optimal transport of embeddings within the Poincaré model of hyperbolic geometry. Our method leverages the gyrobarycenter mapping defined on Möbius gyrovector spaces. As a result of this theoretical framework, we extend several existing Euclidean OT-based domain adaptation techniques to their hyperbolic counterparts. Empirically, we demonstrate that both Euclidean and hyperbolic methods achieve comparable performance in the context of retrieval tasks.

Source code (Context) and its parsed abstract syntax tree (AST; Structure) offer two complementary views of the same computer program. Historically, machine learning model designers have focused primarily on either Structure or Context. In this work, we introduce a novel model that learns jointly from both the Context and Structure of source code. Unlike prior approaches, our model relies solely on language-agnostic features—specifically, source code itself and features derived directly from the AST. 

Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in monolingual code summarization across all five programming languages evaluated in this study. Furthermore, we present the first multilingual code summarization model. We demonstrate that training on non-parallel data from multiple programming languages enhances performance across all individual languages, with particularly significant improvements observed for low-resource languages. Notably, multilingual training based only on Context does not yield similar gains, underscoring the value of integrating both Structure and Context for more effective representation learning in code.

Meta-learning seeks to optimize the hyperparameters of a model class or training algorithm based on observations from a set of related tasks. Following Baxter's framework [1], these tasks are assumed to originate from a common task environment, which is characterized by a distribution over the space of tasks and by per-task data distributions. The statistical structure of this environment determines the degree of similarity among the tasks. The objective of a meta-learner is to identify hyperparameters that yield low loss when applied to a new task drawn from the same environment. The difference between the average loss across the task environment—referred to as the meta-population loss—and the empirical loss computed on the data from the observed tasks—known as the meta-generalization gap—serves as an indicator of the meta-learner's generalization performance. In this paper, we introduce new information-theoretic bounds on the average absolute value of the meta-generalization gap. Unlike previous work [2], our bounds explicitly account for the effects of task relatedness, the number of tasks, and the number of samples per task on the meta-generalization gap. Task similarity is quantified using the Kullback-Leibler (KL) and Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergences. We demonstrate the applicability and tightness of the proposed bounds.

Person Re-Identification (Re-ID) plays a critical role in modern video surveillance systems. Despite its importance, learning discriminative features for Re-ID remains challenging due to significant variations in the image space, such as changes in human pose, lighting conditions, and viewing angles. In this paper, we introduce HAVANA, a novel, extensible, and lightweight hierarchical and variation-normalized autoencoder designed to learn features that are robust to intra-class variations. Unlike existing generative methods that rely on heavy external supervision to reduce variations, HAVANA effectively suppresses intra-class variability through a variation-normalized autoencoder trained without any additional supervision. We also propose a new Jensen-Shannon triplet loss for contrastive distribution learning in Re-ID. Furthermore, we present Hierarchical Variation Distiller, a hierarchical VAE that decomposes the latent representation and explicitly models variations. To the best of our knowledge, HAVANA is the first VAE-based framework specifically designed for person Re-ID.

The effectiveness of deep machine learning in automatically identifying tumor regions has been validated for intraoperative neuronavigation, utilizing active IR-mapping combined with the cold test. The proposed method employs a matrix IR-imager to remotely map the spatiotemporal distribution of surface temperature patterns, which reflect the dynamics of local cerebral blood flow. This technique offers several advantages, including non-invasiveness, zero risk to patients and medical personnel, low implementation and operational costs, as well as ease and speed of use. 

In contrast, traditional IR-diagnostic methods rely on a diagnostician to manually determine tumor boundaries, introducing significant uncertainty that can lead to uncontrolled diagnostic errors. The current study demonstrates that the integration of deep learning algorithms effectively addresses this limitation, improving accuracy and reliability in tumor delineation.

Transfer learning offers a powerful strategy for developing predictive models that integrate both simulation and experimental data within a unified framework. In this approach, a neural network is initially trained on a comprehensive set of simulated data, and then fine-tuned using limited experimental data to improve the alignment of its predictions with real-world observations. This technique has previously been applied to construct more accurate predictive models for Omega and NIF inertial confinement fusion (ICF) experiments compared to simulations alone. In this study, we explore a transfer learning-based hypothetical ICF campaign aimed at maximizing experimental neutron yield through Bayesian optimization. The transfer learning model achieves results within 5% of the theoretical maximum yield in a relatively small design space, requiring fewer than 20 experiments. Additionally, we show that this method outperforms conventional model calibration techniques in optimizing ICF designs. This approach holds significant potential for enabling robust optimization of experimental performance in the face of uncertainty.

Deep learning (DL) has become the state-of-the-art approach for a wide range of medical image segmentation tasks. However, it typically requires large amounts of manually annotated training data, which can be difficult or impractical to obtain in certain applications. Furthermore, DL models often exhibit limited generalizability when applied to out-of-sample data. In contrast, multi-atlas segmentation (MAS) demonstrates strong performance with minimal training data and exhibits better generalizability. A hybrid approach that combines the high accuracy of DL with the robust generalizability of MAS is highly desirable, particularly in scenarios where manually labeled data is scarce or challenging to generate.

Most previous research has focused on enhancing individual components of MAS using DL, rather than directly optimizing the final segmentation performance through an end-to-end pipeline. To date, only one study has explored this concept in the context of binary 2D image segmentation, leaving the effectiveness of such an approach in more complex, multi-class 3D segmentation tasks unclear. In this work, we introduce a novel 3D end-to-end hybrid pipeline called Deep Label Fusion (DLF), which leverages the strengths of both MAS and DL. Experimental results show that DLF significantly outperforms traditional label fusion methods and U-Net, a direct DL-based approach, in the segmentation of medial temporal structures.

The Jacobian matrix (or gradient in the case of single-output networks) is closely connected to several key properties of neural networks, including the function landscape, stationary points, (local) Lipschitz constants, and robustness against adversarial attacks. In this paper, we introduce RecurJac, a recursive algorithm designed to compute both upper and lower bounds for each entry of the Jacobian matrix with respect to the network's input. The method is applicable to networks employing a wide variety of activation functions. As a byproduct, our approach enables the efficient computation of (local) Lipschitz constants, which are essential for verifying neural network robustness and ensuring the training stability of GANs. Experimental results demonstrate that the (local) Lipschitz constants generated by our method are of higher quality compared to existing approaches, leading to improved robustness verification. Our algorithm runs in polynomial time, and its computational efficiency makes it suitable even for relatively large networks. Furthermore, we utilize the Jacobian bounds to analyze the neural network's landscape, such as determining the presence of stationary points in a local neighborhood. The source code is available at \url{http://github.com/huanzhang12/RecurJac-Jacobian-bounds}.

Graph classification is a well-researched problem with extensive real-world applications. However, in many practical scenarios, the availability of labeled graphs for training classification models is limited, making these models susceptible to overfitting. To tackle this challenge, we introduce two approaches based on contrastive self-supervised learning (CSSL) to reduce overfitting. The first approach involves pretraining graph encoders using CSSL on a large set of unlabeled graphs, without the need for human-annotated labels, and then fine-tuning the pretrained encoders on the available labeled graphs. The second approach incorporates a regularizer derived from CSSL, allowing the simultaneous optimization of both the supervised classification task and the unsupervised CSSL task. To apply CSSL to graphs, we generate augmented graphs by applying a sequence of graph transformation operations to the original graphs. A contrastive loss is then used to train the graph encoder by distinguishing whether two augmented graphs originate from the same original graph. Experimental results on multiple graph classification datasets validate the effectiveness of our proposed methods.

Knowledge tracing (KT) models, such as the Deep Knowledge Tracing (DKT) model, monitor a learner's progression in acquiring skills by analyzing their performance on questions associated with those skills. A common limitation in existing KT models is that they treat all questions within a given skill as equivalent indicators of a learner's proficiency, which is often an oversimplification in real-world educational settings. To address this issue, we propose qDKT, a variant of DKT that models the probability of a learner's success on individual questions over time. 

First, qDKT introduces graph Laplacian regularization to smooth predictions within each skill, offering significant benefits when dealing with large numbers of questions. Second, it employs an initialization method inspired by the fastText algorithm, which has proven effective in various natural language processing tasks. Experimental results on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that qDKT achieves state-of-the-art performance in predicting learner outcomes. As a result, qDKT can serve as a simple yet highly competitive baseline for future question-centric knowledge tracing models.

Mobile and embedded applications demand neural network-based pattern recognition systems that operate efficiently within strict computational constraints. Unlike traditional synchronous, frame-based vision systems and convolutional neural networks (CNNs), asynchronous spiking neural networks driven by event-based visual input offer significantly lower latency and higher efficiency by responding selectively to sparse, salient features in the input. However, the discrete nature of event-based data streams presents challenges for directly training asynchronous neural networks. This paper explores asynchronous spiking neural networks derived from conventional CNNs trained on frame-based data. As a case study, we examine a CNN designed to guide a robot in tracking a moving target. We highlight potential issues in the conversion process and demonstrate how our proposed solutions bring the classification accuracy of the asynchronous network to within 3% of the original synchronous CNN, while reducing computational requirements by a factor of 12. Although applied to a relatively simple task, this work represents a critical advancement toward low-power, high-speed, and embedded neural network solutions for robotic vision systems.

In most machine learning tasks, a model $ M $ is evaluated on a given data population $ S $ using a population-level metric $ F(S; M) $. Common examples of such metrics include precision and recall for binary classification, the F1 score for multi-class classification, and the BLEU score for language generation. Meanwhile, the model $ M $ is typically trained by minimizing a sample-level loss function $ G(S_t; M) $ at each training step $ t $, where $ S_t $ is a subset of $ S $ (often referred to as a mini-batch). Popular loss functions include cross-entropy, Dice loss, and sentence-level BLEU scores.

A key assumption underlying this training paradigm is that the expected value of the sample-level loss $ G $, when averaged over all possible samples, should closely approximate the population-level metric $ F $ of the task. In other words, it is assumed that $ \mathbb{E}[G(S_t; M)] \approx F(S; M) $.

In this paper, we systematically examine the validity of this assumption across several natural language processing (NLP) tasks. We present both theoretical and empirical evidence showing that certain widely used sample-level loss functions $ G $ may not align with the true population-level metric $ F $ of the task. As a result, models trained to optimize these losses can be significantly suboptimal with respect to the actual performance metric. This discrepancy, which we refer to as **Simpson's bias**, stems from deep connections to the classic Simpson's paradox.

Protein engineering aims to discover protein sequences that exhibit enhanced or tailored properties. When informed by machine learning, sequence generation techniques can leverage existing knowledge and experimental data to refine and accelerate this endeavor. In this review, we examine recent advancements in the application of machine learning for generating protein sequences, with a particular emphasis on the rapidly evolving area of deep generative methods.

A novel message-passing (MP) approach is introduced for the matrix completion problem commonly encountered in recommender systems. The problem is addressed through a generative factor graph model, which is closely related to probabilistic low-rank matrix factorization. Based on this framework, we propose a new algorithm called IMP, designed to recover a data matrix from incomplete observations. The method combines a clustering step with inference via message passing, hence the name IMP. We evaluate the algorithm against several existing matrix completion techniques using real-world collaborative filtering datasets, such as Netflix. Our experimental results demonstrate that while many methods achieve comparable performance when a large portion of the data is observed, the IMP algorithm significantly outperforms others in scenarios where only a small fraction of entries are available. This advantage is particularly valuable, as it helps mitigate the well-known cold-start problem in collaborative filtering systems.

In this paper, we address the challenge of large-scale multi-agent reinforcement learning. First, we investigate the representation of the pairwise value function to reduce the complexity of agent interactions. Second, we introduce an l2-norm regularization technique to bound the trivial component of the approximated value function.
