Finally, experimental results on a battle game demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach.

Recent advancements in deep learning have demonstrated impressive performance in medical image analysis. However, most deep learning models require high-quality, human-annotated ground truth data for training. In practice, obtaining such annotations is costly and often limited, especially in the context of medical imaging. As a result, there has been growing interest in developing methods that can learn meaningful representations from unlabelled raw data. In this paper, we introduce a self-supervised learning approach for learning informative and transferable representations from medical imaging videos without any human supervision. We posit that understanding anatomical structures is key to learning useful representations, and thus we design the model to perform anatomy-aware tasks using only the information present in the data itself. Specifically, the model is trained to restore the original order of a shuffled video clip and simultaneously predict the geometric transformations applied to it. Experimental results on fetal ultrasound videos demonstrate that our approach effectively captures meaningful and robust representations, which generalize well to downstream tasks such as standard plane detection and saliency prediction.

The automatic digitization of paper maps represents a critical and complex challenge for both academic research and industrial applications. As a key step in the map digitization process, semantic segmentation has traditionally depended on manual visual interpretation, which is time-consuming and inefficient. In this study, we focus on urban planning maps as a representative sample and explore the potential of using a U-Shape fully convolutional network architecture for end-to-end semantic segmentation of maps. Experimental results from the Shibuya district in Tokyo show that our proposed method achieves a high Jaccard similarity coefficient of 93.63% and an overall accuracy of 99.36%. When implemented on a GPGPU with cuDNN acceleration, the processing time for the entire Shibuya district is less than three minutes. These results demonstrate that the proposed method offers a reliable and efficient solution for semantic segmentation of urban planning maps.

This paper primarily addresses the generation of personalized fonts as a problem of image style transfer. The main objective is to develop a network framework capable of extracting and recombining the content and style features of individual characters. These techniques enable the synthesis of an entire font set using only a small number of sample characters. The study integrates various deep learning architectures, including Convolutional Neural Networks, Multi-layer Perceptrons, and Residual Networks, to identify the most effective model for capturing font characteristics. Experimental results demonstrate that the generated characters are highly similar to real ones, as evaluated by the Structural Similarity Index and the Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio.

Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) is a widely used method for sampling from high-dimensional probability distributions in statistics and machine learning. HMC is known for its efficiency in practice, and its popular second-order "leapfrog" implementation has long been conjectured to require only $d^{1/4}$ gradient evaluations. In this work, we prove that this conjecture holds when sampling from strongly log-concave target distributions that satisfy a weak third-order regularity condition related to the input data. Our regularity assumption is less restrictive than the standard Lipschitz Hessian condition, enabling us to establish faster convergence rates for a broader class of distributions than previously possible with the Lipschitz Hessian alone. Notably, many important distributions, such as posterior distributions arising in Bayesian logistic regression, satisfy our regularity condition when the data exhibits an "incoherence" property. Our theoretical results improve upon the best-known bounds for strongly log-concave distributions, which typically scale as $d^{1/2}$. Furthermore, our experiments on synthetic data demonstrate that, under our regularity condition, the leapfrog HMC algorithm outperforms competing methods both in terms of accuracy and the number of gradient evaluations required.

Recent efforts in super-resolution for medical images have leveraged deep learning techniques, particularly Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), to produce perceptually realistic single-image super-resolution results. However, these approaches often struggle with generalization across different scale factors. This limitation necessitates the use of separate neural networks for each integer scale, leading to increased storage and energy demands. 

A recent paper introduced a novel meta-learning approach that employs a Weight Prediction Network, enabling super-resolution at arbitrary scale factors using a single, unified network. In this work, we present a new architecture that integrates this technique with SRGAN, a leading GAN-based super-resolution model, to achieve high-fidelity super-resolution for medical images at arbitrary scales.

By applying our proposed network to images from the Multimodal Brain Tumor Segmentation Challenge (BraTS) dataset, we demonstrate that it outperforms traditional interpolation methods by up to 20% in SSIM scores while maintaining strong generalizability on brain MRI data. Our experiments show that performance remains consistent across various scale factors, and the model achieves competitive results compared to state-of-the-art methods like EDSR—while being fifty times smaller in size. 

Combining efficiency, performance, and generalizability, this approach has the potential to serve as a new foundation for future research and applications in medical image super-resolution.

An orthogonal Haar scattering transform is a deep network that operates through a hierarchical process involving additions, subtractions, and absolute values applied to pairs of coefficients. It offers a straightforward mathematical framework for unsupervised deep learning. This approach incorporates non-linear contractions that are optimized for classification, utilizing an unsupervised pair matching algorithm with polynomial computational complexity. When applied to graph data, a structured Haar scattering generates permutation-invariant representations of connected groups of nodes. If the graph structure is unknown, unsupervised Haar pair learning can effectively estimate dyadic clusters of points. The method has been evaluated on image databases defined on regular grids or graphs, where the connectivity may be either known or unknown.

Normalization techniques are a fundamental component of the deep learning toolkit. They help accelerate and stabilize training, while reducing the need for carefully tuned learning rate schedules. However, when learning from multi-modal data, the performance of batch normalization (BN)—the most widely used normalization method—can be significantly diminished. To address this limitation, we introduce a more adaptable approach: by extending normalization to account for multiple means and variances, we can dynamically identify data modes and jointly normalize samples that exhibit similar characteristics. Our experiments show that this method outperforms BN and other standard normalization techniques across various tasks, including both single- and multi-task settings.

Variable screening is a rapid dimension reduction technique designed to aid in the selection of high-dimensional features. As a preselection method, it identifies a manageable subset of candidate variables that can then be further refined through feature selection to construct the final model. The effectiveness of variable screening relies on both computational efficiency and the capacity to significantly reduce the number of variables while preserving the important ones. When the data dimension $ p $ is much larger than the sample size $ n $, variable screening becomes essential for two reasons: 1) more efficient feature selection algorithms are required; and 2) the conditions that ensure selection consistency may no longer hold. This paper investigates a class of linear screening methods and develops a theoretical framework for their consistency. Specifically, we demonstrate that the restricted diagonally dominant (RDD) condition is both necessary and sufficient for strong screening consistency. As concrete examples, we show that two screening methods—SIS and HOLP—are strongly screening consistent (under additional constraints) with high probability when $ n > O\left((\rho s + \sigma/\tau)^2 \log p\right) $ under random design assumptions. Furthermore, we connect the RDD condition to the irrepresentable condition and discuss the limitations of SIS.

This paper introduces PatchNet, an automated tool that leverages hierarchical deep learning to classify code patches by extracting features from commit messages and code changes. PatchNet features a deep hierarchical architecture designed to reflect the sequential and layered structure of a code change, setting it apart from conventional deep learning models used for source code analysis. The tool offers multiple configurable parameters, enabling users to customize the training process according to their needs. PatchNet has been evaluated in the context of identifying stable-relevant patches within the Linux kernel and shows promise for application in other software engineering tasks that can be framed as patch classification problems. A demonstration video of PatchNet is available at [https://goo.gl/CZjG6X](https://goo.gl/CZjG6X), and the implementation can be accessed on GitHub at [https://github.com/hvdthong/PatchNetTool](https://github.com/hvdthong/PatchNetTool).

Approximate inference in complex probabilistic models, such as deep Gaussian processes, often involves optimizing doubly stochastic objective functions. These objectives introduce randomness through both mini-batch subsampling of the data and Monte Carlo estimation of expectations. When the gradient variance is high, the resulting stochastic optimization problem becomes challenging, leading to a slow convergence rate. While control variates can help reduce this variance, previous methods have failed to account for how mini-batch stochasticity interacts with sampling variability, resulting in suboptimal variance reduction. In this work, we propose a novel approach that leverages a recognition network to efficiently approximate the optimal control variate for each mini-batch, without requiring additional model gradient computations. We analyze the properties of our method and evaluate its performance on logistic regression and deep Gaussian processes.

**Objectives:** This study introduces a novel deep learning-based skull stripping method for magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) that operates directly in the k-space domain, preserving rich information typically lost in conventional image-domain approaches.  

**Materials and Methods:** We trained a deep learning model using two MRI datasets from different institutions, comprising a total of 36,900 slices. The model was designed to process complex raw k-space data directly, without prior transformation into the image domain. Skull stripping results obtained using HD-BET (Brain Extraction Tool) in the image domain were used as the ground truth for training and evaluation.  

**Results:** The proposed method demonstrated strong performance, achieving DICE scores ranging from 92% to 98% and Hausdorff distances below 5.5 mm across both datasets. Notably, performance was particularly high for slices above the eye region, with DICE scores reaching up to 99%. However, accuracy decreased in areas around and below the eyes, where some blurring and smoothing of edges at the brain-skull boundary were observed. Binary masks were generated using an appropriately selected threshold.  

**Conclusion:** This proof-of-concept study demonstrates the feasibility of performing skull stripping in the k-space domain, leveraging preserved phase information and delivering consistent results. Future research should explore additional applications of k-space data for advanced image analysis and improved processing workflows.

Traditional recommendation systems face two enduring challenges: data sparsity and the cold-start problem. These limitations have driven the development of Cross-Domain Recommendation (CDR), which aims to address these issues by leveraging information from other domains. Over the past decade, significant research efforts have been devoted to CDR. More recently, with the advancement of deep learning and neural networks, numerous new methods have emerged. However, there remains a lack of comprehensive and systematic reviews of CDR, particularly regarding the latest approaches, as well as the specific recommendation scenarios and tasks they target. In this survey paper, we present a two-level taxonomy of cross-domain recommendation that categorizes different recommendation scenarios and tasks. We then systematically review and summarize existing CDR methods under various scenarios. Additionally, we compile and organize commonly used datasets in the field. Finally, we outline several promising research directions for future exploration in cross-domain recommendation.

While rule-based attribution methods have proven effective in providing local explanations for Deep Neural Networks, the increasing diversity and complexity of modern architectures present new challenges in generating reliable and trustworthy explanations. This is because traditional rule sets may not be sufficient or applicable to these novel structures. To address this issue, network canonization has been introduced as an elegant solution. This process exploits the implementation-dependency of rule-based attributions by restructuring a model into a functionally equivalent form that is more amenable to established attribution techniques. However, the concept of canonization and its practical benefits have so far been explored primarily in a qualitative manner. In this work, we provide a quantitative evaluation of the effectiveness of network canonization when applied to rule-based attribution methods on VGG-16 and ResNet18 models with BatchNorm layers, thereby extending current best practices for obtaining reliable neural network explanations.

While adversarial training and its variants have emerged as the most effective methods for defending against adversarial attacks, their slow training process poses significant challenges when scaling to large datasets such as ImageNet. Recent efforts to accelerate adversarial training have focused on replacing multi-step attacks (e.g., PGD) with single-step attacks (e.g., FGSM). However, these single-step approaches often lead to catastrophic overfitting, where the model's accuracy against PGD attacks drops sharply to nearly zero during training, severely undermining its robustness.

In this work, we investigate the phenomenon of catastrophic overfitting from the perspective of individual training instances. We demonstrate that this issue is instance-dependent, with instances exhibiting larger gradient norms being more prone to causing catastrophic overfitting. Based on this insight, we propose a simple yet effective method called Adversarial Training with Adaptive Step size (ATAS). ATAS dynamically adjusts the step size for each instance in an inverse proportion to its gradient norm. Theoretical analysis shows that ATAS converges more efficiently than conventional non-adaptive methods. Empirically, ATAS effectively alleviates catastrophic overfitting and achieves superior robust accuracy on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet across a range of adversarial budgets.

Importance weighting is a widely studied and commonly used technique for addressing sample selection bias and covariate shift. It offers attractive properties such as unbiasedness, consistency, and low computational cost. However, weighting can also negatively impact the performance of an estimator. In this work, we empirically demonstrate that the sampling distribution of an importance-weighted estimator can be skewed. Specifically, in settings involving sample selection bias and with small sample sizes, the importance-weighted risk estimator tends to overestimate the risk for datasets that fall within the bulk of the sampling distribution—i.e., the majority of cases—and significantly underestimate the risk for data points in the tails. These inaccuracies in risk estimation can result in suboptimal regularization parameters when the estimator is used for importance-weighted validation.

Creating reliable prediction sets remains a significant challenge for the practical application of neural models: achieving distribution-free conditional coverage is theoretically unattainable, and the exchangeability assumption that supports the coverage guarantees of standard split-conformal methods is often violated in the presence of domain shifts. In light of these challenges, we introduce and analyze a data-driven approach for obtaining empirically reliable approximate conditional coverage. This method computes unique quantile thresholds for each label at each test point. Our approach leverages strong signals of prediction reliability derived from KNN-based model approximations on the training set and constrained samples from the held-out calibration set. We demonstrate the potential for substantial, previously unrecognized under-coverage when using split-conformal methods with marginal coverage guarantees—particularly in tasks such as protein secondary structure prediction, grammatical error detection, sentiment classification, and fact verification. These tasks span supervised sequence labeling, zero-shot sequence labeling (i.e., feature detection), document classification (with sparsity and interpretability constraints), and retrieval-classification, including scenarios with class imbalance and domain shifts.

Cross-validation (CV) is a widely used technique for estimating the generalization error of predictive models. When working with pipeline modeling algorithms—those involving multiple sequential steps—it is generally recommended that the entire pipeline be applied during each CV iteration, in order to simulate how the full pipeline would perform on an external test set. While this approach is theoretically sound, it can lead to significant computational overhead when the pipeline includes resource-intensive operations, such as imputation of missing values.

There is a common assumption that unsupervised variable selection—where the outcome is ignored—can be performed before CV without introducing bias. However, there is less agreement regarding the impact of performing unsupervised imputation of missing values prior to CV. In this study, we empirically evaluated whether conducting imputation before CV would result in biased estimates of generalization error or lead to suboptimal tuning of model parameters, potentially harming the external performance of downstream models.

The results indicate that although imputation conducted before CV may introduce some optimistic bias, the reduced variability associated with this approach compared to imputation performed within each CV replicate leads to a lower overall root mean squared error in estimating the true external R-squared. Moreover, the performance of models tuned using imputation before CV versus imputation during each CV replication shows only minimal differences.

In Franceschi et al. (2018), we introduced a unified mathematical framework rooted in bilevel programming, which integrates gradient-based hyperparameter optimization and meta-learning. We developed an approximate formulation of the problem, where the inner objective is solved iteratively, and established sufficient conditions for convergence to the exact solution. In this work, we demonstrate how to efficiently optimize learning rates, automatically adjust the weights of individual example losses, and learn hyper-representations using Far-HO, a software package built on top of TensorFlow. Far-HO enables seamless handling of both hyperparameter optimization and meta-learning tasks.

Images captured in rainy conditions often suffer from poor visibility, which can significantly degrade the performance of computer vision systems. Rainy scenes are typically classified into two categories: moderate rain and heavy rain. In moderate rain scenes, the primary issue is the presence of rain streaks, whereas heavy rain scenes involve both rain streaks and a veiling effect that resembles haze. While existing methods have shown remarkable success in handling each of these scenarios individually, there remains a lack of a unified framework that can effectively address both moderate and heavy rain conditions.

In this paper, we propose a hierarchical multi-direction representation network based on the contourlet transform (CT) to tackle both types of rainy scenarios. The CT decomposes an image into multi-directional subbands (MS) and a semantic subband (SS). First, rain streaks are extracted into the MS by leveraging the multi-orientation characteristics of the CT. Next, a hierarchical structure is introduced to restore the background information, including the loss of semantic details and the veiling effect present in the SS. Finally, a multi-level subband discriminator equipped with a feedback error map is designed to optimize all subbands effectively. This is the first architecture capable of efficiently addressing both moderate and heavy rain scenarios.

Event detection plays a crucial role in enabling timely decision-making within graph analytics applications. Although recent advances in deep learning on graphs have shown promise, detecting events in dynamic graph structures remains a significant challenge for existing models. Real-world events often manifest as abrupt changes in the normal behavior of a graph. However, current methods for dynamic node embedding fail to effectively capture the broader, graph-level dynamics that are relevant to such events.

In this paper, we introduce DyGED, a simple yet innovative deep learning model designed for event detection in dynamic graphs. DyGED captures the relationship between the macro-level dynamics of the graph—represented as a sequence of high-level graph embeddings—and labeled events. Additionally, our approach integrates structural and temporal self-attention mechanisms to better account for the varying importance of nodes and time steps in different applications.

Extensive experiments on a diverse set of datasets demonstrate that DyGED achieves up to 8.5% higher event detection accuracy compared to existing methods, while also offering improved scalability. We further present case studies that highlight the key characteristics and effectiveness of our model.

For lossy image compression, we have developed a neural-based system that learns a nonlinear estimator to decode from quantized representations. The system employs two recurrent networks that collaborate to reconstruct the same target image patches by leveraging complementary spatial context, with information exchanged through gradient signals. This dual-agent framework builds on prior work that introduced an iterative refinement algorithm for RNN-based decoding, which demonstrated improved image reconstruction compared to traditional methods. Our approach is compatible with any encoder—whether neural or non-neural—and progressively reduces reconstruction error for image patches over a fixed number of steps.

Experiments with various RNN memory cell configurations, both with and without future information, show that our model consistently produces images with lower distortion and higher perceptual quality than alternative approaches. Specifically, on the Kodak Lossless True Color Image Suite, our method achieves up to a 1.64 dB improvement over JPEG, 1.46 dB over JPEG 2000, 1.34 dB over the GOOG neural baseline, 0.36 dB over E2E (a modern competitive neural compression model), and 0.37 dB over a single iterative neural decoder.

With the successful application of deep learning in computer vision, significant progress has been made in the field of image super-resolution reconstruction. However, many studies have highlighted that the limitations of neural networks in extracting image features may lead to a degradation in the quality of reconstructed images. Additionally, generated images can sometimes appear overly smooth and artificial. To address these issues, we propose a novel self-calibrated convolutional generative adversarial network (GAN). The generator architecture comprises two main components: feature extraction and image reconstruction. For feature extraction, we employ self-calibrated convolutions, which are composed of four distinct modules, each serving a specific function. This design not only enhances the receptive field but also captures long-range spatial and inter-channel dependencies. Subsequently, the image reconstruction process is carried out, resulting in a high-quality super-resolution image. Extensive experiments were conducted on multiple datasets, including Set5, Set14, and BSD100, using the SSIM evaluation metric. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed network.

Natural gradient descent improves upon standard gradient descent by incorporating the Fisher information matrix of the underlying statistical model, thereby capturing partial second-order information. Several influential studies have promoted an approximation known as the empirical Fisher, linking approximate second-order methods to popular heuristics such as Adam. However, we challenge this perspective by demonstrating that the empirical Fisher—unlike the true Fisher information—does not generally reflect second-order structure. Furthermore, we argue that the conditions under which the empirical Fisher converges to the Fisher (or the Hessian) are rarely satisfied in practice. Even on simple optimization problems, the empirical Fisher can lead to problematic behaviors with adverse consequences.

Redundancy is widely acknowledged in Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), allowing for the removal of less important filters from convolutional layers, thereby reducing the network's size with minimal performance degradation. Drawing inspiration from the linear and combinational properties of convolution, we aim to make certain filters gradually converge and ultimately become identical, facilitating network compression. To achieve this, we introduce Centripetal SGD (C-SGD), a novel optimization method that trains multiple filters to collapse into a single point within the parameter hyperspace. Once training is complete, the identical filters can be removed without any loss in performance, eliminating the need for fine-tuning. This approach addresses an open challenge in constrained filter pruning for CNNs with complex architectures, where certain layers must be pruned in relation to others. Experimental results on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet demonstrate the effectiveness of filter pruning based on C-SGD. Furthermore, we provide empirical evidence supporting the hypothesis that redundancy in deep neural networks aids in training convergence, as a redundant CNN trained with C-SGD outperforms a similarly sized, conventionally trained network.

We investigate a novel approach to adapting the learning rate (LR) schedule in order to enhance the performance of ReLU-based networks during iterative pruning. Our work contributes four key aspects: (i) We observe that as a ReLU-based network undergoes iterative pruning, the distribution of weight gradients tends to narrow. This insight leads us to conclude that, as the network becomes sparser, a higher learning rate should be employed to train the pruned model. (ii) Building on this finding, we introduce a new LR scheduling strategy called S-Cyclical (S-Cyc), which modifies the conventional cyclical LR schedule by gradually increasing the maximum learning rate (max_lr) in an S-shaped manner as pruning progresses. Notably, S-Cyc is a method-agnostic LR schedule that can be applied across various iterative pruning techniques. (iii) We evaluate the effectiveness of S-Cyc and compare it against four established LR schedule benchmarks. Experimental results on three state-of-the-art networks—VGG-19, ResNet-20, and ResNet-50—and two widely used datasets—CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-200—demonstrate that S-Cyc consistently outperforms the best benchmark by 2.1% to 3.4%, with minimal additional computational overhead. (iv) Finally, we assess S-Cyc against an oracle and show that it achieves comparable or better performance.

Backdoor attacks represent a growing threat to Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), where an adversary injects a hidden backdoor into the model by corrupting the training data. This allows the model to misclassify inputs that contain a specific, adversarially designed trigger. A key challenge in defending against such attacks is that only the attacker is aware of the secret trigger and the target class. This challenge is further compounded by the emergence of "hidden triggers," which are subtly embedded within input samples, making them difficult to detect through visual inspection and rendering traditional anomaly detection methods ineffective.

To counter these subtle and imperceptible attacks, this work conducts a systematic analysis of how backdoor attacks affect the internal representations of DNNs—specifically, the set of neuron activations generated when the network processes training data. Based on our findings, we introduce PiDAn, an algorithm that leverages coherence optimization to clean poisoned data. Our analysis reveals that the representations of poisoned and legitimate data within the target class reside in distinct linear subspaces, leading to differences in their coherence with certain latent spaces. Exploiting this insight, PiDAn learns a sample-specific weight vector that maximizes the projected coherence of weighted samples, demonstrating that the learned weights effectively distinguish between genuine and poisoned data.

Machine learning pipelines frequently depend on optimization procedures to make discrete decisions, such as sorting, selecting the nearest neighbors, or finding the shortest path. While these decisions are computationally efficient, they disrupt the back-propagation process in computational graphs. To broaden the range of learning problems that can be addressed in an end-to-end manner, we introduce a systematic approach for converting optimizers into differentiable operations that remain smooth and non-locally constant. Our method employs stochastically perturbed optimizers, which can be seamlessly integrated with existing solvers. The derivatives of these operations can be efficiently computed, and their smoothness can be controlled through the amplitude of the added noise. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this framework connects to a family of losses used in structured prediction and provide theoretical guarantees for their effectiveness in learning tasks. We validate the performance of our approach through experiments across multiple tasks.

A simple method for weight initialization in deep neural networks, known as Layer-Sequential Unit-Variance (LSUV) initialization, is introduced. The approach involves two main steps: first, initializing the weights of each convolutional or fully connected layer with orthonormal matrices, and second, sequentially normalizing the variance of the output of each layer to one, starting from the first and moving toward the final layer. Experiments with various activation functions—including maxout, ReLU variants, and tanh—demonstrate that the proposed initialization enables the training of very deep networks that achieve (i) test accuracy comparable to or better than standard methods and (ii) training speeds that are at least as fast as more complex techniques designed specifically for deep networks, such as FitNets (Romero et al., 2015) and Highway networks (Srivastava et al., 2015). The method is evaluated on architectures like GoogLeNet, CaffeNet, FitNets, and Residual networks, achieving state-of-the-art performance or coming very close to it on benchmark datasets including MNIST, CIFAR-10/100, and ImageNet.

Computational auditory scene analysis has been gaining increasing attention in recent years. While it lags behind the more established field of speech recognition, general sound event detection has become a focal point of interest. Developing and evaluating effective models relies heavily on having access to sufficient, high-quality data—until recently, such datasets were scarce. In this work, we introduce and present a new database containing 714 high-quality WAV files featuring isolated sound events from 14 distinct categories, along with 303 additional "general" WAV files representing sounds that do not belong to these 14 categories. Each sound event is precisely labeled with perceptual onset and offset times, with in-between silences explicitly excluded. The quantity of isolated sound events, the accuracy of the annotations, and the inclusion of a dedicated general sound class set the NIGENS database apart from other existing datasets.

Big data refers to large-volume, rapidly growing datasets that are complex and sourced from multiple independent origins. Traditional technologies struggled to manage the storage and processing of such vast amounts of data, leading to the emergence of the Big Data concept. Handling unstructured data is a challenging task for users, as it lacks a predefined format. Therefore, there is a need for a mechanism that can organize this unstructured data into a structured format, making it easier for users to access the information they need. Classification techniques applied to big transactional databases help retrieve relevant data from large datasets in a more efficient manner. There are two primary types of classification techniques: supervised and unsupervised learning. This paper focuses on the study of various supervised classification methods and also highlights their respective advantages and limitations.

Neural networks represent data by projecting it onto trained weights within a high-dimensional manifold. These weights serve as a knowledge base that encodes causal relationships among different classes. Inference that relies on features capturing these relationships is referred to as feed-forward inference. Such mechanisms are grounded in classical cause-to-effect inductive reasoning models, which contribute to their widespread use due to their mathematical simplicity and ease of implementation. However, feed-forward models often struggle to generalize to unseen or untrained scenarios. To address this limitation, we introduce an effect-to-cause inference approach based on abductive reasoning. In this framework, features reflect the deviation from existing weight dependencies when a specific effect is observed. We refer to this deviation as *contrast*, and the corresponding reasoning process as *contrastive reasoning*. In this paper, we formalize the structure of contrastive reasoning and present a methodology for extracting a neural network's concept of contrast. We evaluate the effectiveness of contrastive reasoning in two stages of a neural network's decision-making pipeline: in both inferring and visually explaining classification outcomes for object recognition tasks. Our experiments demonstrate the benefits of contrastive reasoning in recognizing images under various distortions, showing improvements of 3.47%, 2.56%, and 5.48% in average accuracy under the proposed contrastive framework.

Difficult image segmentation tasks, such as segmenting the left atrium in MRI scans, can benefit from the incorporation of shape priors to ensure solutions align with known anatomical structures. However, a single multivariate Gaussian distribution is insufficient when dealing with significant nonlinear shape variations or multimodal prior distributions. While nonparametric density estimation offers greater flexibility, it demands large amounts of training data and presents substantial challenges in optimization, particularly in high-dimensional spaces.

In this work, we introduce a maximum-a-posteriori formulation that integrates both local intensity information and global shape priors through a generative image model. To capture complex intensity patterns without relying on manually designed features, we employ deep autoencoders. The shape prior is modeled as a mixture of Gaussians, and its parameters are learned directly in a high-dimensional shape space, avoiding the need for projection into a lower-dimensional subspace.

During segmentation, the identity of the mixture component is treated as a latent variable, which is marginalized within a generalized expectation-maximization framework. We propose a conditional maximization approach that alternates between computing a closed-form solution for component-specific shape parameters—enabling a global update strategy—and performing intensity-based energy minimization, thereby translating the global concept of a nonlinear shape into an efficient optimization process.

The Social Internet of Things (SIoT), which integrates the paradigms of the Internet of Things (IoT) and social networks, has emerged as a framework for creating a network of intelligent nodes capable of forming social connections. To address the challenge posed by misbehaving service provider nodes, service requestor nodes must assess the trustworthiness of their counterparts. In this paper, we introduce a novel trust management mechanism designed to predict the most reliable service providers for each service requestor, thereby reducing the risk of interaction with malicious entities.

We model the SIoT as a flexible bipartite graph, consisting of two sets of nodes: service providers and service requestors. A social network is then constructed among the service requestor nodes using the Hellinger distance to capture their relationships. Subsequently, a social trust model is developed based on node centrality and similarity measures to identify trust-related behaviors within the social network. Finally, a matrix factorization technique is employed to uncover latent features of SIoT nodes, identify trustworthy participants, and address issues such as data sparsity and the cold start problem.

We evaluate the impact of key parameters in our proposed trust prediction mechanism on the accuracy of predictions. The results demonstrate that feedback from neighboring nodes of a specific service requestor, which exhibit high Hellinger similarity, significantly enhances the reliability of trust assessments.

In real-world edge AI applications, model accuracy is often compromised by environmental factors such as noise, sensor placement, calibration issues, and temporal drift. This paper presents a neural network-based on-device learning approach to mitigate these challenges without delving into complex details. Unlike conventional backpropagation-based training, our method is specifically designed for resource-constrained edge devices. The approach is implemented on a wireless sensor node composed of a Raspberry Pi Pico and a low-power wireless module. Experimental results using vibration data from rotating machinery show that on-device retraining significantly enhances anomaly detection performance in noisy environments, while also reducing computational and communication overhead, making it more power-efficient.

Learning to take actions based on observations is essential for artificial agents to perform effectively and reliably in their tasks. Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a widely recognized approach for developing such policies. However, existing RL algorithms often struggle with reward shaping, face challenges in generalizing across different environments, and are typically inefficient in terms of sample usage. In this paper, we investigate active inference and the free energy principle—a theoretical framework from neuroscience that explains how self-organizing biological systems function by maintaining an internal model of the world and treating action selection as an inference process. We apply this framework to a classic problem in the RL community, the mountain car problem, and demonstrate how active inference can integrate both reinforcement learning and learning from demonstrations.

There has been an unprecedented rise in the number of service providers offering a diverse array of machine learning prediction APIs for tasks such as image classification and language translation, thereby monetizing the underlying data and trained models. Typically, a data owner—acting as the API provider—develops a model using proprietary data and relies on cloud vendors to host and serve API requests. This model inherently assumes complete trust between the API provider and the cloud vendor. However, a malicious or faulty cloud vendor could potentially copy the APIs, offer identical services under different branding, under-report model usage metrics, or unfairly disadvantage certain API providers by allocating them a minimal share of the revenue.

In this work, we present the design of a blockchain-based decentralized, trustless API marketplace that enables all stakeholders in the API ecosystem to independently audit the behavior of participants without relying on a single centralized authority. Our system achieves this by splitting an AI model into multiple components and deploying them across several cloud vendors, who then collaboratively execute the API requests. This design ensures that cloud vendors cannot collude to steal the combined model, while also maintaining the integrity and transparency of the entire process.

We demonstrate that model compression can enhance the population risk of a pre-trained model by analyzing the trade-off between reduced generalization error and increased empirical risk resulting from compression. First, we establish that model compression tightens an information-theoretic bound on generalization error, offering a theoretical justification for viewing model compression as a form of regularization that mitigates overfitting. Next, we quantify the increase in empirical risk due to compression using principles from rate-distortion theory. These findings suggest that model compression can lead to improved population risk when the reduction in generalization error outweighs the rise in empirical risk. We illustrate this phenomenon through a linear regression example, showing that population risk can indeed be reduced via model compression. Furthermore, our theoretical analysis indicates that the Hessian-weighted $K$-means clustering method for compression can be enhanced by incorporating regularization into the distance between cluster centers. Experimental results on neural networks are provided to validate our theoretical insights.

In the field of visual decoding, reconstructing visual images from corresponding human brain activity measured by functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) remains a challenging task, particularly when dealing with natural images. Visual reconstruction can be viewed as a conditional image generation problem based on fMRI data, and recent efforts have leveraged generative adversarial networks (GANs) for natural image generation in this context. While GAN-based approaches have shown significant improvements, the quality and realism of reconstructed images still fall short, largely due to the limited number of available fMRI data samples and the inherent instability in GAN training. To address these challenges, this study introduces a novel GAN-based Bayesian visual reconstruction method (GAN-BVRM). This approach incorporates a classifier for category decoding from fMRI data, a pre-trained conditional generator capable of producing natural images of specified categories, and a set of encoding models along with an evaluator to assess the quality of generated images. GAN-BVRM utilizes the pre-trained generator from the widely used BigGAN model to generate a large number of natural images, and selects those that best match the corresponding brain activity using the encoding models as the reconstructed image stimuli. Throughout this process, the semantic content of the reconstruction is controlled by the decoded categories, while the detailed features are guided by the encoding models. By adopting a Bayesian framework, GAN-BVRM effectively mitigates the conflict between image naturalness and fidelity.

This paper introduces a novel end-to-end deep learning framework that simultaneously learns the demand baseline and an incentive-driven agent demand response model, using net demand measurements and incentive signals. The proposed framework is structured into two modular components: (1) the decision-making process of a demand response participant is modeled as a differentiable optimization layer, which takes the incentive signal as input and outputs the user’s response; and (2) the baseline demand forecast is represented by a standard neural network that uses relevant features to predict the user’s baseline demand. These two intermediate predictions are combined to generate the net demand forecast. We then present a gradient-descent-based method that propagates the error in the net demand forecast backward to jointly update the parameters of both the agent model and the baseline demand forecast. The effectiveness of our approach is validated through computational experiments on synthetic demand response data and a large-scale real-world dataset. Results demonstrate that the method accurately identifies the demand response model, even in the absence of prior knowledge about the baseline demand.

Accurate hardware performance models play a crucial role in efficient code generation. They enable compilers to make informed heuristic decisions, serve as optimization objectives for superoptimizers, and assist autotuners in identifying the best configuration for specific programs. However, developing such models is challenging due to the complexity of modern processors, especially with the growing diversity of deep learning accelerators. In this work, we present a method for learning performance models from a large set of tensor computation graph programs tailored for Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). Our results show that the learned model outperforms a highly optimized analytical model on two key tasks—tile-size selection and operator fusion—and enhances an autotuner's ability to find faster programs, even when access to TPUs is restricted or costly.

We present and analyze an algorithm for first-order stochastic optimization over a broad class of functions in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Specifically, we focus on *variationally coherent* functions, which may be either convex or non-convex. For such functions, the iterates generated by our algorithm converge almost surely to the global minimizer $\boldsymbol{x}^*$. Furthermore, when applied to convex functions, the same algorithm with identical hyperparameters ensures that the expected suboptimality gap after $T$ iterations is bounded by $\widetilde{O}\left(\|\boldsymbol{x}^* - \boldsymbol{x}_0\| T^{-1/2 + \epsilon}\right)$ for any $\epsilon > 0$. This represents the first algorithm to simultaneously achieve both convergence guarantees and this optimal rate. Notably, the convergence rate for convex functions aligns closely with that of parameter-free methods. Our approach is based on the Follow The Regularized Leader framework, enhanced by the use of *rescaled gradients* and time-varying linearithmic regularizers.

In this paper, we present and validate a fully automated pipeline for generating hippocampal surfaces using a combination of 3D U-net and active shape modeling (ASM). The proposed method consists of three main stages. First, a 3D U-net is applied to each magnetic resonance image to automatically segment the hippocampus in both hemispheres. Next, ASM is used on a set of pre-defined template surfaces to compute the mean shape and shape variation parameters via principal component analysis. Finally, a hybrid particle swarm optimization algorithm is employed to identify the optimal shape variation parameters that best align with the segmentation results. The hippocampal surface is then reconstructed using the mean shape and the optimized variation parameters. The proposed pipeline demonstrates high accuracy, maintains correct anatomical topology, and produces smooth hippocampal surfaces for both hemispheres.

Image repurposing is a widespread technique used to spread misinformation on social media and online platforms. It involves sharing authentic images with altered metadata to fabricate false narratives and support propaganda efforts. Although manual verification remains an option, the sheer volume of verified information available online, combined with the growing ease of manipulating image semantics, highlights the need for reliable automated methods to assess the semantic integrity of multimedia content.

In this paper, we introduce a novel approach for detecting image repurposing, inspired by the real-world adversarial interaction between a malicious actor who alters image metadata and a watchdog tasked with verifying the consistency between an image and its associated metadata. Both parties have access to a reference dataset of verified content, which they can leverage to achieve their respective objectives. Our method demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in tasks such as location-identity, subject-identity, and painting-artist verification, underscoring its effectiveness across a wide range of applications.

There is growing interest in learning algorithms that involve interaction between humans and machines. One of the most intuitive methods for obtaining human feedback is through comparison-based queries. However, a key challenge in designing such interactive learning algorithms is dealing with noisy responses. The conventional approach to mitigate this issue is to repeat the same query multiple times. Unfortunately, this method is often impractical in real-world scenarios due to high costs and the unrealistic assumption that noise across repeated queries is independent.

In this paper, we introduce a novel weak oracle model in which a non-malicious user provides a response to a pairwise comparison only when they are confident in their answer. This model effectively captures the behavior of a human in uncertain or noisy conditions. We then explore the application of this weak oracle model to the problem of content search—a variant of the nearest neighbor search problem—using comparisons. Specifically, our goal is to develop efficient algorithms for locating a target object in a database that has a defined dissimilarity metric, by leveraging the weak comparison oracle.

We propose two algorithms, named WORCS-I and WORCS-II (Weak-Oracle Comparison-based Search), which provably locate the target object using a number of comparisons that is close to the theoretical minimum.

This study focuses on the challenge of predicting glaucomatous visual field loss using patient-specific disease data. The primary objective is to accurately forecast the progression of the disease for individual patients. However, due to the limited number of measurements available per patient, developing reliable individual predictors remains a significant challenge. A recently introduced clustering-based approach addresses this by improving prediction power through the use of patient data that exhibit similar spatiotemporal patterns. In this method, each patient is assigned to a cluster based on shared characteristics, and a predictive model is then built using the combined data from all patients within that cluster.

The accuracy of such predictions heavily relies on the quality of the clustering process, yet determining the optimal clustering method is often non-trivial. To address this, we propose a strategy for aggregating multiple cluster-based predictors, aiming to achieve more accurate predictions than those obtained from a single clustering approach. Moreover, our method demonstrates exceptional performance by hierarchically combining expert models derived from various clustering techniques. Using real-world datasets, we show that our hierarchical aggregation approach significantly outperforms traditional clustering-based and patient-wise regression methods. This superior performance stems from the mechanism that allows high-quality predictors within smaller communities to emerge and contribute effectively to the overall prediction.

Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks trained using gradient descent and back-propagation have achieved significant success across a wide range of applications. However, relying on point estimates for network weights is susceptible to overfitting and fails to capture the uncertainty inherent in the estimation process. While exact Bayesian neural network methods offer a principled approach to quantifying uncertainty, they are computationally intractable and not well-suited for real-world scenarios. In this work, we introduce an approximate method for estimating weight uncertainty based on the Ensemble Kalman Filter, which is highly scalable to networks with a large number of parameters. Additionally, we enhance the algorithm by optimizing the covariance of the noise distribution during the ensemble update step using maximum likelihood estimation. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we apply it to outlier detection in five real-world events extracted from the Twitter platform.

Interpretable machine learning has recently attracted significant attention. When explaining decisions made by black-box systems, it is essential to balance brevity and comprehensiveness in order to convey a large amount of information in a concise manner. However, existing interpretable machine learning approaches often fail to address both aspects simultaneously, resulting in explanations that are either too verbose or insufficiently informative. To address this challenge, we propose VIBI (Variational Information Bottleneck for Interpretation), a system-agnostic interpretable method that delivers brief yet comprehensive explanations. VIBI is grounded in the information bottleneck principle, an information-theoretic framework used to identify optimal representations. For each instance, VIBI identifies key features that are maximally compressed with respect to the input (ensuring brevity) while remaining highly informative about the decision made by the black-box model (ensuring comprehensiveness). We evaluate VIBI on three datasets and compare its performance with state-of-the-art interpretable methods, assessing both interpretability and fidelity through human evaluations and quantitative metrics.

We present a novel approach to text generation, with a focus on song lyrics, that leverages the speech-like acoustic characteristics of an input audio file. By repurposing a vocal source separation algorithm and an acoustic model originally designed for isolated speech recognition, we instead feed it instrumental music or environmental sounds. By analyzing the "errors" produced by the vocal separator, we derive a transcription of words that could be interpreted as being spoken within the original audio. We outline the core components of our method, provide initial experimental insights, and explore its potential for facilitating human-machine collaboration in creative domains.

Denoising remains a central challenge in scientific imaging. While deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable success in denoising natural images, their application in scientific imaging has been largely unexplored. Most CNN-based denoising methods are trained on real natural images that have been artificially corrupted with simulated noise. However, in scientific contexts, clean reference images—essential for training—are often unavailable.

To overcome this limitation, we introduce a simulation-based denoising (SBD) framework, where CNNs are trained using synthetically generated data. We evaluate the framework on transmission electron microscopy (TEM) data, an imaging modality widely used in material science, biology, and medicine. The SBD approach significantly outperforms existing techniques, both on simulated benchmark datasets and on real-world data.

In addition to producing high-quality denoised images, SBD provides likelihood maps that highlight the consistency between the denoised image and the original noisy data. Our findings expose limitations of current state-of-the-art denoising architectures, particularly their limited field-of-view. Expanding the receptive field of the CNNs enables them to capture non-local periodic structures, which are especially important under high-noise conditions. Furthermore, we investigate the generalization performance of the SBD framework across different imaging scenarios.

We address the problem of selecting the structure of a high-dimensional Ising (or graphical) model. To this end, we propose a straightforward algorithm for estimating the graph structure, which relies on thresholding the empirical conditional variation distances. We introduce a new criterion that identifies tractable graph families for which our method is efficient, based on the existence of sparse local separators between node pairs in the underlying graph. For such graphs, the proposed algorithm achieves a sample complexity of $ n = \Omega(J_{\min}^{-2} \log p) $, where $ p $ denotes the number of variables and $ J_{\min} $ represents the minimum (in absolute value) edge potential in the model. Additionally, we derive nonasymptotic necessary and sufficient conditions for successful structure estimation.

Melanoma is recognized as the most aggressive type of skin cancer. Due to the similarity in appearance between malignant and benign skin lesions, diagnosing these conditions often requires significant time and expertise. Currently, the assessment of malignancy primarily relies on invasive histological examination of suspicious lesions. Developing an accurate and efficient classifier for early detection can help reduce the harmful effects of skin cancer and improve patient outcomes. This paper introduces a multi-class classification approach utilizing the CoAtNet architecture—a hybrid model that integrates the depthwise convolution operations of traditional convolutional neural networks with the strengths of Transformer models and self-attention mechanisms. This combination enables improved generalization and model capacity. The proposed classifier achieves an overall precision of 0.901, recall of 0.895, and average precision (AP) of 0.923, demonstrating superior performance compared to other state-of-the-art models.

Simulation holds great promise for advancing the development of reliable algorithms for mobile agents operating in safety-critical environments. Nevertheless, current simulation platforms often suffer from limited photorealism and a lack of diverse sensor capabilities, which hinder their effectiveness in fully realizing this potential. In this work, we introduce VISTA, an open-source, data-driven simulator designed for autonomous vehicles. VISTA integrates multiple sensor modalities, including RGB cameras, 3D LiDAR, and event-based cameras, all based on high-fidelity real-world datasets. This enables the efficient creation of new viewpoints in simulation, significantly expanding the dataset available for policy learning—particularly for rare or challenging scenarios that are hard to replicate in the real world. Using VISTA, we demonstrate the successful training and evaluation of perception-to-control policies across different sensor types, and validate the approach through deployment on a full-scale autonomous vehicle. The policies developed in VISTA show strong sim-to-real transfer performance without modification, and outperform those trained solely on real-world data in terms of robustness.

Poor sitting habits have been recognized as a significant risk factor for musculoskeletal disorders and lower back pain, particularly among the elderly, disabled individuals, and office workers. In today's computer-driven world, people often spend long hours seated—whether during work or leisure activities—typically at a desk. This prolonged sitting can lead to spinal discomfort and related health issues. As a result, there is a growing need for systems that can monitor and improve sitting habits, offering timely reminders and suggestions such as engaging in physical activity.

Currently, most research on posture recognition has focused on standing postures, with less attention given to seated positions. Various methods have been employed in the literature for posture analysis, including wearable sensors, pressure or force sensors, video recordings, and image-based approaches. 

This study aims to develop Machine Learning models for classifying a person’s sitting posture by analyzing data collected from a chair equipped with two 32x32 pressure sensor arrays on the seat and backrest. Five classification algorithms were used: Random Forest (RF), Gaussian Naïve Bayes, Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Deep Neural Network (DNN). All models were evaluated using K-Fold cross-validation. The paper presents experiments conducted on two distinct datasets—controlled and realistic—and discusses the results obtained.

One-shot Neural Architecture Search (NAS) seeks to reduce the computational cost of identifying high-performing models. However, in recent years, it has become evident that naive random search can achieve performance comparable to that of leading NAS algorithms within the same search spaces. To tackle this challenge, we investigate the impact of significantly expanding the NAS search space and introduce Bonsai-Net, an efficient one-shot NAS approach designed to explore this relaxed space. Built around a modified differential pruner, Bonsai-Net consistently identifies state-of-the-art architectures that outperform random search while using fewer parameters than other cutting-edge methods. Furthermore, Bonsai-Net integrates model search and training in a single process, substantially reducing the time required to produce fully trained models from scratch.

Many critical data analysis applications involve highly imbalanced datasets, particularly with respect to the target variable. A common example is medical image analysis, where positive cases—such as the presence of a disease—are rare, yet accurate detection of these instances is crucial. To address this challenge, we frame the problem as anomaly detection using generative models. Specifically, we train an unsupervised generative model on the "negative" (common) data and leverage it to estimate the likelihood of unseen samples. A well-performing model can then identify "positive" cases as those with low likelihood values.

In this position paper, we explore the application of cutting-edge deep generative models—namely Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)—for estimating data likelihood. Our findings demonstrate that both GANs and VAEs are capable of distinguishing "positive" and "negative" samples in the MNIST dataset. However, in the more complex NLST dataset, neither model was able to fully capture the data's intricacies or effectively detect anomalies at the required level of precision. These results highlight that while generative models have shown promise in similar applications, significant challenges remain in their practical deployment for real-world, imbalanced data scenarios.

We analyze networks of learning agents that collaborate to solve a shared nonstochastic multi-armed bandit problem. These agents communicate over an underlying network, exchanging information about the actions taken by others, while discarding messages that take more than $d$ hops to arrive, where $d$ is a delay parameter. We introduce \textsc{Exp3-Coop}, a cooperative variant of the {\sc Exp3} algorithm, and establish that, with $K$ actions and $N$ agents, the average per-agent regret after $T$ rounds is at most on the order of $\sqrt{\left(d + 1 + \frac{K}{N} \alpha_{\le d}\right) T \ln K}$, where $\alpha_{\le d}$ denotes the independence number of the $d$-th power of the connected communication graph $G$. 

We demonstrate that for any connected graph, setting $d = \sqrt{K}$ yields a regret bound of $K^{1/4} \sqrt{T}$, which is strictly better than the minimax regret $\sqrt{KT}$ achieved by noncooperating agents. With more refined choices of $d$, the regret can be made arbitrarily close to the full-information minimax bound $\sqrt{T \ln K}$ when the graph $G$ is dense. In cases where $G$ has sparse components, we show that a modified version of \textsc{Exp3-Coop}, which allows agents to adjust their parameters based on their centrality in the graph, leads to improved regret performance.

As a secondary contribution, our analysis provides the first characterization of the minimax regret in bandit learning scenarios involving delayed feedback.

Prediction markets are widely used in real-world applications to forecast outcomes of interest, such as presidential elections. This paper introduces a mathematical framework for artificial prediction markets designed for supervised learning tasks, specifically for estimating conditional probabilities. The artificial prediction market is a novel approach to aggregating predictions from features or trained classifiers, with the final output represented as the price of a contract corresponding to each possible outcome.

The market can be trained incrementally by updating participants' budgets based on training examples. Drawing inspiration from real-world prediction markets, the underlying equations of the artificial market are derived from simple and intuitive assumptions. Efficient numerical algorithms are proposed to solve these equations.

It is shown that the resulting artificial prediction market corresponds to a maximum likelihood estimator. This method generalizes several existing techniques, including linear aggregation found in boosting and random forests, as well as logistic regression and certain kernel methods. Moreover, the market mechanism enables the integration of specialized classifiers that only participate in specific instances, enhancing flexibility and performance.

Experimental evaluations demonstrate that artificial prediction markets often outperform random forests and implicit online learning on both synthetic data and real-world UCI datasets. Furthermore, an extensive evaluation for detecting pelvic and abdominal lymph nodes in CT scans shows that the prediction market improves AdaBoost's detection rate from [insert value].
Proceedings of the BMVC 2019 Workshop on Interpretable and Explainable Machine Vision, held in Cardiff, UK, on September 12, 2019.

Data collection and annotation are labor-intensive tasks in machine learning, particularly for large-scale problems. A common solution to this challenge is to transfer knowledge from a related, labeled domain to a target domain. Two widely used approaches for this purpose are adversarial learning and self-training. In this paper, we first investigate the training instability and the issue of mistaken confusion that often occur during the adversarial learning process. Inspired by domain confusion and self-ensembling techniques, we propose a combined model that learns a joint invariant representation for both features and classes, referred to as Domain Confusion with Self Ensembling (DCSE). Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches on multiple unsupervised domain adaptation benchmarks.

Deep generative modeling using normalizing flows has become increasingly popular due to its ability to provide exact, tractable log-likelihood estimates, along with efficient training and synthesis processes. However, flow models face a significant challenge in dealing with high-dimensional latent spaces that match the dimensionality of the input data. To address this issue, Dinh et al. (2016) introduced a multi-scale architecture that progressively factorizes a portion of the total dimensions at regular intervals. Most prior work on generative flow models employing multi-scale architectures relies on static masking for dimension factorization. In this paper, we propose a novel multi-scale architecture that instead performs data-dependent factorization, determining which dimensions should pass through additional flow layers. To enable this, we introduce a heuristic based on the contribution of each dimension to the overall log-likelihood, which reflects the importance of different dimensions. This heuristic can be efficiently computed during the training process, allowing for a flexible implementation of our likelihood-based multi-scale architecture across various flow models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to several state-of-the-art flow models, achieving improvements in log-likelihood scores and sampling quality on standard image benchmarks. Additionally, we conduct ablation studies to evaluate the impact of our proposed method.

Cyber-physical systems (CPS) and Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices are being increasingly integrated into a wide range of applications, spanning from healthcare wearables to critical infrastructure such as nuclear power plants, autonomous vehicles, smart cities, and smart homes. These systems are inherently vulnerable across their entire software, hardware, and network stacks, creating a vast attack surface that can be exploited by malicious actors. In this article, we introduce an innovative approach for identifying unknown system vulnerabilities, effectively managing them, and enhancing incident response when these vulnerabilities are exploited. The core innovation of our method involves extracting insights from real-world CPS/IoT attacks, representing these attacks using regular expressions, and applying machine learning (ML) techniques to this collection of patterns in order to generate new attack vectors and security weaknesses. Our experimental results demonstrate that 10 novel attack vectors and 122 new vulnerability exploits can be successfully generated, each with the potential to compromise a CPS or IoT ecosystem. The ML-based methodology achieves an accuracy of 97.4% and significantly reduces the search space by 87.2%, enabling efficient prediction of potential attacks. We illustrate the practical application of our approach through a case study on the hacking of a connected car's in-vehicle network. To defend against such threats, we propose a proactive strategy that leverages the generated attack patterns to enhance system resilience and improve overall security posture.

ICD coding serves as the global standard for documenting and reporting health conditions and diagnoses, playing a critical role in the revenue cycle management of healthcare systems. However, manually assigning ICD codes is error-prone due to the extensive code vocabulary and the similarities among many codes. Machine learning approaches rely on high-quality labeled data, but inconsistencies among human coders introduce noise into the labeling process, complicating the training and evaluation of ICD classifiers. This paper examines the characteristics of such noise in manually assigned ICD-10 codes and proposes a method for training more robust ICD-10 classifiers despite the presence of labeling noise. Our research reveals that the nature of this noise is systematic rather than random. Most existing methods for handling label noise assume that errors are independent and randomly distributed, which does not hold true for ICD data. To address this, we introduce a new approach for training classifiers that can withstand systematic labeling noise. We first identify ICD-10 codes that are frequently misused or confused by human coders, based on their position within the ICD-10 hierarchy, their code types, and the behavior of a baseline classifier. Subsequently, we develop an innovative training strategy to improve classifier performance in the face of such noise.

In this paper, we address the problem of $\ell_p$ norm linear regression, which finds applications in areas such as sparse recovery, data clustering, and semi-supervised learning. Although the problem is convex, it does not admit a closed-form solution. Existing state-of-the-art algorithms are iterative but often face convergence challenges—either diverging for $p > 3$ or showing sensitivity to initial conditions. Moreover, these methods are typically not applicable for all possible values of $p$. 

To overcome these limitations, we introduce an iterative algorithm called **Parallel IteRative AlgOrithM for $\ell_p$ norm regression via MajorizaTion Minimization (PROMPT)**, which is based on the principle of Majorization Minimization. We establish that the proposed algorithm is monotonic and guaranteed to converge to the optimal solution for any value of $p$. Additionally, PROMPT allows for parallel updates of each component of the regression variable, making it highly efficient for handling large-scale datasets—a common requirement in the current era of data explosion.

We further demonstrate that the algorithm can be effectively applied to graph-based semi-supervised learning problems. Through extensive numerical simulations, we show that PROMPT converges to the optimal solution from any random initialization and outperforms existing methods in terms of both speed and accuracy.

Analyzing the morphology of cells in microscopy images can reveal important insights into the mechanisms of compounds or the functions of genes. Successfully addressing this task requires methods that can extract meaningful biological information while filtering out technical variations—such as differences in experimental procedures or equipment used to capture the images. To tackle this challenge, we introduce **Treatment Exemplars with Mixture-of-Experts (TEAMs)**, an embedding learning framework that trains a set of specialized experts to capture technical variations present in the training data. At inference time, these experts' predictions are aggregated, allowing TEAMs to generate robust embeddings with reduced bias from technical noise. 

To train our model efficiently, we utilize **Treatment Exemplars**, which enable our approach to represent the full distribution of the dataset within each minibatch while remaining compatible with GPU memory constraints. We evaluate TEAMs on three datasets for tasks such as drug discovery, achieving performance improvements of 5.5–11% over state-of-the-art methods in identifying the true mechanism of action of cell treatments.

$(j,k)$-projective clustering is a natural extension of the families of $k$-clustering and $j$-subspace clustering problems. Given a set of points $P$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, the objective is to find $k$ affine subspaces (flats) of dimension $j$ that best approximate $P$ according to a specified distance metric. In this paper, we present the first algorithm that computes an $L_\infty$ coreset with size polynomial in $d$. Additionally, we introduce the first strong coreset construction for general $M$-estimator regression. Our approach yields efficient coreset constructions for a wide range of loss functions, including Cauchy, Welsch, Huber, Geman-McClure, Tukey, $L_1-L_2$, and Fair regression, as well as for general concave and power-bounded losses. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of our method through experiments on real-world datasets.

The remarkable effectiveness of adversarial attacks in deceiving deep neural networks presents a significant challenge to the broader deployment of deep learning in safety- and security-critical applications. Although various adversarial defense techniques have been proposed since the discovery of neural network vulnerabilities, a comprehensive understanding and resolution of this issue remain elusive. In this study, we propose that a key factor behind the potency of adversarial attacks lies in their ability to implicitly access and exploit the gradient flow within a deep neural network. This inherent capability to manipulate gradient dynamics makes defending against such attacks particularly difficult. 

Motivated by this hypothesis, we suggest that if a deep neural network architecture can actively incorporate its own gradient flow during training, it could substantially enhance its resilience to adversarial perturbations. Drawing from this insight, we introduce a novel architectural concept known as *self-gradient networks*, which are specifically designed to improve robustness against adversarial attacks. By explicitly utilizing gradient flow information during training, self-gradient networks achieve greater stability against perturbations than is possible through conventional training methods. We perform a theoretical analysis to deepen our understanding of the behavior and performance of the proposed architecture.

In this paper, we address the challenge of clustering collections of very short texts using subspace clustering techniques. This task is prevalent in various applications, including product categorization, fraud detection, and sentiment analysis. The primary difficulty stems from the high dimensionality and extreme sparsity of the vector representations of short texts—high dimensionality arises from the large number of unique terms in the corpus, while sparsity results from the limited number of words in each text with little to no repetition. To tackle this problem, we introduce a novel and straightforward subspace clustering algorithm based on linear algebra. Experimental evaluations on identifying product categories from product titles sourced from the US Amazon website demonstrate that the proposed method performs competitively against existing state-of-the-art clustering approaches.

Machine learning models can pose significant risks to individual privacy, especially when the training data includes personal information. Recent attacks have demonstrated the ability to extract sensitive details from trained models through techniques such as model inversion and attribute inference. These attacks can expose specific private attributes of individuals who contributed their data to the model's training process. Research has also shown that various factors can increase the vulnerability of a model to inversion attacks, with feature influence being one such factor.

We note that not all features carry the same level of sensitivity or privacy risk. In many cases, certain features—such as those related to personal identity, health, or financial status—are particularly vulnerable and thus more likely to be targeted in inversion attacks. To address this issue, we propose a method for mitigating model inversion attacks in tree-based models by reducing the impact of sensitive features. This approach has not been extensively explored in prior work, with only limited efforts to use feature influence reduction as a defense against attribute inference.

Our research demonstrates that it is often possible to train models in different ways, leading to varying levels of feature influence, without compromising the model’s overall accuracy.
