To enhance its practical utility, we provide a detailed overview of the data collection process, preprocessing steps, and the statistical characteristics of the resulting dataset. Additionally, we present a thorough evaluation of state-of-the-art RecSys methods on a next-period recommendation task, along with an in-depth analysis of their performance across different metrics and datasets.

Predicting the geographical location of social media users, such as those on Twitter, has proven valuable in various fields including health surveillance, emergency response, content personalization, and social science research. In this study, we advance the field by developing and evaluating novel methods that integrate the principles of weighted multigraphs with cutting-edge deep learning techniques. The proposed approaches are built upon a shared structural foundation—an extended mention and/or follower network—but employ distinct information processing strategies. These include information diffusion via transductive and inductive algorithms, specifically RGCNs and GraphSAGE, as well as node embedding techniques like Node2vec+. To further enhance the models, attention mechanisms are incorporated to integrate users' textual content. We evaluate the performance of each method and compare them against baseline models using the publicly available Twitter-US dataset. Additionally, we release a new dataset derived from a large-scale Twitter capture in Latin America. Finally, our work critically examines the limitations and validity of comparisons between methods, considering different label definitions and evaluation metrics.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have garnered significant attention due to their impressive performance in tasks such as node classification. However, there remains a limited understanding of how and why GNNs function, particularly in the context of node representation learning. This paper introduces a theoretical framework to shed light on GNNs, focusing specifically on spectral graph convolutional networks and graph attention networks, from the perspective of graph signal denoising. Our analysis reveals that GNNs implicitly address graph signal denoising problems: spectral graph convolutions serve to denoise node features, while graph attentions help denoise edge weights. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a linear self-attention mechanism can achieve performance comparable to state-of-the-art graph attention methods. Based on our theoretical insights, we propose two new models, GSDN-F and GSDN-EF, which are effective for graphs with noisy node features and/or edges. We validate our theoretical findings and the efficacy of our proposed models through experiments on benchmark datasets. The source code is available at \url{https://github.com/fuguoji/GSDN}.

The geometry of three-dimensional (3D) graphs, composed of nodes and edges, is essential in various critical applications. A prominent example is molecular graphs, where the spatial arrangement significantly affects properties such as reactivity and biological function. To enable the integration of geometric information into deep learning models for 3D graphs, we introduce three geometric graph representations: positional, angle-geometric, and distance-geometric. As a proof of concept, we apply the distance-geometric representation in geometric graph convolutions. To leverage standard graph convolution networks, we implement a simple edge weight–edge distance correlation scheme, with parameters either set using reference values or optimized via Bayesian hyperparameter tuning. Experimental results on the ESOL and Freesol datasets demonstrate that geometric graph convolutions outperform traditional approaches. Our work highlights the effectiveness and potential of incorporating geometric information through distance-geometric representations in deep learning on 3D graphs.

In this work, we demonstrate how to apply the Operational Space Control (OSC) framework under joint and Cartesian constraints for reinforcement learning in Cartesian space. Our approach enables efficient learning with adjustable degrees of freedom, and allows for policy transfer without additional dynamics randomization in a KUKA LBR iiwa peg-in-hole task. Prior to simulation-based learning, we conduct system identification to align the simulation environment as closely as possible with the real robot's dynamics. By incorporating constraints into the OSC controller, we ensure safe learning on the real robot or enable the development of a flexible, goal-conditioned policy that can be effectively transferred from simulation to reality.

Deep reinforcement learning methods have achieved super-human performance across a wide variety of environments. However, these approaches are often highly inefficient, requiring orders of magnitude more data than humans to reach comparable levels of performance. To address this challenge, we introduce **Neural Episodic Control**—a deep reinforcement learning agent designed to quickly incorporate and act on new experiences. Our approach employs a semi-tabular representation of the value function, combining a buffer of past experiences with slowly updated state representations and rapidly changing value estimates. We demonstrate that our agent significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art, general-purpose deep reinforcement learning methods in terms of learning speed across a broad range of environments.

There are many approaches to achieving $\epsilon$-differential privacy (DP). However, determining the appropriate value of $\epsilon$ remains a challenge, as there is no universally accepted threshold for what constitutes a "sufficiently small" $\epsilon$. The choice of $\epsilon$ depends on the specific query and the nature of the data being queried. In this paper, we present a method for computing $\epsilon$ based on $\delta$, which represents the adversary's advantage in correctly guessing a particular property of the output. The attacker's objective can be expressed as a Boolean function over the estimation of specific attributes, potentially within a certain level of precision. For our analysis, we assume that both the input and output distributions are characterized by probability density functions or probability mass functions, and that the attributes involved are independent.

Machine Learning for Software Engineering (ML4SE) is a rapidly evolving research area focused on developing methods that assist software developers in their tasks. For these methods to be effectively applied in practice, they must achieve a sufficient level of quality to support rather than hinder developers. Although advances in code representation and data collection have enhanced model performance overall, they often overlook the specific information that can be derived from individual projects. In this work, we explore how model quality can be improved by tailoring it to a specific project. We propose a framework for evaluating quality improvements when models are fine-tuned for the method name prediction task on a particular project. We assess three models of varying complexity across three scenarios: training on a large dataset of Java projects, fine-tuning on data from a specific project, and training from scratch on that project's data. Our results demonstrate that per-project fine-tuning significantly enhances model performance by capturing the project's domain-specific characteristics and naming conventions. We have open-sourced the tool used for data collection and the code for running the experiments at: https://zenodo.org/record/6040745.

Today, most industrial robotic assembly tasks rely on fixed initial conditions to ensure successful assembly. These rigid constraints lead to high production costs and limited adaptability when new tasks are introduced. In this work, we aim to develop a more flexible and adaptable approach to robotic assembly by leveraging 3D CAD models for all components involved. We focus on a generic assembly task—the Siemens Innovation Challenge—where a robot must precisely assemble a gear-like mechanism into an operational system.

To achieve the millimeter-level accuracy required for this task and similar industrial applications, we employ a depth camera mounted close to the robot’s end-effector. We introduce a high-precision two-stage pose estimation method based on deep convolutional neural networks. This approach includes part detection, initial pose estimation, refinement, and effective handling of both near- and full symmetries in the components. The networks are trained on simulated depth images, with techniques implemented to ensure robust performance in real-world settings.

Our system achieves an average pose estimation error of 2.16 mm and 0.64 degrees, resulting in a 91% success rate for assembling randomly distributed parts. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first fully successful solution to the Siemens Innovation Challenge, with all components assembled at high accuracy and reliability.

Self-supervised learning has emerged as a powerful technique for learning image representations without relying on large labeled datasets. In the context of underwater robotics, developing computer vision algorithms that enhance perception capabilities—such as sonar image classification—is of significant interest. However, due to the sensitive nature of sonar imaging and the difficulty in interpreting sonar images, it is challenging to create publicly available, large-scale labeled datasets for training supervised learning models. 

In this work, we explore the effectiveness of three self-supervised learning methods—RotNet, Denoising Autoencoders, and Jigsaw—in learning high-quality sonar image representations without the need for human-labeled data. We present results from pre-training and transfer learning experiments conducted on real-world sonar image datasets. Our findings demonstrate that self-supervised pre-training achieves classification performance comparable to that of supervised pre-training in few-shot transfer learning scenarios across all three methods. 

Code and the self-supervised pre-trained models are available at [https://github.com/agrija9/ssl-sonar-images](https://github.com/agrija9/ssl-sonar-images).

Test Input Prioritizers (TIP) for Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) play a crucial role in efficiently managing typically large test datasets, thereby reducing computational and labeling costs. This is especially relevant in large-scale, deployed systems, where real-world inputs observed in production are often collected and used as potential test or training data for future system iterations. Feng et al. introduced DeepGini, a fast and straightforward TIP, demonstrating its superior performance compared to more complex methods like neuron coverage and surprise coverage. In a comprehensive study involving 4 case studies, 8 test datasets, and 32,200 trained models, we confirmed their results. However, we also found that other simple baselines from the field of uncertainty quantification—such as the predicted softmax likelihood or the entropy of the softmax probabilities—perform just as effectively as DeepGini.

We present a novel framework for training a model that can learn to segment objects from a collection of images without the need for human annotations. Our approach is based on the observation that the location of object segments can be locally perturbed relative to a background without compromising the realism of the scene. 

The method begins by training a generative model of a layered scene, which consists of three components: a background image, a foreground image, and a mask representing the foreground. A composite image is then created by overlaying the masked foreground onto the background. This generative model is trained adversarially using a discriminator, ensuring that the generated composite images are realistic.

To encourage the generator to produce foreground layers that correspond to actual objects, we introduce random shifts in both the foreground image and its corresponding mask relative to the background. Since the generator is unaware of these shifts during output generation, it must produce layered representations that remain realistic under any such perturbation.

Data augmentation has been extensively explored to enhance the accuracy and robustness of classifiers. However, the potential of image augmentation in improving GAN models for image synthesis remains underexplored in prior research. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive investigation into the effectiveness of various existing augmentation techniques for GAN training across multiple settings. We offer insights and practical guidelines on how to apply image augmentation to both standard GANs and GANs with regularization methods, significantly boosting the quality of generated images. Surprisingly, we find that vanilla GANs can achieve generation quality comparable to recent state-of-the-art results when augmentations are applied to both real and generated images. Furthermore, when combined with other augmentation-based regularization strategies—such as contrastive loss and consistency regularization—these augmentations lead to even higher-quality image generation. Our approach sets new state-of-the-art results for conditional image generation on CIFAR-10 by incorporating both consistency loss and contrastive loss as additional regularizations.

We investigate sequential decision-making problems with the goal of maximizing the expected total reward while adhering to a constraint on the expected total utility. To address the discounted infinite-horizon optimal control problem in Constrained Markov Decision Processes (Constrained MDPs), we employ the natural policy gradient method. Specifically, we introduce a novel Natural Policy Gradient Primal-Dual (NPG-PD) algorithm, which updates the primal variable using natural policy gradient ascent and the dual variable through projected subgradient descent.

Despite the underlying optimization problem involving a nonconcave objective function and a nonconvex constraint set, we establish global convergence with sublinear rates for both the optimality gap and constraint violation under the softmax policy parametrization. This convergence is independent of the size of the state-action space, making it dimension-free. Furthermore, for log-linear and general smooth policy parametrizations, we derive sublinear convergence rates that are affected by a function approximation error due to the restricted policy class.

We also provide theoretical guarantees on convergence and finite-sample complexity for two sample-based variants of the NPG-PD algorithm. Finally, we present computational experiments that demonstrate the effectiveness and advantages of our proposed approach.

High-throughput mRNA sequencing (RNA-Seq) is a widely adopted approach for quantifying gene isoforms. However, RNA-Seq data alone is often insufficient to accurately determine the origin of reads from different isoforms, which limits the precision of transcript quantification. To address this challenge, we propose integrating protein domain-domain interaction information as prior knowledge into an integrative analysis framework with RNA-Seq data. We present Net-RSTQ, a network-based method for RNA-Seq-based transcript quantification that combines protein domain-domain interaction networks with short-read alignment data to improve transcript abundance estimation.

Our key insight is that the expression levels of neighboring isoforms connected by domain-domain interactions are positively correlated. Based on this, Net-RSTQ models the expression of neighboring transcripts using Dirichlet priors on the likelihood of observed read alignments against transcripts within a gene. This allows for a joint estimation of transcript abundances across all genes through an alternating optimization process that solves multiple EM problems.

In simulation studies, Net-RSTQ demonstrated improved accuracy in quantifying isoform transcripts when isoform co-expression patterns were aligned with their interaction networks. Experimental validation using qRT-PCR on 25 multi-isoform genes in stem cell, ovarian cancer, and breast cancer cell lines further supported the effectiveness of Net-RSTQ, as it produced more consistent isoform proportions compared to standard RNA-Seq quantification methods.

Furthermore, experiments on RNA-Seq data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) showed that Net-RSTQ provided more reliable and biologically meaningful transcript abundance estimates, highlighting its potential for improving transcriptome analysis in complex biological systems.

Reinforcement Learning (RL) can be viewed as a sequence modeling problem, where a model sequentially predicts future actions based on a history of state-action-reward interactions. Recently, Transformers have been effectively applied to this task. In this paper, we introduce the State-Action-Reward Transformer (StARformer), which explicitly captures local causal dependencies to enhance action prediction in long sequences. StARformer first generates local representations—referred to as StAR-representations—from short time windows of state-action-reward tokens. These local representations, along with global state information, are then used to make accurate action predictions over extended time horizons. Experimental results demonstrate that StARformer outperforms existing Transformer-based methods on both Atari (image-based) and Gym (state-vector-based) benchmarks, across both offline RL and imitation learning settings. Additionally, StARformer exhibits superior performance with longer input sequences compared to baseline models. The code is publicly available at [https://github.com/elicassion/StARformer](https://github.com/elicassion/StARformer).

This paper introduces a novel convolutional layer called Perturbed Convolution (PConv), designed to simultaneously enhance the performance of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and mitigate the memorization issue in discriminators, where they tend to retain all training images as training progresses. In PConv, perturbed features are generated by randomly modifying the input tensor prior to the convolution operation. Despite its simplicity, this method proves to be remarkably effective. First, to maintain consistent output despite the perturbation, each layer in the discriminator must learn robust features with a small local Lipschitz constant. Second, the random perturbation during training acts similarly to dropout, thereby reducing the risk of memorization. To validate the effectiveness and generalizability of our approach, we conducted extensive experiments across multiple datasets—such as CIFAR-10, CelebA, CelebA-HQ, LSUN, and tiny-ImageNet—and various loss functions. The quantitative results show that PConv significantly improves the performance of both GANs and conditional GANs, as measured by the Frechet Inception Distance (FID).

Approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) is a well-established and widely used technique for likelihood-free inference, with applications across various scientific disciplines. The success of ABC hinges critically on the quality of the summary statistics employed. Selecting effective summary statistics typically relies on domain expertise and manually engineered features, making the process both time-consuming and labor-intensive. Moreover, due to the sensitivity of ABC to data dimensionality, the selection of summary statistics must strike a balance between incorporating informative features and managing the complexity of the feature space.

This paper introduces a novel approach by framing the problem of dynamically choosing an optimal summary statistic from a set of candidate statistics as a multi-armed bandit problem. This enables ABC rejection sampling to adaptively focus on a distribution of high-performing summary statistics rather than relying on a fixed set. The proposed method stands out for its ability to operate without any pre-processing and its scalability to large numbers of candidate statistics. As a result, it facilitates the efficient use of extensive libraries of time series summary statistics without the need for prior feature engineering.

The approach is evaluated against state-of-the-art methods for summary statistic selection using a challenging test problem drawn from the systems biology literature.

The typical application of code smells assumes a causal relationship: identifying a smell, removing it, and thereby improving the code. We empirically examine whether this assumption holds true. We outline a set of properties that code smells should exhibit if they genuinely contribute to lower code quality. Our evaluation involved 31,687 Java files from 677 GitHub repositories, all of which had over 200 commits in 2019. We assessed the impact of these smells on four key metrics related to quality, productivity, and bug detection efficiency.

Out of the 151 code smells identified by the CheckStyle detector, fewer than 20% showed potential causality, with only a small number demonstrating strong, consistent effects. The most impactful smells were related to simplicity, defensive programming, and abstraction. Files that lacked these potentially causal smells were 50% more likely to be of high quality.

Unfortunately, many code smells remain unaddressed. Developers often focus on removing the easier ones rather than those that have the greatest effect on code quality.

We present an efficient computational framework designed to accelerate a wide range of machine learning algorithms with minimal impact on accuracy. The framework leverages projections through a novel class of structured matrices, termed *Structured Spinners*, which are constructed as products of three matrix blocks incorporating rotational transformations. This approach is highly general in several respects:  
i) the structured matrices can be either fully randomized or learned,  
ii) the proposed family encompasses all previously studied structured schemes as special cases,  
iii) it extends naturally to non-linear settings where projections are followed by non-linear functions, and  
iv) it finds broad applicability in areas such as kernel approximation via random feature maps, dimensionality reduction, fast cross-polytope LSH techniques, deep learning, convex optimization using Newton sketches, quantization with random projection trees, and more.

The framework is supported by theoretical guarantees that characterize its performance relative to unstructured counterparts, and is grounded in a general theoretical principle outlined in the paper. As a result of our analysis, we provide the first theoretical guarantees for one of the most effective existing LSH algorithms based on the HD3HD2HD1 structured matrix [Andoni et al., 2015]. Comprehensive experimental evaluations confirm the effectiveness and versatility of the proposed approach.

We introduce any-precision deep neural networks (DNNs), which are trained using a novel method that enables the models to adapt their numerical precision during inference. The same model can be dynamically configured at runtime to different bit-widths by truncating the least significant bits, allowing for flexible trade-offs between speed and accuracy. When all layers are set to low-bit precision, we demonstrate that the model achieves accuracy comparable to dedicated models trained at the same precision level. This capability significantly enhances the practical deployment of deep learning models in real-world scenarios, where balancing accuracy and efficiency is often critical.

Prior work has focused on training separate models for each fixed efficiency or accuracy trade-off point. However, achieving runtime flexibility in numerical precision remains largely unexplored. When the required balance between efficiency and accuracy changes dynamically or frequently, retraining models becomes impractical, and maintaining multiple models may not be feasible due to storage constraints. Our proposed framework provides this flexibility without compromising performance.

Importantly, our approach is architecture-agnostic and applicable across various vision tasks. We have made our code publicly available at https://github.com/SHI-Labs/Any-Precision-DNNs.

We consider a population divided into multiple communities and investigate the problem of identifying the largest community through sequential, random sampling of individuals. The population is also partitioned into several sampling domains, referred to as *boxes*. Each box may contain individuals from different communities, and each community may be distributed across multiple boxes. At any point, the learning agent can sample (with replacement) an individual from any selected box. Upon sampling, the agent learns both the community of the sampled individual and whether this individual has been previously sampled. The objective of the agent is to minimize the probability of incorrectly identifying the largest community within a fixed budget, by optimizing both the sampling strategy and the decision rule. We introduce and analyze new algorithms for this task, and establish information-theoretic lower bounds on the probability of error across all possible algorithms. In several important cases, the exponential decay rates of the error probability under our algorithms are shown to be optimal up to constant factors. Additionally, we validate the performance of our algorithms through simulations on real-world datasets.

Rectified Linear Units (ReLUs) have emerged as the dominant activation function in artificial neural networks. In this paper, we investigate two fundamental learning problems under the assumption that the data are generated by a ReLU network—a neural network with ReLU activations. As a primarily theoretical work, we focus on single-layer networks.  

The first problem involves dictionary learning in the presence of nonlinearity, modeled through ReLU functions. Given a set of observation vectors $\mathbf{y}^i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ for $i = 1, 2, \dots, n$, our goal is to recover the $d \times k$ matrix $A$ and the latent vectors $\{\mathbf{c}^i\} \subset \mathbb{R}^k$, under the model $\mathbf{y}^i = \mathrm{ReLU}(A\mathbf{c}^i + \mathbf{b})$, where $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is a random bias. We demonstrate that, under certain conditions on the distribution of $\mathbf{b}$, it is possible to recover the column space of $A$ with an error bounded by $O(d)$ in the Frobenius norm.  

The second problem concerns the robust recovery of a signal in the presence of outliers—large but sparse noise. Here, we aim to reconstruct the latent vector $\mathbf{c}$ from its noisy nonlinear sketches of the form $\mathbf{v} = \mathrm{ReLU}(A\mathbf{c}) + \mathbf{e} + \mathbf{w}$, where $\mathbf{e} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ represents the outlier component and $\mathbf{w}$ denotes additive noise.

We explore a data-driven approach for constructing uncertainty sets in robust optimization, where the uncertain problem parameters are treated as random variables with an unknown joint probability distribution. Using only independent samples drawn from this distribution, we develop a nonparametric method to estimate uncertainty sets that are guaranteed to capture a specified target probability mass within a given tolerance, with high confidence. The nonparametric estimators considered are shown to satisfy distribution-free finite-sample performance bounds, ensuring their convergence in probability to the desired target mass. Moreover, these estimators are computationally efficient and lead to uncertainty sets that result in tractable robust optimization problems across a wide range of constraint functions.

Inspired by the learned iterative soft thresholding algorithm (LISTA), we propose a general class of neural networks designed for sparse signal reconstruction from limited linear measurements. By incorporating a broad range of weight-sharing strategies across layers, our framework supports a unified analysis of diverse network architectures, from recurrent structures to those resembling standard feedforward networks. Using empirical risk minimization based on training data, we aim to learn the optimal network parameters that enable accurate signal recovery from low-dimensional measurements. We derive generalization bounds by examining the Rademacher complexity of hypothesis classes composed of these deep networks, taking into account both network weights and thresholding parameters. Our results yield sample complexity estimates that scale linearly with the number of parameters and the network depth. We demonstrate the applicability of our findings by deriving specific generalization bounds for several practical scenarios, including various (implicit) dictionary learning algorithms and convolutional neural networks.

Comparing the top $ k $ elements across two or more ranked lists is a common task in various contexts and applications. While several measures have been proposed to assess the similarity of top $ k $ lists, they often exhibit limitations and practical shortcomings despite their appealing mathematical properties. This paper introduces a novel measure for comparing any two top $ k $ lists by analyzing the information content they convey. Our approach leverages the compressibility of the lists, where the length of the message required to losslessly encode them provides a natural and robust indicator of their variability. This information-theoretic measure objectively captures the key factors in assessing (dis)similarity between lists: the extent of non-overlapping elements, the degree of disorder among overlapping elements, and the displacement of ranks for shared items.

Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is widely employed for optimizing non-convex functions. However, the standard convergence theory for SGD in the smooth non-convex setting typically guarantees only sublinear convergence to a stationary point. In this work, we present several convergence theorems for SGD that establish convergence to a global minimum under additional structural assumptions on the non-convex problem. Specifically, we analyze two broad classes of structured non-convex functions: (i) Quasi (Strongly) Convex functions, which generalize convex functions, and (ii) functions satisfying the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition, a generalization of strongly convex functions.

Our analysis relies on an Expected Residual condition, which we demonstrate to be a strictly weaker assumption than previously used growth conditions, expected smoothness, or bounded variance assumptions. We provide theoretical guarantees for the convergence of SGD under various step-size strategies, including constant, decreasing, and the recently introduced stochastic Polyak step-size. Furthermore, our results hold within the arbitrary sampling framework, allowing us to derive insights into the complexity of minibatching and determine an optimal minibatch size.

Finally, we show that for models that perfectly interpolate the training data, the Expected Residual condition can be dispensed with, leading to state-of-the-art performance in this setting.

The issue of data imbalance often hinders the classification performance of neural networks. In this paper, we introduce a novel supervised discriminative feature generation (DFG) approach tailored for datasets with a minority class. The DFG framework is built upon a modified generative adversarial network architecture that incorporates four independent components: a generator, a discriminator, a feature extractor, and a classifier. To enhance the extraction of discriminative features for the minority class, an attention mechanism is employed. The generator is trained for the class-imbalanced task, while the feature extractor and classifier are regularized using pre-trained features from a large-scale source dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that the DFG generator effectively generates label-preserving and diverse features, leading to significant improvements in classification performance on the target task. This feature generation model holds great potential for advancing data augmentation techniques through the integration of discriminative feature generation and supervised attention mechanisms.

We investigate the problem of identifying the best arm in a stochastic multi-armed bandit setting. Consider a set of $ n $ arms, indexed from $ 1 $ to $ n $, where each arm $ i $ is associated with an unknown reward distribution supported on $[0,1]$ with mean $ \theta_i $ and variance $ \sigma_i^2 $. Assume that the means satisfy $ \theta_1 > \theta_2 \geq \cdots \geq \theta_n $. We introduce an adaptive algorithm that leverages both the gaps and variances of the reward distributions, making future decisions based on the collected information through a novel technique called *grouped median elimination*. 

The proposed algorithm ensures that the best arm is selected with probability at least $ 1 - \delta $, while using at most  
$$
O\left( \sum_{i=1}^n \left( \frac{\sigma_i^2}{\Delta_i^2} + \frac{1}{\Delta_i} \right)(\ln \delta^{-1} + \ln \ln \Delta_i^{-1}) \right)
$$
samples, where $ \Delta_i $ (for $ i \geq 2 $) represents the gap between the mean of arm $ i $ and the best arm, and we define $ \Delta_1 = \Delta_2 $. This approach offers a significant improvement over variance-independent algorithms in certain favorable settings and is the first result to eliminate the additional $ \ln n $ factor compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

Furthermore, we establish a lower bound showing that any algorithm aiming to achieve the same goal must sample at least  
$$
\Omega\left( \sum_{i=1}^n \left( \frac{\sigma_i^2}{\Delta_i^2} + \frac{1}{\Delta_i} \right) \ln \delta^{-1}

Belief propagation is a core message-passing algorithm used for probabilistic reasoning and inference in graphical models. Although it is exact on tree-structured graphs, it is commonly applied to graphs with cycles in practice. Understanding the behavior of "loopy" belief propagation has long been a key challenge in machine learning. Existing convergence guarantees for belief propagation typically rely on strong assumptions that imply the underlying model exhibits decay of correlations.

In this work, we show that, under a natural initialization, belief propagation converges rapidly to the global optimum of the Bethe free energy for Ising models on any graph, provided the model is **ferromagnetic**—that is, neighboring variables tend to align. This result holds even when the model exhibits long-range correlations or has multiple suboptimal fixed points. We also establish a similar convergence result for the naive mean-field equations. Notably, both results are **dimension-free**, meaning that a constant number of iterations suffices to obtain a good approximation of the Bethe or mean-field free energy.

To improve the accuracy of protein-protein interaction function prediction, this paper proposes a second-order graph neighbor information feature extraction method based on an undirected simple graph, which extends the traditional first-order graph neighbor feature extraction approach. Additionally, the chi-square test is incorporated into the feature combination process. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed second-order graph neighbor features, four logistic regression models—logistic regression (LR), diffusion kernel logistic regression (DKLR), polynomial kernel logistic regression (PKLR), and radial basis function (RBF)-based kernel logistic regression (RBF KLR)—are applied to two different feature sets. Experimental results on the Yeast Proteome Database (YPD) using protein-protein interaction data from the Munich Information Center for Protein Sequences (MIPS) demonstrate that the second-order graph neighbor information significantly enhances the overall average percentage of protein function prediction, particularly when combined with RBF KLR. Furthermore, by employing a novel top-5 chi-square feature selection method, RBF KLR achieves an impressive average overall prediction accuracy of 99.05% on the second-order neighbor feature set.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as powerful machine learning techniques for solving and identifying partial differential equations (PDEs). In this work, we utilize PINNs to solve the Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) equations for incompressible turbulent flows without relying on any specific turbulence model or assumption, using only boundary data. We first demonstrate the effectiveness of PINNs in solving the Navier–Stokes equations for laminar flows by addressing the Falkner–Skan boundary layer problem. Subsequently, we apply PINNs to simulate four different turbulent flow scenarios: zero-pressure-gradient boundary layer, adverse-pressure-gradient boundary layer, turbulent flow over a NACA4412 airfoil, and flow over a periodic hill. The results highlight the strong performance of PINNs in capturing laminar flows with significant pressure gradients, achieving predictions with less than 1% error. For turbulent flows, the method also delivers highly accurate simulations, including reliable predictions of Reynolds-stress components.

Deep convolutional neural networks have achieved remarkable success in a wide range of image classification tasks. Current methods for interpreting the predictions of pre-trained models typically rely on gradient-based approaches, which often produce saliency maps that highlight the overall foreground object. However, human reasoning involves breaking down an image into smaller, more meaningful concepts and identifying their presence or absence. The final interpretation is usually an aggregation of these individual components.

In this work, we introduce MACE: a Model-Agnostic Concept Extractor. This framework enables the explanation of convolutional network behavior by identifying and leveraging smaller, concept-based features. MACE decomposes the feature maps generated by a convolutional network to extract prototypical explanations grounded in these concepts. Moreover, it quantifies the relevance of each extracted concept to the model's prediction—a crucial element for explaining class-specific decisions, which is often overlooked in existing methods.

We evaluate MACE using popular architectures such as VGG16 and ResNet50, on benchmark datasets including Animals With Attributes 2 (AWA2) and Places365. Experimental results show that the concepts identified by MACE enhance the interpretability of model explanations while maintaining fidelity to the underlying black-box model.

In this work, we introduce a modified neural network model designed to simulate Markov chains. We demonstrate how to formulate and train such a network, ensure that it captures the desired statistical properties from the training data, and present several applications where the model generates non-deterministic outcomes. For instance, it can be used to model a random walker—useful for simulating Brownian motion—or a natural Tic-Tac-Toe network that exhibits non-deterministic gameplay.

A variety of deep learning architectures have been proposed to address the wide range of time series data encountered across different domains. In this article, we provide an overview of typical encoder and decoder structures used in both one-step-ahead and multi-horizon time series forecasting, explaining how each model integrates temporal information into its predictions. We then discuss recent advances in hybrid deep learning models that merge established statistical approaches with neural network components, aiming to enhance the performance of traditional methods. Finally, we explore several ways in which deep learning can support decision-making processes through the analysis of time series data.

Significant advancements in deep learning have made it increasingly easy and cost-effective to create video forgeries. As a result, developing reliable methods for detecting such manipulations has become crucial. This paper presents an effective approach for identifying various types of video forgeries. The problem is formulated as a per-frame binary classification task. To enhance performance across diverse facial manipulation scenarios, we leverage transfer learning from face recognition tasks. Additionally, in low-resolution settings where single-frame detection proves inadequate, we explore the use of neighboring frames to improve the classification of the central frame. Both strategies are evaluated on the public FaceForensics benchmark, achieving state-of-the-art results in terms of accuracy.

This paper presents an analysis of character-level machine translation models in the context of pivot-based translation, particularly when applied to sparse and noisy datasets such as crowdsourced movie subtitles. Our experimental results show that character-level models reduce the number of untranslated words by more than 40%, and they demonstrate significant improvements—up to 2–3 BLEU points—in scenarios with limited training data. We investigate the effects of character alignment, phrase table filtering, bitext size, and the selection of pivot language on translation quality. Additionally, we compare cascaded translation models with the use of synthetic training data generated through multiple pivots, and find that the latter approach yields superior performance. Finally, we highlight that neither word-level nor character-level BLEU scores perfectly align with human judgments, owing to BLEU's sensitivity to sentence length.

Ultra-short laser pulses, ranging from femtoseconds to attoseconds, represent the briefest controlled events achievable by humans. Accurately characterizing these pulses—both in terms of amplitude and phase—is essential in ultrafast science, particularly for studying processes such as chemical reactions and electronic phase transitions. In this work, we present and demonstrate, through both numerical simulations and experimental validation, the first deep neural network approach for reconstructing ultra-short optical pulses. We expect that this method will significantly broaden the range of ultrashort laser pulses that can be characterized, including the ability to detect extremely weak attosecond pulses.

Previous generations of face recognition algorithms have shown variations in accuracy across different racial groups, leading to race bias. In this work, we explore the potential underlying factors contributing to such bias—both data-driven and scenario-based—and discuss methodological considerations for evaluating race bias in these systems. We examine data-driven factors, including image quality, population statistics within the dataset, and algorithm architecture, as well as scenario modeling factors that take into account the role of the algorithm's user, such as threshold settings and demographic constraints.

To illustrate these issues, we analyze data from four face recognition algorithms—three deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) and one previous-generation system—focusing on their performance with East Asian and Caucasian faces. Our findings reveal several key insights: first, dataset difficulty affects both overall recognition accuracy and the extent of race bias, with bias increasing as the difficulty of the test items rises. Second, the level of bias varies depending on the identification threshold used; to achieve equal false accept rates (FARs), East Asian faces generally require higher thresholds than Caucasian faces across all algorithms. Third, demographic constraints in how distributions are defined during testing can significantly influence estimates of algorithmic accuracy.

We conclude that race bias must be assessed on a case-by-case basis, tailored to specific applications. To support this, we provide a comprehensive checklist for measuring and addressing race bias in face recognition algorithms.

Sktime is an open-source, Python-based, and sklearn-compatible toolkit for time series analysis, developed by researchers at the University of East Anglia (UEA), University College London, and the Alan Turing Institute. A primary initial objective of sktime was to offer time series classification capabilities comparable to those found in the Java-based package tsml, also developed at UEA. In this work, we present the implementation of six classifiers within sktime and compare them to their tsml counterparts. We validate correctness by demonstrating equivalent accuracy across a range of standard benchmark problems and evaluate the build times of the different implementations. While we observed only a minor difference in accuracy for one of the six algorithms—Proximity Forest—this discrepancy has presented some challenges during debugging. Additionally, we found a more significant variation in efficiency between the two toolkits. Although this difference was anticipated, it underscores potential areas for improvement in both sktime and tsml.

Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) represent a specific class of learning systems inspired by the functioning of biological neural networks, particularly exhibiting a strong affinity for Hebbian learning—often summarized as "neurons that fire together, wire together." However, unlike their biological counterparts, ANNs feature a tightly coupled structure where the modules of neurons are interdependent. This strict coupling imposes a rigid framework on the network, requiring all layers to update their weights only after completing a full forward and backward pass. While this constraint was acceptable in earlier stages of machine learning, it has become increasingly impractical in the current era of large-scale machine learning, where parallelization across multiple computing platforms is essential.

To address this limitation, synthetic gradients (SG) combined with decoupled neural interfaces (DNI) have been introduced as an alternative to the traditional backpropagation algorithm. This paper presents a speed benchmark comparing the performance of SG-DNI with that of a standard neural interface using a multilayer perceptron (MLP). The results indicate that SG-DNI demonstrates significant promise, not only in effectively capturing the learning task but also in achieving over three times faster training due to its asynchronous learning capabilities.

It is well-established that greedy methods perform effectively in the context of maximizing monotone submodular functions. However, they tend to struggle when dealing with non-monotonic functions. In this paper, we present a surprising yet significant result: by running the classical greedy algorithm $ O(\sqrt{k}) $ times, we obtain the currently fastest deterministic algorithm, known as **Repeated Greedy**, for maximizing a general submodular function under $ k $-independent system constraints. Repeated Greedy achieves a $(1 + O(1/\sqrt{k}))k$-approximation ratio using $ O(nr\sqrt{k}) $ function evaluations, where $ n $ and $ r $ represent the size of the ground set and the maximum size of a feasible solution, respectively.

We then introduce **Sample Greedy**, a randomized algorithm that achieves the best-known approximation guarantee for submodular maximization under $ k $-extendible system constraints—a subclass of $ k $-independent constraints. By employing a careful sampling procedure, Sample Greedy runs the greedy algorithm only once and attains a $(k + 3)$-approximation with just $ O(nr/k) $ function evaluations.

Furthermore, we establish an almost tight lower bound, demonstrating that no polynomial-time algorithm can achieve an approximation ratio better than $ k + 1/2 - \varepsilon $ for any $ \varepsilon > 0 $. To validate our theoretical findings, we evaluate the performance of both Repeated Greedy and Sample Greedy against existing approaches in a concrete application—movie recommendation systems.

In this paper, we introduce three novel error bounds for covariance estimation under differential privacy, expressed in terms of the Frobenius norm. These bounds are: (1) a worst-case bound of $\tilde{O}(d^{1/4}/\sqrt{n})$, which outperforms the standard Gaussian mechanism's $\tilde{O}(d/n)$ in the regime where $d > \widetilde{\Omega}(n^{2/3})$; (2) a trace-sensitive bound that achieves a $\sqrt{d}$-factor improvement over existing results; and (3) a tail-sensitive bound that provides more instance-specific guarantees. The associated algorithms are straightforward and computationally efficient. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that these methods significantly outperform prior approaches.

Communication in parallel systems introduces significant overhead, often becoming a bottleneck in parallel machine learning. To alleviate this burden, this paper introduces EventGraD—a stochastic gradient descent algorithm that employs event-triggered communication for parallel machine learning. The core concept of EventGraD is to replace the standard requirement of communication at every iteration with communication only when necessary, based on predefined events. We provide a theoretical analysis of the convergence properties of our algorithm. Furthermore, we implement EventGraD for data-parallel training of a widely used residual neural network on the CIFAR-10 dataset, demonstrating that it can reduce communication overhead by up to 60% while maintaining the same level of accuracy. Additionally, EventGraD can be effectively combined with techniques such as Top-K sparsification to further minimize communication without sacrificing performance.

While traditional statistical inference methods and machine learning generalization bounds assume that tests are conducted on data that is independent of the hypotheses being tested, real-world data analysis and machine learning are often iterative and adaptive processes. In such scenarios, the same holdout data is frequently reused for testing a sequence of hypotheses or models, where each subsequent test may depend on the results of previous ones. In this work, we introduce RadaBound, a rigorous, efficient, and practical method for controlling generalization error when performing multiple adaptive tests on a holdout sample. Our approach leverages a novel application of Rademacher Complexity bounds, specifically adapted to handle dependent testing scenarios. We validate the effectiveness and practical utility of our method through extensive simulations and comparisons with existing techniques.

Biology serves as both a critical application domain and a driving force behind the advancement of sophisticated machine learning techniques. While significant research has focused on large and complex datasets generated by high-throughput sequencing, recent developments in high-quality video recording technologies have also produced rich data sources that demand advanced methods from both computer vision and time-series analysis. Similarly, just as studying gene expression in one organism can uncover principles applicable to others, investigating complex social interactions in experimentally controlled model systems—such as laboratory ant colonies—can yield insights into the dynamics of broader social structures. In this work, we examine a specific case study from the research on reproductive regulation in small laboratory colonies of more than 50 *Harpegnathos* ants. These ants can be induced to undergo a ~20-day process of hierarchical reorganization. Although the final outcome of this process is readily observable, it remains unclear which behaviors during the transitional phase are essential to its progression. To address this challenge, we investigate the potential of One-class Classification (OC) for detecting abnormal states in ant colonies, where only behavioral data is available.

The growing availability of large-scale healthcare data repositories highlights the need for efficient tools to enable data-driven medicine. In this work, we present a distributed system based on Stratified Locality Sensitive Hashing (SLSH) that enables fast, similarity-based prediction on extensive medical waveform datasets. Our implementation, tailored for an ICU use case, emphasizes low latency and is designed for cloud deployment. We apply our system to the task of predicting Acute Hypotensive Episodes from Arterial Blood Pressure waveforms. On a dataset containing 1.37 million data points, we demonstrate scalability up to 40 processors, achieving a 21× speedup in the number of comparisons compared to a parallel exhaustive search—albeit with a 10% reduction in the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC). Moreover, when a higher tolerance for MCC loss is acceptable, our system can deliver speedups of up to two orders of magnitude.

The recent global outbreak of the novel coronavirus (COVID-19) has presented significant challenges to the research community. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based approaches can play a crucial role in predicting key epidemic parameters, risks, and impacts. These predictions can aid in the effective control and prevention of disease spread. However, the primary challenges in applying AI to such scenarios include limited data availability and inherent uncertainty.

In this study, we propose a shallow long short-term memory (LSTM)-based neural network for predicting the risk category of a country. To enhance performance, we employ a Bayesian optimization framework to automatically design and optimize country-specific models. The results demonstrate that our proposed pipeline outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods when tested on data from 180 countries, making it a valuable tool for risk categorization.

We also explored the integration of trend data with weather data for improved prediction. However, the results indicate that weather factors do not significantly influence the outcomes. This tool has the potential to forecast long-term outbreaks of similar epidemics, enabling early preventive measures and better preparedness.

Applying machine learning to molecules is challenging due to their natural representation as graphs rather than vectors. While several deep learning architectures have been proposed for molecular graph analysis, they often face information bottlenecks by only propagating information between directly connected nodes. To address this, we introduce a more expressive route-based multi-attention mechanism that incorporates features from paths between node pairs. We name this approach Graph Informer. This allows a single network layer to attend to nodes that are multiple steps away. Empirically, our method outperforms existing approaches in two key tasks: (1) predicting 13C Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectra, achieving a state-of-the-art mean absolute error of 1.35 ppm, and (2) predicting drug bioactivity and toxicity. Additionally, we develop an injective variant of Graph Informer that is provably as powerful as the Weisfeiler-Lehman test for graph isomorphism. Furthermore, we show that the use of route information enables the model to capture nonlocal topological features of the graph, thereby surpassing the limitations of the Weisfeiler-Lehman test.

Many data types encountered in data mining applications can be represented as bipartite graphs. Examples include terms and documents in a text corpus, customers and purchased items in market basket analysis, and reviewers and movies in a movie recommendation system. In this paper, we introduce a novel data clustering approach that is based on partitioning the underlying bipartite graph. The partitioning is achieved by minimizing a normalized sum of edge weights between unmatched vertex pairs in the bipartite graph. We demonstrate that an approximate solution to this optimization problem can be efficiently obtained through a partial singular value decomposition (SVD) of the corresponding edge weight matrix. We highlight the relationship between our clustering method and correspondence analysis, a technique commonly used in multivariate statistical analysis. Additionally, we briefly address the challenge of assigning data objects to multiple clusters. To evaluate the performance of our algorithm, we apply it to the task of document clustering and present experimental results that illustrate its effectiveness and efficiency.

Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) represents a promising approach for robotic control, demonstrating the ability to learn effective policies for high-dimensional, continuous control of complex, unmodeled systems. However, the field of robotic reinforcement learning currently lacks well-defined benchmark tasks, which hinders reproducibility and makes it challenging for researchers to compare their work with previous studies. While "Reacher" tasks—essential for robotic manipulation—are frequently used as benchmarks, they often lack formal specifications, omitting critical details necessary for accurate replication. In this paper, we present an empirical analysis that reveals how unstated spatial constraints in standard Reacher task implementations significantly ease the learning of a successful control policy using Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG), a leading DRL algorithm. Our findings suggest that less constrained versions of the Reacher task are considerably more challenging to master, indicating that current de facto benchmarks do not adequately reflect the true difficulty of general robotic manipulation.

We introduce a novel Stochastic Frank-Wolfe (also known as conditional gradient) algorithm tailored for constrained smooth finite-sum minimization problems that involve a generalized linear structure. This class of problems encompasses empirical risk minimization under sparse, low-rank, or other structured constraints. The proposed approach is straightforward to implement, eliminates the need for manual step-size tuning, and maintains a constant per-iteration computational cost that is independent of the dataset size. Moreover, as a byproduct of the algorithm, we derive a stochastic estimator of the Frank-Wolfe gap, which can serve as an effective stopping criterion. Depending on the specific setting, our method achieves or surpasses the best-known computational guarantees for stochastic Frank-Wolfe algorithms. Empirical evaluations on multiple datasets demonstrate regimes where the proposed method converges faster than existing approaches. Finally, we provide an open-source implementation of all the methods considered in this work.

Transferring knowledge across multiple streaming processes remains an underexplored area in current literature, characterized by several unique challenges: the absence of labeled data in the target domain, covariate shift between source and target domains, and differing drift patterns in the source and target domains. To address these challenges, this paper introduces Autonomous Transfer Learning (ATL), a flexible deep learning framework designed for online, unsupervised transfer learning across multiple streaming tasks. ATL employs an online domain adaptation strategy that integrates generative and discriminative phases, along with a KL divergence-based optimization approach, to build a domain-invariant network. It also features an elastic network architecture that enables automatic evolution of the model structure from scratch, either with or without access to ground truth, thereby effectively handling independent concept drifts in both source and target domains. Comprehensive numerical experiments have been conducted, comparing ATL with recent state-of-the-art methods. The results demonstrate that ATL achieves superior performance while significantly outperforming existing approaches in terms of training speed.

Machine learning models are susceptible to data-poisoning attacks, where an adversary manipulates the training data to alter the model's predictions. In a trigger-less attack, the attacker modifies the training set but not the test inputs, whereas in a backdoor attack, the attacker can also tamper with the test inputs. Current model-agnostic defense methods either fail to address backdoor attacks or lack strong guarantees, such as certificates that provide formal proof of security. We introduce BagFlip, a model-agnostic certified defense mechanism that effectively protects against both trigger-less and backdoor attacks. Our evaluation on image classification and malware detection datasets demonstrates that BagFlip performs as well as or better than existing state-of-the-art approaches for trigger-less attacks, and outperforms them for backdoor attacks.

Mouse dynamics offers a promising approach for user authentication. Traditionally, such systems have relied on classical machine learning techniques; however, recent advances have seen the introduction of deep learning methods for this purpose. While prior studies have shown that both machine learning and deep learning models can be compromised by carefully designed adversarial samples, there has been limited exploration of adversarial attacks in the context of behavioural biometrics. To address this gap, we developed a set of attacks based on generative approaches, aiming to create adversarial mouse trajectories that can bypass authentication models. These synthetic mouse sequences serve as adversarial examples within our experimental framework.

We also conduct an analysis of the attack strategies we investigated, highlighting their respective limitations. Unlike previous work, our study considers a more realistic and challenging scenario in which an attacker has access to recorded user data but lacks knowledge of the authentication model or its outputs. We examine three distinct attack strategies: 1) statistics-based, 2) imitation-based, and 3) surrogate-based. Our results demonstrate that these approaches are capable of successfully evading the functionality of authentication models, thereby undermining their robustness.

Federated learning has emerged as a key technology for training machine learning models across distributed data sources without exposing sensitive data. In particular, vertical federated learning—also known as feature-based federated learning—applies when different data sources share the same set of sample IDs but have distinct feature sets. To maintain the long-term participation of data owners, it is essential to fairly evaluate each source's contribution and provide appropriate compensation. The Shapley value (SV), rooted in cooperative game theory, offers a mathematically sound method for assessing contributions. However, calculating the SV involves retraining the model for every possible subset of data sources, which leads to prohibitively high communication costs in federated settings. To address this challenge, we introduce the Vertical Federated Shapley Value (VerFedSV), a contribution valuation metric based on the Shapley value. We demonstrate that VerFedSV not only satisfies important fairness properties but also enables efficient computation and can be integrated with both synchronous and asynchronous vertical federated learning frameworks. Comprehensive theoretical analysis and extensive experiments confirm the fairness, efficiency, and adaptability of VerFedSV.

A key feature that distinguishes the Bayesian approach is the use of marginalization, as opposed to relying on a single set of weights. Bayesian marginalization can significantly enhance the accuracy and calibration of modern deep neural networks, which are often underspecified by the data and capable of representing multiple plausible yet distinct solutions. We demonstrate that deep ensembles offer an effective way to approximate Bayesian marginalization, and we introduce an enhanced method that further refines the predictive distribution by marginalizing within basins of attraction, with minimal additional computational cost. Additionally, we examine the prior over functions induced by a vague distribution over neural network weights, offering a probabilistic explanation for the generalization behavior of such models. From this viewpoint, we clarify phenomena that have previously been considered mysterious or unique to neural network generalization, such as the ability to fit images with random labels, and show that these effects can be replicated using Gaussian processes. We also find that Bayesian model averaging mitigates the double descent phenomenon, leading to consistent performance improvements as model flexibility increases. Finally, we present a Bayesian interpretation of tempering as a technique for calibrating predictive distributions.

Building on the work of MacKay (1992), we contend that traditional model-based active learning methods, such as BALD, suffer from a critical limitation: they do not directly account for the distribution of input variables at test time. This oversight can result in suboptimal acquisition strategies, as the most informative samples for refining model parameters may not necessarily be the most informative for making accurate predictions. For instance, this discrepancy can arise when the pool set exhibits greater variability than the target prediction task, or when the distributions of the pool and test data differ. To address this issue, we revisit an acquisition strategy that aims to maximize the expected information gain regarding future predictions, which we term Expected Predictive Information Gain (EPIG). However, due to its limited scalability for batch acquisition, we also explore a hybrid approach that combines elements of BALD and EPIG, which we refer to as Joint Expected Predictive Information Gain (JEPIG). We evaluate both strategies in the context of active learning with Bayesian neural networks across multiple datasets, with a particular focus on their performance under distribution shifts in the pool set.

In recent years, there has been growing interest in video action recognition systems and models. However, direct comparisons of accuracy and computational performance have remained challenging due to variations in training environments, hardware configurations, hyperparameters, processing pipelines, and inference approaches. This paper presents a comprehensive, fair comparison of fourteen off-the-shelf and state-of-the-art models by maintaining consistency across these key training factors, enabling a more meaningful evaluation of different video action recognition algorithms. Model performance is assessed using standard Top-1 and Top-5 accuracy metrics, as well as a newly proposed accuracy measure. Furthermore, we evaluate the computational efficiency of distributed training across two to sixty-four GPUs on a cutting-edge high-performance computing (HPC) system.

Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) seeks to transfer knowledge from a labeled source domain to a distinct, unlabeled target domain. Most existing UDA approaches focus on learning domain-invariant feature representations, either at the domain level or the category level, typically using convolutional neural network (CNN)-based architectures. A key challenge in category-level UDA is the generation of reliable pseudo labels for target domain samples, which are often noisy and lead to suboptimal domain alignment, thereby degrading overall performance. 

With the growing success of Transformer models across various tasks, we observe that their cross-attention mechanism is more robust to noisy input pairs, making it well-suited for effective feature alignment. Motivated by this, we propose to leverage Transformers for the challenging UDA task. Specifically, to generate more accurate input pairs, we introduce a two-way center-aware labeling algorithm to produce high-quality pseudo labels for target samples. 

Complementing these pseudo labels, we present a weight-sharing triple-branch Transformer framework that employs self-attention for feature learning in both source and target domains, and cross-attention for domain alignment between them. This design explicitly encourages the model to learn both discriminative domain-specific and domain-invariant representations simultaneously. The proposed method is named CDTrans (Cross-Domain Transformer), and it represents one of the earliest efforts to address UDA tasks using a pure Transformer architecture.

Probabilistic hierarchical time-series forecasting is a critical area within time-series analysis, focusing on modeling and predicting multivariate time series that exhibit underlying hierarchical structures. Most existing methods concentrate on point predictions and fail to deliver well-calibrated probabilistic forecasts. Even recent state-of-the-art approaches impose hierarchical constraints on point estimates or sampled distributions, without properly addressing the coherency of the full forecast distribution. Additionally, prior work often assumes that datasets strictly conform to the given hierarchical relationships, neglecting real-world scenarios where such consistency may be lacking.

To address these limitations, we introduce PROFHIT, a fully probabilistic hierarchical forecasting model that jointly models the distribution of the entire hierarchy. PROFHIT employs a flexible Bayesian framework and introduces a novel Distributional Coherency Regularization technique, enabling the model to learn from hierarchical relationships across the full forecast distribution. This approach leads to more robust, well-calibrated forecasts and enhances adaptability to datasets with varying levels of hierarchical consistency.

Extensive evaluations across a wide range of datasets demonstrate that PROFHIT achieves 41–88% improvement in accuracy and calibration compared to existing methods. Moreover, due to its ability to model coherency across the entire distribution, PROFHIT remains effective in providing reliable forecasts even when up to 10% of the input time-series data is missing.

In the healthcare system, patients are often required to use wearable devices for the remote collection and real-time monitoring of health data and their medical conditions. The widespread adoption of these devices has led to a substantial increase in the volume of data being collected and transmitted. However, since these devices are powered by small batteries, their energy can be quickly depleted due to the high processing demands associated with data acquisition and transmission.

Given the critical nature of medical data, it is essential that all transmitted information maintains strict integrity and availability. To extend the battery life of these devices, reducing the amount of data transmitted and the frequency of transmissions can be effective. This can be achieved through the use of inference algorithms that optimize data handling.

A key challenge lies in improving transmission performance while maintaining accuracy and efficiency, as these two factors often conflict—enhancing one may come at the expense of the other. This paper presents a solution using machine learning to analyze complex health data metrics, particularly focusing on the balance between accuracy and efficiency in data transmission. By employing the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm, the study demonstrates how both accuracy and efficiency can be improved simultaneously by transmitting fewer samples without compromising data quality.

The algorithm was tested using a standard heart rate dataset to evaluate its effectiveness in comparison to traditional methods.

With the emergence of the 5th generation wireless standards and the growing demand for higher data rates, enhancing the spectral efficiency of wireless systems has become increasingly critical. In the context of cognitive radio, significant improvements in throughput can be achieved if secondary users make intelligent decisions about which channels to monitor and how frequently to do so. In this work, we introduce an algorithm that not only selects an optimal channel for data transmission but also predicts how long a channel will remain free, thereby reducing the time spent on channel sensing. The algorithm operates in two stages: it employs a reinforcement learning framework for channel selection and a Bayesian method to determine the optimal interval during which sensing can be temporarily skipped. Through extensive simulations, we compare our approach with other learning techniques. Our results demonstrate that the number of channel sensing operations can be significantly reduced with minimal impact on primary user interference. This leads to lower energy consumption by the secondary user and improved overall throughput by minimizing the time spent on sensing.

We study model-free reinforcement learning in infinite-horizon discounted Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) with continuous state spaces and an unknown transition kernel, where only a single sample path generated by an arbitrary policy is available. To learn the optimal Q-function, we employ the Nearest Neighbor Q-Learning (NNQL) algorithm, which leverages nearest neighbor regression techniques. Our primary contribution is a tight finite-sample analysis of the algorithm's convergence rate. Specifically, for MDPs with a $d$-dimensional state space and discount factor $\gamma \in (0,1)$, given a sample path with "covering time" $L$, we show that the algorithm can produce an $\varepsilon$-accurate estimate of the optimal Q-function using $\tilde{O}\left(\frac{L}{\varepsilon^3(1-\gamma)^7}\right)$ samples. For well-behaved MDPs, the covering time under a purely random policy scales as $\tilde{O}\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon^d}\right)$, leading to a total sample complexity of $\tilde{O}\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{d+3}}\right)$. Furthermore, we establish a matching lower bound showing that the dependence on $\varepsilon$ cannot be improved beyond $\tilde{\Omega}\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{d+2}}\right)$.

Despite recent advances in graph neural networks (GNNs) for modeling graph-structured data, training GNNs on large-scale datasets remains challenging due to the risk of overfitting. Adversarial training, which enhances model robustness by incorporating worst-case adversarial examples, has shown promise in improving both robustness against attacks and generalization performance. However, most prior work on adversarial training has focused on defending GNNs against malicious attacks, leaving open the question of how adversarial training can enhance the generalization capabilities of GNNs in graph analytics tasks.

In this paper, we analyze GNNs through the lens of weight and feature loss landscapes—i.e., the behavior of the loss function with respect to model weights and node features, respectively. Our analysis reveals that GNNs are prone to converging into sharp local minima in these landscapes, leading to suboptimal generalization performance. To address this issue, we introduce the Co-Adversarial Perturbation (CAP) optimization problem, which jointly considers perturbations in both weights and features. We propose an alternating adversarial perturbation algorithm to progressively flatten the weight and feature loss landscapes in an iterative manner.

Furthermore, we divide the training process into two distinct stages: the first stage involves standard cross-entropy minimization to ensure rapid convergence of the GNN model, while the second stage applies our alternating adversarial perturbation to enhance generalization. This structured approach aims to balance efficiency and robustness, ultimately leading to more reliable and generalized GNN models.

UMAP has become the preferred method for visualizing high-dimensional datasets across various disciplines, surpassing t-SNE. However, the underlying reasons for its success remain poorly understood. In this study, we conduct a detailed analysis of UMAP's sampling-based optimization approach. We derive UMAP's effective loss function in closed form and reveal that it differs from the one previously reported. This discrepancy shows that UMAP does not aim to reproduce the theoretically derived high-dimensional similarities as originally thought. Instead, it focuses on capturing similarities that are based solely on the shared $k$-nearest neighbor graph, which challenges the conventional interpretation of UMAP's effectiveness. Rather, we argue that the core of UMAP's success lies in its implicit balance between attraction and repulsion induced by negative sampling. This balance enhances the stability and efficiency of gradient descent optimization. Our theoretical findings are supported by experiments on both synthetic data and single-cell RNA sequencing datasets.

The rapid advancement of deep learning is giving rise to a wide array of evolving models, accompanied by an ever-increasing demand for computational resources. However, as deep learning frameworks focus on optimizing performance for commonly used network architectures, they inadvertently limit the flexibility needed for novel and diverse models that are essential for research progress. To address this, we introduce a flexible and user-customizable pipeline for optimizing the training of arbitrary deep neural networks, with a focus on minimizing data movement. 

Starting from standard networks implemented in PyTorch or ONNX, the pipeline performs progressive lowering of computations. We define four levels of general-purpose transformations, ranging from local intra-operator optimizations to global reductions in data movement. These transformations operate on a data-centric graph intermediate representation that captures both computation and data flow at all levels of abstraction, including the expansion of basic operators like convolutions into their underlying operations.

At the core of the design is the interactive and introspectable nature of the pipeline. Each component is extensible via a Python API, and users can tune and explore the optimization process through a graphical user interface. We demonstrate competitive performance and significant speedups across ten different network architectures, with interactive optimizations uncovering new efficiency opportunities in EfficientNet.

The invariance to permutations of the adjacency matrix—commonly referred to as graph isomorphism—is a fundamental requirement for Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Traditionally, this property is ensured through invariant operations during message aggregation, which are insensitive to node permutations. However, such approaches may overlook the relationships among neighboring nodes, potentially limiting the expressive power of GNNs. In this paper, we introduce an efficient permutation-sensitive aggregation mechanism based on permutation groups, which effectively captures pairwise correlations between neighboring nodes. We theoretically establish that our method is strictly more powerful than the 2-dimensional Weisfeiler-Lehman (2-WL) graph isomorphism test and at least as powerful as the 3-WL test. Additionally, we show that our approach achieves linear sampling complexity. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of our proposed model.

This paper introduces a novel collaborative distillation meta learning (CDML) framework tailored for simulation-intensive hardware design problems. While deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has demonstrated promising results in various hardware design tasks, prior research has largely focused on simplified objectives that do not reflect real-world complexity. In practice, evaluating the electrical performance of actual systems through simulation is both time-consuming and computationally expensive, making DRL approaches that require extensive reward computation impractical.
