In this paper, we introduce xAT and xVAT, novel adversarial training algorithms that employ **multiplicative** perturbations to input examples, offering a more perceptible and interpretable form of adversarial training compared to the **additive** perturbations used in AT and VAT. Unlike traditional approaches, which only support transductive implementations, multiplicative perturbations can be generated both transductively and inductively. Extensive experiments reveal that xAT and xVAT achieve or exceed state-of-the-art classification performance across multiple benchmark datasets, while being approximately 30% faster than their additive counterparts. Additionally, the resulting DNNs exhibit distinct weight distribution patterns.

Given the joint probabilities of a pair of random variables, one can calculate various quantities of interest, such as mutual information. In the Bayesian framework, when the underlying probabilities are unknown, they are estimated by computing a posterior distribution based on a second-order prior and the likelihood of the observed data. A common approach to handling incomplete data is to assume ignorability and estimate the probabilities using the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm. While these two methods are well-established, they are typically treated as separate approaches. This paper unifies the two by considering the case of Dirichlet priors, and derives efficient approximations for the mean, mode, and (co)variance of the probabilities as well as for mutual information. Furthermore, we establish the unimodality of the posterior distribution, which guarantees that EM converges to the global maximum within this framework. These results are applied to the problem of feature selection in incremental learning and naive Bayes classification. A fast filter based on the distribution of mutual information is demonstrated to outperform traditional filters relying on empirical mutual information across several real-world incomplete datasets.

We present a versatile family of fairness regularizers designed for both linear and logistic regression models. These regularizers are all convex, enabling efficient optimization, and they encompass a broad spectrum of fairness concepts—from group fairness to stronger notions of individual fairness. By adjusting the weight assigned to the fairness regularizer, we can explore the efficient frontier of the accuracy-fairness trade-off on any given dataset. To quantify the severity of this trade-off, we introduce a numerical measure called the Price of Fairness (PoF). A central contribution of our work is an in-depth comparative analysis of the PoF across six distinct datasets where fairness plays a critical role.

Recently, 3D object detectors based on point cloud data have made significant advancements. However, most existing research has focused primarily on improving detection accuracy through the development of deep learning architectures. In this paper, we introduce an autoencoder-style framework that incorporates channel-wise compression and decompression via interchange transfer for knowledge distillation. To capture the map-view features of a teacher network, features from both the teacher and student networks are independently passed through a shared autoencoder. A compressed representation loss is employed to regularize the channel-wise compression knowledge learned from both networks. The decompressed features are then transferred in opposite directions to minimize discrepancies in the interchange reconstructions. Additionally, we propose an attentive head loss to align the critical detection information extracted by the multi-head self-attention mechanism. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method effectively trains a lightweight model well-suited for 3D point cloud detection, and we validate its effectiveness using widely used public datasets such as Waymo and nuScenes.

This brief note introduces an image classification dataset comprising 10 different types of executable code and around 50,000 virus examples. The malicious classes include 9 distinct families of computer viruses, along with a single benign category. The image format for the first 1,024 bytes of Portable Executable (PE) files resembles the well-known MNIST handwritten digit dataset, allowing many existing algorithmic approaches to be adapted with minimal modification. The classification of the 9 virus families as malware is based on unsupervised learning techniques, specifically KMeans clustering, which excludes non-malicious samples. As a benchmark using deep learning methods, we achieved an overall 80% accuracy in identifying virus families when including benign examples. Furthermore, we found that once malware is detected—whether through signature-based or heuristic methods—the first 1,024 bytes can be visualized as a thumbnail image, enabling classification of the virus type with 87% accuracy. This work demonstrates the generalization of convolutional neural networks, originally designed for image recognition tasks, to a novel domain: pixel-level representations of executable files. The dataset is publicly available on Kaggle and GitHub.

Width-based planning has demonstrated promising performance on Atari 2600 games using pixel inputs, while requiring significantly fewer environment interactions compared to traditional reinforcement learning. Recent width-based methods have generated feature vectors for each game screen using either handcrafted features or a variational autoencoder trained on game screens (VAE-IW), and have pruned screens that lack novel features during the search process. We introduce Olive (Online-VAE-IW), an approach that updates VAE features in an online manner through active learning, thereby maximizing the value of the screens encountered during planning. Experimental results across 55 Atari games show that Olive outperforms Rollout-IW by a margin of 42-to-11 and VAE-IW by 32-to-20. Furthermore, Olive surpasses existing policy-learning-based methods ($\pi$-IW, DQN) trained with a 100x larger budget by 30-to-22 and 31-to-17, respectively. It also outperforms a state-of-the-art data-efficient reinforcement learning method, EfficientZero, which was trained with the same budget and used a 1.8x planning budget, by a score of 18-to-7 in the Atari 100k benchmark—without any policy learning. The source code is available at [github.com/ibm/atari-active-learning](https://github.com/ibm/atari-active-learning).

Most industrial recommender systems rely heavily on collaborative filtering (CF) to deliver personalized recommendations to users. However, the fundamental nature of CF conflicts with the principle of user privacy, as it requires users to share their preferences with others in order to be grouped with similar individuals and receive accurate suggestions. While prior approaches to preserving privacy have succeeded in partially obscuring user preference data from centralized recommendation systems, they have also introduced significant trade-offs in terms of privacy, scalability, and recommendation accuracy. Moreover, these methods remain susceptible to privacy leaks caused by malicious actors.

In response to these challenges, we introduce a novel selective privacy-preserving framework called SP2. This paradigm empowers users to define the scope and extent of their personal privacy by labeling their ratings as either public (shareable) or private (never shared and stored exclusively on the user's device). The SP2 framework operates in two stages: (i) First, it constructs an initial recommendation model using the aggregated public ratings provided by users; and (ii) subsequently, this base model is refined on each user’s device using their private ratings, ensuring that sensitive information remains protected while still improving the quality of personalized recommendations.

We perform a comprehensive analysis of the relationship between the out-of-sample performance and the Bayesian evidence (marginal likelihood) of Bayesian neural networks (BNNs), while also evaluating the performance of BNN ensembles, all using the Boston housing dataset. Leveraging advanced nested sampling techniques, we numerically sample the full posterior distribution of the network—accounting for its non-Gaussian and multimodal nature—and compute accurate estimates of the Bayesian evidence for models with up to 156 trainable parameters. The networks under consideration vary in architecture, ranging from zero to four hidden layers, and use either $\tanh$ or $ReLU$ activation functions, with and without hierarchical priors. BNN ensembles are constructed by combining the posterior distributions of individual networks, where each network is re-weighted according to its corresponding Bayesian evidence. A strong correlation is observed between out-of-sample performance and Bayesian evidence, alongside a notable symmetry in the relationships between evidence and model size, as well as performance and model size. Networks employing $ReLU$ activation functions consistently exhibit higher evidence values compared to those using $\tanh$, which is reflected in their superior out-of-sample performance. Furthermore, ensembling across different architectures leads to improved performance relative to individual BNNs.

Many real-world prediction tasks require modeling multi-order feature interactions within a user's event sequence to improve detection performance. However, existing approaches often face two critical limitations: first, they focus solely on feature interactions while neglecting the sequential influence; second, they emphasize sequence information but overlook the internal feature relationships within each event, leading to suboptimal event representations. In this paper, we propose a two-level framework to capture hierarchical information from user event sequences: (1) learning effective event representations through feature interactions, and (2) modeling the sequence-level representation of user history. Experimental results on both industrial and public datasets demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.

In this paper, we explore various approaches to time series modeling. The study includes forecasting methods based on linear models, the ARIMA algorithm, and the XGBoost machine learning algorithm. Results from different model combinations are presented. For probabilistic modeling, we consider approaches utilizing copulas and Bayesian inference.

The primary objective of Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning (PPML) is to safeguard the privacy and ensure the security of data used in training machine learning models. Several techniques are employed in PPML, including Secure Multi-Party Computation, Differential Privacy, and Homomorphic Encryption (HE). These methods are often integrated with various machine learning and deep learning architectures to protect both data confidentiality and user identity. In this paper, we introduce a fully homomorphic encrypted wavelet neural network designed to preserve privacy without sacrificing model efficiency. We evaluated the proposed approach on seven datasets from the finance and healthcare domains. The experimental results demonstrate that our model achieves performance comparable to its unencrypted counterpart.

Most existing graph neural networks (GNNs) learn node embeddings through a message-passing and aggregation framework. However, these models are inherently limited in their ability to capture the relative positions of nodes within a graph. To address this limitation, some approaches introduce anchor nodes, using the distances from each node to these anchors to infer spatial relationships. Unfortunately, prior methods like P-GNNs often select anchors arbitrarily, which can undermine both position awareness and feature learning. In this work, we show that selecting anchors that are evenly distributed and asymmetric is crucial for enhancing position awareness. Furthermore, we demonstrate that choosing anchors capable of aggregating embeddings from all nodes in a graph is an NP-hard problem, making it impractical to design deterministic optimal algorithms. To overcome these challenges while preserving position awareness, we propose Position-Sensing Graph Neural Networks (PSGNNs), which learn to select anchors in a differentiable and backpropagatable manner. Experimental results show that PSGNNs significantly outperform state-of-the-art GNNs across various synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating stable scalability. Specifically, PSGNNs achieve an average improvement of over 14% in AUC for pairwise node classification and 18% for link prediction compared to existing position-aware methods. The source code is publicly available.

We address the challenge of certifying individual fairness (IF) in feed-forward neural networks (NNs). Specifically, we focus on the $\epsilon$-$\delta$-IF framework, which, given a neural network and a similarity metric derived from data, ensures that the output difference between any two $\epsilon$-similar individuals remains within a specified decision tolerance $\delta \geq 0$. By considering various similarity metrics, including the Mahalanobis distance, we introduce a method to overapproximate the associated optimization problem using piecewise-linear functions. This approach allows us to globally bound the non-linearities of the NN across the input space. We formulate this computation as a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) problem and demonstrate its effectiveness in deriving IF guarantees across four widely used fairness benchmark datasets. Furthermore, we show how this formulation can be integrated into the training process to promote fairness by modifying the NN's loss function. Empirical results confirm that our approach produces neural networks that are significantly fairer—by orders of magnitude—than existing state-of-the-art methods.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable success in a wide range of computer vision tasks. However, their application to high-dimensional problems—such as high-resolution image and video segmentation or 3D medical imaging—has been constrained by several challenges. A major limitation arises during the training phase, where the storage of network activations for backpropagation becomes computationally expensive. In such scenarios, the memory required to store these activations often exceeds the capabilities of current hardware, particularly when dealing with 3D data.

Inspired by the propagation of signals through physical networks governed by the hyperbolic Telegraph equation, this work introduces a fully conservative hyperbolic network tailored for high-dimensional input and output tasks. We propose a coarsening operation that enables completely reversible CNNs by leveraging a learnable Discrete Wavelet Transform and its inverse to both downsample and upsample the network state, while also adjusting the number of channels. 

Our experiments demonstrate that fully reversible networks can achieve performance comparable to state-of-the-art models in challenging tasks such as 4D time-lapse hyperspectral image segmentation and full 3D video segmentation, while maintaining a significantly reduced memory footprint that remains constant regardless of the network depth. Additionally, we extend the applicability of this approach to further domains.

It is well established that Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are susceptible to adversarial attacks, and their robustness can be enhanced through adversarial training, such as the standard adversarial training (SAT), which involves adding adversarial noises to the training data. However, the improper application of such noises may degrade the model's overall performance, resulting in a trade-off between accuracy and robustness. While this trade-off has been extensively studied in the context of image classification, it remains underexplored in medical image analysis tasks, such as image segmentation, landmark detection, and object detection. In this study, we demonstrate that the SAT method faces a critical limitation in medical imaging applications: it applies a uniform level of noise across all training samples, which can either severely harm model performance if the noise is too strong or fail to improve robustness if the noise is too weak. To address this issue, we propose an adaptive-margin adversarial training (AMAT) method that generates sample-specific adversarial noises to enhance robustness while maintaining performance. Unlike conventional adversarial training approaches designed for classification tasks, our AMAT method employs a loss-defined margin strategy, enabling more flexible and effective adversarial training tailored to medical image analysis.

In the medical field, the scarcity of large training datasets and benchmarks often hinders the development of deep neural networks. While manual annotation is costly and time-consuming, computer simulations offer a promising alternative by generating extensive, fully labeled datasets with minimal human intervention. However, models trained on synthetic data typically struggle to generalize to real-world conditions. To address this domain gap between simulated and actual laparoscopic images, we leverage recent advancements in unpaired image-to-image translation. We adapt an existing image translation method to produce a wide variety of realistic-looking synthetic laparoscopic images based on data from a basic laparoscopy simulation. By integrating mechanisms that preserve the content of the original images during the translation process, we ensure that the labels assigned to the simulated images remain valid for their realistic counterparts. This approach enables the creation of a large, fully annotated synthetic dataset of laparoscopic images with lifelike appearance. We demonstrate that this dataset can effectively train models for liver segmentation tasks in laparoscopic imaging. Our results show average Dice scores of up to 0.89 in certain patients without the need for any manual labeling of real laparoscopic images, highlighting the potential of this method for improving medical image analysis.

Typically, research in fair machine learning focuses on a single decisionmaker and assumes that the underlying population remains stable over time. However, many of the real-world domains driving this research are characterized by competitive marketplaces with multiple decisionmakers. In practice, we might expect only a subset of these actors to voluntarily adopt fairness-conscious policies, a scenario referred to by political philosophers as *partial compliance*. This raises critical questions: How does the strategic behavior of decisionmakers in such settings influence the resulting allocation outcomes? If k% of employers were to adopt a fairness-promoting intervention voluntarily, should we anticipate k% progress toward the benefits of full adoption, or will the dynamics of partial compliance dilute those gains? Furthermore, how might an auditor’s perspective—global versus local—affect their conclusions?

In this paper, we present a simple model of an employment market, using simulation as a tool to investigate how interaction effects and incentive structures shape both outcomes and auditing metrics. Our key findings reveal that, at equilibrium: (1) partial compliance—where k% of employers adopt fair practices—can lead to significantly less than proportional (k%) improvement compared to full compliance; and (2) the disparity becomes more pronounced when fair employers align with global rather than local norms.

In this paper, we demonstrate that metric learning can encounter significant inseparability issues in the absence of informative sample mining. Since inseparable samples are often intertwined with hard samples, existing strategies for informative sample mining may introduce undesirable side effects, such as instability in the objective function. To address this challenge, we propose a novel distance metric learning algorithm called Adaptive Neighborhood Metric Learning (ANML). In ANML, we introduce two adaptive thresholds to dynamically identify inseparable similar and dissimilar samples during training, enabling the simultaneous removal of inseparable samples and learning of metric parameters. Due to the non-continuity of the proposed approach, we introduce an innovative function called the *log-exp mean function* to formulate a continuous surrogate, which allows efficient optimization via gradient descent. Similar to the triplet loss, ANML is capable of learning both linear and deep embeddings. Through analysis, we uncover several intriguing properties of the proposed method. For instance, when applied to linear embedding learning, well-known metric learning algorithms such as Large Margin Nearest Neighbor (LMNN) and Neighborhood Components Analysis (NCA) emerge as special cases of ANML.

Explainable AI has become a crucial element for black-box machine learning models, particularly in domains where reliability and transparency are paramount. Applications such as medical diagnostic systems and tools subject to the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) in the European Union highlight the need for transparent decision-making processes. These requirements necessitate the ability to audit and understand the reasoning behind a classifier's predictions.

While visualizations are commonly used as explanations, they often fall short in capturing the full complexity of model decisions. They struggle to differentiate between various manifestations of visual features—such as whether an eye is open or closed—and fail to accurately represent the impact of feature absence or the relationships among features. As an alternative, more expressive symbolic surrogate models could provide better interpretability. However, these models typically require symbolic input, which is not readily available in most computer vision tasks.

In this paper, we explore a novel approach to address this challenge. We leverage the inherent features learned by a deep neural network to construct a global, expressive, and verbal explanation of the reasoning behind a feed-forward convolutional neural network's predictions. The semantic meaning of these features is extracted through a concept analysis method trained on a set of human-interpretable visual concepts. The resulting explanation is derived using an Inductive Logic Programming (ILP) approach.

This paper investigates the problem of vehicle re-identification by analyzing distance comparisons in the latent spaces of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Initially, we examine the effect of different distance metrics—namely, the minimal Euclidean distance (MED), the minimal cosine distance (MCD), and the residue of sparse coding reconstruction (RSCR)—on performance. These metrics are evaluated using features extracted from five distinct CNN architectures: ResNet18, AlexNet, VGG16, InceptionV3, and DenseNet201. The VeRi dataset is used to fine-tune these models and assess their effectiveness. Overall, regardless of the CNN architecture, MCD consistently outperforms MED, which is widely adopted in existing literature. These findings are further validated on additional vehicle retrieval datasets.

Subsequently, we extend the state-of-the-art image-to-track process (I2TP) into a track-to-track process (T2TP). By adapting the three distance metrics to measure similarity between tracks, we enable the T2TP framework. When compared with I2TP using the same CNN models, T2TP demonstrates superior performance, particularly when combined with MCD and RSCR metrics. Notably, the combination of T2TP with DenseNet201 and MCD-based metrics achieves the highest performance, surpassing existing I2TP-based models.

Finally, our experimental results reveal two key insights: first, the critical role of metric selection in vehicle re-identification, and second, the significant improvement in performance achieved by T2TP over I2TP, especially when paired with MCD-based distance measures.

In hardware-aware Differentiable Neural Architecture Search (DNAS), one of the main challenges is computing gradients of hardware metrics to guide the architecture search process. Most existing approaches rely on linear approximations, which offer limited flexibility and support for custom hardware accelerators. To address this, we propose End-to-end Hardware-aware DNAS (EH-DNAS), a comprehensive framework that seamlessly integrates end-to-end hardware benchmarking with fully automated DNAS. This approach enables the design of hardware-efficient deep neural networks across diverse platforms, including Edge GPUs, Edge TPUs, Mobile CPUs, and customized accelerators.

Given a target hardware platform, EH-DNAS introduces a differentiable model that predicts the end-to-end performance of neural network architectures, enabling gradient-based optimization during the search. We also present E2E-Perf, an end-to-end hardware benchmarking tool tailored for customized accelerators. Experimental results on CIFAR10 and ImageNet demonstrate that EH-DNAS achieves an average improvement of 1.4× in hardware performance on custom accelerators and 1.6× on conventional hardware platforms, while maintaining competitive classification accuracy.

This paper introduces a new method for distributed linear filtering and prediction in a multi-agent network of sensors observing a random dynamical system. The network is characterized by sparsity, and the approach is inspired by consensus+innovations frameworks commonly used in distributed estimation. The proposed algorithm integrates the concepts of consensus and innovations to achieve accurate and efficient estimation across the network. A key contribution of the paper is the introduction of a new notion of distributed observability, which serves as a less restrictive condition compared to the combined assumptions of global observability and network connectivity. Based on first principles, optimal gain matrices are derived to minimize the mean-squared error of estimation at each agent. Additionally, a distributed form of the algebraic Riccati equation is developed to compute these gains efficiently.

This paper presents a comprehensive review of previous approaches that have employed deep-learning frameworks to analyze discrete, irregular-patterned, and complex sequential datasets. A typical example of such data is financial time series, where specific events can lead to sudden, unpredictable changes in the sequence. Conventional deep-learning techniques often struggle or fail when applied to these types of datasets. A systematic literature review highlights the prevalence of recurrent neural network (RNN)-based frameworks in this domain. The evaluation of deep-learning models primarily relies on accuracy metrics such as mean absolute error and root mean square error. Key challenges identified include limited performance robustness, methodological opacity, and issues related to both internal and external architectural design and configuration. These challenges present opportunities for further development and refinement of deep-learning frameworks tailored for complex, irregular sequential data.

Recently, a series of papers have presented promising theoretical results regarding the training of over-parameterized neural networks—networks that are larger than necessary to achieve low error. The key insight is that with sufficient over-parameterization, gradient-based optimization methods tend to leave certain components of the network largely unchanged, effectively treating them as fixed at their initial random values. This behavior mirrors the well-established approach of learning with random features, where some parts of the model are held constant during training. In essence, these findings suggest that successful learning with neural networks is possible whenever learning with random features is feasible.

In this paper, we begin by reviewing these techniques, offering a clear and self-contained analysis focused on one-hidden-layer networks. We then highlight that, despite the encouraging theoretical results, random feature approaches have inherent limitations in explaining the full capabilities of neural networks. Specifically, we rigorously demonstrate that random features cannot be used to learn even a single ReLU neuron with standard Gaussian inputs, unless the network size or the magnitude of the weights grows exponentially. Since a single neuron can be learned using gradient-based methods, this implies that we still lack a comprehensive and satisfying explanation for the empirical success of neural networks.

Word vector representations play a crucial role in deep learning models used for natural language processing. Various types of these vectors, referred to as embeddings, have been developed, such as word2vec and GloVe. These embeddings are trained on extensive text corpora and capture the contextual usage of words, thereby encoding semantic relationships between them. However, the semantics captured are typically at the level of individual word types, which can lead to ambiguity—especially when a word can function as different parts of speech, such as a noun or a verb. In tasks like question answering, part-of-speech information and named entity types are essential, but incorporating these features into neural models often increases the input dimensionality. This research introduces a method that uses holographic compression of pre-trained embeddings to encode a token, its part-of-speech, and its named entity type within the same dimensional space as a single token. When implemented in a modified recurrent deep learning network for question answering, this approach maintains semantic relationships while achieving strong performance.

Training machine learning models on sensitive user data has raised growing privacy concerns across various domains. Federated learning has emerged as a widely adopted approach for protecting privacy by aggregating local model updates rather than raw data. One effective method to ensure strong privacy is the integration of local differential privacy (LDP) into federated learning. However, existing approaches face significant challenges due to three key issues. First, the noisy data remains close to its original value with high probability, increasing the risk of information leakage. Second, the introduction of high variance in the estimated average leads to reduced model accuracy. Third, the privacy budget is excessively consumed due to the high dimensionality of deep learning model weights. In this paper, we propose a novel local differential privacy mechanism tailored for federated learning to address these limitations. Our approach enhances the distinction between the perturbed and original data while reducing variance. Furthermore, it mitigates the curse of dimensionality by splitting and shuffling model updates. Empirical evaluations on three widely used datasets—MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10—demonstrate that our solution not only achieves superior deep learning performance but also provides a robust privacy guarantee.

Deep learning algorithms have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in the field of Computer Vision. In recent years, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have been extensively applied to address challenges in the subarea of Image Generation, with widespread applications in domains such as photo editing, image design, computer animation, real-time rendering of large-scale scenes, and visual effects in movies. However, during the texture synthesis process, state-of-the-art CNNs struggle to accurately capture the spatial location of textures within an image, leading to significant distortions after synthesis. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach to image generation by incorporating a semantic segmentation step as a preprocessing stage using deep learning algorithms, and we analyze the resulting outcomes.

This paper introduces the baseline approach for the organized second edition of the COVID-19 Competition, held within the framework of the AIMIA Workshop at the European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV 2022). It presents the COV19-CT-DB database, a collection of approximately 7,700 3D CT scans annotated for the detection of COVID-19. A subset of this database, comprising COVID-19 cases, is further annotated with four severity levels. The database has been divided into training, validation, and test sets, with the first two used for training and validating machine learning models, and the latter for evaluating the performance of the developed models. The proposed baseline approach is based on a deep learning framework utilizing a CNN-RNN architecture, and it reports the results achieved on the COV19-CT-DB database.

Optimal Transport (OT) emerges naturally in a wide range of machine learning applications, but its high computational cost has hindered its broader adoption. To tackle this scalability challenge, we introduce SPOT (Scalable Push-forward of Optimal Transport), a generative learning framework based on implicit modeling. In SPOT, we approximate the optimal transport plan as a pushforward of a reference distribution and reformulate the OT problem as a minimax optimization. This formulation enables efficient solutions using primal-dual stochastic gradient methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the density of the optimal transport plan can be recovered using neural ordinary differential equations. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets show that SPOT is robust and exhibits strong convergence properties. Additionally, SPOT facilitates efficient sampling from the optimal transport plan, which enhances performance in downstream tasks such as domain adaptation.

Machine learning models are frequently integrated with human experts in the decision-making pipeline, allowing the model to defer to a domain expert when it lacks confidence in its predictions. Our objective is to develop mechanisms that ensure both accuracy and fairness in such hybrid systems that combine machine learning inferences with human judgments. Prior research on "deferral systems" in classification tasks has primarily focused on scenarios involving a single expert, aiming to account for the expert's potential inaccuracies and biases while simultaneously learning an inference model and a deferral strategy. In this work, we extend this framework to settings where multiple experts are available, each with their own area of expertise and associated biases. We introduce a framework that jointly learns a classifier and a deferral system, where the deferral system can choose to consult one or more human experts when the classifier's confidence is low. We evaluate our approach on a synthetic dataset and a content moderation dataset featuring biased synthetic experts, demonstrating significant improvements in both accuracy and fairness compared to baseline methods. Additionally, we have collected crowdsourced labels to further validate our findings.

This paper presents a novel loss function called OSM (One-Sided Margin) designed to effectively address maximum-margin classification problems. Unlike the hinge loss, OSM explicitly defines the margin through associated hyperparameters, which then guides the classification process. Experimental results demonstrate that using the OSM loss leads to faster training speeds and improved accuracy compared to binary and categorical cross-entropy in several widely used deep learning models for classification and optical character recognition tasks. 

OSM consistently achieves higher classification accuracy than both cross-entropy and hinge losses across a range of network sizes, from small to large. Furthermore, it enhances the efficiency of the training procedure. On several benchmark datasets, such as CIFAR10 (98.82%), CIFAR100 (91.56%), Flowers (98.04%), and Stanford Cars (93.91%), we achieved state-of-the-art performance with significant improvements over other loss functions. For larger networks, OSM also outperforms cross-entropy and hinge loss in terms of accuracy.

Therefore, we strongly believe that OSM offers a powerful alternative to traditional loss functions like hinge and cross-entropy for training deep neural networks on classification tasks.

Given a dataset, biclustering seeks to identify simultaneous groupings of both samples and features, forming biclusters that exhibit coherent patterns. Consistent biclusterings enable accurate classification of samples based on the known class labels of features, and vice versa, making them highly valuable for supervised classification tasks. The challenge of discovering consistent biclusterings can be viewed as a feature selection problem, where irrelevant features are removed while maintaining a maximal set of features to preserve essential information. This feature selection task can be formulated as a linear fractional 0-1 optimization problem. In this work, we reformulate the problem as a bilevel optimization problem and introduce a heuristic algorithm for its efficient solution. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing heuristic methods in terms of solution quality.

In this study, we introduce a *Discourse-Aware Semantic Self-Attention* encoder that leverages linguistic annotations as its foundation for improving reading comprehension on long narrative texts. By utilizing existing annotation tools, we identify relationships between discourse units, events and their arguments, as well as coreferential mentions. Our experimental results demonstrate that incorporating these structures enhances overall performance, particularly in capturing intra-sentential and cross-sentential discourse relations, sentence-internal semantic role relations, and long-distance coreference. We further show that assigning specific self-attention heads to intra-sentential connections and relations between adjacent sentences improves the model's ability to locate answers within extended contexts. These findings highlight the value of integrating discourse-semantic annotations to boost the generalization capabilities of self-attention models in reading comprehension tasks.

Forecasting particulate matter (PM) concentrations in South Korea has become increasingly urgent due to its significant negative impact on public health. Most statistical and machine learning approaches typically assume independent and identically distributed data, such as a Gaussian distribution; however, time series data like air pollution and weather do not conform to this assumption. In this study, the Maximum Correntropy Criterion for Regression (MCCR) loss is employed to analyze the statistical properties of air pollution and weather data. A rigorous seasonality adjustment was conducted due to the complex seasonal patterns and the heavy-tailed nature of the data, even after deseasonalization. The MCCR loss was applied across various models, including traditional statistical methods and advanced machine learning techniques. The results demonstrate that the MCCR loss is more effective than the conventional mean squared error loss in forecasting extreme values.

Support Vector Machine (SVM) is a powerful machine learning model known for its high accuracy across various classification tasks, and it is widely employed in embedded systems. However, implementing SVM-based classifiers in embedded environments presents significant challenges due to the complex computations involved. This motivates the development of hardware implementations of SVM to achieve high-performance computing at low cost and power consumption. Melanoma, the most aggressive form of skin cancer, is associated with a high mortality rate. Our objective is to develop an optimized embedded SVM classifier tailored for a low-cost handheld device to enable early detection of melanoma in primary healthcare settings. In this paper, we present a hardware/software co-design approach for implementing the SVM classifier on an FPGA, aiming to realize on-chip melanoma detection. The proposed implementation on a modern hybrid FPGA platform (Zynq), utilizing the advanced UltraFast High-Level Synthesis design methodology, demonstrates efficient melanoma classification. The hardware results show a classification accuracy of 97.9%, a remarkable acceleration factor of 21, and a minimal resource utilization of 3% with a power consumption of only 1.69W. These findings confirm that the on-chip system meets critical constraints of embedded systems, including high performance, low resource usage, minimal power consumption, and cost-effectiveness, while delivering efficient and reliable classification.

Most machine learning systems that engage with humans construct some notion of a person's "identity." However, the dominant paradigm in AI research frames identity as composed of fixed, discrete, and static essential attributes. This contrasts sharply with perspectives within critical theory, which view identity as fluid, constructed through social interaction, and more akin to a process or practice than a fixed state.

In this work, we draw from these critical perspectives to offer insights for machine learning practitioners. We propose a theory of identity as autopoiesis—an ongoing, self-referential process of formation and function. We argue that the prevailing default model of identity in AI entrenches existing categories and the power structures that accompany them, due to the lack of iterative feedback mechanisms in our models. This critique extends to current AI fairness practices, which often reinforce the same outdated assumptions.

Finally, we explore how our theoretical framework can inform new approaches to identity in machine learning, such as multilevel optimization and relational learning. While many questions remain open, we envision a future in which machines are capable of understanding and reflecting human identity as a dynamic, evolving relationship.

A common challenge in learning causal models from data is the difficulty of estimating high-order conditional independence (CI) relationships among random variables. While CI tests involving small conditioning sets can be reliably performed with limited data, a practical approach to inferring causal structures often relies solely on low-order CIs. Recent studies have shown that, particularly in sparse true causal models, structures derived from zero- and first-order conditional independencies can provide accurate approximations of the underlying causal relationships. However, a significant challenge remains: developing methods that can faithfully represent a given set of low-order CIs. In this paper, we introduce an algorithm that, given a set of conditional independencies of order at most $k$ (where $k$ is a small fixed number), constructs a faithful graphical representation of the data. Our results extend and generalize prior work on learning from pairwise marginal independencies. Furthermore, they offer improvements over the 0-1 graph model, which is widely used, for example, in the analysis of genome networks.

The adoption of machine learning (ML) methods in the social and health sciences has been relatively slow, with existing research applying ML to these fields often remaining fragmented. This may stem from the distinct development paths of computational/data science and the social/health sciences, as well as the limited availability of comprehensive overviews and proper training in ML techniques for researchers without a data science background. This paper presents a meta-mapping of research questions in the social and health sciences to suitable ML approaches, taking into account the statistical requirements specific to these disciplines. It aligns traditional classification categories—description, prediction, and causal inference—with common research objectives, such as estimating the prevalence of adverse health or social outcomes, predicting the likelihood of an event, and identifying risk factors or causes of negative outcomes. By doing so, this meta-mapping seeks to bridge disciplinary divides and foster a more dynamic exchange between researchers in the social and health sciences and those with methodological expertise. Such a framework could enable a more effective integration of ML, ensuring that domain-specific considerations are addressed while maximizing the potential of these techniques to advance both theoretical and applied research in these fields.

In this paper, we investigate the information-theoretic limits of learning the structure of Bayesian networks (BNs), applicable to both discrete and continuous random variables, from a finite number of samples. We establish that the minimum number of samples required by any method to accurately recover the true network structure scales as $\Omega(m)$ for non-sparse BNs and as $\Omega(k \log m + k^2/m)$ for sparse BNs, where $m$ denotes the number of variables and $k$ is the maximum number of parents per node. 

We present a straightforward approach—based on an extension of Fano's inequality—to derive information-theoretic bounds for structure recovery in any exponential family-based BN. Using this framework, we analyze specific conditional distributions within the exponential family to determine the fundamental limits of learning widely used BN models, including those based on conditional probability tables, Gaussian BNs, noisy-OR networks, and logistic regression networks.

As part of our analysis, we derive tight bounds on the number of sparse and non-sparse essential DAGs. Additionally, as a byproduct of our work, we recover the information-theoretic limits for sparse variable selection in logistic regression.

In the field of intelligent communication, deep learning (DL) has garnered significant attention due to its strong modeling capabilities and data-driven learning approach. While traditional DL feedforward network architectures have been widely used, enhanced structures incorporating direct data feedback have been explored and demonstrated superior performance compared to conventional feedforward networks. However, these simple feedback mechanisms often lack sufficient analytical and learning capacity for the feedback data, limiting their effectiveness in handling more complex nonlinear systems and hindering further performance improvements.

To address these limitations, this paper proposes a novel Multi-Agent Feedback-Enabled Neural Network (MAFENN) framework. This framework enhances the system's feedback learning capabilities and improves intelligence in tasks such as feature abstraction, denoising, and generation. Furthermore, the MAFENN framework is theoretically formalized as a three-player Feedback Stackelberg game, and it is proven to converge to the Feedback Stackelberg equilibrium. The design and algorithm of the MAFENN framework aim to significantly enhance the learning capabilities of standard feedforward DL networks or their variants that employ basic data feedback mechanisms.

To validate the feasibility of the MAFENN framework in wireless communication scenarios, a multi-agent MAFENN-based equalizer (MAFENN-E) is developed for wireless fading channels with inter-symbol interference (ISI). Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

Humans and animals are continuously exposed to a constant flow of sensory information from various modalities. At the same time, they develop more compact representations such as concepts or symbols. In species that use language, this process is further shaped by interaction, requiring a mapping between sensorimotor concepts and linguistic elements. Evidence suggests that children may learn language by disambiguating potential meanings through repeated exposure to utterances in different contexts—a process known as cross-situational learning. Most existing models establish the mapping between modalities in a single step, relying on the co-occurrence frequencies of referents and meanings. In this paper, we extend this one-step approach and introduce a newly proposed sequential mapping algorithm, along with a publicly available Matlab implementation. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we focus on a less conventional scenario: instead of associating objects with their names, we examine body representations. A humanoid robot receives tactile stimuli across its body while simultaneously hearing utterances of body part names (e.g., "hand," "forearm," and "torso"). Our goal is to correctly identify "body categories," and we show how the sequential mapping algorithm outperforms the traditional one-step method.

Cybersecurity threats have become increasingly frequent and complex over the years, necessitating continuous advancements in defensive strategies. While traditional intrusion detection methods and deep packet inspection remain widely used, they are no longer adequate to address the evolving landscape of security challenges. With the rise in computing power and decreasing costs, Machine Learning has emerged as a promising alternative or complementary approach for combating malware, botnets, and other cyber threats. This paper investigates the potential of Machine Learning as an effective solution by evaluating its ability to identify malicious network traffic. A comprehensive data analysis is conducted, resulting in the extraction of 22 relevant features from the original NetFlow datasets. These features are then subjected to a feature selection process to determine their relevance. Following this, five different Machine Learning algorithms are evaluated against a NetFlow dataset that includes common botnet traffic. The Random Forest Classifier demonstrates strong performance, achieving detection rates exceeding 95% in 8 out of 13 scenarios and over 55% in the most challenging datasets. Finally, the study provides insights into improving and generalizing the results, with a focus on the application of bootstrapping techniques.

Multiclass probability estimation involves estimating the conditional probabilities that a given data point belongs to a particular class, based on its covariate information. This task plays a crucial role in statistical analysis and data science. Recently, a class of weighted Support Vector Machines (wSVMs) has been introduced to estimate class probabilities using ensemble learning for $K$-class problems (Wu, Zhang, and Liu, 2010; Wang, Zhang, and Wu, 2019), where $K$ represents the number of classes. These estimators are known for their robustness and high accuracy in probability estimation. However, their learning process relies on pairwise coupling, which results in polynomial time complexity in $K$. 

In this paper, we introduce two novel learning strategies—baseline learning and One-vs-All (OVA) learning—to enhance the computational efficiency and estimation accuracy of wSVMs. The baseline learning approach achieves optimal computational complexity, being linear in $K$, making it highly efficient. Although not the most computationally efficient, the OVA method provides the highest estimation accuracy among all compared procedures. The resulting estimators are distribution-free and have been shown to be consistent. We also present extensive numerical experiments to evaluate their performance in finite samples.

In this paper, we present a realistic and challenging acoustic environment featuring multiple sources and rooms, along with an enhanced algorithm for estimating source-dominated microphone clusters in acoustic sensor networks. Our clustering approach utilizes a single microphone per node and leverages unsupervised clustered federated learning with a lightweight autoencoder model. We introduce an improved clustering control strategy that accounts for the variability of the acoustic scene, enabling the dynamic estimation of cluster numbers with minimal training data. The proposed method is optimized using clustering-based metrics and validated through a network-wide classification task.

This paper explores the uniqueness and temporal consistency of computer usage profiles composed of process-, network-, mouse-, and keystroke-related events within a naturalistic environment, while examining the challenges and potential of leveraging such profiles for continuous authentication. Data was collected from 31 Microsoft Windows 10 users over an 8-week period, and the dataset underwent extensive machine learning analysis using a wide range of online and offline classifiers. The findings reveal that: (i) the majority of users maintained consistent computer usage patterns throughout the study, with 83.9% exhibiting recurring habits on a daily basis; (ii) computer usage profiles hold significant potential for uniquely identifying users, achieving a maximum F-score of 99.90%; (iii) network-related events emerged as the most discriminative features, accounting for 95.69% of the top distinguishing characteristics; and (iv) binary models proved to be the most effective for profile recognition, delivering superior performance in online settings compared to offline ones (maximum F-score of 99.90% versus 95.50%).

Depth estimation plays a crucial role in enabling autonomous driving and advanced driver assistance systems. Among various approaches, monocular depth estimation has attracted significant attention due to its practical advantages—using a single camera is more cost-effective than multi-sensor solutions and eliminates the need for complex calibration processes required by stereo vision systems. Current state-of-the-art methods for monocular depth estimation rely heavily on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). A promising direction involves incorporating additional semantic information about the traffic environment during the training of these networks. In practice, this means that depth data is augmented with images that have pixel-level semantic labels, which are often challenging to annotate, especially in complex urban scenes. Traditionally, it has been assumed that the same raw data is paired with both depth and semantic ground truth. The main contribution of this paper is to demonstrate that this strict assumption can be relaxed. We show that CNNs can be effectively trained for depth estimation by combining depth and semantic information from different, heterogeneous datasets. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we integrate the KITTI depth dataset with the Cityscapes semantic segmentation dataset, achieving superior results compared to existing state-of-the-art methods in monocular depth estimation.

Sign Language serves as an essential communication tool for individuals with speech and hearing impairments, enabling them to interact effectively with others. The identification of Sign Language remains a complex challenge within the domain of computer vision. While recent advancements have led to near-perfect performance in this task, several obstacles still need to be addressed. In this paper, we present a novel machine learning pipeline for identifying American Sign Language (ASL) gestures using hand tracking points. We transform hand gestures into sequences of coordinate data representing hand movements, which are then used as input to our system. To enhance efficiency, we evaluated 28 different combinations of preprocessing techniques across three machine learning algorithms: k-Nearest Neighbors, Random Forests, and a Neural Network. By comparing their performance, we identified the most effective preprocessing method and algorithm combination. Our proposed system achieved an accuracy of 95.66% in recognizing American Sign Language gestures.

User and item features from side information play a critical role in achieving accurate recommendations. However, the high dimensionality of these features—often exceeding 10^7—leads to significant storage and computational costs, making fast recommendation challenging, especially on mobile platforms with limited resources. In this paper, we propose a generic feature-based recommendation model called Discrete Factorization Machine (DFM), designed for both speed and accuracy. DFM converts real-valued model parameters (e.g., float32) of each feature embedding into binary codes (e.g., boolean), enabling efficient storage and rapid user-item scoring. To mitigate the quantization loss caused by binarization, we introduce a convergent updating rule that effectively addresses the discrete optimization problem in DFM. Extensive experiments on two real-world datasets demonstrate that: 1) DFM consistently outperforms existing binarized recommendation models, and 2) it achieves performance comparable to its real-valued counterpart (Factorization Machine), showcasing minimal quantization loss. This work was accepted at IJCAI 2018.

With the rapid advancement of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), synthetic images and videos have become increasingly realistic, creating a pressing need for forensic techniques that can analyze this new class of media. Although GANs have proven valuable in various computer vision tasks, their misuse—such as in the creation of "deepfakes"—has highlighted the importance of developing robust forensic tools. While existing source camera attribution methods have been effective for real-world imagery, they are less applicable to synthetic content. In this work, we tackle the challenge of identifying the specific GAN generator responsible for a synthetic image within a white-box framework. By reversing the generation process, we not only determine whether a given generator could have produced the image but also reconstruct an input that closely matches the synthetic output.

Large-scale object detection datasets continue to grow in both the number of classes and the volume of annotations. However, the number of object-level categories annotated in these datasets remains significantly smaller—by an order of magnitude—compared to image-level classification labels. State-of-the-art object detection models are typically trained in a supervised manner, which restricts their ability to detect new or unseen object classes. In this paper, we introduce a novel Weight Transfer Network (WTN) that effectively transfers knowledge from a pre-trained classification network to a detection network, enabling the detection of novel classes without requiring bounding box supervision. To address underfitting in a basic WTN, we first propose input and feature normalization schemes. We then present Autoencoder-WTN (AE-WTN), which leverages a reconstruction loss to preserve the classification network's information across all classes in the target latent space, thereby improving generalization to novel object categories. Compared to the vanilla WTN, AE-WTN achieves absolute performance gains of 6% on two Open Images evaluation sets with 500 seen and 57 novel classes, respectively, and 25% on a Visual Genome evaluation set with 200 novel classes. The code is available at [https://github.com/xternalz/AE-WTN](https://github.com/xternalz/AE-WTN).

In the Federated Learning framework, a central server coordinates the training of a shared model across a network of distributed devices. A significant challenge in this setting arises when the data exhibits class imbalance, leading to inconsistent training performance. To address this issue, we introduce a novel loss function called Fed-Focal Loss. This approach modifies the cross-entropy loss to reduce the contribution of well-classified examples, drawing inspiration from the focal loss mechanism. Furthermore, by incorporating a flexible sampling strategy, we enable selective aggregation of client models on the central server, thereby enhancing the detector's focus and improving its overall robustness during training. Through extensive experiments using the VIRTUAL (Variational Federated Multi-Task Learning) framework, we demonstrate consistent performance improvements across both balanced and imbalanced scenarios on benchmark datasets such as MNIST, FEMNIST, VSN, and HAR. Notably, we achieve a more than 9% absolute percentage improvement in the unbalanced MNIST benchmark. Additionally, our method is shown to be adaptable across various Federated Learning algorithms, delivering consistent gains in performance.

The application of transfer learning with deep neural networks has become increasingly prevalent for adapting well-established computer vision systems to new domains, particularly those with limited labeled data. In this work, we present a transfer learning case study in a data-scarce environment, where the target dataset contains fewer than 100 labeled samples. We assess the effectiveness of convolutional feature extraction and fine-tuning of overparameterized models, examining how their performance varies with the size of the target training data, as well as their ability to generalize to data affected by covariate shift or out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions. Our experimental results demonstrate that both model overparameterization and feature reuse play critical roles in achieving successful transfer learning for image classification in data-limited scenarios.

One of the key distinctions between human learning and Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) lies in humans' ability to focus on and master one task at a time. In contrast, ANNs typically learn multiple tasks simultaneously. When attempting to learn new tasks incrementally, ANNs often experience a complete loss of previously acquired knowledge—a phenomenon known as catastrophic forgetting. This limitation is considered a significant challenge in the development of true artificial intelligence systems.

In this paper, our objective is to identify and isolate the truly effective approaches to incremental learning from those that only perform well under specific conditions. To achieve this, we conduct a detailed analysis of the state-of-the-art method for incremental learning, iCaRL, and show that its performance is not primarily due to the reasons stated in the existing literature. Instead, we conclude that the success of iCaRL is largely attributed to knowledge distillation. However, we also highlight a critical drawback of knowledge distillation: it can introduce bias into classifiers.

To address this issue, we propose a dynamic threshold-moving algorithm that effectively mitigates this bias. We evaluate the performance of our algorithm on the CIFAR100 and MNIST datasets, demonstrating near-optimal results. Our implementation is available for further exploration and validation.

Quantum machine learning has emerged as a promising and dynamic area within the broader field of quantum technologies. It offers the potential, on one hand, to perform more efficient machine learning tasks using quantum devices, and on the other hand, to leverage machine learning techniques for improved control of quantum systems. Within this domain, quantum reinforcement learning seeks to develop "intelligent" quantum agents capable of interacting with and adapting to their environment in pursuit of specific objectives. Another key area is quantum autoencoders, which aim to reduce the resource requirements of quantum devices through a training process. Additionally, the field of quantum biomimetics explores analogies between biological and quantum systems, uncovering novel connections that could lead to innovative applications. Recent developments include concepts such as quantum artificial life and quantum memristors. In this Perspective, we provide an overview of these topics, highlighting the research conducted by the scientific community in this rapidly evolving field.

Driven by a 2-dimensional (unsupervised) image segmentation task, where local pixel regions are grouped through edge detection techniques, a more general probabilistic mathematical framework is developed. This framework identifies critical thresholds that reveal strong correlations among randomly generated, high-dimensional data points after they are projected into structured partitions within a bounded 2-dimensional space—where an image serves as a specific example. A notion of "neighborhood" for these structures is introduced, and a critical radius is determined. This radius, measured from a central structure within localized regions of the partition, reflects both short- and long-range correlations in the density of occupied structures. The length of a small interval of radii is estimated, beyond which the transition from short- to long-range correlation becomes virtually certain. This interval marks the point at which an image ceases to exhibit significant structural complexity, effectively defining the boundary of what constitutes an "interesting" image.

Recent research in adversarial learning has predominantly focused on neural networks and domains where they perform exceptionally well, such as computer vision and audio processing. In these areas, the data is typically homogeneous, while heterogeneous tabular datasets—despite their widespread use—remain largely unexplored. When searching for adversarial patterns in heterogeneous input spaces, attackers must simultaneously maintain the complex domain-specific validity rules of the data and ensure the adversarial nature of the samples. As a result, applying adversarial manipulations to heterogeneous datasets has proven to be a difficult task, with no general attack method proposed to date. However, we argue that machine learning models trained on heterogeneous tabular data are just as vulnerable to adversarial attacks as those trained on continuous or homogeneous data, such as images. To support this claim, we present a generic optimization framework for identifying adversarial perturbations in heterogeneous input spaces. We define distribution-aware constraints to ensure the consistency of adversarial examples and incorporate them by embedding the heterogeneous input into a continuous latent space. Given the characteristics of the underlying datasets, we focus on $\ell_0$ perturbations and demonstrate their practical applicability. We validate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on three real-world datasets.

In this paper, we explore a multi-issue negotiation scenario in which a seller negotiates both the composition and the price of bundled goods with customers. We provide key insights and introduce a procedure for identifying mutually beneficial alternatives to the bundle currently under discussion. The core of our approach involves integrating aggregate (anonymous) knowledge of customer preferences with real-time data from the ongoing negotiation. The proposed procedure can either utilize existing aggregate knowledge or, when such information is unavailable, acquire the necessary insights dynamically during the negotiation process. We conduct computer simulations using synthetic customers with nonlinear preferences. Our results demonstrate that, across different types of customers employing various negotiation strategies, the procedure significantly improves the speed of reaching agreements, as well as the quantity and Pareto efficiency of the deals achieved, when compared to a standard benchmark.

In the field of hyper-parameter tuning, recent approaches have increasingly leveraged low-fidelity observations—such as training on sub-sampled datasets or for shorter durations—to identify promising configurations for full-scale training. Among these methods, HyperBand has emerged as one of the most widely adopted due to its efficiency and strong theoretical guarantees. In this paper, we propose HyperJump, a novel method that builds upon HyperBand’s robust search strategy while incorporating advanced model-based risk analysis techniques. These techniques enable HyperJump to "jump" over low-risk configurations—those that are unlikely to perform well and would typically be discarded by HyperBand—thereby accelerating the search process. We evaluate HyperJump across a broad range of hyper-parameter optimization tasks and demonstrate that it achieves more than an order-of-magnitude speedup compared to HyperBand and several state-of-the-art optimizers, both in sequential and parallel settings, across diverse domains including deep learning, kernel-based learning, and neural architecture search.

Time series forecasting with limited data remains a challenging yet essential task. Although transformers have demonstrated remarkable performance in this domain, they typically require a large number of training samples due to their high parameter count. In this paper, we introduce a novel training technique for transformers that employs random sampling to construct training windows. By allowing non-consecutive input time steps, the number of distinct samples increases from linear to combinatorial. Furthermore, by disrupting the temporal order, this approach enables transformers to better capture fine-grained dependencies across time steps. Our method achieves competitive results compared to state-of-the-art approaches on real-world datasets.

It has been demonstrated that deep neural networks (DNNs) can be susceptible to adversarial attacks, raising concerns about their robustness, especially in safety-critical applications. In response to the local nature and limitations of existing adversarial attack methods, we introduce a new class of global adversarial attacks aimed at evaluating the global robustness of DNNs. Specifically, we propose a novel concept of global adversarial example pairs—pairs of examples that are close to each other in the input space but are classified differently by the DNN. We then present two families of global attack methods, showing that these approaches can generate diverse and compelling adversarial example pairs located far from the training or testing data. Furthermore, we demonstrate that DNNs that have been hardened through PGD-based (local) adversarial training remain vulnerable to these global adversarial examples, highlighting the necessity of considering global robustness during the training of robust deep learning models.

CycleGAN (Zhu et al., 2017) is a recently successful method for learning transformations between two image distributions. In a series of experiments, we uncover an interesting characteristic of the model: CycleGAN learns to embed information from the source image into the generated images in a nearly imperceptible, high-frequency signal. This technique allows the generator to reconstruct the original input, thereby satisfying the cyclic consistency constraint, while maintaining the realism of the output. We draw a connection between this behavior and adversarial attacks by interpreting the training process of CycleGAN as that of generating adversarial examples. Furthermore, we show that the cyclic consistency loss makes CycleGAN particularly susceptible to such attacks.

The conventional approach to compressive sampling focuses on reconstructing an unknown deterministic signal that exhibits a known structure. This typically involves designing the sub-sampling pattern and recovery algorithm based on prior knowledge of the signal's structure. Such methods often require identifying an appropriate signal representation and solving a non-smooth convex optimization problem, such as basis pursuit.

In this paper, we explore an alternative approach: instead of relying on prior knowledge of the signal structure, we learn an effective sub-sampling pattern using available training signals. The reconstructed signal is then obtained through a computationally efficient linear reconstruction method. We establish theoretical bounds on the recovery error and demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed compressive MRI framework through experiments on real-world MRI data.

Nonnegative Matrix Factorization (NMF) with group sparsity constraints can be formulated as a probabilistic graphical model. Given observed data generated by this model, a variational Bayesian algorithm is derived to estimate the model parameters. In supervised learning settings, NMF is typically used as an unsupervised feature extractor, followed by classification in the resulting feature space. By mapping class labels to a broader notion of groups that influence the sparsity of the coefficient matrix, the proposed group-sparse NMF model enables the integration of label information to learn low-dimensional, label-driven dictionaries. These dictionaries not only aim to accurately represent the data but also enhance class discrimination. Experimental results in face recognition and facial expression recognition demonstrate that classification in such label-driven feature subspaces outperforms classification in features obtained through purely unsupervised methods.

Many AI challenges in robotics and other domains are goal-oriented, focusing on finding paths that lead to specific target states. Reinforcement learning (RL), which is grounded in Bellman’s optimality equation, is inherently designed to optimize for a single goal. However, it can be adapted for multi-goal scenarios by incorporating the goal into the state representation. In contrast, we introduce a novel RL framework derived from a dynamic programming formulation of the all-pairs shortest path (APSP) problem, which naturally supports multi-goal planning. We demonstrate that this approach offers computational advantages in both standard and approximate dynamic programming settings.

Interestingly, our formulation introduces a new method for trajectory generation: rather than predicting the next state based on the previous one, as is typical in standard RL, our approach constructs a goal-conditioned trajectory by first predicting an intermediate state between the start and the goal, thereby splitting the path into two segments. This process is then repeated recursively on each sub-segment, progressively refining the trajectory until the full path is completed. We refer to this hierarchical structure as a sub-goal tree.

Building upon this structure, we extend the policy gradient method to recursively predict sub-goals, leading to new goal-based algorithms. Finally, we apply our approach to neural motion planning, where it significantly outperforms traditional RL methods in navigating a 7-degree-of-freedom robot arm through obstacle-laden environments.

In the future, advanced AI systems may be deployed in high-stakes environments, where a single failure could lead to severe consequences. One approach to enhancing AI safety in such settings is adversarial training, which involves using an adversary to generate challenging examples during training, thereby improving the system's performance under worst-case scenarios.

In this study, we used a language generation task as a testbed to explore how adversarial training can contribute to achieving greater reliability. We developed a range of adversarial training techniques, including a tool designed to assist human adversaries, with the goal of identifying and mitigating failures in a classifier that filters text completions generated by a model.

In our "avoid injuries" task, we found that we could set very conservative thresholds for the classifier without significantly compromising the quality of the filtered outputs. With these thresholds, our baseline classifier reduced the rate of unsafe completions from approximately 2.4% to 0.003% on in-distribution data—nearly reaching the limits of our measurement capabilities.

We observed that adversarial training substantially improved the system's robustness against the specific adversarial attacks it was trained on, while maintaining strong performance on standard, in-distribution data. We hope to see continued research in high-stakes reliability, including more advanced tools to support human adversaries and improved methods for ensuring safe and reliable AI behavior.

This paper introduces a deep learning model designed to simultaneously estimate both target and wall parameters in through-the-wall radar systems. The study examines two scenarios: single-target and two-target configurations. In each case, the model estimates the wall's permittivity and thickness, along with the two-dimensional coordinates and permittivity of the target(s). Specifically, for the single-target case, five parameters are estimated, while for the two-target scenario, eight parameters are simultaneously determined. 

Our findings demonstrate that incorporating more problem-related parameters into the deep neural network enhances the accuracy of target localization. Consequently, we included the wall's permittivity and thickness as part of the estimation process, which not only allowed us to accurately determine these wall properties but also improved the precision of target localization. Using a deep neural network model, we achieved an accuracy of 99% in estimating the wall's permittivity and thickness, as well as the two-dimensional coordinates and permittivity of the targets in both single-target and two-target modes.

We investigate the challenge of estimating conditional average treatment effects (CATE) from observational data in the presence of unobserved confounders. The CATE function provides individual-level causal effect predictions based on baseline covariates, making it essential for personalized decision-making. While recent research has primarily focused on CATE estimation under the assumption of unconfoundedness—where no unobserved confounders exist—this assumption may not hold in practice. When unconfoundedness is violated, the CATE may not be uniquely identifiable. To address this, we propose a functional interval estimator that provides bounds on individual causal effects under plausible violations of unconfoundedness. Our approach employs a weighted kernel estimator with adversarially varying weights, ensuring robustness to hidden confounding. We establish that our estimator is sharp, meaning it converges to the tightest possible bounds on CATE when unobserved confounders are present. Additionally, we analyze personalized decision rules derived from our estimator and show that they achieve optimal minimax regret asymptotically. We evaluate our method through a simulation study and illustrate its practical utility by comparing findings from an observational study on hormone replacement therapy with results from a clinical trial.

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have demonstrated impressive performance in learning complex data distributions across various data types. In this paper, we first demonstrate that a direct extension of existing GAN algorithms is not suitable for point cloud generation, as the discriminators require constraints that are undefined for set-based data. To address this, we introduce PC-GAN, a two-fold modification to the GAN framework designed specifically for generating point clouds. 

First, we integrate concepts from hierarchical Bayesian modeling and implicit generative models by developing a hierarchical and interpretable sampling process. A critical element of our approach is the training of a posterior inference network for the latent variables. Second, rather than relying solely on the state-of-the-art Wasserstein GAN objective, we propose a novel "sandwiching" objective that provides a tighter estimate of the Wasserstein distance compared to the conventional dual formulation. This makes PC-GAN a flexible framework capable of incorporating various existing GAN techniques.

We evaluate our approach on the ModelNet40 benchmark dataset.
