Using the distance between generated point clouds and real mesh data as a metric, we show that PC-GAN trained with the sandwiching objective outperforms existing methods on test data. Additionally, as a secondary benefit, PC-GAN learns expressive latent representations of point clouds that achieve competitive performance in downstream tasks.

Many machine learning models are susceptible to adversarial examples—carefully crafted inputs designed to deceive the model into producing incorrect outputs. Notably, adversarial examples that fool one model often also affect another, even when the models have different architectures or were trained on distinct datasets, as long as they are tasked with the same objective. As a result, an attacker can train a substitute model, generate adversarial examples against it, and then transfer these examples to a target (victim) model, with minimal knowledge of the victim's structure. Recent research has advanced this approach by using the victim model as an oracle to generate labeled synthetic data for the substitute, eliminating the need for the attacker to gather a separate training set. In this work, we build upon these techniques by incorporating reservoir sampling, significantly improving the efficiency of the substitute model's training process. We introduce novel transferability attacks between previously unexplored pairs of model classes, particularly between support vector machines (SVMs) and decision trees. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of these attacks on two commercial classification systems from Amazon (achieving a 96.19% misclassification rate) and Google (88.94%), using only 800 queries to the victim model.

Visual scenes are remarkably diverse, not only due to the vast number of possible object and background combinations, but also because the perception of the same scene can vary significantly depending on the viewpoint. When observing a scene with multiple objects from different perspectives, humans are capable of understanding the scene in a structured way from each viewpoint, achieving what is known as "object constancy" across varying views—even without explicit knowledge of the exact viewpoints. This ability is crucial for recognizing the same object while moving and for efficiently learning from visual input. It is therefore fascinating to develop models that replicate this capability. In this paper, we address a new challenge: learning compositional scene representations from multiple unspecified viewpoints without any supervision. We introduce a deep generative model that disentangles latent representations into viewpoint-independent and viewpoint-dependent components. To infer these latent representations, information from different viewpoints is progressively integrated through neural networks. Experiments on several specially designed synthetic datasets demonstrate that our method can effectively learn from multiple unlabelled viewpoints.

We introduce an ensemble prediction system based on a Deep Learning Weather Prediction (DLWP) model, which recursively forecasts key atmospheric variables with a six-hour temporal resolution. The model employs convolutional neural networks (CNNs) on a cubed-sphere grid to generate global weather forecasts. This approach is computationally efficient, producing a 320-member ensemble of six-week forecasts at 1.4° resolution in just three minutes on a single GPU. The ensemble spread is generated by randomizing the CNN training process, resulting in 32 distinct DLWP models with slightly varied learned weights.

Although the DLWP model does not predict precipitation, it accurately forecasts total column water vapor and provides a reasonable 4.5-day deterministic forecast for Hurricane Irma. Beyond mid-latitude weather systems, the model spontaneously generates tropical cyclones in a one-year free-running simulation. On average, over a two-year test period, the ensemble mean root-mean-square error (RMSE) retains skill relative to climatology beyond two weeks, with anomaly correlation coefficients remaining above 0.6 through six days.

Our primary application is subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) forecasting for lead times ranging from two to six weeks. Current operational systems exhibit limited skill in predicting weather patterns averaged over one or two weeks at these time scales. The continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) and...

This study introduces a Deep Belief Network (DBN) model designed for classifying traffic flow states. The model is capable of handling large-scale, high-density, and noisy datasets collected from smartphone sensors. Statistical features extracted from vehicle acceleration, angular acceleration, and GPS speed data—recorded through smartphone applications—are analyzed and utilized as input for the classification process. Data gathered over a five-day experimental period is used to train and evaluate the proposed model. A total of 747,856 data samples are generated and employed for both traffic flow state classification and the sensitivity analysis of input variables. The results demonstrate that the proposed DBN model outperforms traditional machine learning methods in terms of classification accuracy and computational efficiency.

Variational Bayes (VB) has emerged as a scalable alternative to Markov chain Monte Carlo methods for Bayesian inference. In this work, we analyze a mean-field spike and slab VB approximation applied to commonly used Bayesian model selection priors in sparse, high-dimensional logistic regression. We establish non-asymptotic theoretical guarantees for the VB posterior, demonstrating optimal (minimax) convergence rates in both $\ell_2$ and prediction loss under a sparse true model. Notably, our results show that the VB algorithm achieves optimality without relying on knowledge of the unknown true parameter, offering insights into effective prior design. Numerical experiments further confirm the superior performance of our VB approach compared to standard sparse VB methods.

Zooplankton images, like many real-world data types, possess inherent characteristics that complicate the development of effective classification systems. For example, the number of potential classes in practical applications can be very large, and classes may be ambiguous or overlapping. Moreover, taxonomic classifications often vary among researchers and institutions. While high accuracy has been achieved in benchmarks using standard classifier architectures, biases introduced by rigid classification schemes can significantly impact the reliability of results when these outputs are used for ecosystem assessments and monitoring.

In this work, we propose the use of a deep convolutional neural network to generate a vector embedding of zooplankton images. This approach maps each image into a high-dimensional Euclidean space, where the distances between vectors correspond to the semantic relationships among the images. We demonstrate that such an embedding can produce classifications with accuracy comparable to that of a dedicated classifier, while also uncovering meaningful structures within the data. Additionally, we test the embedding's performance on new classes that were not part of the original training set.

Traditional neural network classifiers tend to perform well when the classes are clearly defined in advance and when sufficient labeled data is available. However, in practical scenarios, these conditions are often not met, making it essential to explore more flexible and robust approaches for classification and data representation.

Structured prediction is typically addressed by training a locally normalized model using maximum likelihood, followed by approximate decoding with beam search. However, this approach can lead to mismatches, as the model is not exposed to its own errors during training and does not use beam search in that phase. Beam-aware training aims to resolve these issues, yet it remains underutilized due to limited understanding of its performance impact, optimal use cases, and stability. Recently, Negrinho et al. (2018) introduced a meta-algorithm that generalizes beam-aware training methods and suggests new ones, though they did not provide empirical validation. In this paper, we initiate an empirical study by training the supertagging model from Vaswani et al. (2016) and a simpler model using instantiations of the meta-algorithm. We investigate the effects of different design choices and offer recommendations for their selection. Our findings show that beam-aware training enhances performance for both models, with more significant improvements observed in the simpler model, which must effectively handle uncertainty during decoding. These results suggest that a model should be trained with search in mind to achieve its full potential.

Web-based interactions are often modeled as attributed graphs, and node clustering in such structures has become a topic of significant research interest. While Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have been widely applied for this task, they face limitations in accuracy due to the over-smoothing problem. Although alternative methods—particularly those based on Laplacian smoothing—have achieved better performance, they suffer from a critical drawback: poor scalability. In this paper, we tackle this challenge by connecting Laplacian smoothing with the Generalized PageRank and introducing a random-walk-based algorithm as a scalable graph filter. This forms the foundation of our scalable deep clustering method, RwSL. By employing a self-supervised mini-batch training approach, RwSL jointly optimizes a deep neural network for assigning samples to clusters and an autoencoder that learns embeddings tailored for clustering. Experimental results on six real-world datasets, evaluated using six clustering metrics, demonstrate that RwSL outperforms several recent state-of-the-art methods. Notably, RwSL is the first deep clustering framework capable of scaling effectively to graphs with over one million nodes, making it suitable for web-scale applications. Furthermore, we show that RwSL can perform node clustering on a graph containing 1.8 billion edges using just a single GPU.

We introduce an algorithm for deep learning on networks and graphs. Our approach is based on the observation that many graph algorithms—such as PageRank, Weisfeiler-Lehman, and Message Passing—can be viewed as iterative updates to vertex states. Unlike prior methods that depend on the designer's insight to define specific update rules, Deep Graphs automatically adapt to the learning task. The algorithm is computationally efficient, with both training and inference operating in $O(|E| + |V|)$ time, where $E$ and $V$ represent the sets of edges and vertices, respectively. In essence, we learn the recurrent update functions rather than specifying them a priori. This leads to a powerful method that achieves high accuracy on both graph labeling and regression tasks.

As next-generation networks continue to evolve, the demand for higher levels of intelligence is growing. Federated Learning has emerged as a critical enabler for building intelligent and distributed network systems. However, like any machine learning approach, it is susceptible to concept drift, which can significantly degrade model performance. In the context of modern networks that support critical and emergency services, such degradation can lead to serious consequences. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a concept drift detection system that utilizes the updates generated during each iteration of the federated learning process. By employing dimensionality reduction and clustering techniques, the proposed framework identifies and isolates nodes experiencing drift. Experimental results using an Intelligent Transportation System as a use case demonstrate the effectiveness of the framework in detecting drifted nodes across various non-IID scenarios, at different stages of drift, and under varying levels of system exposure.

In a recent study, we introduced a discriminative backend for speaker verification that demonstrated strong out-of-the-box calibration performance across various testing conditions with differing levels of mismatch relative to the training data. This backend emulates the conventional PLDA-based process used in most modern speaker verification systems, including the calibration stage. All parameters within the backend are jointly optimized to minimize binary cross-entropy for the speaker verification task.

The robustness of the calibration is achieved by making the calibration parameters dependent on condition-representing vectors, which are derived from a model trained to predict condition labels. In this work, we propose a streamlined version of the backend in which these condition vectors are estimated directly within the backend, eliminating the need for an external condition prediction model. We demonstrate that this simplified approach achieves performance comparable to the original method, while being easier to implement and requiring less extensive training data.

Additionally, we present an analysis of several key aspects of the proposed method, including the impact of initialization, the characteristics of the vectors used for computing calibration parameters, and the influence of the random seed and the number of training samples.

In this study, we integrate the representation learning power of neural networks with domain expertise from agricultural scientists to model environmental heat and drought stresses. We begin by developing deterministic expert models, which serve as a benchmark and guide the design of more flexible neural network architectures. Finally, a sensitivity analysis of these models enables the clustering of hybrid varieties into susceptible and resistant categories.

Reviewing multiple log files from various processes can be a time-consuming and complex task, as these logs often contain a large volume of events, each with numerous attributes. To address this challenge, we developed an automated approach for modeling log files and identifying outlier traces within the data. Our method extends Dynamic Bayesian Networks to capture the normal behavior observed in log files. We also introduce a novel algorithm that learns a model directly from the log data. This model is capable of assigning scores to traces, even when new values or previously unseen combinations of values appear.

A neural network is essentially a high-dimensional, complex mapping model that achieves feature fitting by adjusting its weights. However, the spectral bias inherent in neural network training often results in an excessive number of training epochs required to accurately fit high-frequency components in broadband signals. To address this challenge and improve the efficiency of high-frequency component fitting, the PhaseDNN was recently introduced by integrating complex frequency band extraction with frequency shift techniques [Cai et al., SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 42, A3285 (2020)]. In this paper, we propose an alternative approach for efficiently fitting complex signals containing high-frequency components. Specifically, we introduce a Parallel Frequency Function-Deep Neural Network (PFF-DNN), which reduces computational overhead while maintaining fitting accuracy by leveraging fast Fourier analysis of broadband signals and the spectral bias characteristics of neural networks. The effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed PFF-DNN method are demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments on six typical broadband signals.

Sparse deep neural networks have demonstrated effectiveness in building predictive models for large-scale studies. While prior research has explored the theoretical and numerical properties of sparse neural architectures, most efforts have concentrated on edge-level sparsity. Although edge pruning may seem intuitively appealing, it does not necessarily reduce the overall structural complexity of a network. In contrast, pruning redundant nodes within each layer leads to a structurally sparse network, which can significantly lower computational complexity and memory usage.

To address this, we propose a Bayesian approach that employs spike-and-slab Gaussian priors to enable node selection during training. This method eliminates the need for arbitrary thresholding rules to remove unnecessary nodes. Furthermore, we adopt a variational Bayes framework to overcome the computational limitations associated with traditional Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods.

In the context of node selection, we establish a fundamental result on the consistency of the variational posterior distribution, along with a detailed characterization of the prior parameters. Unlike previous work, our theoretical analysis relaxes the assumptions of equal node counts and uniform bounds on all weights, allowing for greater flexibility in handling sparse networks with layer-specific node structures or varying coefficient constraints. Our approach provides a more general and adaptive framework for achieving structural sparsity in deep learning models.

Multiview representation learning of data can facilitate the creation of coherent and contextually rich user representations on social media. This paper introduces a joint embedding model that integrates users' social and textual information to learn contextualized user representations, enabling a deeper understanding of their lifestyle choices. We apply our model to tweets related to two lifestyle activities—`Yoga` and `Keto diet`—and use it to identify users' activity types and motivations. The paper details the data collection and annotation process and presents an in-depth analysis of users from different classes based on their Twitter content. Experimental results demonstrate that our model achieves performance improvements across both domains.

Currently, the growth of material data generated from experiments and simulations is surpassing manageable limits. This rapid expansion underscores the need for advanced data-driven methods capable of uncovering patterns across multiple length and time scales, as well as establishing structure-property relationships. These data-driven techniques hold significant potential within the field of materials science. This review provides an overview of machine learning applications in the characterization of metallic materials. Numerous parameters related to material processing and microstructure influence the properties and performance of manufactured components. As a result, this study aims to explore the effectiveness of machine learning approaches in predicting material properties. Key material characteristics such as strength, toughness, hardness, brittleness, and ductility are critical in classifying materials or components based on their quality. In industrial settings, conventional material tests—such as tensile, compression, and creep tests—are often time-consuming and costly. Therefore, the adoption of machine learning methods is seen as a valuable tool for more efficiently generating material property information. This study also presents an application of machine learning techniques to small punch test data, with the goal of determining the ultimate tensile strength of various materials. A strong correlation was observed between small punch test data and tensile test results, ultimately enabling the prediction of tensile strength based on small punch measurements.

Message passing on a factor graph provides a versatile framework for implementing approximate inference algorithms in complex, large-scale models. The concept of a factor graph fragment facilitates the modular organization of both algebraic expressions and computational code. We demonstrate that the Inverse G-Wishart family of distributions allows for the elegant and concise representation of fundamental variational message passing fragments. These fragments are commonly used in models involving approximate inference about covariance matrices or variance parameters, and they play a central role in modern statistics and machine learning.

In many real-world applications, obtaining sufficient large-scale labeled data to fully leverage deep neural networks is often challenging and costly. As a result, transferring knowledge learned from a well-labeled source domain to an unlabeled or sparsely labeled target domain has emerged as a promising alternative. However, direct knowledge transfer typically leads to a significant drop in performance due to domain shift. Domain adaptation (DA) aims to address this issue by reducing the discrepancy between the source and target domains. Multi-source domain adaptation (MDA) extends this concept by leveraging labeled data from multiple sources with potentially different distributions. Given the success of DA techniques and the increasing availability of multi-source data, MDA has gained growing interest in both academic research and industrial applications. In this survey, we provide an overview of various MDA strategies, summarize existing datasets for evaluation, compare state-of-the-art MDA methods in the deep learning era—including latent space transformation and intermediate domain generation—and discuss potential future research directions in this field.

Combination therapy has demonstrated the ability to enhance therapeutic effectiveness while minimizing adverse effects. Importantly, it has emerged as a critical strategy for overcoming resistance in antibiotics, antimicrobials, and anti-cancer drugs. However, despite the vast chemical space and the lack of clear design principles for small-molecule combinations, computational approaches to drug combination design have yet to fully realize their potential, particularly in the absence of generative models capable of accelerating the discovery of effective resistance-breaking combinations.

To address this gap, we have developed the first deep generative model for drug combination design, integrating graph-structured domain knowledge with an iterative reinforcement learning-based approach for generating chemical graph sets. 

First, we introduced Hierarchical Variational Graph Auto-Encoders (HVGAE), which are trained end-to-end to jointly encode gene-gene, gene-disease, and disease-disease networks. A novel attentional pooling mechanism is incorporated to derive disease representations from the representations of associated genes.

Second, by targeting diseases based on these learned representations, we reformulated the drug-combination design problem as a graph-set generation task and developed a deep learning model equipped with novel reward mechanisms. In addition to chemical validity rewards, we introduced a novel generative adversarial reward—based on the generalized sliced Wasserstein distance—to promote the generation of chemically diverse molecules that resemble known drugs. We also designed a network principle-based reward to guide the selection of effective drug combinations.

Numerical results show that compared to traditional graph embedding methods, HVGAE learns more informative and generalizable disease representations. Case studies further demonstrate the model's effectiveness in identifying promising drug combinations.

Imaging Cherenkov detectors are widely employed in modern nuclear and particle physics experiments, where advanced solutions are essential to meet the ever-increasing computational challenges. This field presents a promising opportunity for AI-driven approaches, and today we are seeing the emergence of new, highly efficient, and fast applications. This paper explores innovative directions in the application of these techniques to Cherenkov detectors, with a focus on recent advancements in detector design, calibration, and particle identification.

This paper addresses the challenge of estimating the Markov parameters of a linear system using observed data. Recent non-asymptotic system identification studies have analyzed the sample complexity of this problem in both single- and multi-rollout scenarios. In both cases, the number of samples needed to achieve accurate estimates can lead to optimization problems with an excessively large number of decision variables, making them computationally intractable for standard second-order methods. We propose a randomized and distributed Newton algorithm that leverages Hessian-sketching to efficiently compute $\epsilon$-optimal solutions with geometric convergence. Additionally, the algorithm is inherently parallelizable. Our analysis applies to a wide range of sketching matrices, and we support our theoretical findings with numerical experiments.

We introduce two new algorithms for learning formulas in Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) from examples. The first algorithm transforms the learning process into a sequence of satisfiability problems in propositional logic, and it generates the smallest LTL formula (in terms of the number of subformulas) that is consistent with the provided data. The second algorithm integrates the SAT-based approach with classical decision tree learning methods, resulting in a scalable solution suitable for real-world applications involving hundreds of examples. However, this approach no longer ensures the production of minimal consistent LTL formulas. We evaluate both algorithms on a variety of synthetic benchmarks and demonstrate their effectiveness. Furthermore, we show their practical utility in analyzing the execution behavior of a leader election protocol.

In this paper, we introduce a framework for addressing a single-agent task through the collaboration of multiple agents, each specializing in distinct components of the task. This approach offers two key benefits: first, it enables the training of specialized agents on different aspects of the task, and second, it introduces a novel method for knowledge transfer by reusing trained agents. Unlike traditional hierarchical decomposition, where a single agent takes control at any given time until its subtask is completed, our framework allows for a more flexible and integrated approach. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through empirical experiments in two different domains.

Machine learning (ML) applications have experienced significant growth in recent years, largely driven by the increasing availability of data. However, real-world datasets often suffer from inconsistency and incompleteness, and the effects of these issues on ML performance are not yet fully understood. In this paper, we conduct a formal investigation into how data incompleteness affects ML outcomes by extending the concept of "Certain Answers" from Codd tables—long studied in the database community—into the domain of machine learning. 

Specifically, we focus on classification tasks and introduce the concept of "Certain Predictions" (CP). A test instance is considered to be "certainly predicted" if every possible classifier trained on all potential complete versions of the data yields the same prediction. We examine two fundamental CP-related queries: (Q1) the **checking query**, which determines whether a given data example can be certainly predicted; and (Q2) the **counting query**, which calculates how many classifiers support a particular prediction (i.e., a specific label).

Given that solving CP queries in general is computationally challenging without restrictions on the type of classifier, we present a case study focused on **nearest neighbor (NN) classifiers**, for which efficient solutions to both CP queries can be developed. We demonstrate that it is possible to effectively compute certain predictions under this framework.

To enhance the travel experience, researchers have been exploring the role of attitudes in modeling travel behavior. While most studies rely on closed-ended surveys, there is ongoing debate about the most effective method for measuring attitudes. Topic Modeling offers a promising alternative by significantly reducing the time required to extract insights from open-ended responses and minimizing subjective bias, thereby addressing analysts' concerns. In this study, we apply Topic Modeling to analyze open-ended responses and compare its effectiveness with traditional closed-ended questions. Additionally, some respondents may prefer answering using their preferred survey format. To accommodate this, we propose a flexible modeling framework that allows participants to choose their preferred questionnaire type while enabling analysts to employ their preferred modeling approach for predicting behavior. We test this framework using a dataset collected in the U.S., which examines intentions to use Autonomous Vehicles for commuting trips. Participants were presented with both open- and closed-ended versions of the survey. To ensure a fair comparison between the two formats, the survey was carefully designed to eliminate confounding factors such as statement influence, behavioral context, and choice experiment design. The results show that Topic Modeling is effective in extracting meaningful information from open-ended responses, but models based on closed-ended questions still demonstrate superior performance.

We investigate supervised learning problems where clustering constraints are used to impose structure on either features or samples, with the goal of enhancing both predictive performance and model interpretability. Clustering features naturally arises in tasks such as text classification, where it helps reduce dimensionality by grouping related words and identifying synonyms. On the other hand, clustering samples is relevant in multiclass settings where multiple predictions are allowed, and the accuracy of the best prediction is considered. We develop a unified optimization framework that reveals the shared structure underlying these problems, and propose algorithms whose core computational step involves a k-means clustering operation, which can be efficiently approximated. We extend this approach to incorporate both sparsity and clustering constraints, introducing a novel projection algorithm for the space of clustered sparse vectors. We establish convergence guarantees for our algorithms under a random instance setup, leveraging a union of subspaces interpretation of the clustering structure. Finally, we evaluate the robustness of our methods on both synthetic datasets and real-world data from movie reviews.

To succeed in real-world tasks, Reinforcement Learning (RL) must leverage the compositional, relational, and hierarchical nature of the environment, and effectively transfer this understanding to the specific task at hand. Recent advancements in representation learning for language have enabled the development of models that can acquire world knowledge from text data and incorporate it into decision-making processes. This suggests that now is an opportune time to explore a more integrated approach between natural language understanding and RL. In this work, we review the current state of the field, covering areas such as instruction following, text-based games, and the use of textual domain knowledge. Finally, we advocate for the creation of new environments and further exploration of how recent advances in Natural Language Processing (NLP) can enhance RL systems.

This article introduces a novel approach for estimating an existing mutual information-based dependence measure by utilizing histogram density estimates. A critical challenge in this process is determining an appropriate bin width for the histogram, which remains an open issue in statistical analysis. To address this, we propose a new method for calculating the bin length based on a function of the maximum separation between data points. This choice of bin width ensures consistent density estimates when using the histogram method.

The resulting density estimates are then used to compute an estimate of an established dependence measure. The proposed estimator is referred to as the Mutual Information Based Dependence Index (MIDI). Several key properties of MIDI are discussed. The performance of the proposed method is evaluated against widely accepted measures such as Distance Correlation (dcor) and Maximal Information Coefficient (MINE), focusing on accuracy and computational efficiency. This comparison is conducted using various artificial datasets with differing levels of noise.

The method demonstrates the ability to detect a wide range of relationships between variables without requiring any assumptions about the underlying functional form. The power statistics of MIDI highlight its effectiveness in identifying nonlinear relationships. Consequently, the method achieves broad applicability while maintaining a low rate of false positives. Overall, MIDI is found to perform competitively and effectively in comparison to existing techniques.

We explore a strategy to enhance the efficiency of contrastive learning for visual representations by incorporating a limited amount of supervised information during pre-training. We introduce a semi-supervised loss function called SuNCEt, which combines noise-contrastive estimation with neighborhood component analysis. This loss not only supports self-supervised instance-wise pretext tasks but also aims to effectively differentiate between classes. On ImageNet, we demonstrate that SuNCEt achieves comparable semi-supervised learning accuracy to previous contrastive methods while requiring less than half the pre-training data and computational resources. Our key insight is that integrating even a small amount of labeled data during pre-training—rather than just during fine-tuning—provides a crucial signal that significantly accelerates the learning of visual representations. Our code is available on GitHub at github.com/facebookresearch/suncet.

Knowledge distillation (KD) has proven to be an effective technique for enhancing the performance of graph neural networks (GNNs), with the primary objective of transferring knowledge from a more complex, deeper teacher GNN to a simpler, shallower student GNN. However, in practice, training a high-quality teacher GNN remains challenging due to issues such as over-parametrization and over-smoothing, which can hinder the effectiveness of knowledge transfer. To address this limitation, we introduce FreeKD, the first reinforcement learning-based knowledge distillation framework for GNNs that does not rely on a pre-trained, deep, and well-optimized teacher model. The core concept of FreeKD involves collaboratively constructing two shallower GNNs and enabling them to exchange knowledge through a hierarchical reinforcement learning process. Observing that different nodes within a GNN may exhibit varying levels of performance during training, we design a dynamic and flexible knowledge transfer strategy comprising two levels of actions: 1) node-level actions that determine the direction of knowledge transfer between corresponding nodes in the two networks; and 2) structure-level actions that decide which local structures, generated by the node-level interactions, should be propagated. In essence, FreeKD is a general and principled framework that offers a novel approach to knowledge distillation in GNNs, free from the constraints of traditional teacher-student architectures.

Failures and anomalies in large-scale software systems are inevitable. When an issue arises, operators must quickly and accurately pinpoint its source to enable rapid resolution. In this work, we address the challenge of identifying the root cause set that best explains an anomaly in multi-dimensional time series data with categorical attributes. The vast search space presents a significant challenge—even with a small number of attributes and limited value sets, the number of possible combinations becomes prohibitively large for brute-force approaches. Previous methods have attempted to reduce the search space, but they often face limitations such as requiring extensive manual parameter tuning, being too slow for practical use, or failing to detect more complex root causes. To overcome these challenges, we introduce RiskLoc, a novel approach for multidimensional root cause localization. RiskLoc employs a 2-way partitioning strategy and assigns element weights that increase linearly with distance from the partitioning point. Each element is assigned a risk score that combines two key factors: (1) its weighted proportion within the anomalous partition, and (2) the relative change in deviation score adjusted for the ripple effect. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of RiskLoc.

Learning optimal policies in environments with sparse rewards is challenging, as the agent receives minimal or no feedback about the quality of its actions. In such scenarios, effective exploration becomes crucial, as it increases the likelihood of encountering a reward signal that can guide policy improvement. A robust learning algorithm for these settings must be capable of (1) exploring a wide range of agent behaviors and (2) efficiently exploiting any reward that is discovered. While several efficient exploration methods have been proposed, they often require the prior definition of a behavior space—a representation that maps an agent's actions to a structured, exploratory space. This pre-defined structure limits their flexibility and applicability. In this work, we present STAX, an algorithm that dynamically learns a behavior space during training and explores it while simultaneously optimizing any discovered reward. STAX achieves this by decoupling the exploration and behavior space learning from the reward exploitation through an alternating two-step process. In the first step, STAX constructs a diverse set of policies while learning a low-dimensional representation of the high-dimensional observations generated during policy evaluation. In the second step, emitters are used to...

This study represents the first experimental effort to explore the performance bottlenecks that 5G mobile networks may encounter. To achieve this, we utilize a comprehensive set of measurements collected from a prototype testbed designed to reflect the essential characteristics of a cloudified mobile network. We examine the significance of various metrics and evaluate different approaches for effectively and efficiently detecting bottlenecks across multiple network locations and system layers. Our results underscore the complexity of this task within a multi-layered architecture and emphasize the need for innovative monitoring strategies that intelligently integrate metrics across network layers and functions. Notably, we find that distributed analytics demonstrates satisfactory performance in terms of both bottleneck detection accuracy and the associated computational and communication overhead.

Distillation is a powerful technique for knowledge transfer, where the soft predictions of a high-capacity teacher model are used to guide the training of a more compact student model. However, pre-trained teachers with strong capabilities are not always accessible. To address this, recent approaches have introduced online distillation methods that use aggregated intermediate predictions from multiple student models as targets for individual students. While such group-based targets offer a promising solution for teacher-free distillation, the use of simple aggregation functions often leads to rapid homogenization among group members, resulting in early saturation and suboptimal performance.

In this work, we propose Online Knowledge Distillation with Diverse Peers (OKDDip), a framework that performs two-stage distillation using multiple auxiliary peers and a single group leader. In the first stage, each auxiliary peer employs an attention-based mechanism to generate personalized aggregation weights, enabling it to derive distinct target distributions from the predictions of other peers. This diversity in target distributions enhances the overall effectiveness of group-based distillation. In the second stage, the knowledge from the ensemble of auxiliary peers is further transferred to the group leader, which serves as the final model for inference.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that OKDDip consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods without increasing training or inference complexity, validating the efficacy of our approach.

We have introduced a model inspired by flocking behavior on a complex network, and subsequently developed two clustering algorithms based on this framework. In these algorithms, a weighted and directed *k*-nearest neighbor (knn) graph is first constructed among all data points, with each point treated as an agent capable of movement in space. A time-varying complex network is then formed by introducing long-range links for each data point. Additionally, each data point is influenced not only by its *k* nearest neighbors but also by *r* long-range neighbors through spatial fields they collectively establish. As a result, each point moves in the direction of the vector sum of all these fields. Importantly, the long-range links provide hidden information that guides the movement of each data point, while also accelerating its convergence toward a central location. As the data points evolve according to the proposed model, those belonging to the same class gradually gather in the same region, while those from different classes separate. Consequently, the experimental results show that the data points are clustered effectively and reasonably.

Metal artifacts in computed tomography (CT) result from a discrepancy between the actual physics of image formation and the idealized assumptions made during tomographic reconstruction. These artifacts are especially pronounced around metal implants, which significantly hinder the broader use of 3D cone-beam CT (CBCT), despite its potential for real-time intra-operative verification of implant placement—such as in spinal fusion surgery. Through experiments on both synthetic and real data, we show that many of these artifacts can be mitigated by acquiring higher-quality data in a task-aware and patient-specific manner. We present the first step toward a task-aware CBCT protocol. Traditionally, the short-scan CBCT trajectory is planar, offering limited flexibility for scene-specific optimization. We enhance this trajectory by autonomously adjusting the out-of-plane angulation. This allows for C-arm source paths that are tailored to the specific imaging scenario, avoiding the acquisition of "poor-quality" images caused by beam hardening, photon starvation, and noise. The determination of optimal out-of-plane angulation is performed in real-time using a deep convolutional neural network that predicts a detectability rank based on principles of imaging physics.

We introduce semi-random features as a flexible approach for nonlinear function approximation. These features occupy an intermediate position between the fully adaptable units in deep learning and the fixed, randomly generated features used in kernel methods. For single-layer models employing semi-random features, we establish, without relying on unrealistic assumptions, that the model class is universal—meaning it can approximate any target function arbitrarily well as the number of features increases. Furthermore, despite the non-convex nature of the optimization problem, we demonstrate that a near-optimal function can be efficiently found, and that this function generalizes well to unseen data.

For deep models, we similarly prove universal approximation capability, derive a lower bound on the approximation error, provide partial guarantees for optimization, and establish a generalization bound. Notably, the generalization performance of deep semi-random features can be exponentially better than that of standard deep ReLU networks under certain conditions. Our analysis shows that the generalization error bound is independent of key factors such as depth, the number of trainable parameters, and input dimensionality.

Empirically, we show that semi-random features can achieve performance comparable to neural networks by using only slightly more units, while significantly outperforming traditional random features with fewer units. Additionally, we present a novel implicit ensemble method based on semi-random features, further enhancing their effectiveness.

We present a novel class of lower bounds on the log partition function of a Markov random field, leveraging a reversed form of Jensen's inequality. Specifically, our approach approximates the intractable distribution by combining spanning trees with negative weights. This method serves as the lower-bound counterpart to the tree-reweighted belief propagation algorithm, which employs convex combinations of spanning trees with positive weights to derive upper bounds. We propose algorithms for optimizing and refining these lower bounds over the non-convex space of valid parameters. Notably, our approach generalizes mean field methods—including both naive and structured mean field approximations—recovering them as a limiting case.

We investigate fast algorithms for statistical regression problems under the strong contamination model, where the objective is to approximately optimize a generalized linear model (GLM) in the presence of adversarially corrupted data. Previous work in this area has primarily relied on two approaches: the robust gradient descent framework introduced by Prasad et al., which employs biased gradient queries, and the Sever framework developed by Diakonikolas et al., an iterative method that removes outliers by calling a stationary point finder.

In this paper, we introduce nearly-linear time algorithms for robust regression tasks that offer either improved runtime or better estimation guarantees compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. For the general case of smooth GLMs—such as logistic regression—we demonstrate that the robust gradient descent approach can be accelerated, and we show that our algorithm can also be applied to optimize the Moreau envelopes of Lipschitz GLMs, such as support vector machines. This addresses several open questions in the literature.

For the well-studied problem of robust linear regression, we present an alternative method that achieves improved estimation rates over prior nearly-linear time algorithms. Notably, our approach builds upon an identifiability proof originally introduced in the context of the sum-of-squares algorithm by Bakshi and Prasad. While that algorithm achieved optimal error rates, it required a large polynomial runtime and sample complexity. We reinterpret their proof within a more efficient computational framework, enabling both faster execution and stronger theoretical guarantees.

Reinforcement learning has achieved remarkable success across a wide range of applications. However, learning an effective policy typically requires the agent to interact extensively with the environment, which can be computationally expensive and time-consuming. To address this challenge, the framework known as Reinforcement Learning with Expert Demonstrations (RLED) was introduced to leverage supervision from expert demonstrations. While RLED methods can reduce the number of learning iterations, they often assume that the provided demonstrations are perfect, making them vulnerable to performance degradation when faced with noisy or imperfect data in real-world scenarios.

In this paper, we propose a novel framework that enables the agent to adaptively learn a policy by simultaneously interacting with the environment and leveraging expert demonstrations. Specifically, for each step in a demonstration trajectory, we construct an instance and define a joint loss function that aims to both maximize the expected reward and minimize the discrepancy between the agent's behavior and the expert demonstrations. Crucially, we calculate the expected gain of the value function to assign a weight to each instance, reflecting its potential utility. This weighting mechanism allows the framework to emphasize more informative demonstrations while effectively filtering out noisy ones.

Experimental results across multiple environments and with several popular reinforcement learning algorithms demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

Most artificial neural networks used for object detection and recognition are trained in a fully supervised manner. This approach is not only resource-intensive, requiring large sets of labeled data, but also diverges significantly from the way humans learn. In this work, we propose an alternative setup where an artificial agent first learns through self-supervised exploration in a simulated environment. After this initial phase, the representations acquired through interaction with the world can be used to associate semantic concepts, such as different types of doors. To achieve this, we employ a method called *fast concept mapping*, which identifies and defines semantic concepts based on correlated patterns of neural activity. This process operates rapidly with minimal labeled examples, mirroring a human cognitive phenomenon known as fast mapping. Remarkably, the method can already recognize objects with as few as one labeled example, underscoring the quality of the representations learned through self-supervised embodiment and curiosity-driven exploration. This approach thus offers a promising strategy for learning concepts with limited supervision and demonstrates that meaningful environmental representations can be acquired purely through interaction with the world.

A distinctive member of the power transformation family is the Box-Cox transformation. This method can be viewed as a mathematical procedure that identifies the optimal lambda (λ) value, which maximizes the log-likelihood function to transform data into a normal distribution and mitigate heteroscedasticity. In data analytics, the assumption of normality underpins numerous statistical models and tests. While the Box-Cox transformation is widely recognized for its application in one-dimensional data analysis, this paper explores its utility as a preprocessing step for two-dimensional data—specifically digital images—and investigates its impact.

Furthermore, to minimize computational complexity, it is sufficient to estimate the λ parameter in real-time for large two-dimensional matrices by analyzing their probability density function as a statistical representation of the underlying data distribution. We compare the performance of this lightweight Box-Cox transformation with established state-of-the-art techniques for low-light image enhancement. Additionally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through various test datasets, showcasing improvements in the visual quality of images and enhanced performance of a color pattern classification algorithm as a representative application. The results with and without the proposed method are evaluated and compared using...

Hottopixx, introduced by Bittorf et al. at NIPS 2012, is an algorithm designed to solve nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) problems under the separability assumption. Separable NMF has a wide range of applications, including topic extraction from text documents and the unmixing of hyperspectral images. In these scenarios, the algorithm's ability to handle noise is crucial for its effectiveness. Hottopixx has been shown to be relatively robust to noise, and this robustness can be further improved through postprocessing. However, a significant limitation exists: both Hottopixx and its postprocessing step require prior knowledge of the noise level in the input matrix, which is not always easy to estimate. In this paper, we address this limitation by introducing a refined version of Hottopixx and its postprocessing method that does not require prior knowledge of the noise level. We demonstrate that this refinement maintains nearly the same level of noise robustness as the original algorithm.

With the rapid development of mobile applications and cloud computing, mobile cloud computing has garnered significant attention from both academic researchers and industry professionals. However, mobile cloud applications are increasingly vulnerable to security challenges, including data integrity breaches, user privacy leaks, and service disruptions. To mitigate these risks, a proactive strategy involves identifying and isolating cyber threats before they can inflict substantial damage on the mobile cloud infrastructure. In this paper, we introduce a novel framework that employs deep learning techniques to detect cyberattacks within a mobile cloud environment. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed framework is capable of effectively identifying a wide range of cyber threats while achieving a high detection accuracy of up to 97.11%. Additionally, we compare our approach with existing machine learning-based methods to highlight the superior performance and effectiveness of our solution.

Creating new pairs of images and corresponding text is a challenge that integrates computer vision and natural language processing. In this paper, we introduce methods for generating novel image-caption pairs using existing captioning datasets. Our approach leverages recent advancements in generative adversarial networks and sequence-to-sequence models. We extend our framework to generate paired data across multiple domains. Additionally, we explore cyclic generation—converting images to text and then back to images, and vice versa—and examine its relationship with autoencoder architectures.

Diabetes is currently one of the most prevalent, dangerous, and expensive diseases globally, caused by elevated blood sugar levels or insufficient insulin in the body. If detected at a late stage, diabetes can severely impact an individual's health. Today, it poses a significant challenge for healthcare professionals and government authorities alike. Preventive measures are crucial, and ensuring people's well-being without compromising their comfort has become an essential priority.

In this study, we employ an Ensemble training methodology based on genetic algorithms to accurately diagnose and predict the outcomes of diabetes mellitus. The research utilizes experimental data, specifically real-world datasets on Indian diabetics available on the University of California's website. Recent advancements in Information and Communication Technologies (ICT), such as the Internet of Things, machine learning, and data mining, enable the development of more intelligent health strategies. These technologies allow for accurate prediction of disease outcomes in both daily life and clinical settings, helping to prevent the progression of diabetes and its associated complications.

The results demonstrate the high effectiveness of the proposed method, achieving a diagnostic accuracy of 98.8% and 99% in this study.

We consider the setting of vector-valued non-linear dynamical systems governed by the equation $ X_{t+1} = \phi(A^* X_t) + \eta_t $, where $ \eta_t $ is unbiased noise and $ \phi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ is a known link function satisfying a certain **expansivity property**. The objective is to estimate the matrix $ A^* $ from a single trajectory $ X_1, \dots, X_T $ consisting of **dependent or correlated** samples.

Although this problem has been extensively studied in the linear case—where $ \phi $ is the identity function and optimal error rates are achievable even for non-mixing systems—existing results in the non-linear regime are limited to **mixing systems**. In this work, we make several key contributions that advance the understanding and learning of non-linear dynamical systems:

a) We present the **first offline algorithm** capable of learning non-linear dynamical systems without relying on the mixing assumption.  
b) We significantly reduce the **sample complexity** compared to existing methods for mixing systems.  
c) In the more challenging **one-pass, streaming** setting, we analyze a variant of stochastic gradient descent with Reverse Experience Replay ($\mathsf{SGD-RER}$), and show that it achieves the same sample complexity as our offline algorithm for mixing systems.  
d) Finally, we provide a theoretical justification for the expansivity assumption by demonstrating that for the widely used ReLU link function—which is **not expansive** but is easy to learn with independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) samples—any method would require **inherently higher sample complexity**, highlighting the necessity of the expansivity condition in the dependent sampling regime.

We consider a seller who offers a network of $ N $ products over a time horizon of $ T $ periods. The seller is unaware of the parameters governing the linear demand model for the products and must dynamically adjust product prices to learn the demand structure based on observed sales data. The objective of the seller is to minimize its pseudo-regret, defined as the expected revenue loss compared to a clairvoyant seller who knows the true demand model.

To capture the complex relationships among products, we consider a sparse structure of demand interactions, which reflects various connectivity properties of the product network. Specifically, we analyze three distinct sparsity frameworks:

1. **$ L_0 $-sparsity**, which limits the total number of non-zero connections in the network,  
2. **Off-diagonal sparsity**, which restricts the magnitude of cross-product price sensitivities, and  
3. **Spectral sparsity**, a novel concept that imposes constraints on the asymptotic decay of a similarity metric across network nodes.

We propose a dynamic pricing-and-learning policy that integrates the optimism-in-the-face-of-uncertainty principle with PAC-Bayesian techniques. This approach achieves asymptotically optimal performance in terms of both $ N $ and $ T $. Furthermore, we demonstrate that under the conditions of spectral and off-diagonal sparsity, the seller can attain a pseudo-regret that scales linearly with $ N $, even when the underlying product network is dense.

We show that language models trained on codified (discretely-encoded) music audio develop representations that are effective for downstream Music Information Retrieval (MIR) tasks. Specifically, we examine the representations generated by Jukebox (Dhariwal et al., 2020), a music generation system that includes a language model pre-trained on codified audio from one million songs. To assess whether these representations contain valuable information for MIR, we use them as input features to train simple models on various MIR tasks. Compared to representations from traditional MIR models pre-trained on tagging data, Jukebox's representations lead to an average 30% improvement across four MIR tasks: tagging, genre classification, emotion recognition, and key detection. Notably, for key detection, Jukebox's representations significantly outperform those from tagging-pretrained models, indicating that pre-training on codified audio through language modeling may overcome limitations in conventional approaches. We interpret the superior performance of Jukebox's representations as evidence that modeling audio directly, rather than relying on tags, results in more informative and richer representations for MIR tasks.

In this paper, we present Symplectic ODE-Net (SymODEN), a deep learning framework designed to infer the dynamics of physical systems governed by ordinary differential equations (ODEs) from observed state trajectories. To enhance generalization with limited training data, SymODEN integrates appropriate inductive bias by structuring its computational graph in a physics-informed manner. Specifically, it enforces Hamiltonian dynamics with control, enabling the transparent learning of underlying system dynamics. This approach facilitates insights into key physical properties, such as mass and potential energy. Furthermore, we introduce a parametrization that preserves the Hamiltonian formalism even when generalized coordinates are embedded in high-dimensional spaces or when only velocity data is available instead of generalized momentum. By providing interpretable and physically consistent models, this framework paves the way for the development of model-based control strategies.

We present the Chi-Square Test Neural Network, a single-layer backpropagation neural network that incorporates the chi-square test theorem to redefine the cost and error functions. The weights and thresholds are updated using the standard backpropagation algorithm. This approach offers the advantage of maintaining consistent data distribution across both training and testing sets, making it suitable for binary classification tasks. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed method significantly enhances classification accuracy compared to existing approaches.

Current machine translation systems, whether phrase-based or neural, have primarily relied on word-level modeling with explicit segmentation. In this paper, we explore a fundamental question: can neural machine translation generate a character sequence without any explicit segmentation? To address this, we evaluate an attention-based encoder-decoder architecture that employs a subword-level encoder and a character-level decoder on four language pairs—En-Cs, En-De, En-Ru, and En-Fi—using the parallel corpora from WMT'15. Our experimental results demonstrate that models with a character-level decoder consistently outperform those with a subword-level decoder across all four language pairs. Moreover, ensembles of neural models using a character-level decoder surpass state-of-the-art non-neural machine translation systems on En-Cs, En-De, and En-Fi, and achieve comparable performance on En-Ru.

Random feature maps are widely used in modern statistical machine learning, extending the concept of random projections through sophisticated, yet often analytically challenging nonlinear transformations. In this paper, we utilize the "concentration" effect arising from random matrix theory to conduct a spectral analysis of the Gram matrix associated with these random feature maps, specifically in the context of Gaussian mixture models where both the dimension and the number of samples are large. Our findings provide critical insights into how nonlinearity interacts with data statistics, enabling more effective tuning of random feature-based methods.

The Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) provides a rigorous framework for decision-making in robots operating under uncertainty. However, POMDP planning is computationally intensive, especially when long-term planning is required. While temporally extended macro-actions can reduce the effective planning horizon and enhance computational efficiency, the challenge remains: how to acquire high-quality macro-actions? This paper introduces the Macro-Action Generator-Critic (MAGIC), an approach that enables offline learning of macro-actions tailored for online POMDP planning. Specifically, MAGIC trains a macro-action generator end-to-end, using the performance of an online planner as feedback. During online planning, the generator produces context-aware macro-actions on the fly, conditioned on the robot's belief and environmental context. We evaluated MAGIC on multiple long-horizon planning tasks, both in simulation and on a real robot. The results demonstrate that the learned macro-actions significantly outperform primitive actions and handcrafted alternatives in terms of online planning performance.

Generating text from structured data, such as tables, plays a crucial role in various natural language processing tasks, including question answering and dialog systems. Recent research has focused on using neural language models and encoder-decoder architectures for table-to-text generation. However, these approaches often fail to account for the order of content during the text generation process. When humans create summaries based on a table, they typically consider the sequence of information before deciding on the wording. For instance, in a biography, a person's nationality is usually mentioned before their occupation. In this paper, we introduce an order-planning text generation model that captures the relationships between different fields and leverages this structure to produce more fluent and coherent text. Experiments on the WikiBio dataset demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms previous methods, achieving higher scores in BLEU, ROUGE, and NIST metrics.

This paper introduces the Pressure Ulcers Online Website, a foundational step toward an innovative platform designed to assist individuals in detecting, understanding, and managing pressure ulcers. It explains the motivations behind the project and serves as a centralized hub for pressure ulcer analysis and ongoing research. Leveraging advanced technologies such as convolutional neural networks and transfer learning, combined with modern end-to-end web development, the platform enables the analysis of pressure ulcers and the generation of detailed reports. As the system continues to develop through collaborative partnerships, future iterations will offer decision-support tools to better characterize the complexity of pressure ulcers and provide comprehensive wound care information across various user groups. Ultimately, this initiative aims to increase awareness and provide support for those affected by or caring for individuals with pressure ulcers.

This paper introduces a Grounded Language-Image Pre-training (GLIP) model, designed to learn object-level, language-aware, and semantically rich visual representations. GLIP integrates object detection and phrase grounding into a unified pre-training framework. This integration offers two key advantages: first, it enables GLIP to benefit from both detection and grounding data, enhancing performance in both tasks and facilitating the development of a strong grounding model; second, GLIP can utilize large-scale image-text pairs by generating grounding boxes through self-training, resulting in more semantically meaningful representations.

In our experiments, GLIP was pre-trained on 27 million grounding examples, including 3 million human-annotated and 24 million web-crawled image-text pairs. The resulting representations exhibit strong zero-shot and few-shot transferability across various object-level recognition tasks. Specifically:  
1) When evaluated directly on COCO and LVIS (without any exposure to COCO images during pre-training), GLIP achieves 49.8 AP and 26.9 AP, respectively, outperforming many supervised baselines.  
2) After fine-tuning on COCO, GLIP attains 60.8 AP on the validation set and 61.5 AP on the test-dev set, surpassing previous state-of-the-art results.  
3) When applied to 13 downstream object detection tasks, a one-shot version of GLIP performs comparably to a fully supervised Dynamic Head model.  
The code will be made available at [https://github.com/microsoft/GLIP](https://github.com/microsoft/GLIP).

The automation of condition monitoring and workpiece inspection is crucial for ensuring both high product quality and efficient production throughput. In this context, recent advancements in machine learning have significantly enhanced the capabilities of autonomous process supervision. However, as these models become more complex and powerful, they often become less transparent and harder to interpret. A major challenge lies in monitoring the performance of deployed machine learning systems in real time and detecting events that could negatively affect their reliability.

In particular, supervised classifiers are typically trained under the assumption of stationary data distributions. For instance, a visual inspection system designed to identify surface defects in materials may fail to adapt to or even detect gradual changes in the data—commonly referred to as "data drift." This can include the emergence of new types of defects that the model was not originally trained to recognize. Such failures can lead to serious misclassifications, such as new defect types being incorrectly labeled as non-defective. To address this, it is essential to implement real-time performance tracking of classifiers, enabling early detection of potential error sources and supporting timely interventions.

Can machine learning models for recommendations be easily manipulated? While this question has been addressed in the context of manually crafted fake user profiles, the vulnerability of recommendation systems to adversarial attacks generated by machine learning remains underexplored. This paper aims to bridge this gap. We introduce a framework for creating synthetic user profiles that, when used during the training of a recommendation system, can serve an adversarial purpose while appearing indistinguishable from genuine user data. The process is modeled as a repeated general-sum game between two entities: an oblivious recommendation system $ R $ and an adversarial profile generator $ A $, which has two objectives: (G1) to ensure that the rating patterns of the fake users closely resemble those of real users, and (G2) to optimize an attack-specific objective function $ f_A $, such as degrading the top-K recommendation quality for a targeted group of users. We present a learning framework designed to achieve both goals and conduct extensive experiments across various attack scenarios, demonstrating the susceptibility of recommendation systems to such adversarial techniques.

Acoustic monitoring for machine fault detection has emerged as a promising and rapidly growing area of research, with significant potential for industrial applications. However, it remains challenging to collect sufficient data to train models for all possible fault types. As a result, new algorithms have been developed that rely solely on data from healthy machines to perform unsupervised anomaly detection. A major challenge in this approach is the presence of noise in the acoustic signals, which can significantly affect the accuracy of anomaly detection.

In this work, we introduce a robust, data-driven, and quasi non-parametric denoising technique tailored for spectral data, based on the Non-negative Canonical Polyadic (CP) decomposition. This method is particularly well-suited for machines that produce stationary sound. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our denoising strategy through a case study using the Malfunctioning Industrial Machine Investigation and Inspection (MIMII) baseline, showing a notable improvement in the performance of unsupervised anomaly detection. Such approaches enhance the reliability of sound-based monitoring systems in industrial environments.

Deep learning classifiers are increasingly supporting human decision-making, making user trust in these models a critical factor. Trust is typically rooted in consistent behavior: from an AI perspective, this means that given the same input, users expect the same output—particularly when the output is correct, i.e., consistent and accurate results over time. This paper investigates model behavior in the context of periodic retraining of deployed models, where successive model versions may disagree on the correct labels for the same input. We formally define the concepts of consistency and correct-consistency for learning models. We prove that the consistency and correct-consistency of an ensemble learner are at least as high as the average of those metrics across individual learners. Furthermore, we show that correct-consistency can be enhanced with a certain probability by combining learners whose accuracy meets or exceeds the average accuracy of the ensemble components. To validate our theoretical findings, we conduct experiments on three datasets using two state-of-the-art deep learning classifiers. Based on these results, we propose an efficient dynamic snapshot ensemble method and demonstrate its effectiveness.

There is a critical need in modern large-scale data analysis to prioritize samples for manual inspection. For instance, such inspections may focus on identifying mislabeled instances that significantly affect model performance or uncovering vulnerabilities that could be exploited by adversarial attacks. To address the challenge of identifying which samples to inspect—often referred to as the "needle in the haystack" problem—we introduce a new scalable variant of Cook's distance, a well-established statistical method used to detect samples that have an unusually strong influence on the fit of a regression model and its subsequent predictions.

To make this approach applicable to very large and high-dimensional datasets, we propose a novel algorithm called "influence sketching." This method incorporates random projections into the influence computation process, specifically using a randomly projected pseudo-dataset derived from a post-convergence Generalized Linear Model (GLM) to calculate influence scores. 

We demonstrate the effectiveness of influence sketching by applying it to a malware detection dataset comprising over 2 million executable files, each represented by nearly 100,000 features. Our results show that randomly removing approximately 10% of the training samples leads to only a minor drop in predictive accuracy, from 99.47% to 99.45%. In contrast, removing the same number of samples identified as highly influential by our method causes a much more significant decline in accuracy, highlighting the effectiveness of influence sketching in pinpointing critical samples.

Network traffic classification using machine learning has been extensively researched. Most existing approaches classify entire traffic flows, but these methods face significant practical limitations. At a network router, packets must be processed with minimal delay, meaning the classifier cannot wait for the entire flow to complete before making a decision. Additionally, complex machine learning models may be too resource-intensive to deploy within the router.

In this paper, we propose a flow-packet hybrid traffic classification (FPHTC) approach, where the router makes per-packet decisions based on a routing policy derived from a flow-based classifier located outside the router. We analyze the generalization bounds of FPHTC and demonstrate its superiority over traditional packet-based classification methods. Using a real-world traffic dataset, we present experimental results that highlight the effectiveness of FPHTC. The results show that the method is resilient to changes in traffic patterns and can be efficiently implemented with limited computational resources.

In this work, we introduce a novel method for reconstructing multivariate functions from training data by simultaneously determining an appropriate neural network architecture and an initialization based on polynomial approximations. Training deep neural networks using gradient descent can be viewed as navigating the loss landscape to minimize the loss functional. The initial configuration of the network parameters plays a crucial role in the success of iterative optimization methods. Our proposed approach constructs a network whose initial state corresponds to a polynomial approximation of the given training data. This initialization offers a significant advantage, as it allows standard training procedures to refine the network's performance starting from a meaningful baseline. Since the initial network already captures the underlying structure of the data, the training process is more likely to converge to a favorable local minimum. We present the theoretical foundation required to build such networks and demonstrate their effectiveness through several numerical examples. These experiments show that our approach leads to networks that can be efficiently trained from the initialized state, resulting in improved approximations across a wide range of target functions.

Attention mechanisms in biological perception are believed to select subsets of perceptual information for more complex processing, which would be computationally infeasible if applied to all sensory inputs. In computer vision, however, hard attention—where certain information is selectively ignored—has received relatively little attention, despite the success of soft attention, which reweights and aggregates information without filtering it out. In this work, we propose a novel approach to hard attention and demonstrate that it achieves highly competitive performance on a recently released visual question answering dataset, matching and sometimes exceeding the performance of similar soft attention models while completely ignoring certain features. Although hard attention is typically considered non-differentiable, we observe that feature magnitudes correlate with semantic relevance, providing a useful signal for our attention selection mechanism. Since hard attention focuses on the most relevant input features, it can also be more efficient than equivalent soft attention mechanisms. This efficiency is particularly valuable for modern approaches that employ non-local pairwise operations, where computational and memory costs scale quadratically with the number of features.

We investigate the optimization of finite sums of geodesically smooth functions on Riemannian manifolds. While variance reduction techniques have gained significant attention in recent years for optimizing finite-sum problems, prior work has largely focused on vector spaces. In this paper, we introduce Riemannian SVRG (RSVRG), a novel variance-reduced method tailored for Riemannian optimization. We analyze RSVRG for both geodesically convex and nonconvex (smooth) functions. Our analysis shows that RSVRG retains the benefits of the standard SVRG algorithm, but with convergence rates influenced by the curvature of the underlying manifold. To the best of our knowledge, RSVRG is the first provably efficient stochastic Riemannian optimization method. Additionally, our work presents the first non-asymptotic complexity analysis—novel even in the batch setting—for nonconvex Riemannian optimization. Our results have several implications, including a Riemannian interpretation of variance-reduced PCA, which offers a concise and transparent convergence analysis.

In this paper, we investigate the problem of cluster head detection in a two-level unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarm network (USNET) consisting of multiple UAV clusters. The intrinsic follow strategy (IFS) of low-level follower UAVs (FUAVs) relative to high-level cluster head UAVs (HUAVs) is unknown. To address this, we first introduce a graph attention self-supervised learning algorithm (GASSL) for detecting HUAVs within a single UAV cluster, which simultaneously models the IFS. To extend this approach to multi-cluster USNETs, we propose a multi-cluster graph attention self-supervised learning algorithm (MC-GASSL), built upon GASSL. MC-GASSL employs a gated recurrent unit (GRU)-based metric learning scheme to cluster the USNET and then identifies HUAVs within each cluster using GASSL. Numerical results demonstrate that GASSL achieves over 98% average accuracy in detecting HUAVs in single clusters with diverse IFSs. Simulation results further reveal that MC-GASSL improves the clustering purity of the USNET by at least 10% on average compared to traditional clustering methods. Moreover, MC-GASSL efficiently detects all HUAVs in USNETs with varying IFSs and cluster configurations, while maintaining low detection redundancy.
