Machine learning models are frequently employed on human brain imaging datasets to link brain function or structure with behavioral traits, health status, or other individual characteristics. These models often depend on low-dimensional representations derived from intricate processing pipelines. However, the inherent numerical instabilities in these pipelines can compromise the accuracy of the resulting maps and introduce computational biases. To address this, Monte Carlo Arithmetic—a method that introduces controlled numerical noise—was applied to a structural connectome estimation pipeline, generating a range of plausible brain networks for each sample. The variability across these perturbed networks was incorporated into an augmented dataset, which was then used for an age classification task. Our results showed that resampling brain networks through multiple numerically perturbed outcomes enhanced the performance of all tested classifiers, preprocessing methods, and dimensionality reduction techniques. Notably, the performance improvement was not dependent on a large number of perturbations, indicating that even minimal numerical perturbation introduces meaningful variability that can be effectively leveraged by downstream models.

Variable selection plays a crucial role in the analysis of high-dimensional data, and numerous algorithms have been proposed to address this challenge. Ideally, a variable selection method should be flexible, scalable, and theoretically sound; however, most existing approaches fail to achieve all these properties simultaneously. In this paper, we introduce a three-step variable selection algorithm that leverages kernel-based estimation of the regression function and its gradient, followed by a hard thresholding step. The key strength of this approach lies in its ability to operate without explicit model assumptions, accommodate a wide range of predictor effects, support scalable computation, and achieve desirable asymptotic sparsistency.

The algorithm is designed to work within any reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), allowing for the use of various kernel functions. It can also be easily adapted for interaction selection with minimal modifications. Its computational complexity scales linearly with the number of features, and further improvements are possible through parallel computing. We establish the sparsistency of the proposed method under mild conditions for general RKHS, including linear and Gaussian kernels as special cases. The effectiveness of the algorithm is demonstrated through a range of simulation studies and real-world applications.

Although convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have shown great success in learning discriminative features, they often struggle to generalize to unseen domains. Domain generalization seeks to overcome this limitation by training a model on a set of source domains such that it can perform well on any unknown target domain. In this paper, we propose a novel approach called MixStyle, which involves probabilistically mixing instance-level feature statistics across different source domains. Our method is inspired by the observation that visual domains are closely tied to image style (e.g., photo versus sketch). This style information is typically captured by the lower layers of a CNN, where our style-mixing operation takes place. By mixing the styles of training instances, new synthetic domains are implicitly created, thereby increasing the diversity of the source domains and improving the model's generalizability. MixStyle integrates seamlessly into mini-batch training and is straightforward to implement. We demonstrate its effectiveness across a wide range of tasks, including category classification, instance retrieval, and reinforcement learning.

In computed tomography (CT), automatic exposure control (AEC) is commonly employed to minimize the radiation dose delivered to patients. For organ-specific AEC, a preliminary CT reconstruction is typically required to estimate the shape of the organ, enabling optimized dose delivery. However, only a limited number of projections are available for real-time reconstruction in such scenarios. In this study, we evaluate the performance of the Automated Transform by Manifold Approximation (AUTOMAP) in these applications.

As a proof of concept, we first assess AUTOMAP's performance on the MNIST dataset, which consists of images of the 10 digits. The dataset is randomly divided into training and test sets. We train the AUTOMAP model to reconstruct images from either 2 or 4 projections directly. The test results show that AUTOMAP can successfully reconstruct most digits, with false recognition rates of 1.6% and 6.8%, respectively.

In a follow-up experiment, the MNIST dataset is split such that the training set includes 9 digits, while the test set contains only the excluded digit—such as "2." In this setup, the model misclassifies the digit "2" as "3" or "5" when using 2 projections for reconstruction, resulting in a high false recognition rate of 94.4%.

For potential application in medical imaging, AUTOMAP is also trained on patient data.

Deep learning holds great promise in the field of medical imaging. However, the incidence rates of different diseases vary significantly, resulting in imbalanced class distributions in medical image datasets. This imbalance often leads to poor performance, particularly for less frequent classes. One potential approach to address this issue is to augment the dataset by generating synthetic images of rare classes using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). Nevertheless, traditional GANs typically require a substantial number of real images to train effectively. To overcome this challenge, we introduce the General-to-Detailed GAN (GDGAN), a two-stage GAN architecture composed of two sequentially connected networks: one for generating images based on general labels and another for producing more detailed representations. GDGAN was able to generate a wide variety of medical images, and when used to augment the training data, it led to improved performance compared to existing methods, as demonstrated by higher Area-Under-the-Curve (AUC) values on the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve.

Deep convolutional networks frequently incorporate additive constants, commonly referred to as "bias" terms, into their convolution operations. This allows for a more diverse set of functional mappings. Additionally, biases are often used during training to help normalize the responses across batches of images (a key aspect of "batch normalization"). Recent leading blind denoising methods, such as DnCNN, appear to rely on these bias terms for their effectiveness. However, we demonstrate that such networks tend to overfit to the specific noise levels they are trained on. When deployed at noise levels outside this range, their performance drops significantly. In contrast, a bias-free architecture—created by eliminating all constant terms, including those used in batch normalization—exhibits strong generalization across various noise levels while maintaining state-of-the-art performance within the training range. Locally, the bias-free network behaves linearly with respect to the noisy input, enabling straightforward analysis using conventional linear algebra techniques. These analyses reveal that the network's behavior can be interpreted in terms of nonlinear adaptive filtering and projection onto unions of low-dimensional subspaces, thereby bridging learning-based denoising approaches with more classical signal processing methods.

Recent advances in the theory of overparameterized learning have focused on establishing generalization guarantees in the interpolating regime. While such results have been obtained for several standard classes of methods, they remain elusive for ensemble approaches. In this work, we introduce an ensemble classification method that not only interpolates the training data but also achieves consistency across a wide range of data distributions. To accomplish this, we define the manifold-Hilbert kernel for data lying on a Riemannian manifold. We demonstrate that kernel smoothing regression based on this kernel is weakly consistent under the framework established by Devroye et al. (1998). Furthermore, for data distributed on a sphere, we show that the manifold-Hilbert kernel can be expressed as a weighted random partition kernel, which corresponds to an infinite ensemble of partition-based classifiers.

In this paper, we investigate the problem of constrained robust (min-max) optimization in a black-box setting, where the optimizer does not have access to the gradients of the objective function but can query its values. We propose a principled optimization framework that combines a zeroth-order (ZO) gradient estimator with an alternating projected stochastic gradient descent-ascent method. The ZO gradient estimator requires only a small number of function evaluations, while the latter involves a single-step descent or ascent update. We demonstrate that the proposed framework, named ZO-Min-Max, achieves a sub-linear convergence rate under mild assumptions and exhibits good scalability with respect to problem size. On the application side, we explore a promising link between black-box min-max optimization and black-box evasion and poisoning attacks in adversarial machine learning. Our experimental results on these scenarios highlight the effectiveness and scalability of our approach, particularly in high-dimensional settings where recent black-box solvers are impractical.

To address the rapid growth in available data, the efficiency of data analysis and machine learning libraries has gained increasing attention. While significant progress has been made in traditional array-based computations, these approaches are often constrained by the resources of a single computation node. As a result, new methods are needed to leverage distributed computing resources, such as distributed memory architectures. To this end, we present HeAT, a numerical programming framework designed for large-scale parallel processing, featuring an intuitive NumPy-like API. HeAT leverages PyTorch as a local eager execution engine and distributes workloads across arbitrarily large high-performance computing systems using MPI. It supports both low-level array operations and a variety of higher-level algorithms. With HeAT, users familiar with NumPy can fully utilize their computational resources, dramatically reducing the barrier to distributed data analysis. Compared to similar frameworks, HeAT demonstrates speedups of up to two orders of magnitude.

The primary objective of this paper is to compare various commonly used Bayesian methods for model selection in practical scenarios, emphasizing their differences and offering guidance on the most suitable approaches. We focus on variable subset selection in regression and classification tasks, conducting a series of numerical experiments using both simulated and real-world datasets. The findings reveal that optimizing utility estimates, such as cross-validation (CV) scores, can lead to overfitting, particularly when data is limited, due to the high variability in these estimates. This issue may result in significant selection-induced bias and optimism in the evaluation of the selected model's performance. From a predictive standpoint, the best results are achieved by accounting for model uncertainty through the construction of a full encompassing model, such as Bayesian model averaging across the candidate models. When the encompassing model becomes too complex, it can be effectively simplified using the projection method, which transfers the information from the full model to the submodels. This approach demonstrates a much lower risk of overfitting compared to model selection based on CV scores. Overall, the projection method outperforms not only the maximum a posteriori model but also the selection of the most probable model.

Learning features from data has proven to be more effective than using hand-crafted features for a wide range of machine learning tasks. In the field of Music Information Retrieval (MIR), features extracted from windowed spectrograms are highly sensitive to transformations such as transposition or time shifts. These variations can be problematic when they are irrelevant to the specific MIR task at hand. To address this, we introduce an architecture called the Complex Autoencoder (CAE), which learns features that are invariant to orthogonal transformations. By mapping signals onto complex basis functions learned by the CAE, we obtain a transformation-invariant "magnitude space" and a transformation-variant "phase space." The phase space can be used to infer the relationship between data pairs. Leveraging the invariance of the magnitude space, we achieve state-of-the-art performance in audio-to-score alignment and repeated section discovery in audio. A PyTorch implementation of the CAE, along with the repeated section discovery method, is available online.

This paper tackles the challenge of estimating and forecasting instantaneous occupancy levels in dynamic environments. Given the complexity of real-world settings such as urban streets or densely populated areas, effectively integrating temporal dependencies into static occupancy models remains a significant challenge. To address this, we introduce a method that captures the spatial uncertainty of moving objects and integrates this information into a continuous occupancy map within a high-dimensional feature space. Experiments using LIDAR data demonstrate the algorithm's real-time performance.

This paper presents a method for learning a policy for a dynamical system that is guaranteed to be both provably safe and capable of reaching a desired goal. Here, safety is defined as the policy's ability to prevent the system's state from entering any unsafe region, while goal-reaching requires that the system's trajectory asymptotically converges to a target region—a generalization of stability. To achieve this, we jointly learn two additional certificate functions: a barrier function that ensures safety and a Lyapunov-like function that guarantees convergence to the goal. Both functions are represented using neural networks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in learning policies that are simultaneously safe and goal-reaching across a range of systems, including pendulums, cart-pole systems, and UAVs.

In this paper, we introduce a more realistic and challenging problem setup for intent detection in natural language understanding, referred to as Generalized Few-Shot Intent Detection (GFSID). GFSID involves distinguishing between two types of intents: those that have ample labeled data and novel intents that are only represented by a limited number of examples per class. To address this challenge, we propose a novel model called Conditional Text Generation with BERT (CG-BERT). This approach effectively utilizes a pre-trained language model to generate text conditioned on the intent label. By employing variational inference to model the distribution of utterances, CG-BERT is capable of generating diverse examples for novel intents, even when only a few samples are available. Experimental results demonstrate that CG-BERT achieves state-of-the-art performance on the GFSID task across two real-world datasets under both 1-shot and 5-shot settings.

Customers are typically exposed to various online digital advertising channels—such as email marketing, display advertising, and paid search engine marketing—throughout their journey toward purchasing or subscribing to a product (i.e., conversion). Marketers collect and analyze customer journey data to evaluate the effectiveness of each advertising channel. Understanding the influence of each channel is critical for making informed decisions on budget allocation and pricing strategies.

While rule-based and data-driven algorithmic approaches have been widely adopted in marketing, they often fail to account for important factors such as channel interactions, time dependencies, and individual user characteristics. In this paper, we introduce a novel attribution algorithm based on deep learning to better assess the impact of each advertising channel. We present the Deep Neural Net With Attention Multi-Touch Attribution (DNAMTA) model, which employs a supervised learning approach to predict whether a sequence of events leads to a conversion. This enables a deeper understanding of the dynamic interactions among media channels.

Additionally, DNAMTA integrates user-contextual information, such as demographics and behavioral data, as control variables to minimize biases in estimating the effects of different media channels. Using a large-scale real-world marketing dataset, we conduct computational experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model.

Spatial clustering techniques offer effective multi-channel noise reduction across a wide range of microphone configurations, yet they struggle to integrate detailed speech and noise models. On the other hand, LSTM neural networks have demonstrated success in recognizing speech from noise using single-channel inputs, but they often fail to fully leverage the information available in multi-channel recordings. This paper combines the strengths of both approaches by training LSTM speech models to enhance the masks produced by the Model-based EM Source Separation and Localization (MESSL) spatial clustering method. As a result, the system achieves both the spatial separation capabilities and flexibility of multi-channel spatial clustering, along with the signal modeling performance of multiple parallel single-channel LSTM speech enhancers. Experimental results on the CHiME-3 dataset of noisy tablet recordings show that our system improves speech quality as measured by the Perceptual Evaluation of Speech Quality (PESQ) and reduces the word error rate of the baseline CHiME-3 speech recognizer compared to the default BeamformIt beamformer.

Noise is a major factor that degrades the quality of Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) images. Neural network models based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have shown great promise in image denoising. However, OCT image denoising remains challenging due to the high demand for large amounts of labeled data, which can be time-consuming and costly to obtain. Additionally, CNN-based methods often require a large number of parameters and sophisticated tuning techniques, making them resource-intensive.

To address these challenges, we propose a novel Cycle-Consistent Generative Adversarial Network called Dual-Merged Cycle-WGAN for retinal OCT image denoising. Our method achieves excellent performance with minimal labeled training data. The proposed model consists of two Cycle-GAN networks enhanced with an improved generator, discriminator, and Wasserstein loss, ensuring better training stability and overall performance. By incorporating an image merging technique between the two Cycle-GAN networks, our model captures more detailed features, leading to improved training results.

The effectiveness and generalization capability of our approach have been validated through ablation studies and comparative experiments. Compared to state-of-the-art methods, our unsupervised approach delivers superior visual quality and higher objective evaluation metrics.

A neural network operating in real-world environments may encounter inputs that come from a distribution different from the one it was trained on. A significant body of research has shown that it is relatively straightforward to generate or synthesize inputs for which the network exhibits high confidence but makes incorrect predictions. Generative models are often considered robust against such overconfidence, as they model the underlying data distribution and can be used to identify out-of-distribution samples. In this paper, we question this assumption. We demonstrate that the density estimates produced by flow-based models, VAEs, and PixelCNNs fail to distinguish between images of common objects—such as dogs, trucks, and horses (as found in CIFAR-10)—and those of house numbers (as in SVHN). In fact, when trained on the former, these models assign higher likelihoods to the latter. Furthermore, we observe similar behavior across multiple popular image datasets: FashionMNIST vs. MNIST, CelebA vs. SVHN, and ImageNet vs. CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100/SVHN. To better understand this unexpected phenomenon, we focus our analysis on flow-based generative models, which are trained and evaluated using exact marginal likelihood. We find that this behavior persists even when flows are restricted to certain conditions.

End-to-end (E2E) models are frequently combined with language models (LMs) through shallow fusion to enhance overall performance and improve the recognition of rare words. However, prior research has shown that LMs can unintentionally memorize rare or unique sequences from their training data. In this work, we propose a framework for detecting the memorization of random textual sequences—referred to as "canaries"—in the LM training data, under the constraint of only having black-box access to an LM-fused speech recognizer, rather than direct access to the LM itself. Using a production-grade Conformer RNN-T E2E model integrated with a Transformer LM, we demonstrate that it is feasible to detect memorization of singly-occurring canaries within a training dataset of 300 million examples. To address privacy concerns, we further show that applying per-example gradient clipping during LM training significantly reduces such memorization without degrading the overall system performance.

We examine the problem of universal function approximation using two-layer neural networks with random weights that are "nearly Gaussian" in the sense of Kullback-Leibler divergence. This investigation is inspired by recent studies on lazy training, where the weight updates produced by stochastic gradient descent remain close to their independent and identically distributed Gaussian initialization. 

We begin by analyzing the mean-field limit, in which the finite number of neurons in the hidden layer is replaced by a continuous ensemble. Under this framework, the problem reduces to a global minimization task over the space of probability measures on the weights, specifically minimizing a free-energy functional. This functional balances the $L^2$ approximation risk against the Kullback-Leibler divergence from a centered Gaussian prior.

We identify the unique global minimizer of this functional and then construct a controlled nonlinear dynamics in the space of probability measures over the weights. This dynamics corresponds to solving a McKean–Vlasov optimal control problem. Notably, this control problem is closely related to the Schrödinger bridge (or entropic optimal transport) problem, and its value is proportional to the minimum of the free energy.

Finally, we demonstrate that stochastic gradient descent in the lazy training regime—achievable by appropriately tuning the variance of the Gaussian prior and the entropy regularization—effectively implements this optimal control strategy, thereby achieving near-optimal approximation performance.

An implicit objective in research on deep generative models is the ability of these models to generate novel examples that were not present in the training data. In this paper, we examine how well this capability holds for commonly used variational autoencoder (VAE) architectures. VAEs maximize a lower bound on the log marginal likelihood, which suggests that they may overfit the training data when equipped with a sufficiently expressive decoder. In the limit of an infinitely powerful decoder, the optimal generative model becomes a uniform mixture of the training examples. More generally, an optimal decoder should produce a weighted average of the training data, with weights determined by the similarity of examples in the latent space. This leads us to hypothesize that, with sufficiently high-capacity encoder and decoder networks, the VAE's decoder will essentially perform nearest-neighbor matching based on latent space coordinates. To evaluate this hypothesis, we assess the generalization performance of VAEs on the MNIST dataset. We consider both the ability to generalize to new instances of previously seen classes and to completely unseen classes. In both scenarios, we find that the reconstructed samples are closely approximated by the nearest neighbors in the latent space.

In this article, we introduce CANDIES (Combined Approach for Novelty Detection in Intelligent Embedded Systems), a novel method for detecting anomalies in technical systems. We assume that technical systems consist of multiple interacting processes. By monitoring these processes using sensors, we can collect observations (samples) and model them using a probabilistic framework. Ideally, the components of the parametric mixture density model used correspond to the actual processes occurring in the system. However, during operation, new or unexpected processes may arise—such as those caused by unforeseen failures—which result in novel types of samples. These require the model to be adapted accordingly.

CANDIES employs mixtures of Gaussians, a flexible approach that can also be used for classification tasks. Novel processes can emerge in two types of regions within the model’s input space: areas with few previously observed samples (low-density regions) or areas with many existing samples (high-density regions). While both scenarios pose challenges, most existing methods focus primarily on low-density regions. Detecting novelty in high-density regions is more complex and often overlooked.

To address this gap, CANDIES presents a new technique for identifying novel processes in high-density regions through an efficient online approach.

Mini-batch Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with momentum is a core algorithm for training large-scale predictive models. In this paper, we introduce a novel analytical framework to study the behavior of mini-batch SGD on linear models across different momentum values and batch sizes. Our central approach involves representing the sequence of loss values through a generating function, which can be expressed in a compact form under the assumption of a diagonal approximation for the second moments of the model weights. By examining this generating function, we derive key insights regarding convergence conditions, the phase structure of the learning process, and optimal hyperparameter settings. Specifically, we demonstrate that: 1) the optimization trajectory typically transitions from a "signal-dominated" to a "noise-dominated" phase, with the transition time predictable through analytical means; 2) in the "signal-dominated" phase, a larger effective learning rate is beneficial, but its value must be carefully controlled for any finite batch size to prevent divergence; 3) the fastest convergence is achieved with a negative momentum. We validate our theoretical findings through extensive experiments on MNIST and synthetic datasets, observing strong quantitative agreement between theory and practice.

We present a model-free relax-and-round algorithm for k-means clustering, which is based on a semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxation introduced by Peng and Wei. The algorithm treats the SDP solution as a denoised version of the original data and then applies a rounding procedure to obtain a hard clustering. We develop a general framework for establishing performance guarantees for this approach, and we analyze its behavior under subgaussian mixture models. Additionally, we investigate the theoretical limits of estimating Gaussian cluster centers using k-means, allowing us to compare the approximation guarantees of our algorithm with the optimal k-means solution.

Supervised learning-based segmentation methods typically require a large amount of annotated training data to achieve good generalization at test time. In medical applications, creating such datasets is often impractical, as obtaining a large number of expert-annotated samples is both time-consuming and costly. As a result, many approaches have been proposed to address the challenge of learning from limited labeled examples. However, existing methods have not yet surpassed the performance of simple random data augmentation, which itself does not yield high accuracy. In this work, we introduce a novel task-driven data augmentation approach designed for scenarios with limited labeled data. The synthetic data generator in our method is specifically optimized for the segmentation task, incorporating two types of transformations: additive intensity variations and deformation fields. Both transformation sets are jointly optimized using both labeled and unlabeled examples within a semi-supervised framework. Experimental results on three medical datasets—cardiac, prostate, and pancreas—demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms standard augmentation and conventional semi-supervised approaches in the limited annotation setting. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/krishnabits001/task$\_$driven$\_$data$\_$augmentation.

In recent years, the application of machine learning has gained significant traction within the realm of lattice field theories. A key component of these theories is symmetry, and incorporating such symmetries into neural network designs can greatly enhance performance and generalizability. A fundamental symmetry in physical systems defined on a lattice with periodic boundary conditions is equivariance under spacetime translations. In this work, we explore the benefits of using translationally equivariant neural networks compared to their non-equivariant counterparts. The system under study is a complex scalar field with quartic interactions on a two-dimensional lattice, represented in the flux formulation. The networks are tasked with various regression and classification problems. Through a systematic search, we identify both effective equivariant and non-equivariant architectures. Our results show that, in most tasks, the best equivariant models outperform and generalize better than their non-equivariant equivalents—not only for physical parameters outside the training set but also across different lattice sizes.

This paper presents a method for using a Transformer Neural Network to learn a Generative Model from a single path-based example image. Furthermore, we demonstrate how a dataset can be constructed from this example and how the model can generate a large collection of varied images that preserve the original image's style and underlying concept.

The recently introduced "generalized min-max" (GMM) kernel offers efficient linearization, making it suitable for large-scale statistical learning and fast nearest neighbor search. The linearized GMM kernel was extensively compared with the linearized radial basis function (RBF) kernel. Surprisingly, the tuning-free GMM kernel performs competitively against the best-tuned RBF kernel across a wide range of classification tasks. However, one might reasonably expect that incorporating tuning parameters could further enhance the performance of the GMM kernel. In this paper, we explore three simple extensions of the GMM kernel that introduce tunability: (i) the exponentiated-GMM (eGMM) kernel, (ii) the powered-GMM (pGMM) kernel, and (iii) the exponentiated-powered-GMM (epGMM) kernel. Notably, the pGMM kernel retains the efficiency of linearization by modifying the original hashing procedure used for the GMM kernel. Through experiments on approximately 60 publicly available classification datasets, we demonstrate that the proposed tunable GMM kernels consistently outperform the original GMM kernel, with some improvements being remarkably significant. For instance, on 11 widely used datasets for evaluating deep learning and tree-based methods, our results show that the tunable GMM kernels are strong competitors to both decision trees and deep neural networks. Previous work has developed tree-based methods such as "abc-robust-logitboost" and shown their effectiveness in various learning scenarios.

In the EHR, research is considered a tertiary priority, with patient care and billing taking precedence. As a result, the data is often not standardized or structured in a way that is conducive to machine learning applications. Missing data is common, stemming from factors such as variations in individual input practices or differences in clinical decision-making—such as which laboratory tests to order. Additionally, few patients are annotated to the level required for high-quality research, which limits sample sizes and creates a constantly evolving gold standard. Understanding disease progression over time is crucial for many medical conditions, yet many machine learning algorithms rely on a single-point snapshot to generate a usable data vector. Moreover, models that produce "black box" results lack the interpretability necessary for clinical deployment. This chapter explores these and other challenges in applying machine learning techniques to the structured components of the EHR, including Patient Demographics, Family History, Medication Information, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Tests. While it does not address feature extraction from sources like imaging data or free-text patient notes, the approaches discussed can be extended to incorporate features derived from these additional data types.

Chemical kinetics and reaction engineering provide the foundational framework for unraveling reaction mechanisms, enhancing reaction performance, and enabling the rational design of chemical processes. In this work, we employ feed-forward artificial neural networks as basis functions to solve ordinary differential equations (ODEs) subject to differential algebraic constraints that arise in microkinetic models (MKMs). We introduce an algebraic framework for the mathematical representation and classification of reaction networks, elementary reactions, and chemical species. Within this framework, we demonstrate that simultaneous training of neural networks and kinetic model parameters within a regularized multi-objective optimization setting enables the solution of the inverse problem—namely, the estimation of kinetic parameters from synthetic experimental data. We investigate a range of scenarios to determine the extent to which kinetic parameters can be accurately retrieved from transient kinetic data and evaluate the method's robustness in the presence of statistical noise. This approach offers a powerful tool for deciphering reaction mechanisms using transient experimental data.

Currently, Learning Management Systems (LMS) are extensively utilized across various educational levels, ranging from primary to tertiary education. These systems support student administration, record-keeping, progress tracking, reporting, and the delivery of courses, training programs, and learning initiatives. In pursuit of effective assessment of learning outcomes, the problem of generating exam scripts has garnered significant attention in recent years. However, research in this area remains in its early stages, presenting numerous opportunities for improvement in multiple dimensions.

In particular, two critical issues have been largely overlooked by existing approaches. First, given a specific course, there is currently no established method to generate an exam script that produces a desired distribution of student scores within a class or across different classes. Second, while it is common in practice to require equivalent exams with comparable scoring, there is still no clear solution for generating two high-quality exam scripts that are assessment-equivalent—meaning students' performance would be comparable regardless of which exam they take—but contain significantly different sets of questions.

To address these gaps, this paper introduces ExamGAN, a Generative Adversarial Network designed to produce high-quality exam scripts. Furthermore, we extend ExamGAN to T-ExamGAN (Twin-ExamGAN), a model capable of generating pairs of equivalent yet distinct exam scripts.

Collaborative personalization, such as through learned user representations (embeddings), can significantly enhance the predictive performance of neural network-based models. To leverage existing personalization techniques within a Federated Learning (FL) framework, we introduce Federated User Representation Learning (FURL), a simple, scalable, privacy-preserving, and resource-efficient approach. FURL partitions model parameters into federated and private components. While private parameters—such as user-specific embeddings—are trained locally, they are not shared with or aggregated on the central server. We theoretically demonstrate that this parameter division does not hinder training for most personalization methods. By keeping user embeddings on the local device, FURL not only safeguards user privacy but also enhances memory efficiency compared to centralized training. Experimental results on two datasets show substantial improvements in model quality, with 8% and 51% performance gains, and performance levels comparable to centralized training, with only 0% and 4% drops. Moreover, we find that user embeddings learned in both FL and centralized settings exhibit similar structures, confirming that FURL enables collaborative learning through shared parameters while maintaining user privacy.

Rural electrification requires the adoption of cost-effective technologies, such as single wire earth return (SWER) networks. With a growing demand for electricity from remote consumers, the capacity of existing power lines may soon become insufficient. Moreover, high-impedance arcing faults (HIFs) in SWER systems have been known to trigger devastating bushfires, as seen in the 2009 Black Saturday disaster. To address these challenges, reliable and resilient electricity networks can be established by partitioning existing systems into microgrids, with SWER lines serving as interconnection points. The development of such networks, along with improved energy demand management, will depend on the implementation of an integrated, network-wide condition monitoring system.

As the first contribution of this thesis, a distributed online monitoring platform is introduced that integrates power quality monitoring, real-time HIF detection, and transient classification within SWER networks. AI-based techniques are employed to accurately classify faults and transients. The proposed method achieves a high HIF detection accuracy of 98.67% and significantly reduces detection latency to 115.2 ms. 

As the second contribution, a methodology for remote consumer load identification is developed, enabling the determination of load types based on transient characteristics. An edge computing-based architecture is proposed to support high-frequency analysis for more precise load identification. The effectiveness of the approach is validated through real-time evaluation.

The success of semi-supervised learning heavily depends on its ability to scale effectively to large volumes of unlabeled data, which are essential for capturing the underlying manifold structure and improving classification performance. However, computing pairwise similarities between training samples is often computationally prohibitive across various types of input data, making it difficult to develop a general-purpose semi-supervised learning method capable of handling tens of millions or more data points. In this paper, we address this challenge by leveraging two low-rank label propagation algorithms—GLNP (Global Linear Neighborhood Propagation) and Kernel Nyström Approximation—and implementing a parallelized version of these methods accelerated with Nesterov's accelerated projected gradient descent, resulting in the Big-data Label Propagation (BigLP) framework. The proposed parallel algorithms were evaluated on five real-world datasets ranging in size from 7,000 to 10,000,000 samples, as well as a simulated dataset containing 100,000,000 samples. The experiments demonstrate that BigLP can efficiently scale to datasets with up to 100 million samples and hundreds of features, while significantly enhancing prediction accuracy even when only a small fraction of the data is labeled. These results confirm that the BigLP implementation is both highly scalable and effective in leveraging unlabeled data for semi-supervised learning.

In many areas of science, high-dimensional integration is a common and essential task. To address this challenge, various numerical methods have been developed to approximate complex integrals. In this work, we present **i-flow**, a Python package designed for high-dimensional numerical integration using **normalizing flows**—a class of machine-learned, bijective transformations that map between probability distributions. 

Beyond integration, i-flow can also generate samples from complex, high-dimensional distributions. We evaluate the performance of i-flow against existing algorithms for high-dimensional integration and demonstrate that it achieves superior accuracy, particularly in cases involving correlated variables. The i-flow code is publicly available on GitLab at [https://gitlab.com/i-flow/i-flow](https://gitlab.com/i-flow/i-flow).

In machine learning, likelihood-free inference involves conducting data-driven analysis in the absence of an explicit analytical likelihood function. We explore the use of Neural Spline Flows, a type of neural density estimation technique, for addressing likelihood-free inference problems in the context of measuring neutrino oscillation parameters in long-baseline neutrino experiments. A method tailored for physics parameter inference is developed and applied to the analysis of muon neutrino disappearance in the T2K experiment.

We introduce a unified framework that generalizes several well-known loss functions, including the Cauchy/Lorentzian, Geman-McClure, Welsch/Leclerc, generalized Charbonnier, Charbonnier/pseudo-Huber/L1-L2, and L2 losses. By incorporating robustness as a continuous parameter, our proposed loss function enables a more flexible approach to robust loss minimization, leading to improved performance in fundamental vision tasks such as image registration and clustering. Interpreting the loss as the negative logarithm of a univariate probability density yields a general distribution that encompasses both the normal and Cauchy distributions as special cases. This probabilistic formulation allows neural networks to automatically adapt the robustness of the loss during training, enhancing performance on learning-based tasks like generative image synthesis and unsupervised monocular depth estimation, without the need for manual parameter tuning.

We introduce **Sparse Sinkhorn Attention**, a novel and efficient method for learning to attend, which leverages differentiable sorting of internal representations. Specifically, we design a meta-sorting network that learns to generate latent permutations over sequences. By sorting the sequences, we can compute quasi-global attention using only local windows, significantly enhancing the memory efficiency of the attention mechanism. To achieve this, we propose key algorithmic advancements, including **Causal Sinkhorn Balancing** and **SortCut**, a dynamic sequence truncation technique tailored for both encoding and decoding tasks. Extensive experiments across diverse tasks—such as algorithmic sequence-to-sequence sorting, language modeling, pixel-wise image generation, document classification, and natural language inference—demonstrate that our memory-efficient Sinkhorn Attention outperforms not only standard attention mechanisms but also consistently surpasses recent efficient Transformer models like Sparse Transformers.

Sum-Product Networks (SPNs) that incorporate complex probability distributions at their leaves have demonstrated significant potential as tractable models for probabilistic inference. However, while the learning of internal parameters has been extensively studied, the challenge of learning complex leaf distributions remains an open problem, with only limited progress made in specific cases. In this paper, we present an efficient method for learning a broad class of leaf distributions using Expectation-Maximization (EM). The resulting EM updates reduce to simple weighted maximum likelihood problems, enabling the use of any distribution that can be learned via maximum likelihood, even approximately. The algorithm exhibits linear computational complexity with respect to model size and is guaranteed to converge even when only partial optimizations are performed. We evaluate our approach on twenty real-world datasets for density estimation, employing tree-based graphical models as leaf distributions. Despite using SPNs with significantly fewer parameters than state-of-the-art methods, our model achieves superior performance in parameter learning.

Deep reinforcement learning has proven to be an effective framework for learning policies that map complex, high-dimensional sensory inputs to actions in challenging tasks, such as those found in the Atari domain. In this paper, we investigate the use of temporal abstraction through output representation modeling to enhance the convergence and reliability of deep reinforcement learning methods. Focusing on macro-actions, we evaluate their performance across various Atari 2600 games and demonstrate significant improvements in learning efficiency. Furthermore, we show that these approaches can outperform DQN in terms of final performance. We provide analysis and insights into both the convergence behavior and the final results, shedding light on a key challenge faced by deep RL algorithms: the difficulty of handling sparse reward signals.

In this paper, we examine both physics-based and data-driven reconstruction techniques for simultaneous positron emission tomography (PET) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) systems, which offer substantial benefits for clinical imaging of cancer, neurological conditions, and cardiovascular diseases. These methods incorporate prior knowledge—either structural or statistical—alongside a physics-based model of the PET system response. However, the nested nature of the forward problem makes direct PET/MRI reconstruction a nonlinear challenge. We explore how a multi-faceted approach integrates hybrid data- and physics-driven machine learning to achieve 3D PET/MRI reconstruction, highlighting key advancements in deep learning over the past five years that address challenges such as attenuation correction, scatter compensation, low photon counts, and data consistency. Furthermore, we discuss how these multi-modality strategies extend beyond PET/MRI to enhance the accuracy of radiation therapy planning. Finally, we conclude by examining future opportunities for advancing current state-of-the-art techniques, informed by recent trends in physics-based and deep learning-driven computational imaging, as well as next-generation detector technologies.

Solving inverse problems—such as parameter estimation and optimal control—is a critical component of scientific research. Many experiments gather data repeatedly and use machine learning algorithms to efficiently solve the corresponding inverse problems. However, we observe that state-of-the-art training methods are often ill-suited for problems involving complex physical processes, due to the strong variability in both the magnitude and direction of gradients. To address this, we introduce a novel hybrid training approach that integrates higher-order optimization techniques with machine learning. Our method replaces the traditional gradient of the physical process with a new concept called the "physical gradient." This innovation enables the incorporation of domain-specific knowledge by embedding prior information about the solution space directly into the gradient updates. We validate the effectiveness of our approach across a range of canonical physical systems, demonstrating that physical gradients lead to substantial improvements in a wide array of optimization and learning tasks.

In optimization, it is well-established that gradient-based methods can be highly effective when the objective functions are strictly convex and well-conditioned, often achieving an exponential rate of convergence. However, traditional Lasso-type estimators typically fail to attain the optimal convergence rate due to the non-smooth and undesirable behavior of the absolute value function at the origin. 

To address this limitation, homotopy methods have been proposed, which employ a sequence of smooth surrogate functions to approximate the $\ell_1$ penalty used in Lasso-type models. These surrogate functions are designed to converge to the $\ell_1$ norm while maintaining strict convexity, thereby enabling faster numerical convergence rates.

In this paper, we present a novel homotopy approach where the surrogate functions are carefully constructed to achieve a significantly improved convergence rate compared to existing methods. While state-of-the-art algorithms for Lasso-type estimation generally guarantee either $O(1/\epsilon)$ or $O(1/\sqrt{\epsilon})$ convergence rates, our proposed algorithm achieves a much faster rate of $O([\log(1/\epsilon)]^2)$. Furthermore, our numerical experiments demonstrate that the new method not only outperforms existing techniques theoretically but also exhibits superior empirical performance.

A novel method for training variational autoencoders (VAEs) is introduced, leveraging Stein variational gradient descent. A significant benefit of this approach is the elimination of the need for parametric assumptions regarding the encoder's distribution. The method's performance is further improved through the integration of the proposed encoder with importance sampling. Remarkable results are achieved across various unsupervised and semi-supervised tasks, including a semi-supervised analysis of ImageNet data, showcasing the model's effectiveness on large-scale datasets.

We propose a low-complexity decentralized learning algorithm for training a recently introduced large neural network across distributed processing nodes, or workers. In our framework, the communication network among the workers is assumed to be synchronized and represented by a doubly-stochastic mixing matrix, without the need for a central master node. The training data is distributed across the workers, and remains local to each node due to privacy and security constraints. By combining the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) with a layerwise convex optimization strategy, we develop a decentralized learning approach that minimizes both computational and communication costs. We demonstrate that the proposed algorithm achieves learning performance comparable to that of a centralized system where all data is available in one location. Furthermore, we present experimental results that illustrate the algorithm's time complexity and convergence behavior.

The PhD thesis by Maillard (2013) introduces an algorithm for the $ K $-armed bandit problem that is relatively obscure. This algorithm, which we refer to as Maillard Sampling (MS), computes the probability of selecting each arm in a closed form—an advantage not shared by Thompson sampling, a widely used bandit algorithm in industry applications. As a result, data generated by running MS can be directly utilized for counterfactual evaluation, unlike data from Thompson sampling. Inspired by this benefit, we revisit MS and provide an improved analysis, demonstrating that it achieves both asymptotic optimality and a minimax regret bound of $ \sqrt{KT\log T} $, where $ T $ is the time horizon. This performance matches the known bounds of asymptotically optimal Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) algorithms. We then introduce a variant of MS, termed MS$^+$, which improves the minimax bound to $ \sqrt{KT\log K} $. Furthermore, MS$^+$ can be tuned to be more aggressive—i.e., to explore less—without sacrificing asymptotic optimality, a feature that is not available in existing bandit algorithms. Our numerical experiments confirm the effectiveness of MS$^+$.

The modeling unit and model architecture are two critical components in Recurrent Neural Network Transducer (RNN-T) systems for end-to-end speech recognition. To enhance the performance of RNN-T in Mandarin speech recognition, this paper proposes a novel Transformer Transducer that integrates the self-attention mechanism of the Transformer with the structure of RNNs. We also investigate the impact of different modeling units on the performance of the Transformer Transducer. Furthermore, we introduce a new multi-bandwidth training approach to develop a general model capable of accurately recognizing Mandarin speech across various sampling rates. All experiments were conducted on approximately 12,000 hours of Mandarin speech data with sampling rates of 8kHz and 16kHz. The experimental results demonstrate that the Mandarin Transformer Transducer using tone-bearing syllables achieves the best performance, yielding an average of 14.4% and 44.1% relative reductions in Word Error Rate (WER) compared to models using tone-bearing syllable initials/finals and Chinese characters, respectively. Additionally, it outperforms the tone-bearing syllable initials/finals model by an average of 13.5% in relative Character Error Rate (CER) reduction.

Patent data offers valuable insights into technological innovations, but it typically does not reveal the ethnic backgrounds of inventors. In this study, I employ supervised learning methods to estimate this information. To accomplish this, I create a dataset containing 95,202 names with known ethnic labels and train an artificial recurrent neural network with long-short-term memory (LSTM) architecture to predict ethnic origins based on name patterns. The resulting model achieves an overall accuracy of 91% across 17 distinct ethnic categories. Using this model, I classify and analyze the ethnic origins of 2.68 million inventors, uncovering new descriptive evidence about how their ethnic composition has evolved over time and varied across countries and technology sectors. Over the past few decades, the global ethnic diversity of inventors has increased, largely driven by a growing share of Asian-origin inventors. Additionally, the presence of foreign-born inventors is particularly pronounced in the United States, though it has also risen in other high-income economies. This trend is primarily attributed to an influx of non-Western inventors entering emerging high-tech fields in the U.S., whereas such an increase is less evident in other developed countries.

For the universal hypothesis testing problem, where the objective is to distinguish between a known null hypothesis distribution and an unknown alternative distribution, Hoeffding introduced a universal test in the 1960s. Hoeffding's test statistic is expressed in terms of the Kullback-Leibler (K-L) divergence between the empirical distribution of the observed data and the null hypothesis distribution. In this paper, we propose a modification of Hoeffding's test based on a relaxation of the K-L divergence, referred to as the mismatched divergence. The resulting mismatched test is shown to be equivalent to a generalized likelihood-ratio test (GLRT) when the alternative distribution belongs to a parametric family characterized by a finite-dimensional parameter, making it a solution to the corresponding composite hypothesis testing problem. For certain choices of the alternative distribution, it is demonstrated that both the Hoeffding test and the mismatched test achieve the same asymptotic performance in terms of error exponents. This result implies that the GLRT is optimal for distinguishing a specific distribution from others within an exponential family. Furthermore, the mismatched test is shown to offer a significant advantage over Hoeffding's test in terms of finite-sample performance.

Dual decomposition offers a computationally feasible framework for developing algorithms that find the maximum a posteriori (MAP) configuration in graphical models. However, in many real-world inference tasks, the standard decomposition suffers from a large integrality gap caused by frustrated cycles. To address this, one approach is to incorporate additional constraints that enforce cycle consistency. Previous research has demonstrated that cluster-pursuit algorithms—iteratively adding cycle and higher-order consistency constraints—can effectively solve several challenging inference problems. Nevertheless, these methods rely on explicitly enumerating a set of candidate clusters, typically restricting them to small structures such as triplets or short cycles. In this work, we address the challenge of identifying cycle constraints by presenting a nearly linear-time algorithm for detecting the most frustrated cycle of arbitrary length. We integrate this search mechanism with the dual decomposition framework and cluster-pursuit, resulting in a new algorithm that accurately solves MAP inference problems arising in relational classification and stereo vision.

We consider a supervised training setting where task-specific word embeddings are learned. Initially, we start with embeddings pre-trained on unlabeled data and refine them to better capture the characteristics of words in the labeled training data for a specific task. However, when encountering new words in the test set, we are forced to rely on either their initial embeddings or an unknown embedding, which can lead to performance issues. To address this, we train a neural network to map from the initial embedding space to the task-specific embedding space, using a multi-loss objective function. This approach is general in nature, but here we demonstrate its effectiveness in improving dependency parsing—particularly for sentences containing out-of-vocabulary words—and in enhancing downstream tasks such as sentiment analysis.

The National Football League (NFL) and Amazon Web Services collaborated through a Kaggle competition to create an advanced sports injury surveillance and mitigation program. The initiative aims to link specific players to each helmet, enabling precise identification of each player's "exposures" during a football play. Our work focuses on developing computer vision-based machine learning algorithms that can accurately associate detected helmet impacts with the correct players using tracking data. This paper outlines our approach for automatically tracking player helmets and analyzing collision events. Such a system will also enable the NFL to review past plays and analyze trends in player exposure over time.

In this paper, we present a deep residual network-based approach, termed DiCOVA-Net, for identifying COVID-19-infected individuals through the acoustic analysis of their coughs. Given the significant imbalance between healthy and infected individuals in the dataset, this classification task poses a major challenge. To enhance the model's capability to detect the minority class (infected patients), we incorporate both data augmentation and cost-sensitive learning strategies. Additionally, considering the unique nature of this task, we apply fine-tuning techniques to adapt the pre-trained ResNet50 model. To further improve the model's generalization performance, we employ ensemble learning by combining predictions from multiple base classifiers trained with different random seeds. We evaluated the proposed DiCOVA-Net using the DiCOVA challenge dataset, achieving an AUC score of 85.43%, placing it among the top-performing teams in the competition.

Phase retrieval involves reconstructing images from measurements that contain only magnitude information. In many practical scenarios, the problem is underdetermined. When training data is available, generative models offer a promising approach to constrain the solution space. However, not all possible solutions lie within the generator's output range, and those that do may be represented with some degree of error. To address this representation error in the context of phase retrieval, we propose two key improvements. First, we employ a novel variant of intermediate layer optimization (ILO) to expand the generator's effective range while ensuring consistency with the training data. Second, we introduce new initialization strategies that further enhance the quality of the reconstructed images. Through extensive experiments on Fourier and Gaussian phase retrieval tasks, along with comprehensive ablation studies, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our modified ILO method and the proposed initialization schemes.

Mobile malware has been steadily increasing in both scale and complexity as smartphone adoption continues to grow. Among mobile platforms, Android has emerged as the most popular, but this popularity has also made it a prime target for a sharp rise in malware attacks. A concerning trend is the growing sophistication of Android malware, which is increasingly designed to bypass traditional signature-based detection systems. As a result, Android app marketplaces remain vulnerable to hosting malicious applications that can evade detection before being downloaded by unsuspecting users. To address this issue, this paper presents an effective solution based on Bayesian classification models derived from static code analysis. These models are constructed using a set of code and app features that serve as indicators of potentially malicious behavior. The approach is tested using real-world malware samples, and experimental results are presented to demonstrate its effectiveness in identifying malicious applications.

Kernel Ridge Regression (KRR) is a widely used method for non-linear, non-parametric learning. However, traditional implementations of KRR require all data to be stored in main memory, which significantly restricts its applicability in scenarios where the data size exceeds available memory. Such situations are increasingly common in fields like data mining, bioinformatics, and control systems. A promising approach for handling large datasets is the streaming model of computation, where data samples are processed one at a time, with each sample discarded before the next is processed. In this paper, we introduce StreaMRAK, a streaming variant of KRR. StreaMRAK enhances existing KRR methods by structuring the problem into multiple levels of resolution, enabling continuous refinement of predictions. The algorithm minimizes memory usage by efficiently incorporating new samples into the model over time. Additionally, a novel sub-sampling strategy reduces both memory and computational costs by creating a compressed representation of the data. This sub-sampling adapts to the kernel's bandwidth and the local dimensionality of the dataset. We demonstrate the effectiveness of StreaMRAK through a case study on two synthetic problems and the prediction of trajectory data.

We introduce a novel approach for estimating parameters in topic models that diverges from traditional simplex-based algorithms. This method simultaneously estimates the number of topics $ K $ from the observed data. We establish new finite-sample minimax lower bounds for the estimation of the topic-word matrix $ A $, as well as corresponding upper bounds for our proposed estimator. We characterize the conditions under which our estimator achieves minimax adaptivity. Our finite-sample analysis is applicable across a wide range of settings, including arbitrary numbers of documents $ n $, varying document lengths $ N_i $, dictionary sizes $ p $, and topic counts $ K $. Notably, both $ p $ and $ K $ are permitted to grow with $ n $, a scenario that has not been adequately addressed by prior theoretical analyses. Complementing our theoretical findings, we present an extensive simulation study. The results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing methods in terms of speed and accuracy. Importantly, we begin with a computational and theoretical challenge—lacking prior knowledge of the true value of $ K $—while providing competing methods with the correct $ K $ in our experiments.

Considering the worst-case scenario, the junction tree algorithm remains the most general approach for exact MAP inference with polynomial runtime guarantees. However, its primary tractability assumption relies on the treewidth of the corresponding MRF being bounded, which significantly limits the range of applicable problems. In practice, many structured prediction tasks require modeling global dependencies—either through direct introduction of global factors or by imposing global constraints on the prediction variables. Such modeling often leads to fully connected graphs, rendering exact inference via the junction tree algorithm intractable. Prior work [1]–[4] on loss-augmented inference has shown how efficient inference can be achieved in models with specific global factors that represent non-decomposable loss functions within the training framework of SSVMs. In this paper, we extend the efficient exact inference framework proposed in [3], allowing for more refined interactions between the energy of the core model and the sufficient statistics of the global terms, without incurring additional computational costs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach across several use cases, including one that cannot be addressed by previous methods. Finally, we introduce a novel graph transformation technique based on node cloning, which ensures...

Accurate electricity demand forecasting is essential for the development of sustainable power systems. To support informed decision-making, particularly in managing end-user demand flexibility, it is not enough to provide merely accurate forecasts—these forecasts must also be interpretable and actionable. Recent advancements in global forecasting models (GFM), which are trained on time series data, have demonstrated superior performance in various demand forecasting competitions and real-world applications compared to traditional univariate approaches. However, a critical challenge remains: bridging the gap between model accuracy and interpretability.

To address this, we introduce **Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Rule-based Explanations for Forecasting (LIMREF)**, a local explanation framework designed to generate k-optimal impact rules for specific forecasts. LIMREF treats the global forecasting model as a black box and operates in a model-agnostic manner, providing diverse types of rules that clarify the predictions of the global model. Additionally, it offers counterfactual rules that suggest actionable changes to achieve alternative outcomes for given input instances.

We evaluate the effectiveness of LIMREF using a large-scale electricity demand dataset that includes exogenous variables such as temperature and calendar effects. Our assessment focuses on both the qualitative and quantitative quality of the explanations generated by the LIMREF framework.

In this paper, we investigate the concept of UAV-enabled mobile edge computing (UAVE), in which multiple unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are deployed as flying MEC platforms to provide computing resources to ground user equipments (UEs). Compared to traditional fixed-location MEC systems, UAVE is particularly beneficial in scenarios such as temporary events, emergency situations, and on-demand services, owing to its high flexibility, low cost, and ease of deployment. However, the operation of UAVE presents several challenges, including the need to efficiently address 1) the association between multiple UEs and UAVs, and 2) the allocation of resources from UAVs to UEs, while minimizing the overall energy consumption of the UEs. To tackle these challenges, we formulate the problem as a mixed integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) model, which is generally difficult to solve, especially in large-scale scenarios. To address this, we propose a Reinforcement Learning (RL)-based User Association and Resource Allocation (RLAA) algorithm that efficiently and effectively solves the problem. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed RLAA achieves optimal performance compared to exhaustive search in small-scale cases and offers significant performance improvements over other conventional algorithms in large-scale scenarios.

Promptly and accurately addressing product-related questions is crucial for e-commerce platforms. Manually responding to such queries—such as on community Q&A forums—can be slow and does not scale effectively. Recent research has demonstrated that product reviews serve as a valuable resource for real-time, automated product question answering (PQA). In existing literature, PQA is typically framed as a retrieval task, aiming to identify the most relevant reviews that can answer a given product question.

In this paper, we focus on two critical aspects of PQA: answerability and answer reliability. Our work is guided by the insight that many questions may not have answers within a given set of reviews. When a question is unanswerable, a system should avoid returning irrelevant results and instead return "nil" answers, as providing misleading information can severely harm the user experience. Furthermore, for questions that are answerable, only the most relevant reviews that directly address the query should be included in the response.

To address these challenges, we propose a framework based on conformal prediction to enhance the reliability of PQA systems. This approach allows the system to reject unreliable answers, resulting in more accurate and concise responses. It also enables the system to return "nil" answers when no suitable review is available. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in improving both the accuracy and reliability of product question answering systems.

We introduce a novel neural topic model within the Wasserstein Autoencoder (WAE) framework. Unlike traditional variational autoencoder-based approaches, our method directly imposes a Dirichlet prior on the latent document-topic vectors. By leveraging the structure of the latent space, we employ an appropriate kernel to minimize the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), enabling effective distribution matching. We find that MMD outperforms Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) in aligning high-dimensional Dirichlet distributions. Furthermore, we observe that introducing randomness in the encoder's output during training significantly enhances topic coherence. To assess the diversity of generated topics, we propose a simple yet effective metric called topic uniqueness. Combined with the widely used NPMI coherence measure, this provides a more comprehensive evaluation of topic quality. Experimental results on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that our model generates substantially superior topics compared to existing methods.

Variational approximations to Gaussian processes (GPs) commonly employ a limited number of inducing points to construct a low-rank approximation of the covariance matrix. In this work, we take a different approach by leveraging a sparse approximation of the precision matrix. We introduce the Variational Nearest Neighbor Gaussian Process (VNNGP), which incorporates a prior that only maintains correlations among K nearest neighboring observations, resulting in a sparse precision structure. Within the variational framework, VNNGP's objective function can be efficiently factorized over both observations and inducing points, enabling stochastic optimization with a time complexity of O($K^3$). This allows for flexible scaling of the inducing point set, even to the extent of placing inducing points at every observed data location. Through extensive experiments, we compare VNNGP with other scalable GP methods and show that it (1) significantly outperforms low-rank approaches, and (2) exhibits greater robustness to overfitting compared to other nearest neighbor-based methods.

Online meta-learning is gaining traction as a key enabler for achieving edge intelligence within the IoT ecosystem. However, to develop a robust meta-model capable of rapid adaptation within tasks, a single agent must learn across numerous tasks, giving rise to the so-called "cold-start" problem. Noting that in a multi-agent network, the learning tasks across different agents often exhibit some degree of model similarity, we pose a fundamental question: "Can online meta-learning be accelerated across agents through limited communication, and if so, what level of performance gain can be achieved?" To address this, we introduce a multi-agent online meta-learning framework and formulate it as an equivalent two-level nested online convex optimization (OCO) problem. By analyzing the upper bound of the agent-task-averaged regret, we demonstrate that the effectiveness of multi-agent online meta-learning heavily depends on how much each agent can benefit from the network-level OCO process for meta-model updates through limited communication—a factor that remains poorly understood. To overcome this challenge, we propose a distributed online gradient descent algorithm with gradient tracking, where each agent tracks the global gradient using only one communication step with its neighbors per iteration. This approach achieves an average regret of $O(\sqrt{T/N})$ per agent, indicating...

Answer-agnostic question generation is a crucial and challenging task that involves automatically generating questions from a given sentence without relying on a specific answer. In this paper, we introduce two novel strategies to address this challenge: question type prediction and a copy loss mechanism. The question type module enables the model to identify and generate various types of questions for the same source sentence. The enhanced copy loss improves the traditional copy mechanism, ensuring that key words from the original sentence are accurately retained during question generation. Our proposed model achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods in answer-agnostic question generation, attaining a BLEU-4 score of 13.9 on the SQuAD dataset. Human evaluation further confirms the high quality of the generated questions. We will make our code publicly available to support future research in this area.

Langevin diffusion is a powerful technique for nonconvex optimization, as it facilitates escaping from local minima by introducing noise into the gradient updates. The temperature parameter, which regulates the level of noise, introduces a tradeoff between "global exploration" at high temperatures and "local exploitation" at low temperatures. To harness the benefits of both regimes, we propose a replica exchange strategy that swaps states between two Langevin diffusions operating at different temperatures. We theoretically investigate the acceleration brought by replica exchange from two perspectives: (i) convergence in $\chi^2$-divergence, and (ii) the large deviation principle. This acceleration enables faster convergence toward the global minimum. Moreover, by discretizing the replica exchange Langevin dynamics, we derive a discrete-time algorithm. For this algorithm, we rigorously analyze the discretization error and validate its enhanced performance through empirical experiments.

Complex time-varying systems are frequently analyzed by abstracting away from the behavior of individual components, instead focusing on developing a model that captures population-level dynamics from the outset. However, this approach can sometimes lead to an oversimplification, where the role of individual elements and their contributions to the overall system are overlooked. In this paper, we introduce a novel transformer architecture designed to learn from time-varying data while simultaneously capturing both individual and collective dynamics. Instead of aggregating all data at the initial stage, our model employs a separable architecture that processes individual time series first before combining them, thereby achieving permutation invariance. This design enables the model to generalize across systems of varying sizes and complexities. We demonstrate that our model is capable of accurately recovering complex interactions and dynamics in many-body systems, and then apply it to populations of neurons within the nervous system. On neural activity datasets, our multi-scale transformer not only achieves strong decoding performance but also exhibits remarkable transferability. Our results show that it is possible to train a model on neurons from one animal's brain and successfully apply it to neurons in another.

Deep learning models trained in a fully supervised manner have been shown to depend on what are known as "shortcut" features — input patterns that are correlated with the target outcome in the training data but may no longer be relevant or present in testing or real-world deployment scenarios. In this work, we present experiments demonstrating that recent self-supervised models, pre-trained on both images and text, produce more robust image representations and exhibit reduced reliance on visual shortcut features, as illustrated through a realistic medical imaging example. Furthermore, we observe that these self-supervised models tend to "forget" shortcut features more rapidly than their fully supervised counterparts when fine-tuned on labeled data. While not a complete remedy, our findings offer strong evidence that self-supervised learning on images and text can provide some level of resilience against the influence of visual shortcut features.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning often faces challenges due to the exponentially growing action space resulting from a large number of agents. This paper introduces HAVEN, a novel value decomposition framework based on hierarchical reinforcement learning, designed for fully cooperative multi-agent settings. To tackle the instability caused by the simultaneous optimization of high-level and low-level policies, as well as the concurrent optimization among agents, we propose a dual coordination mechanism that integrates both inter-layer and inter-agent strategies. HAVEN is model-agnostic, requiring no domain-specific knowledge or pretraining, and can be seamlessly integrated with any value decomposition approach. Experimental results demonstrate its effectiveness across various decentralized partially observable Markov decision process (Dec-POMDP) environments, offering an efficient way to implicitly partition the decision space.

This paper exclusively presents the efficiency of AIS-INMACA. AIS-INMACA has made a significant impact in addressing key challenges in bioinformatics, such as protein region identification and promoter region prediction, while requiring less computational time (Pokkuluri Kiran Sree, 2014). Several variations of AIS-INMACA have since been developed (Pokkuluri Kiran Sree, 2014) to further establish it as a valuable tool in the field of bioinformatics for tackling a wide range of complex problems. Therefore, this paper will serve as a useful resource for researchers working in the intersection of bioinformatics and cellular automata.

In many academic environments, medical students begin their scientific training early in their studies.
